finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI could substantially reshape educational systems by changing tutoring, curriculum creation, feedback practices, and assessment design, but it also creates institutional risks around transparency, privacy, fairness, and assessment validity. No empirical system-level effect is reported; the discussion is conceptual and forward-looking, drawing on prior studies and examples rather than original data.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of educational system implications; no original outcome measure

finding.finding_summary: The paper contends that GenAI can reduce educator workload and improve efficiency by generating learning resources, producing feedback quickly, and supporting assessment at scale. These claims are based on cited prior studies and examples rather than a new empirical test in this article, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, feedback generation efficiency, resource creation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that GenAI may support critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, and creativity when used as guided support, but overreliance may weaken these same skills and create a performance illusion. This is a synthesis claim supported by examples and cited studies, not a direct empirical estimate from the paper itself.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, creativity, learner agency

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests GenAI may increase engagement, motivation, and positive learning experiences through personalized support, dynamic resources, and multimodal feedback, but it can also reduce agency and increase techno-stress or dependency. These effects are discussed conceptually and through references to prior work, without original data in this paper.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, learner agency, positive emotions, techno-stress

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses GenAI uses in non-specific academic tasks such as curriculum/resource generation, writing support, programming, biology question generation, and assessment design, but it does not test subject-specific learning outcomes. The evidence presented is illustrative and drawn from prior studies, not newly collected data.
finding.measure: Instructional resource quality, assessment authenticity, task-specific academic performance in cited prior studies

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review article examines the emerging role of artificial intelligence in education, with a particular emphasis on chatbots and ChatGPT. The paper asks how AI technologies may transform teaching and learning, what educational functions they can support, and what ethical, practical, and pedagogical constraints accompany their adoption.

Rather than reporting a new empirical study, the authors synthesize prior literature on AI in education, chatbot design, and ChatGPT’s capabilities. They describe AI-supported uses such as personalized learning, instant feedback, automated grading, learner support, and administrative assistance, and organize AI in education into paradigms ranging from AI-directed to AI-empowered learning. The paper also highlights risks including bias, privacy, academic integrity, unreliable outputs, over-reliance on technology, and the need for teacher training and institutional support.

The article’s main conclusion is that ChatGPT and related AI tools have significant potential to improve educational experiences, but successful implementation depends on responsible, ethical, and pedagogically grounded use. The authors argue that educators, researchers, and policy-makers should collaborate to integrate AI thoughtfully into curricula and practice while addressing concerns about fairness, transparency, and accountability.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools, especially chatbots and automated systems, can reduce repetitive instructional and administrative work for teachers by evaluating assignments, scoring work, providing feedback, and answering routine student questions. No original effect estimate is reported, but the review cites prior examples such as auto-grading systems and AI learning management systems as time-saving supports.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, automated grading/scoring, feedback provision, administrative task reduction

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes prior literature suggesting that AI-enabled tools can increase student motivation, engagement, confidence, and reduce anxiety. It notes that personalized learning environments and AI math tutors have been associated with improved motivation and reduced anxiety in cited studies, but the paper itself does not report a pooled or original estimate.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, self-confidence, and anxiety

finding.finding_summary: The article states that AI can support self-reflection, self-directed learning, self-regulation, critical thinking, creativity, and collaboration through individualized feedback and conversational interaction. These claims are based on the literature review rather than new data, and no quantitative effect size is provided.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, creativity, self-regulation, self-directed learning, and collaboration

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights literacy-related uses of chatbots and AI, including writing support, language translation, summarization, and reading comprehension assistance. It cites prior studies showing benefits for writing and reading comprehension, but reports no new empirical results or aggregate effect size.
finding.measure: Writing support, reading comprehension, summarization, and text feedback

finding.finding_summary: The review notes that AI chatbots can facilitate ongoing dialogue, communication practice, and speaking support in language-learning contexts. It cites prior work on improving speaking performance and punctuation/foreign-language learning, but provides no original effect estimate.
finding.measure: Speaking performance, communication ability, and language-learning interaction

paper_profiles.title: Design and evaluation of ChatGPT-MWPS: an AI-enhanced learning system for improving primary students’ mathematical word problem solving
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of primary students’ difficulty in solving mathematical word problems, especially the need to translate text into mathematical representations and sustain step-by-step reasoning. The authors argue that generative AI can provide adaptive scaffolding, but that current educational AI tools often lack alignment with pedagogy, grade level, and usable classroom design.

To address this, the study designs and evaluates ChatGPT-MWPS, a generative AI-enhanced learning system built on the ChatGPT API and intended to support fifth-grade word problem solving through real-time, stepwise hints, personalized feedback, and teacher-configurable prompt constraints. The system was implemented in a Java-based architecture with teacher and student interfaces, batch question import, automated worksheet generation, and learning analytics features.

The evaluation involved 52 fifth-grade students from one public primary school in Guangdong, China, plus three mathematics teachers who provided observations and interviews. Students used the system for a 40-minute task and then completed a 13-dimension usability scale; teachers were interviewed about system performance, content quality, and future improvements. Results showed generally favorable usability and intention to use, with especially strong relations among cognitive engagement, trust, reliability, and adoption intention, but also clear weaknesses in information display and design appeal.

Overall, the paper concludes that generative AI can support personalized mathematics instruction in primary school settings, but its educational value depends heavily on interface clarity, coherent hint presentation, technical stability, and careful prompt/content control. The authors recommend iterative redesign to improve usability, reduce disruptive sequential displays, and better constrain the knowledge level and correctness of generated hints.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT-MWPS was evaluated for supporting fifth-grade mathematical word problem solving, and the paper reports generally favorable usability and perceived educational effectiveness. In the 52-student pilot, the system was described as helping students through step-by-step reasoning, adaptive scaffolding, and real-time feedback, though the study did not report a direct achievement gain on standardized math scores.
finding.measure: Usability scale ratings for a mathematics word-problem solving system; teacher interview feedback on instructional appropriateness

finding.finding_summary: The usability instrument included cognitive engagement and intention to use, and the results showed strong positive associations with system acceptance. Cognitive engagement was especially prominent, correlating almost deterministically with intention to use (r=0.969), and the authors interpret the system as supporting engagement and learner autonomy during problem solving.
finding.measure: Cognitive engagement and intention-to-use dimensions of the usability scale

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the system supports metacognitive and reasoning processes by breaking complex word problems into manageable steps and externalizing problem-solving strategies. Correlations between intention to use and learnability (r=0.720), trust (r=0.743), anthropomorphism (r=0.788), and cognitive engagement (r=0.969) suggest that the platform may promote reflective engagement and structured reasoning, although these were usability-based rather than direct skill outcomes.
finding.measure: Usability dimensions related to learnability, cognitive engagement, trust, and anthropomorphism

finding.finding_summary: The system includes teacher-facing features intended to reduce preparation time, such as batch question import and automated worksheet generation, and teachers viewed the platform as potentially useful if performance and filtering issues were resolved. However, interviews also noted latency at peak usage and limits on free-form question input, so the operational benefits were promising but constrained.
finding.measure: Teacher interview feedback; system functionality for batch processing and worksheet generation

finding.finding_summary: The study discusses classroom integration, teacher oversight, and potential scalability for primary mathematics instruction, but it does not evaluate broader institutional or policy outcomes directly. Teachers highlighted implementation constraints such as server congestion, access limits, and the need for better knowledge-level configuration, indicating that institutional adoption would require further technical and governance support.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about classroom integration, access, and system configuration

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: All levels of education (primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional development); includes elementary, middle/high school, university, and teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT/GPT-3-style systems, for education. Rather than testing a specific intervention, the authors synthesize early research and offer a conceptual review of how LLMs might support learning and teaching, alongside risks related to bias, privacy, hallucination, plagiarism, overreliance, and sustainability.

The paper organizes potential uses by learner and teacher perspective. For learners, it discusses LLMs as tools for generating quizzes, explanations, practice problems, feedback, and dialogue support across subjects, including mathematics, as well as for supporting reading, writing, and language learning. For teachers, it highlights possible uses for lesson planning, adaptive feedback, assessment support, and content generation, while emphasizing that human oversight remains essential.

The paper is not an empirical effectiveness study; it is a normative and integrative discussion of how LLMs could be responsibly integrated into educational practice. Its main conclusion is that LLMs may become valuable educational tools if combined with clear pedagogical strategies, critical thinking and fact-checking practices, teacher training, governance, and safeguards for ethics, fairness, and privacy.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not present original empirical evidence on mathematics achievement, but it explicitly identifies mathematics as a subject area where LLMs may generate practice problems, quizzes, and step-by-step explanations for middle and high school students. These claims are conceptual and illustrative rather than measured, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Not an empirical measure; conceptual discussion of math practice problems, quizzes, and explanations

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally argues that LLMs may support critical thinking, problem-solving, curiosity, and fact-checking, but it does not test these outcomes empirically. The discussion is prospective: it suggests that students should use models to generate hypotheses, compare sources, and reason through outputs rather than passively accept answers.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of critical thinking, problem-solving, curiosity, and fact-checking

finding.finding_summary: A major theme is that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating or assisting with lesson planning, quiz generation, feedback, grading, and content creation. The paper does not report original data, but it repeatedly claims these tools can save time and effort for teachers and make content production more efficient.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of teacher workload, grading effort, and content-generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper devotes substantial attention to institutional issues such as governance, privacy, copyright, bias, sustainability, fairness of access, and the need for policies and teacher training for responsible adoption. It argues that LLMs could broaden access and innovation, but also widen inequities and create compliance, security, and ethical risks if poorly managed.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of policy, governance, access, privacy, bias, sustainability, and institutional adoption

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper conducts a systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education published between 2007 and 2018. The authors ask how the field has developed over time, how AI is conceptualized, what ethical challenges are discussed, and what kinds of applications are being studied in higher education contexts.

Using search results from EBSCO Education Source, Web of Science, and Scopus, the review screened 2,656 records and included 146 peer-reviewed journal articles for synthesis. The review organizes applications into four main areas: profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems/personalisation. It finds that most research comes from Computer Science and STEM, uses quantitative methods, and focuses heavily on learner-facing applications such as dropout prediction, automated feedback, adaptive tutoring, and personalized systems.

The review concludes that AI research in higher education is dominated by technical and predictive applications, with limited educator involvement and very little critical reflection on ethics, privacy, or broader pedagogical implications. Only a small number of studies explicitly define AI or discuss risks. Overall, the paper argues that the field needs stronger connections to educational theory, more attention to ethical governance, and more research on teacher-facing and pedagogically grounded uses of AI.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that AI applications in higher education are frequently used to automate or support tasks such as admission decisions, course scheduling, assessment, feedback, plagiarism detection, and student monitoring. Across the included studies, these tools are often presented as improving efficiency and reducing workload, but the paper is a synthesis of prior work rather than a single intervention study, so no pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Systematic review synthesis of applications related to administrative efficiency, assessment automation, feedback automation, and workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: The review shows that a substantial portion of the literature uses AI for institutional functions such as profiling and prediction, retention, course management, career services, and aligning students with institutional or industry needs. These studies suggest AI can support institutional decision-making and student lifecycle management, though the review emphasizes that ethical and governance concerns are rarely discussed.
finding.measure: Systematic review synthesis of institutional and administrative AI applications

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies use AI to predict or support student engagement, motivation, and retention, including early-warning systems and engagement models. The review characterizes these applications as promising for identifying at-risk or low-engaged students, but results vary by study and are generally reported at the level of predictive accuracy rather than direct learner outcomes.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, retention/dropout prediction, and related learner-behavior indicators

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies a smaller set of studies using AI to support collaboration, self-regulation, and metacognitive processes, especially within intelligent tutoring systems and adaptive environments. These applications are described as providing prompts, feedback, and support for collaborative writing or problem solving, but the evidence base is limited and not synthesized into a quantitative effect estimate.
finding.measure: Collaboration, self-regulation, metacognitive support, and related process measures within AI-supported learning environments

finding.finding_summary: The review includes multiple studies on automated essay scoring, writing feedback, and intelligent tutoring for writing and reading comprehension. These studies generally report that AI systems can provide useful feedback and achieve high agreement with human raters, although concerns remain about feedback quality and suitability for beginning learners; the review does not report a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Writing performance, automated essay scoring agreement, and feedback quality in reading/writing tasks

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies a smaller set of intelligent tutoring studies in mathematics and related quantitative subjects, including one explicitly teaching mathematics content and others in statistics or differential equations. These studies are described as generally showing positive or satisfactory preliminary results, but the evidence is heterogeneous and no pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Mathematics tutoring/learning outcomes and performance in quantitative coursework

finding.finding_summary: Across the review, AI is used in a wide range of non-literacy and non-mathematics academic domains, including computer science, medicine, business, language learning, and general course performance. The overall synthesis suggests many systems perform well on task-specific prediction or feedback functions, but results are mixed across application types and the review does not provide a single effect estimate.
finding.measure: Course-specific academic outcomes across diverse disciplines, including prediction, tutoring, and assessment tasks

paper_profiles.title: Teachers’ Beliefs and Practices About the Potential of ChatGPT in Teaching Mathematics in Secondary Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines secondary school mathematics teachers in Malta to understand how their beliefs and classroom practices relate to their perceptions of ChatGPT as a tool for teaching mathematics. The authors frame the work using TPACK and diffusion of innovation theory, asking whether a short professional development (PD) session changes teachers’ views about integrating generative AI into mathematics instruction and what benefits, limitations, and classroom uses they foresee.

The approach combined pre- and post-PD surveys, field notes from whole-group discussions, and analysis of teachers’ written reflections/pen portraits. The PD session introduced large language models, provided hands-on mathematical tasks with ChatGPT, and prompted discussion of its usefulness and limitations. Participants were 86 consenting secondary mathematics educators from Malta, most of whom had limited prior experience with ChatGPT.

Findings suggest that teachers generally held positive views of ChatGPT, especially those with discovery and connectionist beliefs. They saw the tool as useful for generating practice problems, explanations, assessments, and personalised feedback, and for supporting discussion, exploration, and student engagement. At the same time, teachers identified important constraints, especially errors/inaccuracies and difficulties with visual mathematical representations. The study concludes that teachers felt more confident after PD, but that sustained professional development is needed for effective and thoughtful integration of ChatGPT into mathematics teaching.

finding.finding_summary: The study focused centrally on how ChatGPT could be used in secondary mathematics teaching, but it did not measure student achievement. Instead, teachers reported that ChatGPT could help generate practice problems (59%), explanations/examples for challenging concepts (57%), and support identification of mistakes/misconceptions (65%), while also noting serious limitations for visual mathematics and accuracy. The evidence is about perceived instructional usefulness rather than demonstrated gains in mathematical outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher survey responses and PD discussion field notes about potential uses of ChatGPT in mathematics instruction

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that ChatGPT could enhance student engagement, interest, and self-directed learning in mathematics. In the post-PD survey, 65% said it could help identify mistakes and misconceptions, and 43% said it could facilitate group discussions or projects; in the benefits table, 56% highlighted improved engagement and interest, and 71% said it could support learning at students’ own pace and style. These are perceived rather than measured student outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher survey responses on perceived benefits for student engagement and learning

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed ChatGPT could support critical thinking, discussion, collaboration, and exploration, especially for connectionist and discovery-oriented teachers. The most common classroom uses described were facilitating discussion, helping students identify errors, and creating collaborative tasks, but again these were perceptions from teachers rather than direct observations or student outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher survey responses and qualitative reflections on instructional uses of ChatGPT

finding.finding_summary: A major theme was that ChatGPT could reduce teacher workload by assisting with lesson planning, generating practice materials, creating assessments, rewording questions, and producing examples. Teachers repeatedly described it as a tool for preparation efficiency and a 'sophisticated search engine,' with 59% endorsing use for practice problems/assessments and 57% for explanations/examples. No productivity metric was measured, so the finding is based on teacher perceptions.
finding.measure: Teacher survey responses and field notes on perceived teacher uses of ChatGPT

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that sustained professional development is necessary for effective ChatGPT integration and suggests that teachers’ beliefs align with adoption readiness. This is framed as an institutional implication rather than a measured system-level outcome: 58% of teachers felt they needed more training, and teachers called for ongoing PD to support classroom implementation. No policy or institutional outcome was directly measured.
finding.measure: Teacher survey responses and qualitative statements about professional development needs

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emergence of ChatGPT and asks what it means for learning, teaching, and assessment in higher education. The authors frame the piece as one of the first peer-reviewed journal articles on ChatGPT’s relevance for higher education, with a particular emphasis on assessment, and they situate ChatGPT within the broader history and research literature of Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd).

Methodologically, the paper combines a desktop literature review with hands-on experimentation using ChatGPT. The authors review early peer-reviewed and preprint studies, then test ChatGPT on several tasks such as explaining statistics, generating a short essay, and writing in Chinese. Their examples are used to illustrate strengths such as quick conceptual explanations and fluent text generation, alongside weaknesses including factual unreliability, limited higher-order reasoning, poor performance in lower-resource languages, and inability to reliably produce academic citations.

The paper’s main conclusion is that ChatGPT is best understood as part of a longer continuum of AI-powered writing and assessment tools rather than as a wholly new educational phenomenon. The authors argue that institutions should avoid both hype and panic, and instead adapt assessment practices, teaching strategies, and policies to account for generative AI. They suggest that ChatGPT will likely challenge conventional essays and plagiarism detection, while also creating opportunities for more innovative, formative, and student-centered assessment and instruction.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT produced fluent prose and could draft a short essay quickly, but the output lacked breadth, depth, evidence, and reliable referencing. In the authors’ test, it generated an approximately 500-word essay within about 120 seconds in response to a 2000-word prompt, but the result was described as generic, descriptive, and unsuitable for serious academic writing.
finding.measure: Essay generation quality; ability to produce academic prose and references

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that ChatGPT can communicate in a human-like way and produce responses rapidly in English, but it performed poorly in Chinese. The Chinese composition test showed that the generated text was structurally weak, grammatically poor, and often illogical, suggesting strong performance in high-resource language contexts but weaker performance in lower-resource languages.
finding.measure: Language generation quality in English and Chinese

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that ChatGPT is weak at higher-order thinking tasks such as critical and analytical writing. In their example prompt asking for an argumentative essay, the model failed to demonstrate depth of reasoning or evidence use, leading the authors to conclude that it is less competent at tasks requiring critical thinking than at simple explanation or paraphrase.
finding.measure: Performance on higher-order thinking tasks embedded in essay writing

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT can generate explanations and draft text very quickly, often within 60-120 seconds, which suggests efficiency benefits for drafting, brainstorming, and basic explanatory tasks. The authors also note potential uses for reducing workload in teacher-facing contexts, though no formal workload study was conducted.
finding.measure: Task completion speed and perceived productivity in generating explanations and drafts

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT may disrupt assessment systems, especially essays and plagiarism-checking workflows, while also motivating institutions to redesign policies and assessment approaches. The authors report that anti-plagiarism software did not detect ChatGPT-generated text in their tests and discuss implications for institutional assessment governance, but they do not provide quantitative institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Assessment integrity, plagiarism detection, and implications for institutional assessment policy

paper_profiles.title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces LLaMA, a family of large foundation language models ranging from 7B to 65B parameters, and studies how model size, training data mix, and architectural choices affect language model performance. The central problem is how to build competitive large language models using only publicly available data and relatively efficient training, while improving inference efficiency compared with very large proprietary models.

The approach is to pre-train transformer-based models on roughly 1.4T tokens from public sources including CommonCrawl, C4, GitHub, Wikipedia, books, arXiv, and Stack Exchange. The paper describes architectural modifications such as pre-normalization, SwiGLU activations, and rotary embeddings, plus efficiency techniques including optimized attention and checkpointing. It then evaluates the resulting models on a broad suite of NLP benchmarks, including commonsense reasoning, closed-book QA, reading comprehension, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and MMLU, alongside bias, toxicity, and truthfulness evaluations.

The paper’s main conclusions are that LLaMA-13B can outperform GPT-3 on many benchmarks despite being much smaller, and LLaMA-65B is competitive with leading models such as Chinchilla-70B and PaLM-540B on several tasks. The models also show meaningful but limited capabilities on mathematical and code benchmarks without task-specific fine-tuning, while bias, toxicity, and hallucination issues remain important limitations. Because this is a model-development and benchmark-comparison paper rather than a study of educational deployment, it does not directly examine K-12 learners or classroom implementations.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates LLaMA on MATH (12K middle/high school math problems) and GSM8k (middle school math problems). LLaMA-65B achieves 10.6% on MATH and 50.9% on GSM8k in the base setting, rising to 20.5% and 69.7% with majority voting (maj1@k), and it outperforms Minerva-62B on GSM8k despite not being fine-tuned on mathematical data.
finding.measure: Exact-match accuracy on MATH and GSM8k; majority-vote accuracy (maj1@k)

paper_profiles.title: Editorial: Generative AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial introduces a special Research Topic on generative AI in education and synthesizes the themes across 11 included papers. Rather than testing a single intervention, it frames the field’s emerging questions around personalized feedback, AI tutors, assessment generation, critical thinking, whole-learner modeling, career mentoring, and ethical integration.

The editorial argues that generative AI can support individualized learning by tailoring content, feedback, and assistance to learner needs and by extending support beyond class time. At the same time, it emphasizes major constraints, including response accuracy, emotional appropriateness, interpretability, privacy, fairness, and the need for human-in-the-loop oversight.

Several papers summarized in the editorial concern adolescent schoolwork use, pre-service teacher mathematics proof construction, interactive assessment, and AI-mediated mentoring, but the editorial itself does not report original empirical data. Its main contribution is to map opportunities and challenges in the field and to highlight that responsible implementation requires careful design, ethics, and further research.

finding.finding_summary: The editorial summarizes one included exploratory study on pre-service teachers using ChatGPT to construct mathematical proofs in geometry. It reports varied usage patterns and limited understanding of the model’s inner workings, suggesting potential for teacher support but no direct evidence of improved mathematical performance.
finding.measure: Use of ChatGPT for constructing mathematical proofs in geometry; qualitative patterns of instrumental genesis

finding.finding_summary: Across the research topic, the editorial highlights potential benefits of generative AI for student engagement, motivation, and emotional support, especially through personalized feedback and whole-learner support. However, these claims are synthesized from included papers rather than reported as original effect estimates in the editorial itself.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, emotional support, and perceived usefulness

finding.finding_summary: The editorial emphasizes generative AI’s role in fostering critical thinking, strategic use of AI tools, and human interaction skills. It specifically notes case studies and discussion points about using AI to enhance communication skills and data structures/algorithms instruction, but provides no original quantitative estimate.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, strategic AI use, communication skills, and human interactions

finding.finding_summary: The editorial reports that one included study found older students used generative AI more frequently for schoolwork and that students with more executive functioning challenges perceived it as more useful. It also states there was no significant link between generative AI use and academic achievement.
finding.measure: Frequency of generative AI use for schoolwork, perceived usefulness, and academic achievement

finding.finding_summary: The editorial frames generative AI as a tool that can provide immediate clarification and ongoing support beyond class hours, potentially reducing delays in getting help and increasing efficiency in learning workflows. It does not present original outcome data, but it does describe improved access and streamlined support as recurring themes across the included papers.
finding.measure: Immediate clarification and availability of support outside class hours

paper_profiles.title: How Does ChatGPT Perform on the United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE)? The Implications of Large Language Models for Medical Education and Knowledge Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can answer multiple-choice medical knowledge questions at a level relevant to USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 Clinical Knowledge. The authors ask whether a conversational large language model can function as a useful educational tool and whether its responses are sufficiently interpretable to support learning.

To study this, the authors tested ChatGPT (December 15, 2022 version) on four question sets: AMBOSS Step 1 and Step 2 items, plus NBME free Step 1 and Step 2 items. They compared ChatGPT with GPT-3 and InstructGPT, and also examined the structure of ChatGPT’s explanations using qualitative coding for logical reasoning, internal question information, and external information. In the AMBOSS sets, they also tested whether adding an Attending Tip improved accuracy. Questions with images or table-formatted answers were excluded, and all prompts were standardized before model testing.

ChatGPT outperformed the two comparison models on all datasets, reaching 44% on AMBOSS-Step1, 42% on AMBOSS-Step2, 64.4% on NBME-Free-Step1, and 57.8% on NBME-Free-Step2. The model’s accuracy decreased with higher AMBOSS difficulty on Step 1 without the tip, and the Attending Tip improved performance in some cases. Qualitatively, ChatGPT’s answers always included logical justification, and nearly all responses used information from the question stem; correct responses more often incorporated external information than incorrect ones. The authors conclude that ChatGPT shows promise as an interactive medical education tool and as a support for small-group or self-directed learning, while also noting that further study is needed before educational use can be recommended broadly.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT showed substantially better performance on medical knowledge question answering than GPT-3 and InstructGPT across four USMLE-aligned datasets. Accuracy was 44% (44/100) on AMBOSS-Step1, 42% (42/100) on AMBOSS-Step2, 64.4% (56/87) on NBME-Free-Step1, and 57.8% (59/102) on NBME-Free-Step2; the authors interpret the >60% result on NBME-Free-Step1 as roughly passing-level performance for a third-year medical student.
finding.measure: Accuracy on USMLE-style multiple-choice medical knowledge questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that ChatGPT consistently provided explanations that were logically coherent and often drew on both internal and external information, suggesting support for reasoning and explanation quality. Every response across the NBME datasets contained logical reasoning, and 96.8% (183/189) of responses across NBME-Free-Step1 and NBME-Free-Step2 used internal information from the prompt.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of logical reasoning, internal information, and external information in model responses
finding.study_size: n=189 NBME responses for qualitative analysis

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT’s performance suggests meaningful ability to apply biomedical knowledge to clinical-style reasoning tasks, with accuracy above chance and above comparator LLMs. On AMBOSS-Step1, accuracy dropped significantly as question difficulty increased (P=.01), indicating that the model’s reasoning performance was sensitive to task complexity rather than flat across difficulty levels.
finding.measure: Accuracy by question difficulty on AMBOSS Step 1 and Step 2 question sets
finding.study_size: n=200 AMBOSS questions total (100 Step 1, 100 Step 2)

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing healthcare: the role of artificial intelligence in clinical practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical practice and argues that AI has the potential to improve diagnosis, treatment selection, population health management, patient education, and workflow efficiency in healthcare. The paper is not an empirical study of a single intervention; instead, it synthesizes indexed literature from PubMed/Medline, Scopus, and EMBASE to describe current applications of AI, including machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, large language models, predictive analytics, and decision-support systems.

The review focuses on healthcare settings and professional users, not K-12 education. It highlights examples where AI systems improved diagnostic performance in imaging, supported personalized treatment and dose optimization, aided predictive analytics for readmissions and chronic disease risk, and reduced burden through virtual assistants and chatbot-based education. The paper also emphasizes constraints such as data quality, privacy, bias, hallucination, cybersecurity, regulatory uncertainty, and the need for human expertise and oversight.

Overall, the article concludes that AI can enhance accuracy, efficiency, and personalization in healthcare, but safe implementation requires robust governance, collaboration, training, and ethical safeguards. Because it is a broad narrative review rather than a controlled evaluation, it provides conceptual and illustrative evidence rather than causal estimates of impact.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that AI can improve workflow efficiency, reduce costs, and save time in clinical practice, especially through automation, decision support, triage, and virtual assistants. No single pooled effect size is reported; the paper summarizes multiple examples such as faster diagnosis, workload reduction, and improved resource allocation across healthcare settings.
finding.measure: Workflow efficiency, time savings, cost reduction, and clinician workload

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI has implications for guideline development, regulatory frameworks, cybersecurity, and institutional implementation in healthcare systems. It emphasizes that responsible adoption depends on governance, data protection, ethics, and organizational collaboration, but reports no quantitative institutional outcome estimates.
finding.measure: Guideline development, regulatory and governance considerations, implementation readiness

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education students; teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it synthesizes early research and offers a conceptual discussion of how LLMs might support learning and teaching through content generation, personalized feedback, tutoring, assessment assistance, and productivity gains.

The paper discusses use cases across educational levels, with examples relevant to elementary, middle, high school, university, and teacher professional contexts. It highlights potential benefits for students such as practice problems, explanations, quizzes, step-by-step solutions, and conversational support, and for teachers such as lesson planning, feedback generation, and semi-automated assessment. The paper also emphasizes important risks including bias, privacy, overreliance, plagiarism, misinformation, sustainability, and inequitable access.

Overall, the authors argue that LLMs may become a powerful educational tool if used responsibly, with strong human oversight, critical thinking instruction, and clear institutional guidance. The paper does not report original empirical outcomes; instead, it proposes mitigation strategies and calls for further research on best practices for integrating LLMs into education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by assisting with lesson planning, personalized feedback, semi-automated grading, and generation of quizzes, prompts, and teaching materials. It cites prior work such as NLP-based feedback systems that reduced grading effort by up to 85%, but this position paper itself reports no original empirical evaluation.
finding.measure: Teacher workload; grading effort; content generation productivity

finding.finding_summary: The paper specifically notes that LLMs can generate practice problems, explanations, step-by-step solutions, and math word problems for middle and high school learners, which may support mathematics learning. However, these claims are conceptual and drawn from cited examples rather than from an in-paper study of math achievement.
finding.measure: Math practice problems; math word problem generation; problem-solving support

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLMs may support durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and fact-checking by generating prompts, explanations, and diverse perspectives. At the same time, it warns that overreliance on model-generated answers may weaken these same skills, so the net effect is framed as mixed and dependent on instructional design.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, fact-checking behaviors

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can improve student engagement, participation, curiosity, and interaction, especially through conversational tutoring and curiosity-prompting pedagogical agents. These are presented as plausible benefits supported by prior studies, but the paper itself provides no new empirical estimates.
finding.measure: Student engagement; curiosity expression; interaction/participation

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is institutional governance: it discusses copyright, bias, privacy, sustainability, fairness, and the need for policies, oversight, and guidance for responsible adoption of LLMs in schools. The paper concludes that these risks are manageable but require institutional strategies, human monitoring, and equitable access policies.
finding.measure: Policy/guidance considerations; governance and responsible adoption practices

paper_profiles.title: The cognitive paradox of AI in education: between enhancement and erosion
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (conceptual/opinion paper; discusses learners broadly, including undergraduate and K-12 examples)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This opinion paper argues that artificial intelligence in education has a “cognitive paradox”: it can enhance learning through personalization, efficiency, and accessibility, but it may also erode important cognitive skills if students over-rely on it. Using Cognitive Load Theory, Bloom’s Taxonomy, and Self-Determination Theory as organizing frameworks, the authors discuss how AI may reduce extraneous load and support lower-order skills while also encouraging cognitive offloading, weakening retention, critical thinking, and intrinsic motivation.

The paper does not report a new empirical study. Instead, it synthesizes prior literature and illustrates the argument with examples from studies on memory retention, critical thinking, creativity, and AI-supported learning. The discussion includes K-12-relevant examples such as AI tutoring in STEM and a report that Turkish high school students using ChatGPT performed worse on conceptual understanding despite better procedural problem solving. The main conclusion is that AI should complement, not replace, human instruction, and should be implemented with reflection, teacher guidance, and safeguards to preserve deep learning, autonomy, and equity.

finding.finding_summary: The paper cites a report of AI tutoring in STEM/mathematics showing improved standardized test scores, with a stated 15% increase for students using AI platforms compared with traditional instruction. However, it also cites evidence that students using ChatGPT for practice on math-like problem solving answered 48% more problems correctly but scored 17% lower on a concept-understanding test, suggesting gains in procedural performance without deeper conceptual learning.
finding.measure: Standardized test scores; problem-solving accuracy; concept understanding test

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can support engagement and competence through personalized learning, but overuse may reduce motivation and intrinsic engagement. The discussion is theoretical rather than based on a single primary dataset, drawing on cited studies to claim that dependence on AI can undermine autonomy and relatedness.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, autonomy, relatedness

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally focuses on durable cognitive skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, retention, and creativity. It synthesizes cited evidence that AI may improve some lower-order or divergent-thinking outcomes while also fostering cognitive offloading, reduced critical scrutiny, and weaker conceptual understanding; one cited example reports 48% more correct problems but a 17% lower concept-understanding score.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, memory retention, creative thinking, conceptual understanding

finding.finding_summary: The paper makes claims about implementation, equity, transparency, explainability, and fairness-aware AI design in educational systems. It does not evaluate a policy intervention empirically, but argues that institutions should adopt monitored, teacher-guided AI integration to avoid bias and educational inequity.
finding.measure: Equity, transparency, explainability, bias mitigation, implementation guidance

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review of artificial intelligence in education, with particular attention to chatbots and ChatGPT. It addresses the broad question of how AI technologies may transform teaching and learning, while also surfacing ethical, practical, and pedagogical concerns associated with their use.

Rather than testing a specific intervention, the authors synthesize existing literature on AI-supported learning tools such as intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment, learning analytics, and chatbots. The paper discusses potential benefits for students and teachers, including personalized learning, immediate feedback, improved motivation and engagement, reduced teacher workload, and support for assessment and administration.

The paper is not focused on a specific population or K-12 implementation study; its examples span multiple educational levels and contexts, including higher education and general schooling. The main conclusion is that AI and ChatGPT hold promise for enhancing learning and instructional efficiency, but responsible adoption requires attention to bias, privacy, accuracy, teacher preparation, and academic integrity. The authors call for further research to determine when and how these tools can be used effectively in education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues, based on prior literature, that AI-supported learning can increase student motivation, engagement, confidence, and reduce anxiety. No new data were collected in this review, so the evidence is synthesized from cited studies rather than reported directly in this article.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, confidence, and anxiety outcomes reported in prior studies

finding.finding_summary: The review claims AI tools can support durable skills such as critical thinking, creativity, self-regulation, and self-directed learning through personalized feedback and step-by-step guidance. These conclusions are conceptual and literature-based, without original effect estimates in this paper.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, creativity, self-regulation, self-directed learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that AI can reduce teacher and administrator workload by automating grading, scoring, feedback provision, and other repetitive tasks. No original quantitative evaluation is presented here, but the review cites examples such as automated homework and test grading tools that save substantial time.
finding.measure: Teacher/administrator workload, grading, scoring, feedback efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The article discusses AI's potential institutional effects, including support for administration, student monitoring, early-warning systems, and the need for governance around ethics, privacy, fairness, and teacher preparation. These are presented as implications from the literature rather than empirically tested outcomes in this study.
finding.measure: Administrative support, monitoring, dropout prevention, ethical and governance considerations

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a conceptual discussion of how AI should be integrated into education, with a focus on higher education. It asks what skills are needed for responsible AI use in classrooms and academic work, arguing that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking are the key competencies students and educators need in the AI era.

The paper is based on the author’s experience at a Swiss University of Applied Sciences, informal discussions with students and staff, and a narrative literature review. It describes the institution’s internal AI guidelines, the tensions between banning and unrestricted use of generative AI, and practical recommendations for building an AI-supportive culture through workshops, policies, and broader training.

The article does not test an intervention or report student outcome data. Instead, it proposes that schools should teach students how to use AI transparently and critically, including how to document AI use and evaluate outputs for hallucinations and other limitations. It also outlines prompt engineering methods and AI literacy components as educational priorities, but provides no empirical evidence on achievement or other measured effects.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is primarily a conceptual and policy-oriented discussion of institutional responses to generative AI in higher education. It describes the development of internal AI guidelines at a Swiss University of Applied Sciences, but it does not evaluate the guidelines’ effects with empirical outcome data.
finding.measure: Institutional AI guidelines, policy discussion, and implementation practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking are essential durable skills for students and educators. However, these claims are presented as conceptual conclusions and literature-based recommendations rather than as measured outcomes from a study.
finding.measure: AI literacy, prompt engineering proficiency, critical thinking

paper_profiles.title: Design and evaluation of ChatGPT-MWPS: an AI-enhanced learning system for improving primary students’ mathematical word problem solving
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge that primary students often face in mathematical word problem solving, particularly the need to translate textual descriptions into structured mathematical reasoning. The authors design and evaluate ChatGPT-MWPS, a generative AI-enabled learning system that uses OpenAI’s ChatGPT API to provide adaptive scaffolding, step-by-step hints, and real-time feedback for fifth-grade mathematics word problems.

The study was conducted in a public primary school in Guangdong, China, with 52 fifth-grade students and three mathematics teachers. Students used the system in a 40-minute task and then completed a 13-dimension usability scale; teachers also participated in interviews. The evaluation focused primarily on usability and perceived educational value rather than direct learning gains on achievement tests.

Results showed generally favorable student perceptions, with especially strong relationships between intention to use and cognitive engagement, reliability, information quality, learnability, design attraction, and anthropomorphism. However, students rated information display and design appeal less favorably, and teachers identified issues such as latency, imperfect content filtering, sequential hint presentation that may disrupt thinking, and limited flexibility in question input and knowledge scope. The paper concludes that generative AI can support primary mathematics instruction through personalized scaffolding, but its educational effectiveness depends heavily on interface clarity, pedagogical alignment, and system stability.

finding.finding_summary: The study evaluated a ChatGPT-based system specifically for fifth-grade mathematical word problem solving and concluded that the tool showed promising educational potential for supporting math reasoning. However, the paper did not report pre/post achievement gains or comparison-group effects on test scores; its evidence for math learning is indirect and based on usability, teacher feedback, and the system’s perceived ability to scaffold problem solving.
finding.measure: Mathematical word problem solving usability and perceived educational effectiveness

finding.finding_summary: Students reported generally favorable experiences with the system, and cognitive engagement emerged as a particularly strong correlate of intention to use (r=0.969, p<0.05). Across the usability scale, cognitive engagement received relatively positive responses, suggesting the AI-supported environment was engaging for many learners.
finding.measure: Usability scale dimension: Cognitive Engagement; Intention to Use

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to support step-by-step reasoning, structured problem solving, and learner autonomy, and the authors interpret the results as evidence that ChatGPT-MWPS can foster metacognitive engagement during mathematical word problem solving. Empirically, cognitive engagement and learnability were positively associated with intention to use, but the paper does not provide direct measures of metacognition or critical thinking gains.
finding.measure: Usability scale dimensions: Learnability, Cognitive Engagement; teacher interview themes on reasoning flow

finding.finding_summary: The system included batch question import, automated test generation, and worksheet generation features intended to reduce teacher preparation time and support classroom use. Teachers, however, reported latency during peak usage and requested improvements to system capacity and workflow, indicating that operational gains were present in design but constrained in practice.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes; system functionality and workflow features

finding.finding_summary: The paper offers implications for integrating generative AI into primary mathematics instruction, but it does not evaluate policy, governance, or institution-level outcomes directly. Teachers suggested changes to content controls, access, and configurability, showing that broader implementation would require institutional decisions about system deployment and oversight.
finding.measure: Teacher interview feedback on implementation and future updates

paper_profiles.title: Shaping integrity: why generative artificial intelligence does not have to undermine education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an opinion/argument piece about whether generative artificial intelligence (GAI) should be seen as a threat to education or as a tool that can support learning and academic integrity when used responsibly. The authors focus on ethical concerns around cheating, plagiarism, bias, privacy, and over-automation, and they argue that these risks can be mitigated through transparent policies, digital literacy instruction, and thoughtful classroom use.

Rather than reporting a primary empirical study, the paper synthesizes ethical frameworks and learning theories, especially deontological ethics, consequentialism, constructivist learning, and self-determination theory. It proposes that GAI can support personalized feedback, authentic assessment, student autonomy, competence, relatedness, and collaborative learning, all of which may strengthen intrinsic motivation and reduce dishonest behavior.

The context is broad K-12 and higher education, with examples drawn from history, language arts, science, business, and general classroom assessment. The paper's main conclusion is normative: GAI does not inherently undermine education, but responsible integration requires educator professional development, explicit instruction in ethical AI use, and iterative policy review to ensure that AI supports genuine learning and academic integrity.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can improve writing and language-related learning by providing real-time feedback on grammar, tone, narrative structure, and revision. However, this is presented as a conceptual claim supported by citations rather than as a directly tested effect; no original sample, effect size, or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Writing quality, grammar, tone, narrative structure, and academic writing skill

finding.finding_summary: The central argument is that GAI can foster intrinsic motivation by supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness, which in turn may increase student engagement and reduce dishonest behavior. The paper discusses these effects conceptually across classroom examples, but it does not report a primary empirical evaluation, sample size, or effect size.
finding.measure: Intrinsic motivation, autonomy, competence, relatedness, and engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims GAI can support durable skills such as critical thinking, collaboration, reflection, and metacognition by promoting authentic assessment, interactive simulations, and collaborative project work. These are theoretical assertions grounded in constructivist learning theory rather than measured outcomes in an empirical study.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, collaboration, reflective/self-assessment, and knowledge construction

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that AI-driven tools can make formative assessment and feedback more efficient by helping students revise drafts, practice skills, and receive immediate guidance. The discussion is descriptive and does not include empirical workload or productivity data.
finding.measure: Feedback delivery speed, formative assessment support, and revision assistance

finding.finding_summary: A substantial portion of the paper focuses on institutional guidance for ethical AI adoption, including transparency, professional development, policy development, and iterative evaluation. The claimed impact is that these practices can help schools govern AI use responsibly, but the paper does not present a measured institutional intervention or outcome data.
finding.measure: AI governance, policy guidance, transparency, professional development, and ethical implementation

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (conceptual perspective; no empirical sample studied)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective article examines the promises, challenges, and research needs surrounding generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as a tool for human learning. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it synthesizes prior work on large language models, diffusion models, chatbots, generative agents, and multimodal tools to argue that GenAI may scale personalized support, diversify learning resources, improve feedback, and enable more authentic assessment.

The paper is not an empirical study of a student sample or school setting; instead, it discusses educational implications across learning contexts, including K-12 and higher education. It highlights potential benefits such as adaptive tutoring, AI-generated feedback, and assessment innovations, while emphasizing limitations including hallucinations, ethical risks, inequity, privacy concerns, and assessment validity problems. The authors conclude that rigorous, human-centered, evidence-based research is needed before GenAI can be relied on as a learning tool, especially to understand its effects on cognition, metacognition, creativity, and learner agency.

finding.finding_summary: This perspective argues that GenAI could substantially reshape educational systems by changing how learning support, resources, feedback, and assessment are designed and delivered. At the same time, it warns that unresolved issues around transparency, privacy, fairness, and assessment validity could undermine institutional trust and require new regulations, standards, and governance frameworks.
finding.measure: conceptual analysis of educational systems, policy, and assessment practices

paper_profiles.title: Retrieval-augmented Generation to Improve Math Question-Answering: Trade-offs Between Groundedness and Human Preference
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS’23 Workshop on Generative AI for Education (GAIED)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve the quality and groundedness of large language model responses for middle-school mathematics question answering. The authors are motivated by the need for conceptual math tutoring support in K-12 settings and by concerns that generative models may hallucinate or misalign with curricular materials.

The intervention is a RAG-based chatbot setup that uses the OpenStax Prealgebra textbook as a retrieval corpus and GPT-3.5-turbo as the response model. The authors compare three prompt-guidance conditions with varying levels of textbook anchoring (None, Low, High) plus a retrieval-only baseline, using 51 real student math questions from Math Nation. They first evaluate groundedness with automated metrics, then conduct a human preference study with 9 educators/designers, and finally analyze whether retrieved-document relevance predicts groundedness and preference.

Across studies, the paper finds that prompt guidance can increase groundedness, and that humans prefer the low-guidance RAG responses over both no-guidance and high-guidance responses. However, the most grounded responses are not always the most preferred: high-guidance answers are judged as more grounded, but are not preferred over no-guidance responses, suggesting a trade-off between strict grounding and conversational usefulness. Document relevance is associated with groundedness, but not with human preference. The study is exploratory and does not measure student learning outcomes, but it offers evidence relevant to designing AI math tutors that balance correctness, curricular alignment, and user preference.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies conceptual middle-school math question answering rather than student achievement. In a survey of 9 educators/designers over 51 student math questions, low-guidance RAG responses were preferred over no-guidance and high-guidance responses, while high-guidance responses were judged as most grounded in the textbook. The study shows that RAG can improve response groundedness and preference relative to some prompt settings, but it does not test learning gains.
finding.measure: Human preference rankings and groundedness judgments for generated answers to middle-school algebra/geometry questions

paper_profiles.title: AI tutoring can safely and effectively support students: An exploratory RCT in UK classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory study asks whether a generative AI tutor can safely and effectively support K-12 mathematics learning in real classroom conditions, relative to standard platform hints and to human tutoring. The authors evaluate LearnLM, a pedagogically fine-tuned generative AI model embedded in the Eedi mathematics platform and supervised by expert human tutors, to see whether it can provide high-quality tutoring dialogue without introducing harm.

The trial was conducted across five UK secondary schools with 165 students in Years 9 and 10 (ages 13–15). Students were randomized to receive either static, pre-written hints or interactive tutoring; within the tutoring arm, sessions were randomized to human tutor alone or LearnLM supervised by a tutor. The study measured immediate mistake remediation, misconception resolution, and near-transfer knowledge transfer on successive mathematics study units. LearnLM-generated tutoring was judged safe and pedagogically reliable, with tutors approving most messages with no or minimal edits and no harmful content detected.

On learning outcomes, interactive tutoring outperformed static hints for immediate correction and misconception resolution, and LearnLM performed at least as well as human tutors on those near-term outcomes. The most notable result was that supervised LearnLM produced better knowledge transfer to the next unit than human tutoring alone: 66.2% vs. 60.7%, a 5.5 percentage-point advantage with a reported credible interval of [–1.4, +12.4] and 93.6% credibility. The authors conclude that pedagogically tuned genAI, when directly supervised by humans, may scale effective individualized mathematics support, though they emphasize that longer-term and broader subject-area effects remain untested.

finding.finding_summary: In an exploratory RCT with n=165 secondary students, supervised LearnLM tutoring improved mathematics learning outcomes relative to standard hints and performed at least as well as human tutoring on immediate correction and misconception resolution. For knowledge transfer to the next unit, students tutored by LearnLM were more likely to solve the novel problem correctly (66.2%) than those tutored by human tutors alone (60.7%), a 5.5 percentage-point advantage with a reported 95% credible interval of [–1.4, +12.4].
finding.measure: Correctness on immediate retry, misconception resolution within the unit, and correctness on the first question of the next mathematics study unit

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: All learners and educators (primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional development); not limited to a studied sample
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper asks how large language models, especially ChatGPT, could be used in education and what risks such systems introduce. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it surveys anticipated applications and synthesizes emerging research on large language models in teaching and learning, with examples spanning content generation, feedback, assessment support, dialogue agents, and tutoring.

The paper discusses potential uses for primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional learning contexts. For students, it highlights possible support for reading, writing, question generation, problem solving, and math word-problem practice; for teachers, it emphasizes lesson planning, personalized materials, feedback, assessment, and professional development. The authors argue that these tools could improve engagement, personalization, and efficiency, but only if accompanied by human oversight, critical thinking, verification practices, privacy protections, and responsible governance.

The article’s main conclusion is normative rather than empirical: large language models are promising educational technologies, but their benefits depend on careful integration into pedagogy and strong safeguards against bias, plagiarism, overreliance, privacy violations, and inequitable access. It frames many open research questions and proposes mitigation strategies, but it does not report primary outcome data or comparative effects on student achievement.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not report an empirical evaluation of generative AI on K-12 mathematics achievement. It only argues that large language models could be used to generate practice problems, step-by-step solutions, and math word problems for middle and high school students, but no sample, effect size, or outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses likely support for problem-solving, critical thinking, and out-of-the-box thinking, especially through explanations and step-by-step solutions in math and other subjects, but these claims are speculative and not based on empirical testing. No measured outcomes, sample, or effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that large language models might improve student engagement, participation, and curiosity, including curiosity-prompting agents and language-learning support, but it does not present primary evidence from an experiment or observation study. No quantitative engagement or motivation outcomes are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models can reduce teacher workload by automating or assisting with lesson planning, quiz generation, feedback, grading support, and content creation. These efficiency claims are supported only by cited prior work and examples, not by new empirical results in this paper; no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: teacher workload, grading effort, content-generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is institutional governance, including privacy, copyright, bias, fair access, sustainability, and policies for responsible deployment of large language models in education. The paper is conceptual and prescriptive, not empirical, so it does not report measured institutional outcomes or effect sizes.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Retrieval-augmented Generation to Improve Math Question-Answering: Trade-offs Between Groundedness and Human Preference
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS 2023 Workshop on Generative AI for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve the quality of generative AI responses for middle-school math question answering, and how prompt guidance shapes the trade-off between groundedness and human preference. The authors are motivated by concerns that LLMs may produce plausible but incorrect or curriculum-misaligned explanations, so they test whether retrieving from a vetted OpenStax prealgebra textbook helps generate better responses for student math questions.

The system was evaluated on 51 real student questions drawn from the Math Nation discussion board, spanning pre-algebra, Algebra 1, and geometry. Study 1 compared three prompting conditions (no guidance, low guidance, high guidance) plus an information-retrieval baseline and found that stronger prompt guidance increased groundedness metrics, but the most retrieval-grounded outputs were not necessarily the most useful conversational responses. Study 2 surveyed 9 educators/designers who ranked responses and judged groundedness; they preferred the low-guidance RAG responses over both no-guidance and high-guidance responses, while high-guidance responses were judged most grounded. Study 3 showed that retrieved-document relevance predicted groundedness, but not human preference. Overall, the paper concludes that RAG can improve math QA response quality, but overly grounded prompting may reduce perceived usefulness, highlighting a trade-off relevant to educational deployment.

finding.finding_summary: Across three studies, RAG and prompt guidance improved groundedness of generated math QA responses, but the most grounded responses were not the most preferred. In the survey of 9 educators/designers across 51 student questions, low-guidance responses were preferred over no-guidance and high-guidance responses, while high-guidance responses were judged most grounded; automated groundedness metrics also increased with more guidance.
finding.measure: Human preference rankings; groundedness judgments; automated groundedness metrics (K-F1++, BLEURT, BERTScore) on generated responses to middle-school math questions
finding.study_size: n=51 queries for generation/evaluation; n=9 survey respondents; n=153 groundedness judgments

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating large language models in analysing classroom dialogue
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a generative AI system based on GPT-4 can analyze classroom dialogue as reliably and efficiently as human experts. The motivation is methodological: classroom discourse analysis is important for teaching diagnosis and instructional improvement, but manual coding is labor-intensive, slow, and difficult to scale.

The authors built a customized GPT-4-based workflow, using retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering, to code classroom dialogue from middle-school mathematics and Chinese lessons in Beijing. They compared GPT-4 outputs with expert manual annotations across a 15-category dialogue coding scheme, focusing on time efficiency, inter-coder agreement, and Cohen’s kappa reliability.

The study found that GPT-4 substantially reduced coding time, with a roughly 30-fold speedup on a representative math lesson (5 minutes vs. 150 minutes for manual coding), while achieving high overall agreement with human coders (about 90% agreement in both math and Chinese datasets). Reliability varied by code category: several codes showed near-perfect agreement, but some coordination-related and context-dependent categories had weak or even near-zero agreement, indicating that GPT-4 is promising for scalable classroom dialogue analysis but still requires refinement for more nuanced coding tasks.

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 dramatically improved coding efficiency for classroom dialogue analysis. For one representative math lesson with 82 dialogue turns, manual coding took about 150 minutes, whereas ChatGPT/GPT-4 coding took about 5 minutes, a roughly 30-fold speedup; across the larger set of lessons, total automated analysis time did not exceed one hour.
finding.measure: Time required to code classroom dialogue transcripts
finding.study_size: Math lesson n=82 dialogue turns for timed comparison; broader datasets included 6 math lessons (576 turns) and 6 Chinese lessons (348 turns)

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates GPT-4 as a tool for analyzing dialogic features linked to reasoning, synthesis, and dialogue quality, rather than measuring student skills directly. Human-GPT agreement was high overall (about 90%), but performance varied substantially by code: near-perfect agreement for some categories such as ELI and EL, and weak or near-zero agreement for coordination-related codes such as CI, SC, and RC in some settings.
finding.measure: Dialogue coding categories representing reasoning, elaboration, coordination, and related discourse moves
finding.study_size: 6 math lessons (576 turns) and 6 Chinese lessons (348 turns); additional timed comparison on 1 math lesson (82 turns)

paper_profiles.title: Editorial: Generative AI in education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (editorial; synthesizes studies across education contexts, including adolescents and pre-service teachers)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial introduces a Frontiers Research Topic on generative AI in education and frames the central question of how large language models and other generative AI tools may reshape teaching, learning, assessment, and student support. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, it summarizes the contributions of 11 papers in the volume and highlights recurring themes such as personalized feedback, AI tutors, whole-learner support, assessment generation, academic integrity, and emotional considerations in AI-mediated interactions.

The article describes several use cases across educational settings: ChatGPT answers compared with human answers on Stack Overflow, adolescents’ use and perceived usefulness of generative AI for schoolwork, pre-service teachers using ChatGPT for mathematical proof construction, AI-supported personalized assessment, AI mentors for STEM career exploration, interactive listening assessment task generation, and deception detection with generative AI robots.
