GPT-4 is the only model reported to reach success (accuracy =60%) across all grades, while ChatGPT succeeds through grades 1–4 and the remaining models largely fail; accuracy declines as grade level, reasoning steps, and number of digits increase.
finding.measure: Accuracy on elementary school math word problems, analyzed by grade, number of reasoning steps, number of digits, and distractor robustness

finding.finding_summary: The authors interpret CMATH performance as reflecting general reasoning complexity, not just arithmetic, and report that accuracy decreases as the number of reasoning steps rises. This suggests current LLMs struggle with multi-step problem solving and reasoning persistence on elementary math tasks, with reasoning complexity having a larger impact than arithmetic complexity in their analysis.
finding.measure: Accuracy as a function of estimated reasoning steps and problem complexity

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central motivation is to create a more interpretable benchmark for assessing model capability, and it evaluates an automated answer-extraction script for scoring model outputs. The authors report 96% precision and 98% recall for the automated evaluation on a random sample of 200 problem-response pairs, indicating high efficiency for large-scale grading of LLM outputs.
finding.measure: Precision and recall of automated answer extraction/scoring procedure

paper_profiles.title: Investigating the Effectiveness of ChatGPT in Mathematical Reasoning and Problem Solving: Evidence from the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how well ChatGPT can solve multiple-choice mathematics questions from the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination (VNHSGE). The authors use 250 questions from exams spanning 2019–2023, organized by Bloom’s taxonomy difficulty levels (knowledge, comprehension, application, high application) and by topic areas such as algebra, geometry, calculus, derivatives, exponential/logarithmic functions, and spatial calculus.

The study evaluates ChatGPT by comparing its generated answers with official answer keys. Results show strong performance on easier items but much weaker performance as difficulty increases: overall accuracy is highest on knowledge-level questions and drops sharply for application and high-application questions. The paper also compares ChatGPT’s scores across years, across math topics, against other exams such as SAT Math and AP/GRE/AMC tests, and against Vietnamese students’ performance on the same exam. ChatGPT performs better on some routine topics and lower-level questions, but it struggles with harder problems and with items requiring interpretation of graphs, tables, or other visual information.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT has some potential as a support tool for mathematics learning, but its current capabilities are inconsistent and limited for higher-order mathematical reasoning. The authors emphasize that the model cannot reliably handle graphical data and that its performance is well below that of Vietnamese students on the same exam. They argue that further work is needed before such tools can be trusted for high-stakes K-12 mathematics support.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT performed well on easier mathematics items but poorly on more difficult ones. Across 250 VNHSGE questions, it answered 85/103 knowledge-level items correctly (83%), 48/77 comprehension items (62%), 12/41 application items (27%), and 3/29 high-application items (10%); overall accuracy was 147/250 (58.8%).
finding.measure: Accuracy on multiple-choice mathematics questions from the VNHSGE, broken down by Bloom's taxonomy level and topic

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation Report on Large Language Models Solving High School Mathematics Questions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report evaluates how several large language models (LLMs) perform on high school mathematics exam questions. The authors use college entrance examination math items from 2019–2023 as test data and compare at least eight models, including GLM-4-Flash, ERNIE-Speed-128K, Spark-lite, Hunyuan-lite, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, gemma-2-9b-it, Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Yi-34B.

The paper examines single-solution and multi-solution answering under multiple prompt conditions and scores models on accuracy, response time, logical reasoning, guidance responsiveness, and creativity. Question types include multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, and comprehensive problems, with difficulty stratified by exam-derived difficulty coefficients.

Overall, the report finds substantial variation across models and metrics. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and ERNIE-Speed-128K perform best on accuracy for comprehensive questions, while Spark-lite and gemma-2-9b-it are among the fastest on some tasks. GLM-4-Flash produces the most and most diverse multi-solution outputs but is slowest overall in multi-solution processing. The authors conclude that LLMs show promise for educational use, but logical reasoning and creative problem-solving still need improvement, and prompt design meaningfully affects performance.

finding.finding_summary: Across eight LLMs tested on high school mathematics exam questions, performance varied widely by question type, difficulty, and model. For single-solution accuracy, top performance on comprehensive questions reached 0.95 (ERNIE-Speed-128K) and 0.85 (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and gemma-2-9b-it), but multiple-choice and fill-in-the-blank accuracy was substantially lower overall (e.g., multiple-choice accuracy ranged from 0.10 to 0.20; fill-in-the-blank from 0.10 to 0.25).
finding.measure: Accuracy on high school mathematics exam questions (multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, comprehensive; single-solution and multi-solution settings)

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively evaluates logical reasoning and prompt-guided reasoning performance, treating these as a core metric for model quality. Reported logic scores ranged from 0.28 (Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) to 0.42 (Hunyuan-lite), and guidance attempts to recover incorrect answers varied from about 3 to 6 attempts depending on model, indicating uneven reasoning quality across systems.
finding.measure: Logical reasoning score; average attempts/success rate for guided correction using chain-of-thought prompting

finding.finding_summary: The report directly measures response time as an operational performance outcome. In single-solution tasks, average times varied substantially by model and question type, with examples such as 0.32 s for Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on multiple-choice items versus 16.01 s for GLM-4-Flash on question-and-answer tasks; for multi-solution tasks, Spark-lite was fastest at 688 s overall while GLM-4-Flash was slowest at 7400 s.
finding.measure: Model response time on math questions in single-solution and multi-solution settings

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes prompt-based evaluations that indirectly reflect adaptive support and user-facing guidance, such as using a 'college entrance examination student' prompt or teacher-style prompting to improve response accuracy. Accuracy improved for most models under guidance prompts, with gains as high as 22% for GLM-4-Flash and 17% for Spark-lite, suggesting prompt framing can increase task engagement or responsiveness, though this is not a direct measure of student motivation or persistence.
finding.measure: Accuracy improvement under different guidance prompts

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses educational applications, model selection, and implications for future instructional use, but it does not directly measure institutional outcomes. Its main institutional-relevance finding is that LLMs may support educational practice and that prompt engineering and model choice can materially change performance, which could inform adoption decisions in schools and development workflows.
finding.measure: Not directly measured; inferred from model evaluation and educational application discussion

paper_profiles.title: AMO-Bench: Large Language Models Still Struggle in High School Math Competitions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces AMO-Bench, a new benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on advanced mathematical reasoning tasks drawn from olympiad-level or harder high school mathematics. The authors argue that existing competition-style benchmarks such as AIME and HMMT are becoming saturated, easier to memorize, and less useful for discriminating among top-tier models.

To address this, the benchmark contains 50 entirely original, human-crafted problems that were cross-validated by multiple experts to meet at least IMO difficulty standards. Unlike many olympiad datasets that require proof-based manual grading, AMO-Bench uses final-answer questions so that responses can be graded automatically with parser-based methods for most items and LLM-based majority-vote grading for descriptive items. The paper also includes human-written solution paths, originality checks, and a difficulty filter that excluded problems solvable by multiple advanced models.

The experimental study evaluates 26 LLMs on AMO-Bench with repeated sampling (32 runs per model). Results show that even the best model reaches only 52.4% average accuracy, while most models score below 40%, indicating that current frontier models still struggle substantially with hard mathematical reasoning. The authors further report that performance improves with increased test-time compute and that pass@k rises with more samples, suggesting that the benchmark has headroom for future model improvements. The paper is best understood as an evaluation/benchmarking study rather than an educational intervention study in K-12 classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: Across 26 LLMs, performance on the 50-problem AMO-Bench was low, showing that current models still struggle on olympiad-level mathematics. The best model, GPT-5-Thinking (High), achieved only 52.4% AVG@32 accuracy, and most models scored below 40%; the benchmark is therefore useful as a stringent test of advanced mathematical reasoning rather than as evidence of strong math performance.
finding.measure: AVG@32 accuracy on 50 advanced math benchmark problems

paper_profiles.title: Cognitive network science reveals bias in GPT-3, ChatGPT, and GPT-4 mirroring math anxiety in high-school students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models (GPT-3, ChatGPT, and GPT-4) exhibit biased perceptions of academic disciplines, especially math, in ways that mirror human math anxiety. The authors frame the work as a cognitive/network analysis of model-generated word associations rather than an intervention study, using behavioral forma mentis networks (BFMNs) to quantify the emotional valence and semantic structure of associations elicited from the models.

The study compares outputs from the three models to a prior dataset from 159 high-school students who completed the same continued free-association task. For each cue word (including math, physics, science, school, teacher, STEM, and others), the models produced three associated words and valence ratings, which the authors analyzed using network measures, valence labels, and circumplex-model visualizations. The main finding is that GPT-3 and ChatGPT frame math negatively, with math often surrounded by negative associations such as boring, difficult, stressful, and frustrating; GPT-4 is less negative and more neutral/positive overall, but still retains stereotypical anxiety-related associations.

The paper concludes that LLMs can mirror societal math anxiety and may reinforce harmful stereotypes if used by students and educators without caution. The authors argue that GPT-4 shows some reduction in negative bias relative to earlier models, but that negative connotations remain present, particularly around math and related academic concepts. They also emphasize important methodological limits: the task probes model behavior in a way inspired by human psychology, but LLM outputs should not be assumed to correspond directly to human semantic memory or cognition.

finding.finding_summary: Across GPT-3, ChatGPT, and GPT-4, math was the central cue studied and was framed negatively by the older models, with associations such as boring, difficult, tedious, stressful, and frustrating. GPT-4 showed a substantial shift toward neutrality and positivity, but negative anxiety-related associations persisted; in the paper's summary table, the math semantic frame size was 30 for GPT-3, 134 for ChatGPT, and 149 for GPT-4, with estimated valence changing from 1.8±0.1 (negative) and 2.0±0.1 (negative) to 3.3±0.2 (neutral).
finding.measure: Semantic frame valence for the cue word 'math'; fraction of negative/positive/neutral associates; estimated valence; non-emotional associates
finding.study_size: LLM outputs: sample sizes comparable to human dataset; math frame summary table reports GPT-3 n=30 associates, ChatGPT n=134, GPT-4 n=149; human comparison n=159 students

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly connects the negative math framings in LLM outputs to math anxiety, arguing that such associations could exacerbate students' anxiety and avoidance of math. It reports that GPT-3 and ChatGPT framed math, school, and teachers with negative emotional jargon, and that GPT-4 reduced but did not eliminate anxiety-related associations.
finding.measure: Valence labels and circumplex-model emotional distributions for cue words and semantic frames; anxiety-related association patterns

finding.finding_summary: The models' perceptions of science, physics, chemistry, and STEM were examined alongside math. Science was generally framed more positively than math, while physics and chemistry showed mixed or polarized frames; GPT-4 was especially more positive for math and physics than earlier models, but some negative domain-related associations remained.
finding.measure: Semantic frame valence for science, physics, chemistry, and STEM; circumplex-model distributions of associated words

finding.finding_summary: School, teacher, art, and scientist were also analyzed as academic concepts. GPT-3 portrayed school and teacher more negatively than ChatGPT, while both models produced overwhelmingly positive semantic frames for art and scientist; GPT-4 reduced negativity around school but still linked it to exam anxiety, boredom, and bullying.
finding.measure: Semantic frame valence and associate content for school, teacher, art, and scientist

paper_profiles.title: SKYLENAGE Technical Report: Mathematical Reasoning and Contest-Innovation Benchmarks for Multi-Level Math Evaluation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This technical report introduces SKYLENAGE, a pair of benchmark suites for evaluating large language models on mathematical reasoning. The paper asks whether current math benchmarks have become too easy for frontier models and whether a harder, more structured evaluation can better distinguish strengths and weaknesses across models, subjects, and grade levels.

The authors present SKYLENAGE-REASONINGMATH, a 100-item structure-aware diagnostic set with metadata on length, numeric density, symbolic complexity, and other features, and SKYLENAGE-MATH, a 150-item contest-style suite spanning high school through doctoral difficulty across seven math subjects. They evaluate 15 contemporary LLMs under a common prompting and grading protocol, using exact-match scoring and detailed analyses by subject, grade band, and item structure.

The main conclusion is that current public math benchmarks show ceiling effects and mask important differences at the frontier, while SKYLENAGE restores headroom and reveals stronger separation among models. Performance drops substantially from high school to doctoral items, leadership rotates by subject, and numeric density and symbolic form expose robustness gaps that are not captured by final-answer accuracy alone. The authors argue that future math evaluations should incorporate process-based checks and richer diagnostic metadata to distinguish correct-by-guess from correct-by-reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that SKYLENAGE meaningfully discriminates mathematical reasoning performance among 15 LLMs, with the top model reaching 81% on the 100-item reasoning set and 44.0% on the 150-item contest set. However, performance varies sharply by subject, grade, and item structure: accuracy drops from high school to doctoral items, and harder slices reveal substantial robustness gaps, indicating that final-answer accuracy alone can overstate mathematical competence.
finding.measure: Exact-match accuracy on SKYLENAGE-REASONINGMATH (100 items) and SKYLENAGE-MATH (150 items), plus subject- and grade-conditioned accuracy
finding.study_size: n=15 models; n=100 items; n=150 items

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark analyses suggest that longer-horizon reasoning, plan integrity, and constraint fidelity vary substantially across models, and that hardest-slice retention is a sharper discriminator than overall score. The paper repeatedly emphasizes failures such as shortcutting, inconsistent intermediate steps, and loss of plan consistency, which are presented as evidence that some systems lack robust multi-step reasoning rather than merely computational skill.
finding.measure: Hardest-quintile retention, structure-sensitive accuracy, and qualitative diagnostics of intermediate-step validity

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that existing public math benchmarks suffer from ceiling effects and ability masking, making them less useful for frontier evaluation. SKYLENAGE is presented as a new benchmark infrastructure intended to improve model selection, routing, and future evaluation practice through richer metadata, subject/grade stratification, and process-based scoring.
finding.measure: Benchmark design and comparative evaluation utility for frontier model assessment

paper_profiles.title: BanglaMATH : A Bangla benchmark dataset for testing LLM mathematical reasoning at grades 6, 7, and 8
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces BanglaMATH, a new benchmark dataset of 1.7k Bangla elementary-school math word problems designed to evaluate large language models’ mathematical reasoning in a low-resource language. The authors ask whether current LLMs can solve grade 6–8 math problems in Bangla, and whether performance changes with problem complexity, distractor information, and translation into English.

The dataset was assembled from Bangla school workbooks, quizzes, and exams, then annotated with grade level, answer, number of reasoning steps, digits involved, and other metadata. The study evaluates several commercial and open-source LLMs in zero-shot settings, including GPT-4, LLaMA 4 Maverick, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Grok 3, and DeepSeek-V3. Across grades 6–8, performance generally declines as grade level, arithmetic complexity, and reasoning complexity increase.

The main findings are that Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek-V3 perform best on the benchmark, but even these models are vulnerable to irrelevant distractor information and show a clear language bias: accuracy improves when Bangla questions are translated into English. The authors conclude that current LLMs remain limited for multilingual mathematical reasoning and that more research is needed on robustness and equitable performance in low-resource languages.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark evaluates LLM performance on elementary math word problems in Bangla across grades 6, 7, and 8. Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek-V3 are the strongest models, reaching at least 80% accuracy across all three grades, but accuracy falls as grade level, digit count, and reasoning-step count increase; for four or more reasoning steps, all models fall below 50% accuracy.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Bangla elementary math word problems; also accuracy by grade level, number of digits, and number of reasoning steps

finding.finding_summary: The paper is not about human productivity directly, but it does evaluate whether LLMs can reliably automate math problem solving and reduce manual effort in educational contexts. Results suggest limited operational reliability because even top models are easily misled by distractors and show substantial degradation in Bangla, which would constrain dependable deployment for automated math support.
finding.measure: Robustness and baseline task performance of LLMs on benchmark math problems

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central contribution is a new public benchmark intended to support evaluation of multilingual LLMs in education and to expose language bias in low-resource settings. By releasing BanglaMATH and documenting performance gaps, the study aims to inform future benchmark development and more equitable model assessment for Bangla-speaking communities.
finding.measure: Creation and release of the BanglaMATH benchmark; comparative evaluation across languages

paper_profiles.title: The Invalsi Benchmarks: measuring the Linguistic and Mathematical understanding of Large Language Models in Italian
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces three Italian-language benchmarks for evaluating large language models (LLMs): Invalsi MATE for mathematical understanding, Invalsi ITA for language understanding, and Olimpiadi MATE for more difficult mathematical reasoning. The benchmarks are constructed from Italian national assessment items and math-olympiad questions, with manual checking by annotators, and are intended to fill a gap in native Italian evaluation resources for generative models.

The authors evaluate 10 LLMs spanning English-pretrained, multilingual, and Italian-fine-tuned models, using zero-shot likelihood-based evaluation and, for a subset of Invalsi MATE, human inspection. They also compare model accuracy to aggregated student results from Italian national tests. The strongest model is Llama 3.1 405B instruct, which leads on all benchmarks, but multilingual models generally outperform English-first models in Italian, and Italian fine-tuning does not close the gap. Models transfer mathematical reasoning across languages better than language understanding, and current LLMs struggle more on the harder Olimpiadi MATE set. Compared with students, LLMs are close on math but often outperform students on Italian language items.

finding.finding_summary: Across 420 Invalsi MATE questions, the best model (Llama 3.1 70B instruct) achieved 0.71 accuracy, with Llama 3.1 405B instruct reaching 0.45 on the harder Olimpiadi MATE benchmark (n=619). Multilingual models such as Mixtral instruct outperformed English-first models, while Italian fine-tuning produced only marginal gains over the base English models. Compared with Italian students, only Llama 3.1 70B instruct clearly outperformed student averages on the math benchmark.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Invalsi MATE and Olimpiadi MATE mathematics benchmarks
finding.confidence_interval: ± 0.01 to ± 0.04 reported for model accuracies; exact 95% CI not_reported

finding.finding_summary: On the 1,117-question Invalsi ITA benchmark, Llama 3.1 70B instruct achieved 0.88 overall accuracy, while Mixtral instruct reached 0.80 and several other models scored around 0.71-0.78. The authors report that most models outperform Italian students on the language benchmark, especially on multiple-choice items, but performance drops for binary items and later-grade questions, indicating that language understanding remains harder than math reasoning for these models.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Invalsi ITA language-understanding benchmark
finding.confidence_interval: ± 0.01 to ± 0.04 reported for model accuracies; exact 95% CI not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly measure durable skills as a learner outcome, but it reports that multilingual pre-training and Italian fine-tuning affect models' cross-lingual reasoning and information-retrieval performance. The authors conclude that LLMs transfer mathematical reasoning across languages better than language understanding, implying a limited but notable cross-task reasoning capability rather than a pure memorization effect.
finding.measure: Comparative performance across mathematical reasoning and language-understanding benchmarks in Italian

paper_profiles.title: MathRobust-LV: Evaluation of Large Language Models’ Robustness to Linguistic Variations in Mathematical Reasoning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models that perform well on standard math benchmarks remain reliable when the same mathematical problems are reworded in linguistically different but mathematically equivalent ways. The authors argue that such robustness matters for real educational use cases such as tutoring, homework help, and automated assessment, where students and instructors often phrase equivalent problems differently.

To study this, the paper introduces MathRobust-LV, a benchmark built from 130 seed high-school-level problems drawn from the MATH dataset and AoPS competition problems. The authors generate 520 variants by preserving numerical structure, solution logic, and final answers while changing variables, contexts, or both; the main reported experiment uses zero-shot pass@1 accuracy across 34 open- and closed-source models. They also run a small preliminary comparison across four variation types and a related analysis on GSM-Symbolic/GSM8K to calibrate expected robustness drops.

The main conclusion is that many models, including strong ones, are sensitive to benign linguistic variation: most open-source models drop by roughly 2-6 percentage points on variants, with especially large declines for smaller models such as OpenMath-Nemotron-1.5B (-11.52%) and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (-9.59%). Larger frontier models are more stable, with GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-pro showing minimal or no decline, but the overall pattern suggests that benchmark accuracy alone overstates true mathematical robustness in educational settings.

finding.finding_summary: Across 34 models evaluated on high-school-level math problems, linguistic rephrasings generally reduced accuracy, indicating brittle mathematical reasoning under surface-form changes. Most open-source models lost about 2-6 percentage points from baseline to variants, with larger drops for smaller checkpoints such as OpenMath-Nemotron-1.5B (-11.52%) and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (-9.59%), while some frontier models remained comparatively stable (e.g., Gemini-2.5-pro +0.21%, GPT-5 -0.77%).
finding.measure: Zero-shot pass@1 accuracy on baseline math problems vs. meaning-preserving linguistic variants

paper_profiles.title: PARAMANU-GANITA: Can Small Math Language Models Rival with Large Language Models on Mathematical Reasoning?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a small, domain-specific generative language model trained from scratch can achieve mathematical reasoning performance comparable to much larger general-purpose and math-specialized LLMs, while also reducing training cost and compute. The authors also frame the work as a sustainability and efficiency question, comparing training hours, checkpoint size, and inference practicality against larger models.

To investigate this, they build PARAMANU-GANITA, a 208M-parameter decoder-only transformer pretrained from scratch on a curated mathematical corpus of web text, textbooks, lecture notes, source code, and templated math Q&A pairs, with a custom math/code BPE tokenizer. They then apply Chain-of-Thought instruction fine-tuning on MetaMathQA and evaluate the model on GSM8K, MATH, LogiQA, MMLU math subsets, and AGIEVAL math benchmarks using zero-shot or prompt-based decoding.

The paper reports that the small model is competitive with, and in some cases better than, several 7B–62B baselines on mathematics benchmarks, while requiring far fewer training resources. However, the evidence is limited to benchmark evaluation of a model trained and tested by the authors, with no K-12 learners, classrooms, or instructional deployment, so the work is best read as adjacent technical evidence about model capability rather than direct educational impact evidence.

finding.finding_summary: PARAMANU-GANITA 208M achieved strong benchmark performance on mathematical reasoning tasks after pretraining from scratch on 31.5 billion tokens and CoT fine-tuning. On GSM8K, it reached 36.77% test accuracy, outperforming many generalist and math-specialized LLMs such as LLaMA-1 7B (11.00%) and LLaMA-2 7B (14.60%), though some larger math models performed better. On MATH, it scored 10.34%, again above many generalist baselines but below the strongest specialized models.
finding.measure: Benchmark accuracy on GSM8K and MATH math reasoning tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper also evaluates broader reasoning-related benchmarks, suggesting the model generalizes beyond direct arithmetic to logical and quantitative reasoning. On LogiQA, it scored 30.57% normalized accuracy, slightly above LLaMA-2 7B (30.41%) and CodeLlama-7B (30.72% is actually higher on the table; the paper’s text frames results as competitive), indicating mixed but non-trivial gains on reasoning tasks adjacent to mathematical problem solving.
finding.measure: LogiQA normalized accuracy and related reasoning benchmark performance

paper_profiles.title: Automated Feedback in Math Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLMs for Open-Ended Responses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can improve automated scoring and feedback generation for open-ended middle-school mathematics responses. The authors compare three approaches: a fine-tuned open-source LLM (GOAT, based on Mistral 7B with LoRA), a prior similarity-based benchmark (SBERT-Canberra), and GPT-4 used zero-shot with a rubric prompt.

The study uses a dataset from an online learning platform containing 50 open-response math problems with teacher scores and feedback, split into 4,000 training examples and 1,000 test examples. Two teachers also rated 100 sampled test responses for feedback accuracy, relevance, motivation, and preference. For scoring, GOAT performs best overall (AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, Kappa=0.422), outperforming SBERT and GPT-4. For feedback quality, GPT-4 is preferred by human raters and is rated highest on accuracy (86% consensus), relevance (91% consensus), and overall preference (77.5%), while GOAT performs better than SBERT but still lags GPT-4 on qualitative feedback.

The paper concludes that fine-tuning an LLM on teacher-scored student responses can improve auto-scoring, but high-quality feedback generation remains challenging when training data contain vague, irrelevant, or inconsistent teacher comments. The authors emphasize that model performance is constrained by teacher feedback quality and grading variability, and they suggest that future work should use more refined datasets and possibly combine teacher and GPT-generated feedback.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly evaluates automated scoring of open-ended middle-school math responses. GOAT achieved the best scoring performance among the three models (AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, Kappa=0.422) on 1,000 test responses, outperforming SBERT-Canberra (AUC=0.662, RMSE=1.364, Kappa=0.362) and GPT-4 (AUC=0.639, RMSE=1.160, Kappa=0.266). However, the authors note that GOAT's accuracy is only fair and that more refinement is needed before deployment.
finding.measure: Auto-scoring accuracy for open-ended middle-school math responses (AUC, RMSE, Cohen’s Kappa)

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies automated scoring and feedback as a way to reduce teacher workload in evaluating open-ended math responses. The models are intended to support faster grading and feedback generation, and the discussion explicitly frames the system as alleviating the cognitive load of composing feedback from scratch. No direct workload effect size is reported, but the study positions GOAT and GPT-4 as tools that can improve grading efficiency.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / efficiency in scoring and feedback generation

finding.finding_summary: The feedback evaluation includes motivational quality and demotivating language, which are relevant to student engagement and affect. GPT-4 was rated as slightly more motivating than GOAT and SBERT (52% vs. 48% and 46% consensus motivation) and least demotivating (1% vs. 5% and 11%), suggesting a modest advantage for student-facing encouragement. The paper does not measure student outcomes directly, only human judgments of motivational tone.
finding.measure: Human ratings of feedback motivation and demotivation
finding.study_size: n=100 sampled student answers evaluated by 2 teachers

finding.finding_summary: The feedback rubric and discussion emphasize conceptual understanding, reasoning, and the quality of explanations in student math responses, which aligns with durable skills such as reasoning and metacognition. However, the study does not directly measure these skills in students; it infers them through teacher scoring and feedback quality. No effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Quality of open-ended mathematical reasoning and explanatory feedback
finding.study_size: n=1000 test responses; n=100 evaluated for feedback

paper_profiles.title: LLM-Driven Rubric-Based Assessment of Algebraic Competence in Multi-Stage Block Coding Tasks with Design and Field Evaluation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of assessing students’ mathematical understanding in online environments where final-answer grading is insufficient to capture problem-solving process, reasoning quality, and rubric-aligned competencies. The authors propose a rubric-based assessment framework powered by a large language model (LLM) that evaluates multi-stage algebra tasks embedded in a block-coding context, with an emphasis on quadratic equations and the solution of consecutive-number problems.

The approach decomposes a complex task into segments mapped to rubric dimensions covering knowledge and understanding, procedural skills, and values/attitudes. A web-based platform records intermediate submissions, applies rule-based scoring for objective items, and uses few-shot LLM prompting for open-ended explanations and holistic rubric synthesis. The study was field-tested with 42 middle school students from two schools during a guided classroom session; students completed multi-stage quadratic-equation and block-coding tasks and also provided self-assessments.

Results suggest that the system can produce rubric-level judgments that align closely with expert ratings, with strong correlations between LLM and expert scores (r=0.79, ρ=0.76), modest bias, and acceptable error levels (MAE=12.4, RMSE=15.8). Rubric analyses showed stronger performance on conceptual knowledge and structured application than on block-coding and proactive tool-use tasks, and cluster/path analyses indicated meaningful heterogeneity among learners. The authors conclude that LLM-assisted rubric scoring is a promising, scalable method for process-sensitive mathematics assessment, while noting that the evidence is limited to a small dataset and a narrow problem domain.

finding.finding_summary: The LLM-based rubric assessment captured students’ algebraic competence in multi-stage quadratic-equation and block-coding tasks and aligned strongly with expert judgments. Across 42 middle school students, LLM and expert rubric scores were strongly correlated (r=0.79, ρ=0.76), with modest average bias (M=5.1 points) and acceptable error (MAE=12.4, RMSE=15.8), indicating that the system can validly approximate mathematics achievement judgments.
finding.measure: Rubric-based algebraic competence scores across five rubric dimensions; expert-vs-LLM agreement on student performance in quadratic-equation/block-coding tasks

finding.finding_summary: The task design and self-check component were intended to capture persistence and willingness to tackle challenging real-world problems, and the paper reports meaningful variation in these attitudes across students. Rubric 4 (challenging attitude toward problem solving) averaged relatively high scores, while self-check responses were incorporated as auxiliary evidence for motivation/persistence and reflective engagement; however, no direct causal effect on these skills was tested.
finding.measure: Rubric 4 (attitude toward problem solving) scores; five-item self-check survey and one-sentence reflection

finding.finding_summary: The framework directly assessed metacognitive explanation, process-oriented reasoning, and the ability to connect symbolic algebra to block-coding procedures. Students showed stronger performance on conceptual and structured items than on higher-order procedural tasks, and the paper used self-assessments plus open-ended explanations as evidence of metacognitive awareness and process understanding; no single causal effect size was reported for these durable skills.
finding.measure: Rubric scores for procedural reasoning and explanation; open-ended explanation stage; self-assessment and reflection responses

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that the LLM-based rubric system reduces manual grading burden while preserving rubric-level interpretability. They report that the LLM-generated synthesis substantially reduced the cognitive and temporal burden of manual grading, and the platform provided immediate grading/feedback across up to four attempts per item; however, no direct time-on-task comparison or workload effect size was measured.
finding.measure: Teacher/manual grading burden; automated grading and feedback workflow efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Models and Mathematical Reasoning Failures
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how large language models perform on 50 newly constructed high-school-level mathematical word problems. The authors are interested not only in whether models arrive at the correct final answer, but also whether their solution steps are logically valid, since correct answers can be produced by flawed reasoning.

Eight state-of-the-art models were queried once each through their APIs, including Mixtral, Llama, Gemini, GPT-4o, and OpenAI’s o1/o3 variants. The problems covered counting, arithmetic, geometry, probability, strategy, and other high-school topics, with an emphasis on natural-language word problems rather than symbolic algebra. The first author manually judged both final answers and solutions for correctness.

The main conclusion is that newer reasoning-oriented models perform better overall, but all models still exhibit substantial reasoning failures, especially in spatial reasoning, strategic planning, and multi-step deduction. The paper highlights common error patterns such as unwarranted assumptions, over-reliance on superficial numerical patterns, and failure to account for physical or combinatorial constraints. The authors argue that evaluating only final answers can substantially overestimate model competence, and that reasoning-process evaluation is necessary for a more accurate assessment of LLM mathematical ability.

finding.finding_summary: Across 50 high-school-level math word problems, performance varied widely by model: mixtral-8x7B solved 0/50 correctly, llama-3.3-70B solved 10/50, gpt-4o 14/50, o1-preview 30/50, o1 37/50, o3-mini 40/50, and deepseek-r1 36/50. The paper also reports 21 instances where a model gave the correct answer but an incorrect solution, showing that answer accuracy alone overstates reasoning quality.
finding.measure: Correct solutions and correct answers on 50 constructed mathematical word problems; manual assessment of both final answer and solution steps

paper_profiles.title: PHYBench: Holistic Evaluation of Physical Perception and Reasoning in Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces PHYBench, a human-curated benchmark of 500 original physics problems designed to evaluate the reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs). The authors argue that existing reasoning benchmarks are limited by oversimplified tasks, contamination from publicly available problems, and weak verification, and they propose PHYBench to address these issues with novel, text-only physics problems spanning high school to Physics Olympiad difficulty.

The benchmark requires models to produce symbolic expressions for answers, and the paper also introduces a new scoring metric, Expression Edit Distance (EED), to provide partial credit for near-correct mathematical expressions. The benchmark was built through iterative expert review and human validation with 81 Peking University physics students, including 50 Physics Olympiad gold medalists, who also served as a human baseline. The evaluation compares many frontier and general-purpose LLMs on PHYBench and finds that even the best model substantially underperforms human experts, with most model errors arising from multi-step semantic reasoning failures.

The paper’s main conclusions are that PHYBench is more discriminative than several existing benchmarks, that EED improves evaluation sensitivity relative to binary scoring, and that current LLMs still struggle with robust long-horizon physical reasoning. The work is primarily a benchmark and evaluation paper rather than an intervention study, and its relevance to K-12 education is indirect: it concerns physics problem-solving at high-school and Olympiad levels, but it does not study classroom use or student learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark itself is intended to measure scientific reasoning in physics, and model performance shows large gaps between LLMs and human experts. Across 500 problems, the best model (Gemini 2.5 Pro) reached 36.9% accuracy and 49.5 EED, while human experts averaged 61.9% accuracy and 70.4 EED (n=81 human participants; 559 valid answer sheets).
finding.measure: Physics reasoning benchmark accuracy and EED Score
finding.study_size: n=81 human participants; 559 valid answer sheets; 500 benchmark problems
finding.confidence_interval: Human baseline reported as 61.9 ± 2.1% accuracy and 70.4 ± 1.8 EED (bootstrap 95% CI not explicitly stated)

finding.finding_summary: The paper introduces and evaluates Expression Edit Distance (EED), a symbolic-math scoring method for final-answer evaluation. Compared with binary scoring, EED is reported to improve sample efficiency by 204% (SD=80%), meaning 500 problems scored with EED provide discriminative power comparable to about 1500 problems under binary accuracy scoring.
finding.measure: Symbolic expression scoring quality / sample efficiency for math-like answer evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The error analysis suggests models struggle with multi-step reasoning, semantic derivation, and self-correction, which are facets of metacognition and robust problem solving. However, the study measures these only indirectly through benchmark behavior rather than directly assessing learner durable skills.
finding.measure: Reasoning robustness, error detection, and correction during multi-step solution traces

paper_profiles.title: Augmenting Math Word Problems via Iterative Question Composing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of improving mathematical reasoning in large language models, particularly open-source models that lag behind proprietary systems on competition-level math benchmarks. The authors propose a new data augmentation approach called Iterative Question Composing (IQC), which uses an LLM to iteratively compose new math questions from seed problems and another LLM to reject-sample answers for correctness.

The resulting dataset, MMIQC, combines filtered web-derived mathematics Stack Exchange data with several synthetic question-response sources, including question bootstrapping, similar-problem generation, IQC, and a filtered subset of MetaMathQA. The paper evaluates fine-tuned base models (including Mistral-7B, Llemma-34B, DeepSeek-67B, and Qwen-72B) on the MATH benchmark and on Hungarian high school finals. Across model sizes, MMIQC fine-tuning improves benchmark performance over MetaMathQA-based fine-tuning, with Qwen-72B-MMIQC reaching 45.0% accuracy on MATH and showing some transfer to the Hungarian exam set.

The work is primarily a data construction and benchmark evaluation paper rather than a K-12 classroom study. Its main conclusion is that combining filtered pretraining-like math text with synthetic question-answer augmentation, especially through IQC, can materially improve LLM math problem-solving performance. The authors also report a contamination check suggesting low risk of direct memorization from the MATH test set.

finding.finding_summary: Fine-tuning on MMIQC improved math benchmark performance across multiple base models. For example, Mistral-7B improved from 28.2% with MetaMathQA to 36.0% with MMIQC, Llemma-34B from 34.8% to 38.6%, DeepSeek-67B from 36.8% to 41.0%, and Qwen-72B from 41.7% to 45.0% on MATH pass@1 accuracy.
finding.measure: MATH benchmark pass@1 accuracy; Hungarian National High School Mathematics Finals scores

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Love Edge Cases in Formative Math Assessment: Using the AMMORE Dataset and Chain-of-Thought Prompting to Improve Grading Accuracy
paper_profiles.population: Middle School (Grades 6-9), primarily students in West Africa
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically grading open-response math answers in K-12 settings, where student responses can be mathematically correct but formatted in unexpected ways. The authors argue that existing rule-based grading systems are accurate overall but still misclassify a small but important set of edge cases, which can reduce feedback quality and distort downstream estimates of student mastery.

To investigate this, the paper introduces AMMORE, a dataset of about 53,000 open-response math answers from 2,508 at-home users of Rori, an AI-powered WhatsApp math tutor used in several African countries. The authors then compare several grading approaches on a hard subset of 4,463 challenging responses: naive string matching, text processing, zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, and chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting with GPT-4o. CoT performed best, scoring 92% of the hard cases and increasing overall grading accuracy from 98.7% to 99.9%.

The paper also examines whether better answer-level grading changes student-level mastery estimates using Bayesian Knowledge Tracing. Small improvements in grading accuracy produced meaningful changes in mastery estimation: the share of students whose lesson mastery was misestimated dropped from 6.9% with string matching to 2.6% with the LLM CoT approach. The study concludes that LLMs can improve grading of open-response math answers, but also highlights important limitations, including inconsistency across runs, occasional faulty mathematical reasoning, latency costs, and uncertainty about real-world learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: On a hard subset of 4,463 challenging math responses, GPT-4o chain-of-thought prompting correctly graded 92% of edge cases and raised overall grading accuracy from 98.7% to 99.9% when used to handle cases that the rule-based system missed. In the full comparison, chain-of-thought grading achieved 0.97 accuracy, 0.98 recall for wrong answers, 0.95 F1 for correct answers, and 0.93 linear weighted kappa against human labels.
finding.measure: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and linear weighted kappa for automatic grading of open-response math answers
finding.study_size: n=4,463 hard cases; n=53,031 total dataset answers

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that LLM-based grading can automate difficult-to-grade math responses and potentially reduce educator grading burden, but it is slower than rule-based text processing. Average processing time was 0.68 seconds for zero-shot, 0.73 seconds for few-shot, and 2.79 seconds for chain-of-thought, compared with 0.006 seconds for text processing.
finding.measure: Average and longest processing time per grading approach
finding.study_size: n=4,463 hard cases for main evaluation; latency reported on grading runs

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that more accurate automated grading could support wider adoption of open-ended formative assessment and improve intelligent tutoring system student modeling. Using LLM chain-of-thought grading reduced the share of students whose lesson mastery was misestimated from 6.9% (165/2,388) to 2.6% (61/2,388), suggesting downstream benefits for institutional assessment systems.
finding.measure: Student mastery estimation error from Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) using different grading methods

paper_profiles.title: SMRC: Aligning Large Language Models with Student Reasoning for Mathematical Error Correction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a gap in generative AI for education: most LLM math-correction methods focus on repairing the model’s own reasoning, whereas educational use requires correcting a student’s work while preserving the student’s original problem-solving path. The authors frame this as a student-aware mathematical reasoning correction problem, emphasizing that a useful educational correction should both produce the right answer and retain correct intermediate steps from the student’s attempt.

To tackle this, the paper proposes SMRC (Student Mathematical Reasoning Correction), a framework that combines a reward model with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). The reward model is trained using process-level supervision constructed from sparse outcome labels via breadth-first search and reward back-propagation; MCTS then searches over possible corrected reasoning paths while trying to preserve valid student steps. The authors also introduce MSEB, a benchmark of 158 authentic high-school student solution records spanning algebra, geometry, matrices, and trigonometry, with multiple correct solution strategies per item.

Experiments compare SMRC against direct correction, thought-preserving correction, self-refinement, and self-check baselines on ProcessBench, MR-GSM8K, and MSEB. SMRC generally improves the balance between answer accuracy and correct-step retention, and the paper reports especially strong results on MR-GSM8K and MSEB. The paper concludes that structured search plus an external reward model can better support student-aligned math correction than generation-only approaches, while also noting limitations in the uniform reward-allocation scheme and suggesting more nuanced process supervision in future work.

finding.finding_summary: SMRC improved student-oriented math error correction performance relative to baseline prompting and self-correction methods. On the high-school MSEB benchmark (n=158), SMRC achieved ACC=40.1, CSRR=73.7, and HM=51.8, outperforming the compared baselines on the overall balance metric; on MR-GSM8K it reached ACC=91.4, CSRR=94.5, HM=92.9. The paper reports no effect sizes or confidence intervals, but the results indicate strong gains in both answer correctness and preservation of correct reasoning steps.
finding.measure: Math error-correction accuracy (ACC), correct-step retention rate (CSRR), harmonic mean (HM)
finding.study_size: n=158 (MSEB); additional benchmark evaluations on ProcessBench and MR-GSM8K not reported as single sample size

paper_profiles.title: FormalMATH: Benchmarking Formal Mathematical Reasoning of Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces FormalMATH, a large-scale Lean4 benchmark for formal mathematical reasoning. The benchmark contains 5,560 formally verified problems spanning high-school Olympiad-level questions through undergraduate theorems across algebra, calculus, number theory, discrete mathematics, geometry, and related areas.

The paper’s main contribution is a human-in-the-loop autoformalization pipeline that combines specialized and general-purpose LLMs, compiler-based syntax checking, multi-LLM semantic verification, negation-based disproof filtering, and final expert review by 12 IMO medalist-level mathematicians. The authors report that this pipeline retains 72.09% of statements before manual verification and substantially reduces annotation effort, while producing a curated dataset for theorem proving research.

The paper also evaluates several state-of-the-art LLM-based theorem provers on FormalMATH and FormalMATH-Lite. Results show that current provers remain far from solving the benchmark: the best single-pass model reaches 16.46% success under practical budgets, and domain bias is pronounced (e.g., strong on algebra but weak on calculus and discrete mathematics). The authors further report limited benefit from large test-time scaling, and find that adding natural-language solution guidance can hurt proof success in formal settings. Overall, the paper is primarily a benchmark and error-analysis study, not an intervention study in K-12 classrooms, but it provides adjacent evidence about the current limits of generative AI for mathematical reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: FormalMATH evaluates formal mathematical reasoning performance of LLM-based theorem provers on 5,560 Lean4 problems spanning high-school Olympiad to undergraduate level. The strongest model, Kimina-Prover, reached only 16.46% success on FormalMATH-Full under Pass@32, while BFS-Prover achieved 11.13% under Pass@1×32×100, indicating that current generative models are still far from robust mathematical proof performance despite some gains from specialized prompting and search.
finding.measure: Pass@K proof success on formal mathematics benchmark (Lean4 theorem proving)

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how ChatGPT, a newly released large language model, may affect higher education, especially assessment, learning, and teaching. Rather than evaluating a formal intervention, the authors combine a desktop literature review with hands-on experimentation using ChatGPT to probe its capabilities and limitations across tasks such as conceptual explanation, basic statistics, essay writing, language generation, and plagiarism evasion.

The paper situates ChatGPT within the broader history of AI in education and reviews adjacent tools such as automated essay scoring, automated writing evaluation, Grammarly, and Wordtune. The authors argue that ChatGPT is best understood as part of an existing ecosystem of AI-powered writing and assessment tools, while also noting that it is unusually capable at producing fluent text that can threaten traditional written assessments.

The main conclusions are cautious: ChatGPT can be useful for generating explanations, brainstorming, and some forms of writing support, but it is weak at higher-order reasoning, may produce inaccurate or fabricated content, and can be used to circumvent plagiarism checks. The authors recommend that institutions adapt assessment practices rather than rely on blanket bans, and they emphasize the need to redesign teaching and assessment for an environment in which generative AI tools are increasingly available.

finding.finding_summary: In informal testing, ChatGPT could quickly generate coherent prose and draft a short essay, but the output lacked depth, had weak structure, and sometimes produced bogus references or poor-language outputs. The paper reports that the model can help with drafting and explanation, but it is unreliable for academically rigorous writing tasks.
finding.measure: ChatGPT-generated essay quality, coherence, citation behavior, and Chinese composition quality

finding.finding_summary: When prompted to produce a Chinese composition, ChatGPT generated text that was grammatically poor, illogical in places, and appeared directly translated from English. The authors conclude that the model is much weaker in low-resource or distant languages such as Chinese than in English and German.
finding.measure: Quality of ChatGPT-generated Chinese composition

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was able to explain statistical ideas such as mean, standard deviation, and z-scores clearly and provide a real-world example with step-by-step calculations. However, the paper frames this as basic conceptual support rather than evidence of robust mathematical reasoning or verified problem-solving performance.
finding.measure: Ability to explain mean, standard deviation, z-scores, and provide worked examples

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that ChatGPT performs poorly on tasks requiring higher-order thinking, especially critical and analytical writing. Their example essay on schizophrenia was generic and descriptive, suggesting limited support for critical thinking despite fluent surface-level output.
finding.measure: Ability to produce critical, analytical writing

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that ChatGPT can increase efficiency by generating text rapidly, answering questions within about 60-120 seconds, and supporting brainstorming or drafting. The authors also note that related AI writing tools can save time for writers and teachers, although these gains come with accuracy and quality risks.
finding.measure: Speed of response and usefulness for drafting/explanation tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT poses a substantial challenge to traditional assessment systems because it can produce passable prose that may evade plagiarism detectors, pushing institutions to rethink assessment design and policy. At the same time, the authors suggest it could be harnessed to improve teaching, feedback, and assessment innovation if institutions adapt appropriately.
finding.measure: Implications for assessment integrity, plagiarism detection, and institutional assessment redesign

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT in higher education: Considerations for academic integrity and student learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines how ChatGPT was being discussed in mainstream news coverage about higher education in Australia, New Zealand, the United States, and the United Kingdom in early 2023. The central question is whether public discourse framed generative AI primarily as an academic integrity threat or as a tool that could support student learning and inclusion.

The authors conducted a content analysis of 100 news articles, coding themes such as academic integrity concerns, university responses, assessment redesign, AI limitations, policy positions, opportunities for learning, and stakeholder voices. The paper is not an intervention study; rather, it analyzes media discourse to understand how institutions and commentators were responding to the rapid emergence of ChatGPT.

The findings show that news coverage was dominated by concerns about cheating, plagiarism, and detection, with many articles recommending assessment redesign or bans. At the same time, the paper identifies a smaller but important set of arguments that ChatGPT could improve learning through plain-language explanations, feedback, brainstorming, and support for diverse students, especially multilingual and accessibility-related use cases. The authors conclude that universities should move beyond reactive integrity responses toward clearer policy, more constructive assessment design, and more student-inclusive discussions about ethical AI use.

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that public and institutional responses to ChatGPT were mixed: most news articles emphasized academic integrity concerns, while fewer discussed learning opportunities or inclusive uses. In the corpus of 100 articles, themes included university policy responses (banned n=18, allowed n=10, undecided n=22), assessment redesign (n=62), and academic integrity concerns (n=88), indicating substantial institutional disruption but not a measured intervention effect.
finding.measure: Content analysis of news articles about university responses, policy positions, and academic integrity framing

finding.finding_summary: The article substantively discusses critical thinking and information literacy as key capacities students need to use ChatGPT appropriately. It argues that reliance on ChatGPT may weaken critical thinking if students bypass the learning process, while careful use could support higher-order thinking through better task design and analysis of outputs; however, no direct student learning outcome was measured.
finding.measure: Thematic content analysis of how media articles described critical thinking, learning processes, and student use of ChatGPT

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies both risks and opportunities related to writing. Articles frequently noted that ChatGPT could be used to generate essays, produce first drafts, and create citations, raising plagiarism concerns, while also potentially supporting writing through grammatical feedback, organizational suggestions, and plain-language explanations. This is a discourse analysis rather than a direct assessment of writing performance.
finding.measure: Themes in news coverage about essay writing, drafting, feedback, and plagiarism

paper_profiles.title: Using ChatGPT in academic writing is (not) a form of plagiarism: What does the literature say?
paper_profiles.venue: Online Journal of Communication and Media Technologies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether using ChatGPT in academic writing should be considered plagiarism and, more broadly, how the literature characterizes the ethical and academic-integrity implications of generative AI in scholarly writing. The authors frame the issue as one of citation, attribution, authorship, and responsible use, and they position the work as a systematic literature review conducted with PRISMA guidelines.

The review searched multiple academic databases and screened 500 records, ultimately including 20 peer-reviewed papers focused on ChatGPT or related chatbot use in academic writing and plagiarism/academic integrity. Most included studies were conceptual, perspective, or small empirical evaluations of ChatGPT-generated text in scholarly contexts rather than studies of K-12 learners.

Across the reviewed literature, the dominant conclusion is that ChatGPT can be useful as a writing aid for drafting, paraphrasing, idea generation, and productivity, but that unacknowledged use can create plagiarism and integrity risks. The paper emphasizes that human judgment, proper citation/attribution, institutional policies, and careful regulation are necessary to use the tool responsibly; it also notes limitations such as inaccurate or fabricated content, weak detectability by plagiarism tools, and unequal access across contexts.

finding.finding_summary: The review found that ChatGPT can support academic writing by generating drafts, improving language quality, and helping users paraphrase or organize text, but that uncritical use may also encourage plagiarism or weak writing quality. The synthesis is based on 20 included papers, many of which described ChatGPT as a useful writing aid while warning that AI-generated content must be reviewed, rephrased, and attributed appropriately.
finding.measure: Academic writing quality, drafting support, paraphrasing, and plagiarism/attribution concerns in scholarly writing

finding.finding_summary: The review consistently reports that ChatGPT can increase writing productivity and speed up drafting, editing, and idea generation. Several included papers described it as a tool that can streamline academic writing workflows and reduce effort for routine text production, though no pooled effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived productivity, drafting speed, and writing workflow efficiency in academic writing

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests ChatGPT may support higher-order writing-related skills such as brainstorming, revising, and exploring alternative formulations, but it also warns that overreliance can weaken independent judgment and critical thinking. The paper repeatedly emphasizes that human evaluation and critical thinking are necessary to transform AI-generated output into acceptable scholarly work.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, judgment, and revision practices in academic writing contexts

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that ChatGPT creates policy and governance challenges for institutions, journals, and educators because existing rules often do not clearly define acceptable use, citation requirements, or misconduct boundaries. The review argues for updated institutional policies, citation guidelines, detection approaches, and regulation to protect academic integrity while allowing beneficial use.
finding.measure: Institutional policies, academic integrity governance, and plagiarism-detection/regulation concerns

paper_profiles.title: Welcome to the Era of ChatGPT et al. The Prospects of Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial discusses the rapid emergence of large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Bard, LaMDA, and Copilot, and reflects on their implications for work, research, education, and society. Rather than reporting a formal empirical study, it synthesizes early examples, media reports, and prior research to explain why LLMs have become a major technological inflection point.

The paper argues that LLMs are powerful but fundamentally limited tools: they can generate fluent text, improve productivity, and support tasks such as drafting, coding, and language assistance, but they also hallucinate facts, reproduce biases, and can be used carelessly or maliciously. It highlights risks around accuracy, copyright, environmental costs, policy, and academic integrity, and suggests that education will need to adapt assessment and disclosure practices to account for AI use.

In the education section, the authors focus mainly on secondary and higher education as a context where students may use LLMs for essays, homework, and theses. The article recommends pragmatic responses rather than simple bans, emphasizing transparency, prompt quality, and human responsibility for outputs. Overall, it is a forward-looking editorial that frames LLMs as transformative infrastructure while warning that their benefits will depend heavily on user skill and institutional governance.

finding.finding_summary: The editorial argues that LLMs are already forcing institutions to reconsider policies, governance, and assessment practices, especially in education and publishing. It cites school bans, academic integrity concerns, journal policies, and possible copyright/legal constraints, but provides no original empirical evaluation of these institutional effects.
finding.measure: policy and governance implications discussed qualitatively

finding.finding_summary: The article claims LLMs can improve productivity by automating drafting, proofreading, grammar checking, coding support, and other text-related tasks. These benefits are illustrated through examples such as GitHub Copilot and text assistants, but the paper does not present original quantitative evidence or a measured effect size.
finding.measure: productivity and task-efficiency claims from prior examples and reports

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses heavily on text generation, writing support, and academic writing implications, arguing that LLMs can help users draft and revise text but may also generate hallucinated citations, bland prose, and low-quality or misleading academic writing. The evidence is descriptive and example-based rather than from a direct study of writing outcomes.
finding.measure: writing quality, drafting, proofreading, and citation generation examples

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the potential of artificial intelligence tools in educational measurement and assessment
paper_profiles.venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.population: Educators and assessment professionals (general education context; not K-12-specific)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review article examines how artificial intelligence tools, especially large language models, may be used across the educational measurement and assessment cycle. The paper focuses on test purpose specification, test blueprint development, item generation, instruction preparation, item assembly, test administration, scoring, interpretation, analysis/appraisal, and reporting. It also discusses the changing role of teachers when AI is used in assessment systems.

The article is not an empirical intervention study; instead, it synthesizes conceptual applications and potential uses of AI in assessment practice. It argues that AI tools may improve efficiency, consistency, personalization, and feedback in assessment, while also raising concerns about bias, transparency, privacy, limited scope, and the need for human oversight. The paper is positioned around educational assessment broadly, with examples that include classroom and computer-based testing, but it does not report original data from a defined student sample.

Overall, the authors conclude that AI can support assessment processes and reduce teacher workload, but it cannot replace educators. They emphasize that teachers remain necessary for assessment design, contextual judgment, ethical oversight, interpretation, and individualized support. The paper recommends collaborative development of transparent, ethical AI systems and professional training to mitigate risks and improve responsible use.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools can automate multiple assessment tasks, including item generation, scoring, reporting, and analysis, thereby saving time and reducing teacher workload. No original effect estimate is reported; the article is a conceptual review rather than an empirical study.
finding.measure: Assessment task automation, grading efficiency, reporting/analysis speed, teacher workload

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames AI as potentially transformative for educational assessment systems, but it also highlights institutional risks such as bias, privacy, lack of transparency, lack of stakeholder participation, and the need for governance and ethical oversight. No original quantitative evidence is reported.
finding.measure: Policy/implementation considerations for AI-based educational assessment

finding.finding_summary: The article claims AI-supported assessment and feedback may increase student engagement, motivation, and reduce anxiety, but these are literature-based assertions rather than findings from a direct study. No sample, effect size, or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Student motivation, engagement, and anxiety in AI-supported assessment contexts

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests AI tools and LLMs can support critical thinking and reflective learning through feedback, adaptive instruction, and assessment interpretation. However, this is presented as a conceptual possibility, not as an empirically measured outcome.
finding.measure: Critical thinking and reflective learning

paper_profiles.title: Educational Applications of the ChatGPT AI System: A Systematic Review Research
paper_profiles.population: K-12, higher education, and general education contexts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews early literature on ChatGPT in education, aiming to synthesize the initial claims, concerns, and proposed uses of the tool shortly after its release in late 2022. The authors conducted a systematic review of 40 studies drawn from multiple databases and Google Scholar, focusing on papers published between December 2022 and February 15, 2023.

The review organizes findings into positive and negative themes. On the positive side, it argues ChatGPT may support literature review, summarization, translation/paraphrasing, generating complex answers, identifying student needs, personalized learning, grading, data analysis, cybercrime/cyberbullying prevention, cataloguing, directing, and material generation. On the negative side, it highlights cheating, bias, ethical issues, legal issues, and incorrect answers as important risks.

The paper is not an evaluation of a specific classroom intervention or product implementation; instead, it is a thematic synthesis of very early evidence and commentary about ChatGPT’s educational implications. The authors conclude that ChatGPT may create a new paradigm in education, but that its adoption also raises substantial concerns about academic integrity, reliability, bias, and governance. The study is broad and cross-disciplinary, with education as the main context but including adjacent domains such as law, medicine, and psychology when relevant to educational use cases.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that ChatGPT may support literacy-related tasks such as abstracting, literature review, generating literature, translation, and paraphrasing, suggesting clear potential for writing support and text processing. At the same time, it highlights risks of inaccurate or fabricated text and plagiarism-related misuse, meaning the literacy impact is presented as both useful and problematic rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Thematic synthesis of reported ChatGPT capabilities and risks in literature review, abstracting, generation, translation, and paraphrasing tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes that ChatGPT has been described in prior literature as able to solve mathematical problems and generate complex answers, and it includes mathematics among the scientific content areas eligible for inclusion. However, this is not presented as a direct evaluation of math learning outcomes; the paper mainly treats mathematics as an adjacent application domain with potential rather than measured impact.
finding.measure: Thematic synthesis of prior claims about solving mathematical problems and generating exam responses

finding.finding_summary: The review links ChatGPT to durable-skill development and risks, especially critical thinking and problem solving. It argues that ChatGPT may help learners by supplying complex answers and study support, but warns that overreliance could reduce students’ independent critical-thinking and problem-solving development.
finding.measure: Thematic synthesis of claims about exam answering, study support, and effects on critical-thinking/problem-solving development

finding.finding_summary: A major theme of the review is that ChatGPT may improve operational efficiency in education by accelerating summarization, literature review, grading, data analysis, cataloguing, and helping students study. The paper does not report a quantitative effect size, but it consistently frames these uses as time-saving and workload-reducing applications for educators and researchers.
finding.measure: Thematic synthesis of productivity-oriented tasks such as grading, abstracting, literature review, data analysis, and cataloguing

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes institutional risks and governance implications, including cheating, ethical concerns, legal issues, bias, and the need to redesign assessment systems and institutional policies. It points to school-level restrictions and broader calls for regulation, showing that ChatGPT is framed as an issue of institutional governance as much as classroom use.
finding.measure: Thematic synthesis of ethical, legal, assessment, and policy implications across included studies

paper_profiles.title: Beyond the Imitation Game: Quantifying and extrapolating the capabilities of language models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces BIG-bench, a large and diverse benchmark designed to probe language model capabilities beyond the narrow tasks used in many existing evaluations. The authors argue that current benchmarks are too limited in scope, too easy, and often too short-lived to reveal new or emerging capabilities as models scale, so they assembled 204+ tasks contributed by a large community of researchers and expert task authors.

The paper evaluates multiple families of large language models, including dense and sparse transformer models and GPT-style models, across tasks spanning math, linguistics, common sense, biology, physics, social bias, and more. It also collects expert human rater baselines. The main conclusions are that performance generally improves with scale and more prompting shots, but remains far below expert human performance overall; calibration improves with scale but remains poor in absolute terms; sparse models outperform dense models at matched inference cost in some settings; and model behavior can be brittle and highly sensitive to task formatting and metric choice.

Although the benchmark includes some math-related tasks, the paper is not an education study and does not evaluate K-12 learners or instructional interventions. Its relevance to education research is indirect: it provides adjacent evidence about the strengths, limitations, and risks of generative language models for tasks that resemble educational problem solving, including mathematical reasoning and answer selection. The paper emphasizes that apparent breakthroughs may depend heavily on task specification and that model outputs can be unreliable, overconfident, or biased, all of which are important cautions for future educational uses of generative AI.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark includes math-related tasks, but the paper does not evaluate mathematics learning or K-12 student performance. On tasks such as modified_arithmetic and periodic_elements, model performance sometimes shows breakthrough-like jumps at critical scale, while other math-adjacent tasks improve gradually; overall performance remains far below expert human raters and is poor in absolute terms.
finding.measure: Task performance on BIG-bench math and math-adjacent benchmark tasks, including exact string match, multiple-choice grade, and normalized preferred metrics

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language models on German middle school content across nine subjects. The authors argue that existing multimodal benchmarks are often English-only, overly multiple-choice, and insufficiently representative of real-world, curriculum-grounded tasks, especially when visual reasoning must be combined with subject knowledge. To address this, they assembled 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions drawn from German textbooks and related materials, with some questions self-constructed to avoid text-only solving and to include adversarial items that are intentionally unanswerable from the image alone.

The study evaluates thirteen open-weight vision-language models, using a panel-of-LLMs judge setup for scoring free-text answers. Results show that even the strongest model reaches under 45% overall accuracy, with especially weak performance in mathematics, music, and adversarial questions. The authors further find that benchmark performance does not always transfer cleanly across datasets: models that score highly on MMMU do not necessarily do as well on VLM@school, and some model families underperform relative to their leaderboard standing.
