The paper concludes that middle-school, German-language multimodal tasks are a useful stress test for current AI systems and that current models remain brittle when asked to combine image understanding, background knowledge, and rejection of misleading prompts.

finding.finding_summary: Math was one of the central benchmark domains. The best model scored 34.09% on math (Qwen2.5VL 32B), while several models were far lower (e.g. Ovis2 4B at 9.09%). The authors report that models were better at calculation than at counting and struggled with geometry, identifying shapes, and reading diagram details, indicating substantial limitations on middle-school mathematical reasoning tasks.
finding.measure: Open-ended math questions on geometry, counting, area, circumference, and diagram interpretation

finding.finding_summary: Physics was a major subject in the dataset, and the authors describe repeated failures on explanation-based items and diagram interpretation. Best reported physics accuracy reached 47.65% (Qwen2.5VL 32B), but many models performed notably lower and struggled to explain phenomena such as stellar evolution or circuit behavior even when they could identify the relevant diagram type.
finding.measure: Open-ended physics questions involving diagrams, explanations, and basic scientific reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark substantively covers non-STEM school subjects including arts, history, geography, religion, music, and sports. Performance varied widely by domain, with best scores around 54% in history and religion, but much weaker performance in music (~31% best) and substantial errors in map reading, art-style identification, and sports-game interpretation. The authors argue these results show major weaknesses in real-world multimodal understanding beyond standard benchmark tasks.
finding.measure: Open-ended subject-specific questions across arts, geography, history, music, religion, and sports
finding.study_size: n=1,189 questions across 289 images in these non-math/non-physics/non-biology domains

finding.finding_summary: Although not the primary framing of the paper, the benchmark repeatedly tests abilities closely tied to durable skills such as reasoning with visual evidence, interpreting ambiguous cues, and recognizing when a question is unanswerable. The authors report that models often hallucinate rather than say 'I don't know,' and perform especially poorly on adversarial questions that require careful judgment and refusal of misleading prompts.
finding.measure: Adversarial unanswerable questions and reasoning-heavy open-ended responses
finding.study_size: adversarial subset included in the 2,038 questions; exact adversarial n not reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main contribution is a benchmark intended to reveal limitations of current VLMs and to improve evaluation practice, especially for non-English and curriculum-grounded tasks. It does not study institutional outcomes directly, but it argues that benchmark design affects what systems appear capable of, and shows that leaderboard performance can diverge from performance on realistic educational tasks.
finding.measure: Benchmark comparison between VLM@school and public leaderboards such as MMMU/Open VLM

paper_profiles.title: Democratizing Signal Processing and Machine Learning: Math Learning Equity for Elementary and Middle School Students
paper_profiles.venue: Submitted to IEEE Signal Processing Magazine
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that strong early mathematics foundations are essential not only for later success in signal processing and machine learning, but also for equity in STEM pathways more broadly. The authors frame elementary arithmetic and middle-school algebra as cumulative prerequisites for later technical learning, and they highlight systemic barriers that prevent many students from developing these foundations, including resource inequities, low expectations, language barriers, and pandemic-related learning loss.

Rather than testing a new intervention through a controlled study, the paper is a perspective/experience-based article describing three university- and foundation-run out-of-school tutoring and mentoring programs: CyMath at Iowa State, Algebra by 7th Grade at Purdue, and Math Motivators from the Actuarial Foundation. The programs serve grades 3-8 (and in one case grades 3-12), using tutoring, mentoring, adaptive software such as ALEKS, parent engagement, and STEM enrichment activities. The article also offers lessons learned from program implementation, including the importance of tutor-student fit, hybrid formats, school partnerships, parent awareness, homework and practice, and access to technology.

The main conclusion is that early math support, especially supplemental tutoring and mentoring, can help close cumulative learning gaps before they become harder to repair in later grades. The authors report descriptive gains from their own programs, including percentile improvements for a small number of CyMath students and a cited finding from Ab7G that students who completed a full ALEKS grade level each year showed significant growth in mathematics proficiency. However, the article is primarily a practitioner-oriented commentary and advocacy piece rather than a rigorous evaluation of intervention effects.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that early math support can improve arithmetic fluency and later algebra readiness, and it reports descriptive gains from the CyMath and Ab7G programs. For CyMath, the authors note percentile increases for several students (e.g., one student moved from the 40th percentile in Sept. 2023 to the 85th in May 2024 and the 92nd in Jan. 2025), but these are presented as noisy school-test percentiles rather than a formal effect estimate. For Ab7G, they cite an external report that students who completed a full grade level in ALEKS each year (n=20) showed significant growth in mathematics proficiency and higher likelihood of achieving proficiency or higher on ILEARN, but no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Standardized math test percentiles (MAP, iReady) and mathematics proficiency on ALEKS/ILEARN
finding.study_size: n=6 (CyMath earliest cohort described); n=20 (cited Ab7G subgroup)

finding.finding_summary: The article repeatedly emphasizes motivational and self-efficacy supports as part of the tutoring/mentoring model, especially in Ab7G, where student self-efficacy, mentorship, and parental engagement are described as foundational pillars. However, the paper does not present a formal psychometric evaluation of motivation, engagement, or self-efficacy; its evidence is mainly programmatic and descriptive, such as students being recognized for meeting ALEKS time/topic goals and tutors using encouragement and game time to sustain participation.
finding.measure: Program participation, goal completion on ALEKS, and informal observations of engagement/self-efficacy

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that university/community partnerships can expand access to supplemental math learning for underserved students and improve institutional coordination around math support. It describes operational features such as school-district busing, principal support, district recruitment partnerships, parent communication, and report sharing with districts, but does not quantify institutional outcomes with a formal evaluation design.
finding.measure: Program implementation features, partnership participation, and school-district coordination

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary school students and teachers perceive creative mathematical writing supported by generative AI. The authors are motivated by a classroom problem common in elementary mathematics: students often struggle to generate original, coherent math stories and to connect creative writing with mathematical understanding. They ask what educational benefits and what challenges emerge when GenAI is used to scaffold this process in authentic classrooms.

The study implemented a GenAI-powered learning technology in six 5th-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools with 79 students and six teachers. The instructional sequence had three parts—Ask, Represent, and Transform—through which students first analyzed math stories, then modeled ideas visually, and finally used GenAI (GPT-4 and DALL·E 3) to draft and revise culturally relevant mathematical stories. After several class sessions, the researchers collected focus-group interviews with 10 students, one-on-one interviews with all six teachers, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations. They analyzed these data using inductive and deductive thematic analysis.

The study found that students and teachers perceived several benefits: GenAI appeared to support divergent and convergent thinking, originality, flexible thinking, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and positive affect such as interest, curiosity, and ownership. At the same time, they identified important limitations and risks, including students’ weak critical evaluation of AI-generated content, difficulty formulating coherent stories, the AI being perceived as too perfect, lack of adaptive feedback, reduced opportunities for autonomous work, limited social interaction, and insufficient accessibility features such as speech-to-text. Overall, the paper argues that GenAI can support creative mathematical writing, but only when carefully designed to balance scaffolding with human learning goals and classroom interaction.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers reported that GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing helped students better understand mathematical problems, represent mathematical ideas, and uncover misconceptions. The study is qualitative and does not report effect sizes, but it describes improved understanding through the Ask and Represent steps and richer mathematical reasoning in story creation across 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers.
finding.measure: Interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observation of mathematical understanding, representation, and misconception uncovering during story-based math tasks

finding.finding_summary: Participants perceived that GenAI made math learning more interesting, sparked curiosity, and increased students’ ownership of learning. Students described the activity as fun and motivating, while teachers noted greater engagement and focus during the 5th-grade classroom implementation.
finding.measure: Interview themes on interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership; survey responses and observations

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that GenAI-supported math writing encouraged divergent and convergent thinking, originality, flexible thinking, prompt engineering, and evaluation of AI strengths and weaknesses. However, it also found that some students struggled to critically evaluate AI-generated content and to formulate coherent stories aligned with the system’s capabilities.
finding.measure: Interview themes on creativity, prompt engineering, critical evaluation, and story formulation

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that GenAI supported creative writing in a mathematics context by helping students draft, revise, and elaborate stories. Students reported that AI corrected mistakes, added detail, and helped them produce more original and interesting stories, although some also noted that the system could reduce opportunities to write independently.
finding.measure: Interview and observation themes about creative mathematical writing and story drafting/revision

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and students described GenAI as helping students generate story drafts more quickly and reducing the burden of starting from scratch. The paper does not quantify time savings, but it presents the system as a productivity aid for drafting and refining math stories.
finding.measure: Perceived productivity/efficiency in drafting and revising math stories

paper_profiles.title: CMATH: Can Your Language Model Pass Chinese Elementary School Math Test?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what grade level of Chinese elementary school mathematics popular large language models can handle, and whether they are robust to irrelevant information in word problems. To study this, the authors introduce CMATH, a 1.7k-item dataset of Chinese elementary school math word problems collected from real workbooks and exams, with fine-grained annotations for grade level, answer, number of reasoning steps, and number of digits.

The authors evaluate several commercial and open-source LLMs in a zero-shot setting, including GPT-4, ChatGPT, Chinese-Alpaca, MOSS, Ziya-LLaMA, Baichuan, RWKV, and ChatGLM. They find that GPT-4 is the only model that achieves at least 60% accuracy across all six elementary grades, while other models deteriorate sharply as grade level increases and many fail even on grade 1. Performance also declines as problems become more complex in terms of reasoning steps and number of digits.

The paper additionally constructs a small distractor dataset to test robustness to irrelevant but numerically salient information. GPT-4 remains comparatively robust, whereas the other models, especially ChatGPT, are often misled by distractors and produce incorrect reasoning or answers. Overall, the paper argues that elementary math word problems remain challenging for most general-purpose LLMs and that fine-grained, grade-level evaluation can reveal important limitations in arithmetic, reasoning, and distractor resistance.

finding.finding_summary: Across 1.7k Chinese elementary school math word problems, GPT-4 was the only model to achieve at least 60% accuracy across all six grades, while other evaluated models degraded markedly with increasing grade level and many failed even on grade 1. On the full benchmark, accuracy fell as grade, number of reasoning steps, and number of digits increased, indicating that elementary-level mathematical problem solving remains difficult for most general-purpose LLMs.
finding.measure: Accuracy on CMATH elementary school math word problems, stratified by grade, reasoning steps, and number of digits

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that model performance drops as the number of reasoning steps increases, suggesting limited multi-step reasoning and problem decomposition ability in most models. GPT-4 performs best, but the general pattern is that more complex reasoning demands lead to lower accuracy.
finding.measure: Accuracy as a function of annotated number of reasoning steps per problem

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.population: Middle School (7th grade mathematics teachers and students)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether teachers should remain “in the loop” when generative AI is used to personalize middle school mathematics tasks, and what tradeoffs arise between personalization quality, teacher effort, and student reactions. The authors focus on context personalization: modifying existing Illustrative Mathematics problems so that they connect to students’ interests, especially popular culture references, while preserving the underlying math structure.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers from six U.S. schools were trained to use ChatGPT/GPT-4o to personalize 143 problems from two curriculum units (Unit 4 on proportional relationships and percentages; Unit 6 on expressions, equations, and inequalities). Teachers’ prompt logs and audio/video were analyzed to characterize their prompting moves, and 521 students provided closed-ended ratings of interestingness and closeness to their interests; a subset also gave open-ended feedback. The study found that teachers most often adjusted grain size, realism, and ownership of the personalized content, but doing so was time-consuming: personalizing a problem took about 4 minutes on average and did not clearly become faster with experience. Students generally preferred finer-grained, specific references, but they also focused more on surface-level interest than on realism/depth. Overall, the paper concludes that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can improve task quality and professional learning, but it is not yet time-efficient and may not satisfy students’ desire for more individualized, small-grain personalization.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers used generative AI to personalize 143 middle school math problems, but the study did not measure math achievement or learning gains. Students’ ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to their interests were modest overall, and problems personalized with 3-5 prompts received significantly higher ratings than those created with fewer or more prompts (B=0.240, SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073), suggesting some optimization of problem quality within mathematics tasks.
finding.measure: Student ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to students’ interests for personalized mathematics problems

finding.finding_summary: The study found that personalization modestly supported students’ interest in mathematics tasks, though ratings were low overall. Mean interestingness ratings were 2.46/5 and mean closeness ratings were 2.53/5 across 53 problems, and Unit 6 problems were rated significantly higher than Unit 4 problems (interestingness/closeness combined: B=0.33, SE=0.095, t=3.49, p=0.0012), indicating improved student receptivity over time.
finding.measure: Student self-reported interestingness and perceived closeness of problems to their interests
finding.study_size: n=521 students; ratings collected for 52-53 problems depending on measure

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-in-the-loop personalization was not especially efficient. Across 143 problems, teachers used 558 prompts total, averaging 3.2 prompts per problem (SD=2.6), and each problem took about 246 seconds (SD=165.7) to create. Efficiency did not improve; in fact, Unit 6 required more prompts and more time than Unit 4 (prompts: B=1.26, SE=0.41, t=3.08, p=0.0025; time: B=70.4, SE=29.6, t=2.38, p=0.0189).
finding.measure: Number of prompts per problem and time spent creating each personalized problem
finding.effect_size: B=1.26 for prompts from Unit 4 to Unit 6; B=70.4 seconds for time from Unit 4 to Unit 6

finding.finding_summary: The paper mainly examined prompting behavior and teacher problem-posing rather than student durable skills, but it does provide evidence about teacher learning and iteration with generative AI. Teachers improved in crafting interesting problems over time, yet this came with increased effort rather than greater efficiency, indicating growth in prompting/revision practice but not streamlined expertise.
finding.measure: Teacher prompting behavior across units and iterative refinement of personalized math tasks

paper_profiles.title: Peak into the Past: An Archaeo-Astronomy Summer School
paper_profiles.population: Year 5-8 pupils (upper primary to lower secondary), Gifted and Talented students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article describes an archaeo-astronomy summer school designed as an outdoor, interdisciplinary learning experience for Year 5-8 Gifted and Talented pupils. The paper asks, in effect, how ancient monuments, archaeology, astronomy, ecology, and hands-on fieldwork can be used to engage students and support transition from primary to secondary school. It is not a controlled evaluation study; rather, it presents the rationale, planning, activities, and reported outcomes of the summer school.

The intervention ran for five days in 2009 with 27 pupils from Meden School and Technology College in Worksop. Students completed school-based preparatory activities, visited local Peak District monuments (Arbor Low and Nine Ladies), analyzed collected data in a university science setting, and then presented their work to parents. Activities included monument surveying, density and construction estimation, ecological sampling, astronomy and shadow activities, and an archaeobotany workshop. The paper also describes preparatory focus-group input from four pupils, risk planning for the field trips, and follow-up activities over the next year using a wiki, CPD resources, and museum visits.

The main conclusion is that the summer school was perceived as successful: students reportedly met the predefined outcomes, showed retention of knowledge, improved confidence and social skills, and were able to communicate their learning through presentations, drama, poetry, and online work. The authors argue that the project demonstrated the value of the outdoor classroom for STEM-enriched learning and that interdisciplinary field-based activities can be embedded in the curriculum. However, the evidence is descriptive and based on participant work and observations rather than formal pre/post testing or comparison groups.

finding.finding_summary: The summer school explicitly used numeracy to scale up measurements from field and classroom tasks to real monuments, such as estimating mass, volume, area, and density. Students carried out calculations in activities like surveying Arbor Low, measuring limestone density, and comparing construction effort; the paper reports that these activities helped transform the outdoor classroom into a "mathematics laboratory," but no quantitative learning gains are reported.
finding.measure: Area, volume, mass, density calculations; estimating work required to construct ancient monuments

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students used scientific reasoning in archaeology, ecology, and astronomy by making observations, testing assumptions, comparing sites, and interpreting data from quadrats, transects, soil pH, monument orientation, and plant remains. The authors state that pupils became more confident in making observations and placing findings in context, but the evidence is descriptive and does not include effect sizes or formal outcome tests.
finding.measure: Observation, site comparison, ecological sampling, alignment checking, archaeobotany interpretation

finding.finding_summary: The authors report improved confidence, individual growth, and social skills across the group, especially among the initial focus students. Students also appeared engaged and motivated during the week and follow-up activities, and the final presentations suggest increased self-assurance in sharing work with parents and peers. No standardized engagement or self-efficacy measure was used.
finding.measure: Observed confidence, engagement, social interaction, willingness to present work

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on collaboration, planning, communication, and metacognitive reflection. Students worked in small groups, designed displays, presented to an audience, used a wiki to reflect on their work, and developed CPD materials, with the authors concluding that these experiences improved collaboration, self-confidence, and the ability to communicate findings through multiple modes.
finding.measure: Group collaboration, presentation performance, wiki-based reflection, communication products

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively covers archaeology, ecology, astronomy, and interdisciplinary STEM enrichment rather than a single academic domain. It reports that students learned key concepts such as stratigraphy, relative dating, ecology of different sites, and solar alignments, and that they used appropriate keywords in presentations and performances. No formal academic achievement metrics are provided.
finding.measure: Content knowledge in archaeology, ecology, astronomy, and interdisciplinary STEM topics

paper_profiles.title: A mathematical model for the bullying dynamics in schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a mathematical compartmental model of bullying in schools to study how bullying may spread and persist in a school population. The model divides individuals into four states: susceptible, bullies, exposed to bullying, and violent individuals, and uses ordinary differential equations plus agent-based simulations on a two-dimensional grid to examine transitions among these states.

The author treats bullying as a socially contagious process influenced by interactions among students and by intervention from parents and schools. Parameters represent recruitment into bullying, victimization, recovery from bullying, escalation to violence, and return from violence, allowing the model to explore when bullying-free versus endemic bullying equilibria occur. Analytical stability analysis and simulations indicate that bullying dies out when the bullying contagion parameter is below the control parameter (α < γ in the mean-field model), but persists when contagion is stronger. The paper concludes that robust anti-bullying school programs and parental actions can reduce or eradicate bullying, while weaker control allows bullying and related violence to persist.

finding.finding_summary: The model suggests that school and parent interventions can control bullying if anti-bullying programs are sufficiently robust. In the mean-field analysis, the bullying-free equilibrium is stable when α < γ (equivalently R0 < 1), while the endemic bullying equilibrium is stable when α > γ; the paper argues that increasing school control (γ) reduces endemic bullying.
finding.measure: Analytical stability of bullying-free vs endemic equilibria; model parameter thresholds (α, γ, R0)

paper_profiles.title: Creating and Evaluating Privacy and Security Micro-Lessons for Elementary School Children
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a gap in school-based digital privacy and security education for young children. The authors argue that, although K–8 students increasingly use digital devices in classrooms, teachers lack ready-to-use, age-appropriate lessons that teach privacy, security, and related digital citizenship skills. The study asks what K–8 teachers need, how privacy/security lessons can fit into existing instruction, and how such lessons may support children’s learning.

The project used an iterative co-design process with teachers from two public elementary schools in two U.S. metropolitan areas. First, the authors conducted formative interviews with 14 teachers to identify curricular needs and design constraints. They then developed four sets of micro-lessons, each made up of three 15–20 minute lessons, covering digital citizenship, digital security, digital privacy, and critical data literacy. The lessons were refined through co-design sessions, classroom implementation by seven teachers, and additional evaluation interviews with six outside teachers.

The main conclusions are that teachers want short, flexible, and age-differentiated materials grounded in children’s everyday experiences, along with stronger instructional supports and ongoing professional development. Teachers viewed the micro-lesson format as easy to integrate into existing curricula, but also noted limits related to school infrastructure and the need for more differentiation across grade bands. The study reports qualitative evidence that both teachers’ and children’s awareness of digital privacy and security concepts improved after engaging with the micro-lessons, but it does not provide quantitative effect sizes.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the micro-lesson format was flexible, short, and relatively easy to integrate into existing curriculum plans. Across interviews, they said the structure could be inserted into regular instruction with manageable lesson length (3 lessons per module, 15–20 minutes each), though some schools might lack the infrastructure needed to use all resources.
finding.measure: teacher interviews about feasibility, integration, and lesson manageability
finding.study_size: n=13 evaluation teachers (plus formative interviews with n=14 teachers)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports qualitative evidence that the micro-lessons helped children engage with privacy and security topics in ways teachers found motivating and relatable. Teachers described the lessons as engaging and suggested they supported children’s awareness of safe and responsible online behavior, but no quantitative engagement or self-regulation measures were reported.
finding.measure: teacher-reported child engagement and awareness during/after micro-lessons
finding.study_size: n=7 classroom-implementation teachers; child sample size not reported

finding.finding_summary: Teachers indicated that the lessons supported children’s ability to evaluate credibility, think about trade-offs in sharing information, and respond to risky online situations, which are durable-skills-like critical thinking and self-protection practices. The evidence is qualitative and based on teacher feedback rather than direct standardized assessment of critical thinking or metacognition.
finding.measure: teacher-reported child understanding of credibility evaluation, privacy trade-offs, and response strategies
finding.study_size: n=13 evaluation teachers (plus formative interviews with n=14 teachers)

finding.finding_summary: The study found that schools and districts often lacked formal privacy/security curricula and teacher professional development, creating a systemic gap the micro-lessons were designed to address. Teachers emphasized the need for curricular support, administrative resources, and ongoing professional development, suggesting the intervention has potential institutional relevance even though policy-level outcomes were not directly measured.
finding.measure: teacher interviews on district curriculum availability, professional development, and school implementation constraints
finding.study_size: n=14 formative teachers; n=13 evaluation teachers

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Applications of Generative AI in High School STEM Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can improve high school STEM learning outcomes, with a specific focus on physics. The motivating problem is that existing claims about generative AI in education have largely been speculative or based on adjacent evidence, so the author uses an experimental pre-test/post-test design to test the tool in a real classroom setting.

The study compares four conditions across AP Physics 1 and on-level physics classes at a Texas high school: a no-tool control group, a search-engine condition, a generative-AI-only condition, and a generative-AI-plus-literacy-program condition. Students completed a lecture, then used their assigned tool for a short study period, followed by a post-test and survey. The sample included 171 students in the quantitative analysis and 60 survey respondents.

Results suggest that generative AI by itself did not improve outcomes and may have been harmful in this short-term setting: the GAI-only group scored worse than the control and search-engine groups in both sections, and in AP Physics the differences across groups were statistically significant. By contrast, the GAI literacy program improved performance relative to GAI alone, especially in AP Physics, though the study did not find statistically significant differences between the control group and any experimental group overall, and survey measures of engagement, understanding, and enjoyment did not show significant differences. The author concludes that generative AI may be useful only when paired with instruction on responsible, effective use, and notes important limitations including short duration, subject specificity, and the use of a general-purpose AI tool rather than an education-specific system.

finding.finding_summary: The study tested whether generative AI changed physics learning outcomes using pre-test/post-test score differences in AP Physics 1 momentum/impulse and on-level electricity/circuits. In AP Physics, the ANOVA was significant (p=0.011), and post hoc tests showed the search-engine group outperformed the GAI-only group (p=0.0062) while the GAI-literacy-program group outperformed the GAI-only group (p=0.0256); in on-level physics, the ANOVA was not significant (p=0.619).
finding.measure: Pre-test to post-test physics score difference on unit assessments
finding.study_size: n=171 quantitative participants (AP Physics n=91, on-level physics n=80)
finding.std_deviation: AP Physics SDs: control 1.355, SE 1.387, GAI-LP 1.225, GAI 1.791; On-level SDs: control 1.700, SE 2.250, GAI 2.199, GAI-LP 1.569

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examined student engagement, understanding, and enjoyment during the learning process via post-survey responses. Although descriptive means suggested the GAI group had slightly higher engagement and the SE group slightly higher understanding, the MANOVA was not significant (Pillai’s Trace p=0.115), indicating no statistically reliable differences across experimental groups on these affective measures.
finding.measure: Post-survey ratings of understanding, engagement, and enjoyment
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CIs overlapped substantially across groups; exact values not reported

finding.finding_summary: Although the study’s main outcome was academic performance, it also directly discussed responsible use, self-confidence, and literacy around generative AI as mechanisms affecting how students learn with the tool. The GAI literacy program was associated with better test performance than GAI alone in AP Physics, but survey responses suggested many students perceived the program as having little or no impact on their performance, indicating a mismatch between objective and perceived effects.
finding.measure: GAI literacy-related survey responses and comparison of GAI-LP vs GAI performance
finding.study_size: n=60 survey respondents; n=171 quantitative participants

paper_profiles.title: A Large Language Model Supported Synthesis of Contemporary Academic Integrity Research Trends
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (research synthesis of academic integrity literature; no direct participant population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what the current research landscape in academic integrity looks like and whether a large language model (ChatGPT/GPT-4) can be used to synthesize that literature. Rather than studying a school intervention or student treatment effect, it uses the LLM as an analytic tool to review academic integrity publications up to April 2023 and identify recurring themes, methods, and geographic patterns.

The study was conducted in January 2024 with human oversight, using ChatGPT Pro to qualitatively analyze its internal knowledge base of journal articles, conference papers, and educational reports. The model produced seven themes and thirteen key focus areas, including plagiarism detection, policy and ethics, cheating behaviors, faculty responses, cross-cultural comparisons, technology in academic integrity, and legal/institutional frameworks. The paper argues that academic integrity research is heavily shaped by technology, that AI-based detection and online proctoring create both opportunities and risks, and that more traditional research and better policy frameworks are still needed.

The main conclusion is that LLM-assisted synthesis may be a useful adjunct for mapping a fast-moving field, but it should not replace conventional scholarship. The paper emphasizes that technology can support detection and analysis, yet also threaten trust, privacy, and the broader culture of integrity. It is best understood as a case study of LLM-enabled literature synthesis and research-trend mapping rather than as an empirical evaluation of educational outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that contemporary academic integrity research is strongly shaped by technology and that institutions are increasingly using policy, detection tools, and operational frameworks to address misconduct. At the same time, it warns that surveillance-oriented tools such as online proctoring may undermine privacy, trust, and the teaching-student relationship, creating both benefits and harms at the institutional level.
finding.measure: Qualitative synthesis of academic integrity research themes, methodologies, and recent developments

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights the use of technology to prevent and detect academic misconduct, including AI-based detection systems and online proctoring, which can improve institutional monitoring and enforcement. However, it also notes that these tools may create implementation burdens and ethical concerns, so the operational benefits are presented as context-dependent rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Qualitative review of detection tools, proctoring, and technology-mediated integrity practices

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Models to the Rescue: Reducing the Complexity in Scientific Workflow Development Using ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether ChatGPT can help domain experts understand, modify, and extend scientific workflows. The authors conducted three user studies in two scientific domains—biomedicine and Earth observation—using real workflow scripts and expert participants to evaluate ChatGPT’s performance on workflow comprehension, tool substitution, and workflow extension.

Study I asked experts to judge ChatGPT’s ability to explain workflow purpose, steps, inputs/outputs, and possible follow-up research questions. ChatGPT performed well on reconstructive tasks such as identifying the general aim and individual steps, but it was weaker on more exploratory reasoning, such as generating valid research questions. The main failure mode was misunderstanding domain-specific abbreviations or workflow-specific context, which could cascade into incorrect explanations.

Study II focused on swapping tools in a bioinformatics workflow, where ChatGPT could often suggest plausible alternative tools and explain differences, but struggled to rewrite executable workflow code correctly. Problems included incorrect handling of tool-specific data formats, linking indexing and alignment steps incorrectly, and occasional hallucinations about tool capabilities. Study III further showed that ChatGPT had substantial difficulty extending partial workflows, especially for more complex, script-heavy Earth observation workflows. Overall, the paper concludes that general-purpose LLMs can support workflow comprehension and tool exploration, but they are not yet reliable for accurate workflow modification or extension without expert correction.

finding.finding_summary: Across three user studies, experts judged ChatGPT to be useful for explaining workflows and suggesting alternative tools, indicating time-saving potential for workflow understanding and tool exploration. For workflow comprehension, domain experts gave high ratings overall (mean ratings around 4.2-4.7/5 in the reported items), and for tool exploration the model provided a fully valid list of 10 alternative tools in the studied cases.
finding.measure: Expert ratings of workflow explanations and tool suggestions; counts of correctly identified tasks/tools and valid alternative tools
finding.study_size: n=4 experts across 5 workflows in Study I; n=1 biomedical expert in Study II; n=2 extension scenarios in Study III

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines whether ChatGPT can help generate and explain scientific workflows, which are a form of scientific reasoning and data-analysis planning. Performance was strong for reconstructing existing workflows but weaker for exploratory reasoning, such as proposing research questions or extending workflows; the authors describe this as reduced performance for more complex, open-ended tasks.
finding.measure: Validity/correctness of generated workflow explanations, research questions, and workflow extensions assessed by domain experts

paper_profiles.title: A Benchmark for Math Misconceptions: Bridging Gaps in Middle School Algebra with AI-Supported Instruction
paper_profiles.population: Middle School (Grades 4-8; especially middle school algebra students)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how AI systems can better identify and respond to middle school students’ algebra misconceptions and common errors. The authors argue that current educational AI tools often lack grounding in authentic student misconceptions and that better diagnosis of wrong answers could support more equitable and responsive mathematics instruction, especially for underserved students.

To address this, the paper introduces a benchmark dataset of 55 algebra misconceptions/common errors with 220 diagnostic examples, assembled from 145 peer-reviewed and related scholarly sources. The benchmark is organized by algebra topic and designed for compatibility with large language models. The authors then evaluate GPT-4-turbo using in-context learning under two settings: (1) random train/test splits across the full dataset and (2) topic-constrained testing. They also collect feedback from five middle-school algebra educators through a survey and interviews to assess clarity, relevance, and potential classroom use.

Results show that GPT-4-turbo performs substantially better when prediction is constrained by topic, reaching 0.753 precision and 0.748 recall per misconception in the topic-constrained setup, and 83.91% accuracy after expert educator relabeling of disputed cases. Performance is uneven across topics, with ratios and proportional thinking being especially difficult. Educators largely confirmed that the misconceptions are common in their classrooms and expressed interest in using the benchmark with AI for diagnosis or teacher training. The paper concludes that topic-constrained testing, educator expertise, and multimodal inputs are important for making AI-supported misconception diagnosis more useful in practice.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that a GPT-4-turbo-based diagnostic approach can identify middle-school algebra misconceptions with moderate to strong accuracy, especially when predictions are constrained by topic. In the full-dataset evaluation the model achieved precision=0.526 and recall=0.529 per misconception (5,500 iterations), while topic-constrained testing improved performance to precision=0.753 and recall=0.748 per misconception (1,100 iterations). After two expert educators reclassified some disputed cases as correct matches, reported accuracy rose to 83.91% in the topic-constrained condition.
finding.measure: Precision/recall for misconception diagnosis; accuracy after expert relabeling
finding.study_size: n=55 misconceptions, 220 diagnostic examples; 5,500 iterations in Experiment 1; 1,100 iterations in Experiment 2

paper_profiles.title: Incorporating Equity into the School Bus Scheduling Problem
paper_profiles.population: K-8 public school districts and students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the school bus scheduling problem (SBSP), a transportation optimization problem in which a district must determine school start times and bus route schedules while minimizing the number of buses required. The authors argue that focusing only on transportation efficiency can create inequitable changes to school start times across schools, which may have unequal effects on students and communities.

To address this, the paper extends a time-indexed integer programming formulation of the SBSP to incorporate equity. The authors define disutility for changing each school’s start time, then develop two equity-centered objectives: a minimax model that minimizes the maximum disutility across schools, and a lexicographic minimax procedure that further improves fairness by sequentially reducing the next-largest disutilities. They also introduce a price-of-fairness analysis to quantify the trade-off between equity and transportation efficiency.

The empirical study uses randomized instances based on a real urban public school district serving grades K-8, with scenarios ranging from 15 schools and 118 routes (morning and afternoon combined) to 30 schools and 200 routes. Results show that the lexicographic minimax approach consistently improves equity relative to both the base efficiency-only model and the basic minimax model, while remaining computationally tractable on the tested instances. The paper concludes that equity should be explicitly modeled in school transportation planning and notes limitations around constant route transition times and scalability to larger instances.

finding.finding_summary: Across randomized instances based on a K-8 district, the optimization models found substantial reductions in the number of buses required while maintaining feasible school start and route schedules. For the 15-school cases, the base model required z*=23 or 24 buses depending on the instance; the authors also report that equity-constrained solutions can be computed efficiently, with nearly all base and minimax problems solved in under 5 minutes. In the larger 30-school cases, the base model required 40-42 buses and the minimax problems remained tractable, though with longer solve times.
finding.measure: Number of buses required; CPU solve time for optimization models
finding.study_size: 15 schools / 59 morning and 59 afternoon routes across 10 instances; 30 schools / 100 morning and 100 afternoon routes across 5 instances

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that explicitly modeling equity changes the resulting school start-time schedules and provides a practical framework for district-level decision-making. In the managerial trade-off analysis, the authors show that districts can achieve meaningful bus savings with bounded start-time changes, and they estimate potential annual savings of over $750,000 for their partner district under some fairness constraints. The paper positions the approach as a policy-relevant planning tool for school districts deciding how to balance transportation budgets, equity, and community acceptance.
finding.measure: Price of fairness; bus savings under maximum start-time-change constraints; schedule composition under equity constraints
finding.study_size: 10 instances in Scenario I-III; 5 instances in Scenario IV

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats start-time changes as a source of disutility that can affect communities and students, and it models these effects as fairness-relevant outcomes. However, it does not directly measure motivation, engagement, self-regulation, or persistence; instead, it infers that more equitable distributions of start-time change may reduce negative community impact and improve acceptability of schedules.
finding.measure: Modeled disutility from changing school start times

paper_profiles.title: Interacting with educational chatbots: A systematic review
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education (mixed; includes mathematics papers but primarily general education, computer science, language, and other fields)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapid growth of educational chatbots and the lack of a focused synthesis of how these systems are designed, deployed, and evaluated in education. The authors aim to compare educational chatbot studies across seven dimensions: field of application, platform, educational role, interaction style, design principles, empirical evidence, and limitations.

The review includes 36 papers published between 2011 and 2021, identified through ACM Digital Library, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and SpringerLink. Across the reviewed studies, chatbots were most often web-based, used mainly in computer science and general education, and typically served as teaching agents or peer agents. Most systems used chatbot-driven, flow-based interactions; a smaller subset used intent-based or user-driven conversational styles.

The review also synthesizes the educational design principles used, such as personalized learning, experiential learning, social dialog, collaborative learning, affective learning, learning by teaching, and scaffolding. Empirical evidence across the included studies was generally positive, with many experiments and evaluation studies reporting improved learning, engagement, satisfaction, or interest, though the review emphasizes that evidence quality and reporting vary widely. The authors conclude that educational chatbots often show promise, but future work should improve dataset quality, usability, design rigor, and consideration of personality/localization effects.

finding.finding_summary: The review includes two mathematics-focused chatbot studies (Rodrigo et al., 2012; Matsuda et al., 2013), and it reports that the mathematics chatbot interventions generally improved learning. For example, the experiment by Matsuda et al. (n=183) found improved learning with p < 0.001, and Rodrigo et al. (n=126) reported no statistically significant difference on learning outcomes (p = 0.65).
finding.measure: Learning outcomes on mathematics tasks / post-test performance

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed chatbot studies, many interventions improved student engagement, subjective satisfaction, interest in learning, or motivation, but at least one longitudinal study found declining interest in interacting with the chatbot over time. Reported experiments include Ruan et al. (n=56, p < 0.0001) with improved engagement, Coronado et al. (n=28, p < 0.001) with improved interest in learning, Tegos et al. (n=56, p = 0.03) with improved subjective satisfaction, and Fryer et al. (n=122, p < 0.05) finding no evidence for sustained engagement.
finding.measure: Engagement, interest in learning, subjective satisfaction, motivation
finding.study_size: multiple studies; e.g., n=56, n=28, n=122

finding.finding_summary: The review reports some evidence that chatbots can support durable skills such as argumentation and collaboration. For example, Wambsganss et al. (n=55, p < 0.05) found improved learning in writing with better formal argumentation quality, and the collaborative-learning studies describe chatbots scaffolded group discussion and pair work, though the review provides limited quantitative detail for these outcomes.
finding.measure: Formal argumentation quality; collaborative learning/discussion quality

paper_profiles.title: Generative artificial intelligence empowers educational reform: current status, issues, and prospects
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review/opinion piece that surveys the development of generative artificial intelligence and discusses its current and prospective uses in education. It focuses on the technical foundations of generative AI, broad educational applications such as intelligent teaching systems, homework grading, tutoring, and speech interaction, and the challenges these tools create for education systems.

The paper is not an empirical student outcome study and does not evaluate a specific intervention with K-12 learners. Instead, it argues that generative AI may support personalized education, intelligent assessment, collaborative education, and virtual teaching, while also raising concerns about opacity, privacy, fairness, and reliability. The authors propose technical and policy responses such as explainable algorithms, encryption, access control, and improved datasets, but provide no quantitative effect estimates.

Because the article is conceptual and based on macro-level logic analysis, its main contribution is framing opportunities and risks rather than measuring learning effects. It discusses examples like Duolingo, Mathway, Knewton, Turnitin, Yixue, and VIPKID to illustrate application types, but it does not present original data on student outcomes or comparative evidence for generative AI tools in K-12 mathematics.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT and large language models in academia: opportunities and challenges
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial examines the emergence of ChatGPT and related large language models (LLMs) and discusses their possible roles in academia. The paper focuses on how LLMs might support academic writing, education, grant writing, programming, and broader research workflows, while also highlighting concerns about hallucinations, bias, plagiarism, access, and computational cost.

Rather than reporting an intervention study, the article offers an expert perspective on the opportunities and limitations of using LLMs in educational settings. In the education section, the authors argue that LLMs could serve as classroom aids, interactive study guides, and tools for immediate feedback, and they suggest that educators will need to adapt pedagogy and assessment if student use becomes widespread. The paper is not an empirical evaluation of a student-facing tool, and it does not present quantitative evidence on learning outcomes, including mathematics outcomes.

The article concludes that LLMs should be embraced cautiously as academic tools, while institutions also develop bias metrics, plagiarism guidance, and safeguards against inaccurate outputs. Overall, it is a conceptual and normative discussion about how academia might incorporate LLMs responsibly, not a comparative study of generative AI effectiveness in K-12 mathematics education.

paper_profiles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence on learner–instructor interaction in online learning
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students and instructors perceive the impact of AI systems on learner–instructor interaction in online learning. Rather than testing a live AI intervention, the authors used an exploratory design with storyboards and Speed Dating interviews to surface perceived benefits and risks of several hypothetical AI uses in online courses.

The study focused on 12 undergraduate students and 11 instructors in higher education during the COVID-19 period. The storyboards represented AI tools for communication, support, and presence, such as an AI teaching assistant, adaptive quizzes, intelligent suggestions, virtual avatars, AI analytics, and facial analytics. Participants discussed how these tools might affect communication, support, connection, agency, responsibility, and surveillance in online learning.

The main conclusion is that AI is seen as a double-edged sword: it may improve the quantity and quality of communication, provide just-in-time personalized support, and strengthen connection, but it also raises concerns about unreliable answers, over-standardization of learning, loss of student agency, and invasive surveillance. The paper argues for design safeguards such as explainability, human-in-the-loop decision-making, and transparent data norms. Because the study is qualitative and perception-based, it does not estimate student achievement effects, but it provides a useful account of social and institutional boundaries for AI in online education.

finding.finding_summary: Participants perceived that AI could improve instructional efficiency by answering repetitive questions, speeding grading and feedback, and freeing instructors to focus on more meaningful communication. Instructors specifically valued AI teaching assistant and grading-assistance scenarios as time-saving tools, but no quantitative effect size was reported because the study was qualitative (n=11 instructors; n=12 students).
finding.measure: Perceived instructor time savings and reduced handling of repetitive questions/faster feedback

finding.finding_summary: Students and instructors expected AI to improve comfort, confidence, connection, and engagement, especially by reducing self-consciousness and enabling just-in-time support. At the same time, participants worried about anxiety, loss of autonomy, and discomfort with surveillance-like features, indicating mixed perceived effects rather than a single positive outcome.
finding.measure: Perceived motivation, engagement, comfort, confidence, and anxiety in online learning interactions

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that AI support could help students with collaboration and planning in group projects, but participants feared over-reliance would reduce exploration, discovery, creativity, and independent problem solving. These are qualitative perceptions from 12 students and 11 instructors, not measured skill outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceived collaboration, creativity, exploration, and independent learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally examines governance-related implications of AI in online learning, especially responsibility, explainability, human-in-the-loop decision-making, and surveillance/privacy norms. Participants saw institutional benefits in scaling support, but also warned that unclear accountability and data collection practices could make AI feel invasive; no quantitative institutional effect was estimated.
finding.measure: Perceived responsibility, explainability, agency, surveillance, and data-governance implications

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Effect of Activity-Based Method of Teaching Mathematics on Nigerian Secondary School Students’ Achievement in Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether an activity-based method of teaching mathematics improves Nigerian secondary school students’ achievement more than the conventional lecture method. The paper was motivated by persistent poor mathematics performance in Nigeria and focused on whether a more hands-on, student-centered approach could address low achievement in topics that students often struggle with.

The intervention compared activity-based instruction with lecture-based instruction in two senior secondary schools in Calabar Metropolis, Cross River State. Ninety-six Senior Secondary II students were assigned to an experimental group (activity-based method, n=48) or a control group (lecture method, n=48) in a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design using intact classes. Achievement was measured with a 20-item Mathematics Test covering circle geometry and construction; the instrument had a reported Cronbach alpha reliability of 0.86.

Results from ANCOVA showed a statistically significant posttest difference favoring the activity-based group after controlling for pretest scores (F=114.461, p<0.001, partial eta squared=0.261). The experimental group’s mean posttest score increased from 27.19 to 51.71, while the control group increased only from 27.39 to 29.56. The author concludes that activity-based teaching improved mathematics achievement and recommends wider adoption and teacher training in this approach.

finding.finding_summary: Students taught with the activity-based method outperformed those taught with the lecture method on a 20-item Mathematics Test covering circle geometry and construction. After controlling for pretest scores, the difference in posttest mathematics performance was statistically significant (F=114.461, p<0.001, partial eta squared=0.261) in favor of the experimental group (n=48) over the control group (n=48).
finding.measure: 20-item Mathematics Test (pretest and posttest) on circle geometry and construction
finding.std_deviation: Experimental pretest SD=9.56, posttest SD=8.84; Control pretest SD=9.73, posttest SD=6.22

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Design Features of an Intelligent Tutoring System for Advanced Mathematics Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates two design features of Xiaomai, an intelligent tutoring system for advanced mathematics: the use of free-response questions with automatic feedback and a metacognitive error-reflection prompt. The authors ask whether these design choices improve students’ learning outcomes and in-system practice performance compared with conventional multiple-choice questions and no reflection.

The study was conducted with 120 Chinese college students who had taken advanced mathematics courses. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions in a 2x2 factorial design: multiple-choice vs. free-response items, and reflection vs. no reflection. Students completed a pretest, a 40-minute practice session in Xiaomai on three knowledge components, and a posttest.

Results showed that multiple-choice practice produced better practice performance and higher posttest scores than free-response practice, although the item-format effect on posttest was only marginally significant after controlling for pretest. Error reflection did not significantly improve either practice performance or learning gains, and it did not interact with prior knowledge. The authors conclude that the current free-response implementation and reflection feature do not enhance Xiaomai’s effectiveness and may need redesign.

finding.finding_summary: The experiment found that item format affected mathematics learning outcomes. Students in the multiple-choice conditions achieved higher posttest scores than those in the free-response conditions after controlling for pretest scores (estimated marginal means 9.21 vs. 7.94), with a marginal item-format effect (F(1,115)=3.72, p=0.06). Pretest-to-posttest effect sizes were reported as large for multiple-choice conditions and small for free-response conditions.
finding.measure: Pretest and posttest mathematics scores; practice performance in Xiaomai

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly tested the metacognitive feature of error reflection, but reflection did not significantly improve posttest scores, practice performance, or learning gains. The authors also found no significant interaction between prior knowledge and reflection, suggesting that the reflection prompt as implemented did not support metacognitive learning in this system.
finding.measure: Posttest scores, pretest-to-posttest learning gain, practice performance, number of attempts, answer correctness, and time per item

paper_profiles.title: Confucius3-Math: A Lightweight High-Performance Reasoning LLM for Chinese K-12 Mathematics Learning
paper_profiles.population: K-12 (Chinese primary, middle, and high school students); also relevant to educators
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents Confucius3-Math, an open-source 14B-parameter reasoning language model optimized for Chinese K-12 mathematics. The authors’ goal is not to run a student outcome experiment, but to develop a low-cost, high-accuracy model that can solve mainstream Chinese K-12 math problems and provide step-by-step solutions suitable for learning contexts.

The model is built through a multi-stage pure reinforcement learning post-training pipeline using a mix of open-source math/reasoning data and proprietary K-12 math questions gathered from the authors’ business operations. Key technical contributions include targeted entropy regularization, policy-specific hardness weighting, and recent sample recovery, which are intended to stabilize training and improve data efficiency. The paper reports benchmark evaluations on several math datasets, including an internal Chinese K-12 benchmark (CK12-MATH), where Confucius3-Math outperforms its base model and several strong open models.

The study is centered on model development and benchmark performance, not direct classroom deployment or student learning measurement. The main conclusion is that strong K-12-focused math reasoning can be achieved at comparatively low training and inference cost, with the model reaching high accuracy on Chinese K-12 math benchmarks and being feasible for practical educational applications. However, the paper does not provide causal evidence that the model improves student outcomes in real educational settings.

finding.finding_summary: Confucius3-Math substantially improved benchmark math performance relative to its base model and several strong baselines. On the internal CK12-MATH benchmark (n=500), it reached 96.24% accuracy, outperforming DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B (82.86%) and DeepSeek-R1 (92.74%), with a reported gain of +13.38 points over its base model. On other math benchmarks it also improved, e.g., GAOKAO-Bench (Math) 98.46% (+11.71) and AIME2025 69.95% (+26.98).
finding.measure: Math benchmark accuracy / pass@1 on CK12-MATH, GAOKAO-Bench (Math), MathBench (K12), CMATH, MATH-500, AIME24, and AIME25
finding.study_size: n=500 for CK12-MATH; other benchmark sizes not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how elementary school students and teachers perceive a generative AI-powered tool designed to support creative mathematical writing. The authors focus on a classroom implementation of a three-step instructional approach—Ask, Represent, and Transform—where students first analyze a math story, then visually represent their thinking, and finally co-create a math story with GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 using prompts and editable drafts.

The study was conducted in six 5th-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools with 79 students and six teachers. Data came from student focus-group interviews, teacher interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations, and were analyzed using inductive/deductive thematic analysis. The paper does not test learning gains with a control group; instead, it identifies perceived benefits and challenges of GenAI-supported math writing.

The main perceived benefits were that GenAI could foster creativity in math, deepen mathematical understanding, promote AI literacy, and improve affective learning outcomes such as interest, curiosity, and ownership. Reported challenges included students’ weak critical evaluation of AI output, difficulty generating coherent stories, the system being perceived as too perfect, lack of formative feedback, reduced autonomy, weak social connectivity, and limited communication modes. Overall, the paper argues that GenAI can support math learning experiences, but only if tools and instruction are intentionally designed to preserve student agency, provide pedagogical feedback, and support inclusive classroom interaction.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived the GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing activities as improving mathematical understanding. The Ask and Represent steps helped students break down story problems, represent mathematical ideas visually, and uncover misconceptions; however, the study reports qualitative perceptions only and does not provide quantitative effect sizes.
finding.measure: Perceptions of mathematical understanding, problem interpretation, knowledge representation, and misconception uncovering from interviews, open-ended surveys, and observations

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that working with GenAI made math learning more interesting, fun, and curiosity-provoking, and it increased learners’ sense of ownership over their work. These outcomes were derived from thematic analysis of interviews and survey responses rather than a measured intervention effect.
finding.measure: Interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership in learning reported by students and teachers

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that GenAI-supported math writing encouraged creative thinking, flexible thinking, and prompt-engineering-related AI literacy, which the authors frame as durable skills. Students described learning to refine prompts, evaluate AI strengths and weaknesses, and iteratively improve their stories, but the study provides no quantitative estimate of skill gains.
finding.measure: Creative thinking, prompt engineering, and AI literacy as perceived through interviews and observations

finding.finding_summary: The activity involved creative mathematical writing, and participants perceived that GenAI supported story drafting, elaboration, and revision. The paper treats writing as part of the math-learning intervention, but it does not report standardized writing outcomes or other quantitative literacy measures.
finding.measure: Creative mathematical writing quality and writing process perceptions

paper_profiles.title: Improving Student Learning with Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring: A Three-Study Quasi-Experimental Investigation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK '24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether hybrid human-AI tutoring can improve mathematics learning for middle school students, especially those from low-income backgrounds. The authors focus on the problem that high-quality human tutoring is effective but too costly and difficult to scale, while math software alone may not sufficiently engage students or direct help to those who need it most.

Across three urban, low-income middle school sites, the study compares student outcomes under software-only conditions versus hybrid tutoring models that combine adaptive math software with remote human tutors. The systems varied by site: IXL, i-Ready, and MATHia were used with different tutoring structures, including round-robin tutor support and a prototype live dashboard intended to guide tutor attention. The study uses quasi-experimental interrupted time-series and mixed-effects modeling to examine learning process outcomes such as time spent, questions answered, skills proficient, lessons passed, and MATHia workspaces completed.

The findings suggest that hybrid human-AI tutoring consistently increased student engagement and intermediate learning outcomes relative to software alone or earlier phases with less intensive support. In Site 1, adding a math teacher and then tutors increased time spent, questions answered, and skills proficient; in Site 2, tutoring increased time on task and lesson completion, especially for students below grade level; in Site 3, increasing tutor availability from roughly 1:8 to 1:4 improved MATHia workspace completion rates. The strongest benefits were generally observed for lower-pretest or lower-performing students, suggesting the model may help reduce inequities in access to effective learning opportunities, though the paper does not directly measure external test-score gains in this study.

finding.finding_summary: Across three quasi-experimental site studies, hybrid human-AI tutoring improved math-related learning process outcomes versus software alone or less intensive support. In Site 1 (n=125), adding a math teacher and then tutors increased time spent, questions answered, and skills proficient; for time spent, tutoring added a positive effect of β=0.202 (95% CI [0.057, 0.347]) and lower-pretest students benefited more (pretest:Tutoring β=-0.212, 95% CI [-0.325, -0.096]). In Site 2 (n=385), tutoring increased lessons passed per week (β=0.244, 95% CI [0.106, 0.381]), especially for students below grade level. In Site 3 (n=75), moving from about 1:8 to 1:4 tutor:student ratios increased MATHia workspace completion by 0.36 per hour (95% CI [0.02, 0.70]).
finding.measure: Math software engagement and learning process measures: time spent, questions answered, skills proficient, lessons passed, MATHia workspaces completed

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly frames part of the intervention effect as increased engagement and usage, which it interprets as improved student participation in the math software. In Site 1, tutoring increased time spent and questions answered; in Site 2, weekly time on task increased from 24 to 33 minutes during the tutoring period. These are engagement-oriented outcomes rather than direct affective measures, but they are central to the paper’s conclusions about how hybrid tutoring affects student learning processes.
finding.measure: Engagement / participation indicators: time spent on task, questions answered, time using software

finding.finding_summary: The study positions hybrid human-AI tutoring as a scalable and lower-cost alternative to traditional high-dosage tutoring, emphasizing tutor-to-student ratios, dashboard-guided allocation of tutor time, and approximate annual costs per student of about $700. It reports that tutor availability changes from 1:8 to 1:4 in Site 3 increased progress, suggesting a potentially more efficient use of tutor time, though the paper does not present a formal efficiency effect size or cost-effectiveness analysis.
finding.measure: Tutor-to-student ratios, cost per student, progress per hour of software use

paper_profiles.title: Do intelligent tutoring systems benefit K-12 students? A meta-analysis and evaluation of heterogeneity of treatment effects in the U.S.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) improve K-12 student achievement in U.S. schools, and under what conditions those effects are larger or smaller. It responds to a gap in prior meta-analyses by focusing specifically on rigorous experimental studies and by examining heterogeneity in effects across study design, student characteristics, intervention features, outcome measures, and school settings.

The authors screened studies published from 2011 to 2021 across multiple databases and retained 18 experimental studies yielding 77 effect sizes from 11 ITS. Across these studies, ITS produced a statistically significant positive overall effect on learning outcomes (Hedges’ g=0.271, SE=0.011, p=0.001). The meta-analysis found that effects were similar across elementary and middle school settings, and across targeted versus non-targeted student groups, but were smaller in rural schools and in studies with longer durations. The analysis also suggested that specific design and implementation features matter: worked-out examples, intervention duration, intervention condition, type of learning outcome, and immediate measurement were among the strongest moderators. Overall, the paper concludes that ITS are beneficial for U.S. K-12 students, but effects vary meaningfully by implementation context and intervention design.

finding.finding_summary: Across 18 experimental studies and 77 effect sizes, ITS improved U.S. K-12 students’ learning outcomes overall, with a meta-analytic effect of g=0.271 (SE=0.011, p=0.001). For mathematics outcomes specifically, the paper reports a positive and statistically significant pooled effect of g=0.253 across 22 effect sizes.
finding.measure: Student learning outcomes / mathematics achievement
finding.study_size: n=77 effect sizes from 18 studies; mathematics subset K=22 effect sizes

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly analyzes motivational and help-seeking-related ITS features, including motivation support, just-in-time hints, on-demand hints, and worked-out examples, as moderators of achievement effects. These supports showed positive pooled effects on learning outcomes, with motivation support g=0.265 (SE=0.027, p=0.024), on-demand hints g=0.316 (SE=0.041, p=0.031), and worked-out examples g=0.324 (SE=0.020, p=0.018); just-in-time hints were positive but not statistically significant.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes associated with ITS supports related to motivation and help-seeking
finding.study_size: K=23 effect sizes for motivation support; K=37 for on-demand hints; K=59 for worked-out examples; K=18 for just-in-time hints
finding.effect_size: g=0.265 (motivation support); g=0.316 (on-demand hints); g=0.324 (worked-out examples); g=0.337 (just-in-time hints, ns)
finding.confidence_interval: motivation support (0.102, 0.428); on-demand hints (0.085, 0.547); worked-out examples (0.176, 0.472); just-in-time hints (-0.147, 0.820)

finding.finding_summary: The study substantively examines worked-out examples and immediate measurement as moderators, which are relevant to problem-solving and metacognitive support in ITS. Worked-out examples had the largest permutation importance in the MetaForest model and a positive pooled effect (g=0.324), indicating that structured problem-solving demonstrations were associated with stronger learning gains; immediate measurement also showed larger effects than delayed measurement.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes and moderator importance for worked-out examples / immediate measurement
finding.study_size: K=59 effect sizes for worked-out examples; K=23 for immediate measurement

paper_profiles.title: Learning From Failure: Integrating Negative Examples when Fine-tuning Large Language Models as Agents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies whether large language models can learn from failed interaction trajectories when fine-tuned as agents. Prior agent-tuning work typically keeps only successful trajectories, discarding failed ones as noise. The authors ask whether these negative examples can be used productively, and if so, how they should be formatted during training.

They propose Negative-Aware Training (NAT), which retains failed trajectories but adds explicit textual markers indicating whether a trajectory is correct or incorrect. The experiments use LLaMA-2-Chat 7B and 13B models fine-tuned on GPT-3.5-generated trajectories for math word problems, multi-hop question answering, and strategic QA. The math datasets include GSM8K, ASDiv, SVAMP, and MultiArith; the QA datasets include HotpotQA and StrategyQA. The paper reports that simply adding negative examples can help, but NAT usually performs better than both positive-only fine-tuning and naïvely mixing positives and negatives.

The strongest results are on mathematical reasoning. On math tasks, NAT improves average accuracy over vanilla positive-only fine-tuning, with gains that are larger in low-data settings and for smaller models. The paper also finds that the quality of negative trajectories matters substantially: high-quality negatives help, while low-quality negatives can hurt performance. Overall, the paper concludes that failed trajectories can be useful training data for agent-style LLM fine-tuning, especially when the training signal distinguishes positive from negative examples and when negative data is of reasonably high quality.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that negative-aware training (NAT) improves math word problem performance over both positive-only fine-tuning and naïve inclusion of negative examples. For LLaMA-2-7B with 2k positive examples, average accuracy increased from 55.90 (Vanilla) to 64.64 (NAT), an 8.74-point gain; with 5k positives, accuracy rose from 64.17 to 67.42. Gains were also seen on individual datasets such as GSM8K, ASDiv, SVAMP, and MultiArith.
finding.measure: Accuracy on GSM8K, ASDiv, SVAMP, and MultiArith math word problem benchmarks
finding.study_size: varies by setting; 2k or 5k positive examples plus up to 10k negative examples

paper_profiles.title: Search for stable hadronising squarks and gluinos with the ATLAS experiment at the LHC
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports a particle physics search, not an education study. The ATLAS Collaboration searched for slow-moving, long-lived massive charged particles (R-hadrons) produced in proton-proton collisions at 30 TeV at the LHC, using 34 pb1 of data collected with the ATLAS detector. The analysis focused on identifying candidate events through measurements of ionisation energy loss in the pixel detector and time-of-flight in the tile calorimeter, which together allowed reconstruction of an estimated particle mass.

The study compared observed event yields with data-driven background estimates and signal simulations for gluino-, stop-, and sbottom-based R-hadrons.
