No significant excess over Standard Model expectations was observed. The paper therefore set 95% confidence-level lower mass limits on stable sbottoms, stops, and gluinos, with the most conservative limits reported as 294 GeV, 309 GeV, and 562 GeV, respectively.

The work is a direct search in high-energy collider data and uses simulation, detector calibration, and statistical limit setting, but it does not involve students, educators, schools, or any educational intervention. Because it is unrelated to AI in education and K-12 mathematics outcomes, no education-relevant outcome assignments apply.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI and Its Impact on Personalized Intelligent Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI, especially large language models such as GPT-4, can be integrated into intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) to support personalized learning. Rather than testing a specific deployed intervention, it surveys and synthesizes recent work on applications including automated question generation, personalized feedback, and interactive dialogue systems, with an emphasis on how these capabilities might improve instructional adaptation.

The paper focuses on educational technology in general and does not report a specific K-12 sample, experimental setting, or student outcome dataset. It discusses potential benefits such as more adaptive questioning, more context-specific feedback, and more conversational support, while also highlighting risks related to pedagogical accuracy, bias, equity, and sustained learner engagement. The conclusion is forward-looking: generative AI may make ITS more effective and responsive, but robust validation, oversight, and ethical governance are needed before such systems can be relied on in education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI-based ITS may improve learner engagement and motivation by delivering more personalized, interactive, and context-relevant support. However, this is a conceptual claim rather than a tested result; no effect size, sample, or quantified engagement outcome is reported.
finding.measure: learner engagement, motivation

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that generative AI can increase the efficiency of ITS by automating question generation and producing personalized feedback at scale. These productivity benefits are described qualitatively, without empirical measurement of time savings, teacher workload, or implementation efficiency.
finding.measure: content generation and feedback automation efficiency

paper_profiles.title: AI and the EU Digital Markets Act: Addressing the Risks of Bigness in Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 202
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether the European Union’s Digital Markets Act (DMA) is sufficient to address concentration and gatekeeping risks in generative AI markets. The authors argue that, although the DMA was designed for established digital platform services, its logic should extend to generative AI because a small number of firms may gain entrenched control over access, data, computing power, and downstream services.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or a K-12 population. Instead, it analyzes the structure of generative AI markets and the legal provisions of the DMA, proposing that certain generative AI systems be designated as core platform services and that some developers be treated as gatekeepers. The discussion focuses on how existing DMA obligations could curb unfair practices, prevent data and service tying, and preserve contestability and diversity in the generative AI ecosystem.

The article’s conclusions are normative and policy-oriented: it contends that without regulatory action, a few firms are likely to consolidate durable advantages in generative AI. The authors recommend amending the DMA so that generative AI services are explicitly covered, thereby supporting fairness, innovation, and user choice in AI markets.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that extending the EU Digital Markets Act to generative AI would improve contestability, fairness, and diversity in AI markets by limiting gatekeeping power and data/service tying. This is a policy analysis rather than an empirical impact study; no sample, effect size, or statistical estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Policy and legal analysis of DMA applicability to generative AI markets

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging Affect Transfer Learning for Behavior Prediction in an Intelligent Tutoring System
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of predicting student problem-solving outcomes in an intelligent tutoring system from video of the learner’s face and upper-body gestures. The authors argue that accurate prediction of outcomes such as solved, skipped, or solved-with-hint could enable real-time interventions like hints or encouragement, with the goal of improving learning in an online math tutor.

The proposed approach, ATL-BP, combines a deep affect representation transferred from the AffectNet facial-expression dataset with traditional facial-analysis features from OpenFace and a two-layer LSTM to model the temporal structure of student videos. The main evaluation uses the MathSpring and MathSpringSP+ datasets, which contain webcam videos of college students solving math problems in the MathSpring intelligent tutoring system; a smaller children’s dataset is also used for follow-up experiments.

Across five-fold cross-validation on random splits, ATL-BP with affect embeddings outperforms prior work by improving mean F-score from 0.228 to 0.330 and accuracy from 46.2% to 60.2% on MathSpringSP+, and from 0.270 to 0.362 mean F-score and 54.0% to 61.0% accuracy on the original MathSpringSP dataset. In the more challenging leave-users-out setting, user personalization further improves performance, with the best personalized model reaching 0.308 mean F-score and 55.1% accuracy. The paper concludes that affect transfer learning plus personalization can improve behavior prediction for math tutoring systems, but the work evaluates prediction quality rather than direct student learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies prediction of math problem outcomes in an intelligent tutoring system, not direct math test performance. On MathSpringSP+ (n=54 students, 2,749 problems), ATL-BP with affect embedding achieved 60.2% accuracy and mean F-score 0.330, improving over Joshi et al. [22] (46.2% accuracy, F-score 0.228). On the original MathSpringSP dataset, the same model reached 61.0% accuracy and mean F-score 0.362 versus 54.0% and 0.270 for the prior method.
finding.measure: Math problem outcome classification in the MathSpring intelligent tutoring system (7 classes: attempted, give up, guess, not read, solved with hint, skip, solved on first attempt)

paper_profiles.title: Randomized co-training: from cortical neurons to machine learning and back again
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how learning systems can exploit abundant unlabeled data to improve performance when labeled data are scarce. Framed as a neuroscience-to-machine-learning translation, it argues that cortical learning may benefit from randomized co-training: using multiple correlated but distinct views of the same input, with randomization supplying those views when natural ones are unavailable.

The paper develops a theoretical and algorithmic bridge from discretized neuronal plasticity to semi-supervised learning. It first derives selective linear regression and a multi-view neuronal co-optimization objective from simplified models of synapses and neuromodulation, then maps these ideas to Correlated Nystr�f6m Views (XNV), a semi-supervised regression algorithm using random Nystr�f6m features and a canonical correlation analysis penalty.

The empirical portion reports benchmark results on 18 non-educational datasets, where XNV is described as faster than prior semi-supervised methods and generally lower error than kernel ridge regression and a randomized SSSL baseline. However, the paper is not a K-12 education study, does not involve students or classrooms, and does not evaluate mathematics interventions or educational outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Contextualizing Problems to Student Interests at Scale in Intelligent Tutoring System Using Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a large language model, specifically GPT-4, can be used to contextualize existing intelligent tutoring system problems to student interests at scale. The motivating problem is that teachers can improve engagement and learning by personalizing problem contexts, but doing so manually is time-consuming and difficult to scale.

The authors explore a prompt-engineering workflow inside the CTAT intelligent tutoring system, where an instructor or author can enter an interest and have GPT-4 rewrite the contextual cover story of an existing problem while preserving the original values, difficulty, and solution structure. They test this approach on several algebra problem sets in TutorShop and report that the model can generate meaningful contextualizations for many interests, though geometry and diagram-dependent problems remain challenging.

The paper is primarily a systems/feasibility paper rather than a student outcome study. It does not present learner-level experimental evidence of improved achievement or engagement; instead, it concludes that LLMs may support scalable contextualization for authoring and calls for future systematic studies to measure effects on learning outcomes, efficiency, and accuracy.

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents a GPT-4-based workflow intended to reduce the manual effort required for contextualizing problems to student interests in CTAT. The authors argue that this approach can support scalable mass production of individualized problem contexts for teachers and instructional designers, but they do not report quantitative productivity metrics or a controlled evaluation of efficiency gains.
finding.measure: authoring workflow feasibility and scalability for contextualizing problems

finding.finding_summary: The paper is motivated by the claim that interest-based contextualization can increase student engagement, and the authors designed the system specifically to align problems with learner interests. However, engagement was not directly measured in this study, so the evidence is limited to the intended function and prior literature rather than an empirical student-level effect.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether teachers should remain “in the loop” when using generative AI to personalize middle school mathematics tasks. The authors focus on context personalization: adapting existing Illustrative Mathematics problems to match students’ interests, especially popular culture references, and they examine both the teacher prompting process and students’ reactions to the personalized problems.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers from six U.S. schools used ChatGPT (GPT-4o) to modify 143 problems across two curriculum units: Unit 4 on proportional relationships and percentages, and Unit 6 on expressions, equations, and inequalities. The study combined chat log analysis, classroom video/audio transcripts, and student surveys (closed-ended ratings and open-ended feedback) from 521 students. Teachers’ prompts were coded for how they handled grain size, depth, and ownership in personalization; students reported whether problems were interesting and whether they matched their interests.

The main findings were that teachers typically personalized at a broad grain size, while students preferred more specific, finer-grained references to their own interests. Teachers spent substantial time refining realism, numeric plausibility, and readability, and the process was not clearly time-efficient: creating a problem took about 4 minutes on average, and efficiency did not improve much over time. Student ratings were low overall, but personalization was somewhat better received when teachers used an intermediate number of prompts (about 3-5 prompts per problem), and problems created in the second unit received higher ratings than those in the first unit. The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop personalization supports teacher learning and oversight, but it is labor-intensive and may not align well with students’ desire for highly specific personalization.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers used ChatGPT to personalize 143 middle school mathematics problems, but the study did not measure student math achievement directly. The paper reports that student ratings of the personalized math problems’ interestingness and closeness to interests were low overall (interestingness M=2.46/5; closeness M=2.53/5), though ratings improved in Unit 6 compared with Unit 4 (interestingness 2.27 to 2.56; closeness 2.28 to 2.66) and were highest when teachers used 3-5 prompts per problem (B=0.240, SE=0.085, p=0.0073).
finding.measure: Student ratings of personalized mathematics problems’ interestingness and closeness to interests; teacher prompting and time spent creating math problems
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.24 (interestingness), SD=1.28 (closeness); problem-creation time SD=165.7 seconds

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that personalized math tasks were associated with students’ reported interest, a motivational outcome, although ratings were modest overall. Students gave more positive feedback when problems matched their preferred specific popular culture references, and average ratings increased from Unit 4 to Unit 6 (interestingness: 2.27 to 2.56; closeness: 2.28 to 2.66).
finding.measure: Student self-reported interest/interestingness and perceived closeness of math problems to their interests

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined whether teacher-in-the-loop personalization saved time, and it found it did not appear to become efficient. Teachers used 558 prompts to create 143 problems (3.2 prompts/problem) and spent an average of 246 seconds per problem (about 4 minutes), with substantial variation across teachers; in Unit 6, teachers actually used more prompts and spent more time than in Unit 4 (prompts: B=1.26, SE=0.41, p=0.0025; time: B=70.4 seconds, SE=29.6, p=0.0189).
finding.measure: Number of prompts per problem and time spent per problem creating personalized tasks
finding.effect_size: B=1.26 (prompts increase from Unit 4 to Unit 6); B=70.4 seconds (time increase from Unit 4 to Unit 6)

finding.finding_summary: The paper indirectly addresses teacher/LLM prompting as a form of problem-solving and iteration, but it does not measure durable skills in students. The authors report that teachers improved in crafting personalized problems over time and that moderate prompting (3-5 prompts) was associated with better student ratings, suggesting some benefits for iterative refinement and task design, though this is not a direct student durable-skills outcome.
finding.measure: Teacher prompting strategies and iterative refinement of problem design

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education (broad, not a single studied sample)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than testing a specific intervention, the authors synthesize early examples and prior work to argue that LLMs may support learning, teaching, assessment, and educational content generation, while also introducing concerns around bias, privacy, misuse, overreliance, and integrity.

The paper discusses potential applications across learner and teacher perspectives, including personalized feedback, quiz generation, tutoring support, writing assistance, and automated assessment. It also highlights use cases in mathematics education such as generating math word problems and step-by-step explanations, but these are framed as possibilities and prior examples rather than rigorously evaluated K-12 student interventions.

Overall, the authors conclude that LLMs have promising educational potential if integrated responsibly, with strong human oversight, ethical safeguards, and attention to transparency, fairness, and access. The paper is primarily a conceptual and agenda-setting contribution that outlines research directions and mitigation strategies rather than presenting empirical results.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not report a direct empirical effect of ChatGPT or any other LLM on K-12 mathematics outcomes. It only notes, in a general discussion of opportunities, that language models could generate practice problems, explanations, and math word problems to support mathematics learning.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper conceptually argues that LLMs may support critical thinking, problem-solving, and fact-checking, but it does not present direct quantitative evidence. The discussion is framed as a recommendation for responsible classroom use rather than a measured outcome study.
finding.measure: critical thinking, problem-solving, fact-checking (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating quiz generation, personalized feedback, and some assessment tasks such as grading textual responses. These claims are supported only by cited prior studies and examples, not by new empirical results in this paper.
finding.measure: teacher workload / grading effort / content-generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: A central contribution of the paper is its discussion of institutional, ethical, and governance implications of LLM adoption in education, including privacy, bias, copyright, sustainability, and equitable access. These are not measured outcomes, but they are substantively analyzed as system-level risks and requirements for adoption.
finding.measure: policy, governance, privacy, fairness, sustainability, access

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT-generated help produces learning gains equivalent to human tutor-authored help on mathematics skills
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether ChatGPT-generated worked-solution hints can support mathematics learning as effectively as human tutor-authored hints. The authors focus on a direct comparison between AI-generated help, human-authored help, and a no-hint control, asking both whether ChatGPT’s outputs are educationally effective and how often they contain errors or hallucinations.

The intervention was implemented in an online Open Adaptive Tutor environment using OpenStax-derived problems in four math subjects: Elementary Algebra, Intermediate Algebra, College Algebra, and Statistics. Mechanical Turk participants (n=274 after exclusions) were randomly assigned to one of three hint conditions and one of four subject areas in a 3 x 4 design. Learning was measured with repeated pre- and post-tests, while hint quality was separately checked by raters and also tested with a self-consistency mitigation procedure.

Results showed that the ChatGPT condition produced statistically significant pre-to-post learning gains overall (17%) relative to no help (1.85%), and these gains were not statistically significantly different from human tutor-authored hints (11.62%). Time-on-task was higher in both hint conditions than in the control, but ChatGPT and human hints did not differ significantly on time. A major limitation was that raw ChatGPT hints failed quality checks on 32% of problems; self-consistency reduced error rates to near zero in algebra and 13% in statistics. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can generate effective math help, but supervision or error mitigation is needed before deploying raw output directly to students.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized 3 x 4 study (n=274 analyzed), ChatGPT-generated worked-solution hints produced statistically significant math learning gains compared with a no-hint control. Overall pre-test to post-test performance increased from 43.51% to 60.52% in the ChatGPT condition (17.00% gain), and the condition was significantly better than control in post-hoc comparisons (p=0.011), while not differing significantly from human tutor-authored hints (p=0.416).
finding.measure: Repeated mathematics pre-test and post-test scores on OpenStax-derived problems in Elementary Algebra, Intermediate Algebra, College Algebra, and Statistics

finding.finding_summary: The paper also evaluates efficiency-related aspects of generating instructional content, finding that ChatGPT-produced hints were much faster to create than human tutor-authored help, while maintaining comparable learning effectiveness. The authors note that ChatGPT hints were produced in roughly 1/20th the time required for human-authored hints, although exact authoring time for human hints was not fully reported in the original system.
finding.measure: Hint authoring time / content-generation time and time-on-task during learner sessions

paper_profiles.title: How Does ChatGPT Perform on the United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE)? The Implications of Large Language Models for Medical Education and Knowledge Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates ChatGPT’s performance on multiple-choice medical knowledge questions drawn from USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 content. The authors ask whether a large language model can answer licensure-style questions accurately enough to be useful as a medical education tool, and whether its responses are coherent and interpretable.

The study compares ChatGPT with GPT-3 and InstructGPT on four text-only question sets: AMBOSS Step 1 and Step 2 questions, and NBME free Step 1 and Step 2 questions. ChatGPT’s accuracy ranged from 42% to 64.4% depending on dataset, outperforming the two comparator models on all sets. Performance declined as AMBOSS question difficulty increased for Step 1 without the Attending Tip (P=.01). In qualitative analysis, ChatGPT always gave a logical explanation, used internal question information in nearly all responses, and more often included external information in correct than incorrect answers. The authors conclude that ChatGPT shows promise as an interactive educational support tool, though they note that it was not studied as a live student-facing intervention and the work is limited to benchmark question answering rather than learning outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative, practice-oriented discussion of ChatGPT and its implications for higher education assessment, teaching, and learning. The authors review early literature on GPT-3/ChatGPT, describe the system’s functionality, and report their own informal experimentation with the tool across a few prompts, including technical explanations, essay writing, and Chinese composition generation.

The paper is not an intervention study and does not evaluate student learning outcomes experimentally. Instead, it argues that ChatGPT is capable of producing fluent responses, can support some student-facing and teacher-facing uses, but is limited in factual reliability, higher-order reasoning, and non-English language performance. The authors conclude that ChatGPT is likely to disrupt conventional assessment practices and that institutions should adapt assessment design, policy, and pedagogical strategies rather than simply ban the tool.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT can rapidly generate essays and clear explanations, but its writing quality was shallow, generic, and sometimes inaccurate. In the authors' own testing, it produced an approximately 500-word essay in about 120 seconds instead of the requested 2000 words and failed to provide proper in-text citations; the authors also note it generated a grammatically weak Chinese composition.
finding.measure: Informal prompt-based writing output quality (essay drafting, citation use, and Chinese composition quality)

finding.finding_summary: In one prompt, ChatGPT was able to explain mean, standard deviation, and z-scores clearly and provide a real-world example with step-by-step calculations. The paper treats this as evidence that the tool can support conceptual and procedural explanations in mathematics/statistics, although no quantitative learning effect was measured.
finding.measure: Quality of explanations for statistical concepts (mean, standard deviation, z-scores) and worked example generation

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that ChatGPT may support experimentation, problem-solving, and collaborative learning, but they also note that it is weak at higher-order thinking tasks that require critical and analytical reasoning. Their own examples suggest the tool can assist idea generation and scenario exploration, yet it does not demonstrate deep understanding.
finding.measure: Prompt-based demonstrations of higher-order thinking support and analytical writing capability

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents ChatGPT as a fast tool for generating explanations and draft text, often within 60-120 seconds, and suggests it may reduce workload for students and potentially teachers. The authors also note that it can aid rapid brainstorming and drafting, though its usefulness is constrained by errors, character limits, and unreliable factual accuracy.
finding.measure: Perceived speed and productivity in generating text, explanations, and drafts

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT may force institutions to rethink assessment, plagiarism detection, and academic policy, and it may eventually be incorporated into mainstream educational software ecosystems. At the same time, the authors emphasize risks for integrity, governance, and the credibility of traditional assessment methods, concluding that institutional adaptation is necessary.
finding.measure: Implications for assessment policy, plagiarism detection, and institutional responses to AI

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing healthcare: the role of artificial intelligence in clinical practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review surveys the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical practice, with emphasis on how machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and large language models are being applied across healthcare workflows. The paper is organized around major application areas: diagnostics, genomic medicine, treatment planning, dose optimization, population health management, drug information support, virtual health assistance, mental health support, patient education, and healthcare system governance.

The article does not test a new intervention on patients directly; instead, it synthesizes indexed literature to describe potential benefits, limitations, and implementation challenges of AI in healthcare. The population/context is adult healthcare practice and medical education rather than K-12 schooling. Across the reviewed examples, the authors conclude that AI can improve accuracy, efficiency, and decision support, but responsible adoption requires attention to data quality, privacy, bias, human oversight, and regulatory frameworks.

Although the review briefly notes that intelligent tutoring systems have improved learning outcomes in math and science, this is not the paper’s substantive focus and no K-12 educational intervention is evaluated. The main contribution is a broad conceptual and narrative overview of AI in clinical practice and the associated ethical and operational considerations.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI can improve workflow efficiency, reduce costs, and save time in healthcare settings by automating tasks, supporting triage, and speeding up diagnostic and laboratory processes. No single pooled effect size is reported because this is a narrative review, but the paper repeatedly cites examples such as improved diagnostic throughput, faster laboratory turnaround, and reduced clinician workload.
finding.measure: Workflow efficiency, turnaround time, workload, cost, and time savings in clinical settings

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI can shape institutional practice through guideline development, regulatory frameworks, population health management, and healthcare system-level decision support. It highlights that AI may influence policy and governance by enabling real-time evidence synthesis, but stresses that human oversight, transparency, privacy protections, and regulation are necessary.
finding.measure: Guideline development, regulatory frameworks, population health management, and institutional decision-making

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual catchword article that introduces generative AI, explains its mathematical foundations, and systematizes it at the model, system, and application levels. Rather than evaluating a specific educational intervention, it surveys how generative AI systems such as GPT-style language models, diffusion models, and RLHF-based conversational agents work and what kinds of socio-technical changes they may bring about across business and information systems contexts.

The article focuses on limitations of current generative AI, including incorrect outputs, bias and fairness issues, copyright concerns, and environmental costs. It then outlines a research agenda for the Business & Information Systems Engineering community across areas such as process management, decision analytics, digital leadership, economics of information systems, enterprise engineering, human-computer interaction, and information systems engineering. Education is mentioned as one application area where conversational agents may reshape teaching and assessment, but the paper does not present a K-12 study, student sample, or quantitative evaluation.

For education, the authors argue that generative AI may support digital teaching assistants, supplemental instructional materials, and new guidance for learners on prompt engineering and output verification. These are forward-looking implications rather than empirical findings. The paper is therefore best understood as a conceptual overview and agenda-setting piece, not as a comparative or outcomes-focused education study.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI will reshape educational governance, assessment practices, and instructional design, but it does not test any educational policy or institutional intervention empirically. Its claims are conceptual and future-oriented, describing potential shifts such as adapted examinations, digital teaching assistants, and the need for guidelines on verification and prompt use.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary school students and teachers perceive a generative AI-powered learning tool designed to support creative mathematical writing. The central question is not whether the tool improves test scores, but how students and teachers experience its use during math story-writing activities, including perceived benefits, challenges, and design implications.

The study implemented a three-step instructional sequence—Ask, Represent, Transform—in six fifth-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools. Students worked with a multimodal GenAI system built with GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 to create and revise culturally relevant math stories, while teachers and researchers observed the classrooms. After four class periods, 10 students and 6 teachers were interviewed, and their responses were triangulated with open-ended survey items and observation notes.

Using inductive/deductive thematic analysis, the authors identified six themes: four benefits and two challenge categories. Reported benefits included fostering creativity in math, supporting mathematical understanding, promoting AI literacy, and improving affective outcomes such as interest, curiosity, and ownership. Challenges included limited student critical evaluation, difficulty generating coherent stories, lack of adaptive pedagogical feedback, reduced autonomy, weak social connection support, and limited communication modes. The paper concludes that GenAI can support creative math writing and learning experiences, but effective educational use requires careful instructional and interface design rather than simply maximizing AI performance.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers reported that the GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing activities helped students better understand mathematical problems, represent mathematical knowledge, and uncover misconceptions. The paper is qualitative and does not report effect sizes, but it describes the 79-student classroom implementation as supporting mathematical understanding through the Ask, Represent, and Transform sequence.
finding.measure: Perceived mathematical understanding, problem understanding, mathematical knowledge representation, and misconception detection from interviews, surveys, and observations

finding.finding_summary: The intervention centered on creative mathematical writing and story generation, and participants reported that the GenAI tool supported drafting, revising, and making stories more original and coherent. The paper presents this as improved creative writing support rather than a quantitative literacy outcome; no effect sizes or test scores are reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions of creative mathematical writing quality, drafting, revising, and story development

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived that the GenAI-supported activity increased interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning. Participants described the math-writing process as fun, motivating, and engaging, but these are interview-based perceptions rather than measured gains, so no quantitative effect estimates are reported.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and sense of ownership in learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that working with GenAI promoted divergent and convergent thinking, flexible thinking, and prompt engineering strategies, all framed as aspects of creativity and AI literacy. Students reportedly learned to give more specific prompts, evaluate AI strengths and weaknesses, and refine ideas through iterative interaction, but the study is qualitative and does not provide numerical outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceived divergent/convergent thinking, flexible thinking, prompt engineering, and critical evaluation of AI outputs

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that the findings have design implications for GenAI tools, curriculum, and classroom practice, especially regarding feedback, autonomy, accessibility, and social interaction. However, the paper does not evaluate policy or institutional outcomes directly; the impact is conceptual and design-oriented rather than measured.
finding.measure: Design implications for GenAI-powered learning technologies and classroom implementation

paper_profiles.title: Improving Student Learning with Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring: A Three-Study Quasi-Experimental Investigation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK '24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a hybrid human-AI tutoring model can improve middle-school mathematics learning compared with math software alone. The motivating problem is that high-dosage human tutoring is effective but expensive and difficult to scale, while AI-enabled software often lacks the motivational and relational support some students need to engage productively.

Across three quasi-experimental studies in urban, low-income U.S. middle schools, the authors examine different implementations of hybrid human-AI tutoring during the school day. Students used different math platforms (IXL, i-Ready, and MATHia), with human tutors providing support remotely; in some sites a math teacher was also present, and in one site a live tutor dashboard guided tutor attention. The designs compare periods or groups with software only versus software plus teacher support versus software plus teacher and remote tutoring, using learning-process data such as time spent, questions answered, skills proficient, lessons passed, and workspaces completed.

The main conclusion is that hybrid human-AI tutoring generally increased student engagement and intermediate learning outcomes, especially for lower-pretest or below-grade-level students. In Site 1, adding a math teacher and then tutoring increased time spent, questions answered, and skills proficient, with tutoring showing a positive effect on time spent (β=0.202, 95% CI [0.057, 0.347]). In Site 2, tutoring increased average time on task from 24 to 33 minutes per week and increased lessons passed more for students below grade level; in Site 3, improving tutor access from a 1:8 to 1:4 ratio increased MATHia progress by 0.36 workspaces per hour (95% CI [0.02, 0.70]). The paper argues that human-AI tutoring can be a scalable and lower-cost alternative to human-only tutoring, though it emphasizes that the evidence is preliminary and quasi-experimental.

finding.finding_summary: Across three quasi-experimental site studies in low-income middle schools, hybrid human-AI tutoring improved intermediate math learning indicators relative to software-only conditions. In Site 1, tutoring increased IXL time spent (β=0.202, 95% CI [0.057, 0.347]) and was associated with more skills proficient; in Site 2, tutoring increased lessons passed especially for students below grade level; in Site 3, a higher tutor ratio improved MATHia progress by 0.36 workspaces per hour (95% CI [0.02, 0.70]).
finding.measure: IXL time spent, questions answered, skills proficient; i-Ready lessons passed and time on task; MATHia workspaces completed per hour

finding.finding_summary: The intervention increased student engagement and usage, which the authors treat as an important learning-process outcome. In Site 2, average time on task rose from 24 to 33 minutes per week during tutoring, and in Site 1 tutoring significantly increased time spent using IXL (β=0.202), indicating stronger participation and persistence in the math software.
finding.measure: Time spent on task / engagement with math software

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames hybrid human-AI tutoring as a scalable, lower-cost model that increases tutor reach and improves use of tutor time via dashboards and tutor-student ratios. Although not a direct productivity experiment, Site 3 suggests that changing tutor access from 1:8 to 1:4 improved student progress, implying more efficient allocation of tutor effort, and the authors estimate marginal costs of about $700 per student annually.
finding.measure: Tutor-to-student ratio, cost per student, progress per hour

paper_profiles.title: Automated Feedback in Math Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLMs for Open-Ended Responses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can improve automated scoring and feedback generation for open-ended middle-school mathematics responses. The authors compare three approaches: a fine-tuned Mistral-based model (GOAT), a prior state-of-the-art sentence-embedding method (SBERT-Canberra), and GPT-4 used in a zero-shot prompting setup.

The study uses a dataset of 50 open-response math problems from an online learning platform, each with 100 student responses, teacher scores, and teacher-written feedback. Models are trained on 4,000 responses and evaluated on 1,000 held-out responses for scoring, while feedback quality is judged by two teachers on a sample of 100 responses using criteria for accuracy, relevance, motivation, and preferred model. The paper is not a student learning-outcomes experiment; it evaluates model performance against teacher judgments.

For scoring, GOAT performs best across all reported metrics (AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, Kappa=0.422), outperforming SBERT-Canberra (AUC=0.662, RMSE=1.364, Kappa=0.362) and GPT-4 (AUC=0.639, RMSE=1.160, Kappa=0.266). For feedback generation, GPT-4 is preferred by teachers and is judged most accurate and relevant (86% consensus accuracy, 91% consensus relevance), although GOAT is a substantial improvement over SBERT on these same measures. The authors conclude that fine-tuned open-source LLMs can improve automated scoring, but GPT-4 currently produces the strongest teacher-preferred feedback.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly evaluates automated scoring of middle-school open-ended math responses. GOAT outperformed SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4 on teacher-score prediction, with AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, and Kappa=0.422 on n=1,000 test responses; SBERT had AUC=0.662, RMSE=1.364, Kappa=0.362, and GPT-4 had AUC=0.639, RMSE=1.160, Kappa=0.266. These are model-prediction outcomes rather than student achievement gains.
finding.measure: Predicted teacher scores on open-ended math responses (AUC, RMSE, Cohen’s Kappa against teacher ratings)

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively evaluates automated scoring and automated feedback as tools to reduce teacher workload in grading open-ended math responses. The authors frame GOAT and SBERT-Canberra as systems that can support teachers with scoring and feedback generation, and report that GPT-4 and GOAT can produce usable feedback, with GOAT improving over SBERT on scoring and feedback quality in several dimensions.
finding.measure: Model utility for automated scoring and feedback generation; teacher preference and rubric-based feedback judgments
finding.study_size: n=50 problems, n=4,000 training responses, n=1,000 test responses; 2 teacher raters for feedback evaluation

paper_profiles.title: AI tutoring can safely and effectively support students: An exploratory RCT in UK classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a generative AI tutor can safely and effectively support secondary students’ mathematics learning in real classrooms. The motivation is the longstanding challenge that one-to-one tutoring is highly effective but difficult to scale, and the authors test whether a pedagogy-fine-tuned model, LearnLM, can help expand access to individualized support.

The study was an exploratory classroom RCT conducted over seven weeks in five UK secondary schools with 165 Year 9–10 students (ages 13–15). Students were randomized to either static, pre-written hints or interactive tutoring; within the tutoring condition, sessions were randomized to a human tutor alone or a human tutor supervising LearnLM. The AI tutor drafted Socratic responses that expert tutors could approve, edit, or rewrite before sending, allowing the researchers to evaluate both safety/quality of the model’s drafts and its learning effects relative to human tutoring and static hints.

Results suggest LearnLM was a reliable instructional aid when supervised: tutors approved most drafted messages with no or minimal edits, and a review found zero harmful content and only five factual errors out of 3,617 messages. On immediate learning outcomes, LearnLM performed about as well as human tutors and substantially better than static hints for mistake remediation and misconception resolution. On the key transfer outcome, students supported by LearnLM were more likely to solve a novel problem on the next topic than students tutored by humans alone (66.2% vs. 60.7%, a 5.5 percentage-point advantage; 95% credible interval [–1.4, +12.4]). The paper concludes that responsibly supervised genAI tutoring may be a promising scalable supplement to human tutoring, especially for mathematics.

finding.finding_summary: The trial found that supervised LearnLM tutoring improved mathematics learning outcomes in a secondary-school context. Students tutored by LearnLM were 5.5 percentage points more likely than those tutored by human tutors alone to solve a novel problem on the next study unit (66.2% vs. 60.7%; 95% credible interval [–1.4%, +12.4%]).
finding.measure: Performance on Eedi mathematics study units, especially knowledge transfer to the first question of the next unit after tutoring

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.population: K-12 mathematics educators/teachers (elementary, middle, and high school contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether K-12 mathematics educators prefer lesson plans generated by generative AI systems or by human curriculum designers, and which lesson-plan components are most affected by those preferences. The study is motivated by the growing use of GenAI tools for lesson planning and the lack of rigorous comparative evidence about how teacher-created and AI-created materials are perceived in practice.

The authors conducted a controlled, blind pairwise preference study in which 20 experienced K-12 mathematics educators evaluated 529 lesson-plan pairs, each presented as anonymized versions of human-created plans, customized GPT-4 outputs, or fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b outputs. Educators rated plans on warm-up activities, main tasks, cool-down activities, and overall quality, and also left written comments that were analyzed using topic modeling and manual thematic coding. The quantitative results showed that human-authored plans were generally preferred for warm-up, main task, and overall quality, especially in elementary grades, while GenAI plans were more competitive in cool-down activities and became more competitive at higher grade levels, particularly in middle and high school. The qualitative findings suggest that educators valued human plans for differentiation, student discourse, scaffolding, and inclusive supports, whereas GenAI was seen as stronger in structure and concise lesson wrapping.

Overall, the paper concludes that GenAI should be viewed as a support tool for lesson planning rather than a replacement for educator expertise. It argues for human-AI collaboration and domain-specific tuning, especially if AI tools are to better align with pedagogical expectations across grade levels and instructional components.

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests GenAI can reduce educator workload by assisting with lesson planning, and the authors explicitly frame the tools as potentially lowering the cognitive and time burden on teachers. However, the study did not measure actual time savings or workload reduction directly; it measured educator preferences for lesson plans generated by human designers, customized GPT-4, and fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b across 529 lesson-plan pairs rated by 16 educators.
finding.measure: Educator preferences for lesson-plan source and perceived usefulness for lesson planning
finding.study_size: n=16 educators, 529 lesson-plan pairs, 2116 total evaluations

paper_profiles.title: SMRC: Aligning Large Language Models with Student Reasoning for Mathematical Error Correction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of correcting students’ mathematical reasoning errors with large language models (LLMs) in a way that preserves the student’s original reasoning path. The authors argue that existing LLM self-correction methods are not pedagogically aligned because they optimize for final-answer correctness without retaining correct intermediate steps that matter for learning.

To address this, the paper proposes SMRC (Student Mathematical Reasoning Correction), a search-based framework that combines a fine-tuned reward model with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). The system treats student solution correction as a sequential decision problem, using reward signals derived from breadth-first search over reasoning trees and back-propagated process supervision. A benchmark dataset, MSEB, is also constructed from 158 real high-school student solutions spanning algebra, geometry, matrices, and trigonometry.

The experiments compare SMRC against direct correction, thought-preserving correction, Self-Check, and Self-Refine across ProcessBench, MR-GSM8K, and MSEB. Results show that SMRC generally improves both answer accuracy and correct-step retention, with especially strong performance on MR-GSM8K and MSEB. However, this is a methodology paper with benchmark and model evaluation rather than a student intervention study, so the evidence is about model performance on student-like reasoning traces rather than direct educational outcomes for learners.

finding.finding_summary: SMRC improved mathematical error-correction performance relative to baselines across benchmark datasets. On MSEB, SMRC achieved ACC=40.1 and CSRR=73.7 with HM=51.8, outperforming all compared baselines; on MR-GSM8K it reached ACC=91.4 and CSRR=94.5 with HM=92.9. The study uses these metrics to show that the method can both correct answers and preserve correct reasoning steps in high-school mathematics problems.
finding.measure: Reasoning accuracy (ACC), correct step retention rate (CSRR), harmonic mean (HM) on mathematical error-correction benchmarks
finding.study_size: n=158 for MSEB; public benchmark sizes for ProcessBench and MR-GSM8K not_reported in the paper text

paper_profiles.title: Findings of MEGA: Maths Explanation with LLMs using the Socratic Method for Active Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a new generative-AI-based mathematics explanation approach, MEGA (Mathematics Explanations through Games by AI LLMs), improves students’ learning experience compared with a traditional chain-of-thought (CoT) explanation style. The core question is whether combining the Socratic method, chain-of-thought reasoning, simplified gamification, and formative feedback produces explanations that students judge as better for understanding math problems.

The intervention was implemented as a system prompt for large language models and tested on two benchmark math datasets: GSM8K (easier word problems) and MATH (harder competition-style problems). After initial capability screening of six LLMs, the authors evaluated GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet using 60 sampled problems from each dataset. University master’s students at Luleå University of Technology completed pairwise blind comparisons of MEGA versus CoT explanations and provided qualitative feedback. The study also reported model accuracy under MEGA, Socratic sub-questions, and CoT, and analyzed results by dataset difficulty and question type.

The main conclusion is that students generally preferred MEGA over CoT, especially for harder MATH problems, where MEGA was judged better in 47.5% of cases versus 26.67% for CoT. For easier GSM8K problems, MEGA was only slightly better than CoT, suggesting interactive Socratic explanations are more helpful when problems are difficult and less helpful when problems are simple. The paper also finds that LLM hallucinations still occur within the Socratic interaction, sometimes at sub-question steps, and that model performance varies across datasets, problem difficulty, and LLM backend. Overall, the authors argue that MEGA is a promising student-centered, personalized AI tutoring approach, but not all current LLMs can reliably support it.

finding.finding_summary: Students judged MEGA explanations as better for learning mathematics than traditional CoT explanations, especially on the harder MATH dataset. MEGA was preferred in 47.5% of MATH cases versus 26.67% for CoT (n=60 sampled problems), while on GSM8K the advantage was small (26.67% vs 24.17%), indicating stronger benefit for more difficult math problems.
finding.measure: Student pairwise preference judgments of explanation quality for math problems; model accuracy on math question answering
finding.study_size: n=120 sampled problems total (60 GSM8K, 60 MATH); 34 students assigned the task
finding.confidence_interval: p=0.0201 for MATH preference difference; p=0.6731 for GSM8K preference difference

finding.finding_summary: The intervention increased engagement for many students, but not all. The authors report that MEGA was perceived as more interactive and engaging, particularly for harder problems, yet 22.22% of students preferred non-interactive learning, and some found the interactive format tedious on simpler tasks.
finding.measure: Student feedback on engagement/interaction preference and qualitative comments

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues MEGA supports active learning, critical thinking, and problem solving by forcing students to respond to sub-questions before proceeding. Student comments suggest the approach can help build understanding and make reasoning more manageable on complex problems, though some students reported confusion or distraction on easier items.
finding.measure: Student qualitative feedback on understanding, step-by-step reasoning, and perceived cognitive support

paper_profiles.title: Combining Large Language Models with Tutoring System Intelligence: A Case Study in Caregiver Homework Support
paper_profiles.venue: LAK 2025 (The 15th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how large language models (LLMs) can be combined with an intelligent tutoring system’s instructional model to generate useful conversational support for caregivers helping children with math homework. The authors focus on a hybrid tutoring setting in which a caregiver supports a middle-school student working through equation-solving problems in the Lynnette tutoring system. They aim to overcome known limitations of LLMs in education by grounding prompts in real-time student context from the tutoring system and in examples of effective tutoring practice.

The intervention is the Caregiver Conversational Support Tool (CCST), which uses Llama 3 8B Instruct to generate caregiver chat recommendations. The system incorporates live problem-solving context such as correctness, hint use, current equation, and suggested next steps from the tutoring system, then prompts the LLM with tutoring best practices and example responses. The paper reports prompt-engineering experiments across seven prompt rounds and a prototyping study with ten middle-school caregivers, using a qualitative thematic analysis of interview and annotation data.

The main findings are that caregivers preferred messages that provided content-level math support and prompted students to explain their thinking, rather than purely motivational messages. Caregivers valued the contextual relevance of recommendations, especially when the messages reflected student errors or hint use, though they found some generated messages too long and sometimes too slow to appear. The study concludes that tutoring-system intelligence plus LLM prompting can produce more contextually relevant and pedagogically aligned support for caregivers, but the work remains a design study rather than a student-outcome evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test student learning outcomes directly, but it substantively studies a math tutoring context and shows that LLM-generated caregiver messages can be made contextually relevant to equation-solving. In simulated prompt trials and caregiver testing (n=10 caregivers), the system generated math-specific suggestions such as asking about dividing both sides by 6 or explaining an error, indicating improved instructional support for middle-school algebra practice.
finding.measure: Quality and contextual relevance of generated caregiver messages for equation-solving support
finding.study_size: n=10 caregivers; plus simulated prompt trials

finding.finding_summary: The study found that caregivers especially preferred prompts that asked students to self-explain their reasoning, which the authors interpret as support for metacognition. In the caregiver interviews (n=10), five caregivers explicitly favored messages that elicited explanation of thought processes, suggesting the tool may support student reflection and deeper reasoning during math problem solving.
finding.measure: Caregiver preferences for metacognitive / self-explanation prompts

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports usability and responsiveness concerns in live tutoring, including that six of nine caregivers found the messages too long and two of six felt generation was somewhat slow, with average latency around 25 seconds. At the same time, caregivers generally found the three-message output adequate and some said generation was reasonably quick, so the operational impact was mixed.
finding.measure: Caregiver feedback on message length, number of recommendations, and latency

paper_profiles.title: The Invalsi Benchmarks: measuring the Linguistic and Mathematical understanding of Large Language Models in Italian
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces three new Italian-language benchmarks for evaluating large language models (LLMs): Invalsi MATE for mathematical understanding, Invalsi ITA for language understanding, and Olimpiadi MATE for more difficult mathematics. The motivating problem is that there are few natively Italian benchmarks for generative models, especially for mathematics, and the authors want to measure whether multilingual or Italian-fine-tuned models perform better than English-first models on Italian educational tasks.

The authors assemble benchmark datasets from Italian standardized assessments used across grades 2 through 13, manually verify the items, and evaluate 10 open LLMs with likelihood-based zero-shot scoring. For Invalsi MATE they also compare model performance against aggregated Italian student results, and they additionally run human-inspected and pattern-matching evaluations for subsets of the math benchmark. The study is not an intervention with students; it is a model benchmark/evaluation paper focused on direct student-facing test items.

Main findings are that larger multilingual models perform better in Italian than English-first models with Italian fine-tuning alone, and that Llama 3.1 70B/405B models are strongest overall. On Invalsi MATE, only Llama 3.1 70B instruct clearly exceeds student average performance, while on Invalsi ITA most models outperform students on language items; however, all models struggle more on Olimpiadi MATE, indicating limits in complex mathematical reasoning in Italian. The authors conclude that multilingual pretraining helps more than Italian fine-tuning, and that current LLMs transfer mathematical reasoning across languages better than language understanding.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates mathematical understanding on Invalsi MATE (n=420) and Olimpiadi MATE (n=619). Llama 3.1 70B instruct achieved 0.71 accuracy on Invalsi MATE and 0.45 on Olimpiadi MATE; the authors also report that only Llama 3.1 70B instruct clearly outperformed the average Italian student performance on the math benchmark, while other models were at or below student levels. Fine-tuning on Italian alone did not close the gap, and multilingual pretraining was generally stronger.
finding.measure: 0-shot accuracy on math benchmark questions; comparison to aggregated student accuracy on Invalsi math items
finding.study_size: n=1039 total math questions across benchmarks; benchmark-specific n=420 (Invalsi MATE) and n=619 (Olimpiadi MATE)

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates language understanding on Invalsi ITA (n=1264) and finds that LLMs, especially Llama 3.1 70B instruct, perform strongly on Italian language questions. The best model reached 0.88 accuracy overall on Invalsi ITA, and the authors report that most models outperform the aggregated Italian student average on language items, especially multiple-choice questions.
finding.measure: 0-shot accuracy on Italian language comprehension benchmark questions; comparison to aggregated student accuracy on Invalsi Italian items

paper_profiles.title: Elementary Math Word Problem Generation using Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically generating elementary mathematics word problems (MWPs) for classroom practice. The authors argue that manually writing MWPs is time-consuming and that prior automated approaches often require extra inputs such as equations, seeds, or context, and do not reliably control grade level or question type.

To address this, the paper proposes an LLM-based MWP generation system that takes only three inputs: number of problems, grade, and question type. The authors compare open-source 7B instruction-tuned models (Llama-2, Mistral, Zephyr), different prompt templates, decoding settings for diversity, and post-training strategies including QLoRA fine-tuning on a manually created MWP dataset, preference optimization (DPO/KTO/CPO), few-shot prompting, and a secondary LLM-based solvability filter. They also create and release the Mathwizards dataset, a 4K MWP corpus aligned to Common Core grade/section specifications, plus a 4K error-annotated corpus from human and LLM evaluation.

The evaluation is entirely on generated text quality rather than student learning outcomes. Human and LLM-based judgments show that the generated problems are generally grammatical, solvable, and topic-safe, but models still struggle to consistently match the requested grade and section. The best configuration reported is fine-tuned Llama-2 with 5-shot prompting plus solvability filtering, which improves grade/section relevance compared with the zero-shot baseline, though the paper does not report effects on student mathematics performance.

finding.finding_summary: The system is designed to reduce tutor workload by automatically generating math word problems instead of requiring manual authoring. The paper reports that generating MWPs via LLMs can produce high-quality, mostly grammatical questions with minimal spelling issues, suggesting practical efficiency gains for educators, but it does not quantify time saved.
finding.measure: Quality of automatically generated math word problems; qualitative claim about reduced manual authoring effort

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on generating elementary math word problems for practice in mathematics, aiming to support problem-solving and math skill development. The best model configuration improved grade relevance and section relevance relative to baseline, but the study evaluates generated problem quality rather than student achievement, so no direct learning effect is reported.
finding.measure: Grade relevance and section relevance of generated math word problems; solvability and realism of generated problems

paper_profiles.title: Seeing the Big Picture: Evaluating Multimodal LLMs’ Ability to Interpret and Grade Handwritten Student Work
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Educational Data Mining Conference
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can interpret and grade handwritten student mathematics work, with a particular interest in whether such systems could support classroom assessment and feedback. The authors separate the problem into two components: visual interpretation (reading what the student wrote) and grading (judging correctness), because failures may come from either seeing or evaluating student work.

The study uses two experiments. Experiment A analyzes 288 scanned handwritten arithmetic responses from Ghanaian middle school students on fractions, percentages, and basic algebra problems with objective answers. Experiment B examines 150 student-drawn mathematical illustrations from a U.S. elementary dataset (DrawEDU), comparing model performance when grading directly from images versus when given human-written descriptions of the images.

Results show that the best model, Gemini 2.5 Pro, achieved near-human performance on routine handwritten arithmetic (95% grading accuracy, LWK=0.90), suggesting MLLMs can handle objective numerical work reasonably well. However, performance dropped sharply on mathematical illustrations: image-only agreement was low (kappa up to 0.38), and even with human descriptions models only reached moderate agreement (kappa about 0.43-0.47), near the initial human inter-rater ceiling but still insufficient for autonomous deployment. The paper concludes that current MLLMs may be useful for screening routine arithmetic work, but they still lack the visual and tacit pedagogical knowledge needed to interpret more open-ended student mathematical thinking reliably.

finding.finding_summary: Across 288 handwritten middle-school arithmetic responses, the best-performing model (Gemini 2.5 Pro) achieved 95% grading accuracy and LWK=0.90, which the authors characterize as near-human performance. However, performance varied by model and there were non-human error modes, including false positives and false negatives, indicating that while MLLMs can grade routine handwritten numeracy work well, they are not uniformly reliable.
finding.measure: Grading accuracy and Linear Weighted Kappa on handwritten arithmetic responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that MLLMs could reduce teacher workload by automating or pre-screening routine handwritten arithmetic grading. This claim is supported by high grading accuracy on objective work (e.g., Gemini 2.5 Pro at 95% accuracy on n=288), but the authors emphasize that human review remains necessary for ambiguous or illustration-based tasks.
finding.measure: Potential grading automation / reduction in teacher grading burden
finding.study_size: n=288 for arithmetic; n=150 for illustrations

paper_profiles.title: Stepwise Verification and Remediation of Student Reasoning Errors with Large Language Model Tutors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a core problem in LLM-based dialog tutoring for math: large language models often misdiagnose student reasoning errors and then generate tutor feedback that is factually incorrect, poorly targeted, or hallucinatory. The authors propose a modular verify-then-generate framework that separates student-solution verification from response generation, inspired by human tutoring practice where teachers first identify the error and then decide how to respond.

To support this approach, the paper introduces a dataset of 1,002 teacher-annotated student reasoning chains in K-12 math word problems, derived from MathDial/GSM8K-style multi-step problems. Teachers annotate the first erroneous step, and the authors evaluate several verification strategies: binary overall verification, stepwise error classification, free-form error description, and step alignment to a reference solution using a modified Needleman-Wunsch alignment algorithm. They compare prompted and fine-tuned models including GPT-3.5, Llama2, Llama3, and Flan-T5.

The results show that verification is difficult even for strong LLMs, but reference solutions and fine-tuning improve verification performance. More importantly, conditioning tutor response generation on an explicit verification output yields responses that are more targeted to the student's actual mistake, more correct, and more actionable, with fewer hallucinations than direct generation baselines. The strongest improvements come from textual error descriptions and, to a lesser extent, step alignment; the paper concludes that adding a verification stage is a promising way to improve LLM tutors for math problem solving, though the work evaluates teacher-centered proxy metrics rather than student learning outcomes directly.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that a verify-then-generate tutoring pipeline improves the quality of math tutoring responses relative to direct generation baselines. In human evaluation, responses conditioned on Error Description were more targeted, correct, and actionable than baseline responses (e.g., for the prompted GPT-3.5 model, targetedness rose from 30.0% to 57.5% and correctness from 37.5% to 62.5%; for finetuned Flan-T5-3B, targetedness rose from 7.5% to 20.0% and correctness from 20.0% to 35.0%).
finding.measure: Teacher-rated quality of math tutor responses (targetedness, correctness, actionability) and automatic text-generation metrics (sBLEU, KF1, BF1) on K-12 math word-problem tutoring dialogs
finding.study_size: n=40 conversations for human evaluation; dataset n=1002 verification annotations

finding.finding_summary: The approach is intended to improve the efficiency and reliability of tutor response generation by separating error detection from response generation, reducing hallucinations and making responses more actionable. The paper reports that the modular architecture produces more targeted and less hallucinated teacher utterances, implying less need for manual correction or repeated tutoring turns, but it does not directly measure time saved or workload reduction.
finding.measure: Teacher-rated response quality as a proxy for tutor utility and reduction in hallucinated or unhelpful responses
finding.study_size: n=40 conversations for human evaluation; n=1002 annotated verification examples

paper_profiles.title: Take Out Your Calculators: Estimating the Real Difficulty of Question Items with LLM Student Simulations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether open-source large language models can be used to simulate student responses well enough to estimate the difficulty of K-12 mathematics multiple-choice items. The motivating problem is that real item piloting for assessments is expensive and slow, so the authors investigate whether simulated student data can substitute for human response data when screening items for difficulty.

The study uses 631 NAEP math multiple-choice items from grades 4, 8, and 12. The authors compare several approaches: direct text-based difficulty estimation, direct prompting of LLMs to predict percentage-correct rates, and a simulation-based method in which LLMs role-play students at four NAEP proficiency levels (Below Basic, Basic, Proficient, Advanced). Simulated individual responses are aggregated and also fit to Item Response Theory models to estimate item difficulty. They test multiple open-source models (Gemma, Llama, Qwen), prompt conditions (no identifier, student IDs, single name, diverse names), and class sizes.

Results show that direct text-based and direct prompting methods are weak, while simulation-based methods produce moderate-to-strong alignment with real NAEP performance. Best correlations reach 0.75, 0.76, and 0.82 for grades 4, 8, and 12 in the weighted ensemble condition, and IRT-derived difficulty estimates achieve AUC values roughly from 0.78 to 0.90. The authors conclude that LLM student simulations can be a useful low-cost preliminary screening tool for math item difficulty, especially when diverse names, larger simulated class sizes, and weaker math-performing models are used.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that LLM-simulated student responses can moderately to strongly predict real-world NAEP math item difficulty and correctness rates. Using 631 multiple-choice math items across grades 4, 8, and 12, the best simulated/real correlations reached r=0.75, 0.76, and 0.82 (weighted ensemble across grades), and IRT-based difficulty estimates achieved AUC values of about 0.78-0.90, indicating meaningful discrimination between easier and harder items.
finding.measure: NAEP math item correctness rates and IRT-estimated item difficulty for multiple-choice mathematics questions

paper_profiles.title: SUPERCORRECT: Advancing Small LLM Reasoning with Thought Template Distillation and Self-Correction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes SUPERCORRECT, a two-stage training framework for improving the mathematical reasoning and self-correction abilities of small language models. The first stage, hierarchical thought-based supervised fine-tuning (HSFT), distills structured reasoning from larger teacher models into small student models using XML-formatted step-by-step solutions, detailed "Key" explanations for difficult steps, and a generalized summary. The second stage uses cross-model collaborative direct preference optimization (DPO), where teacher models identify and correct erroneous reasoning steps in student-generated solutions, and these correction traces are used to train the student model.

The paper is centered on mathematical problem solving with benchmark datasets such as MATH, GSM8K, and GaoKao Bench, and evaluates models like Qwen2.5-Math-7B, DeepSeek-Math-7B, and Llama3.1-8B. It reports improved benchmark accuracy for the trained models, including 70.2% on MATH and 89.5% on GSM8K for SUPERCORRECT-Qwen-7B, along with gains in self-correction accuracy and error localization. The authors conclude that teacher-guided hierarchical reasoning and cross-model correction traces help small LLMs overcome reasoning bottlenecks and improve both accuracy and stability on difficult math problems.

finding.finding_summary: SUPERCORRECT improved mathematical reasoning accuracy on benchmark tests for small LLMs. The strongest reported model, SUPERCORRECT-Qwen-7B, reached 70.2% on MATH and 89.5% on GSM8K, compared with 55.1% and 83.2% for the base Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct model. The paper also reports a 7.1-point gain over a base HSFT model on MATH and a 2.7-point gain on GSM8K after Cross-DPO.
finding.measure: Benchmark accuracy on MATH and GSM8K mathematical reasoning tasks
finding.effect_size: 70.2% vs 55.1% on MATH; 89.5% vs 83.2% on GSM8K

finding.finding_summary: The method improved reasoning stability and self-correction-related skills such as error localization and correction of reasoning steps. In a stability analysis on 300 hard MATH problems repeated 256 times, the authors report higher mean accuracy and lower variance for SUPERCORRECT than the base model, indicating more stable reasoning performance. On a separate 500-error-solution sample, Cross-model DPO improved locate correctness and correction accuracy (e.g., for Qwen2.5-Math: 0.43 to 0.67 and 0.12 to 0.46).
finding.measure: Reasoning stability, error localization correctness, and correction accuracy
finding.study_size: n=300 for stability analysis; n=500 erroneous solutions for correction analysis
finding.std_deviation: Lower variance reported in Figure 5; exact values not reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims the hierarchical thought format and cross-model correction traces improve the efficiency of training and correction procedures for small LLMs by providing structured templates and targeted error correction. However, the paper does not report direct workload or time-saved metrics for educators or users, so the evidence is indirect and model-centric rather than operational in a school setting.
finding.measure: Training/evaluation workflow efficiency of model reasoning and correction

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Automated Distractor Generation for Math Multiple-choice Questions via Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies whether large language models (LLMs) can automatically generate plausible wrong answer choices (“distractors”) for math multiple-choice questions (MCQs). The motivating problem is that writing high-quality distractors is time-consuming for teachers and content designers, especially when distractors should reflect common student errors or misconceptions rather than just be mathematically incorrect.

The authors evaluate five approaches for distractor generation on a real-world dataset of 1.4K English math MCQs from Eedi, targeted primarily at students aged 10 to 13. The methods include in-context learning with nearest-neighbor example selection (kNN), chain-of-thought prompting, fine-tuning, a rule-based baseline, and a sampling-based baseline. They compare generated distractors to human-authored distractors using exact/partial/proportional match metrics, an exploratory distribution-based metric, and human ratings of mathematical validity and plausibility.

Across experiments, kNN-based in-context learning performs best on alignment-based metrics, outperforming prompting, fine-tuning, and baselines. However, human evaluation shows that while LLM-generated distractors are often mathematically valid, they are less plausible than human-authored distractors and less effective at capturing common student misconceptions. The paper concludes that LLMs can support teacher workflow as an auxiliary tool, but current methods are not yet reliable enough to replace human judgment when designing distractors for students.

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests automated distractor generation could reduce teacher and content-designer workload by partially automating a labor-intensive MCQ authoring task. On a 1.4K-item math MCQ dataset, the authors show LLMs can generate distractors that are often mathematically valid, and they frame the method as an auxiliary tool for saving educators time, though no direct time-saving effect was experimentally measured.
finding.measure: Task automation / distractor generation quality as a proxy for authoring efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Final Answers: Evaluating Large Language Models for Math Tutoring
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models (LLMs) are reliable enough to serve as math tutors, and whether standard benchmark-style evaluation of final answers is sufficient for educational use. The authors argue that correct final answers do not guarantee high-quality tutoring, because students also need accurate scaffolding, stepwise feedback, and pedagogically sound guidance.

To investigate this, the paper uses two complementary approaches on college algebra tasks from the Apprentice Tutors intelligent tutoring system. First, it evaluates five ChatGPT-family models (GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4o, o1-mini, and o1-preview) as problem solvers by comparing their solutions to tutor-generated answers on 110 algebra problems. Second, it has human evaluators interact with the same models as if they were students seeking tutoring help on 30 problems, then rates the resulting dialogues for quality and correctness using a rubric and independent reviewer coding. The study is not a student learning experiment; it is an offline model-evaluation study conducted on college algebra content.

The main finding is that LLMs can often produce correct final answers, but their tutoring dialogues are much less reliable than their headline answer accuracy suggests. In the tutor-based benchmark, overall accuracy was 85.5%, with GPT-4o performing best at 97.3%; in the interactive tutoring condition, final-answer accuracy averaged 88.6%, but only 56.6% of dialogues were fully correct across all steps. The authors conclude that these models are not yet suitable as standalone math tutors without human oversight or additional correctness mechanisms, although they may still be useful for narrower functions such as hint generation, alternative explanations, question generation, and positive reinforcement.
