finding.finding_summary: Across 110 college algebra problems, the models achieved 85.5% overall final-answer accuracy in the tutor-based benchmark, with GPT-4o reaching 97.3% (107/110) and GPT-3.5 Turbo 77.3% (85/110). However, when the same models were evaluated as interactive tutors, only 56.6% of dialogues were fully correct across all steps, indicating that strong final-answer performance did not reliably translate into correct tutoring support.
finding.measure: Final-answer correctness on college algebra problems; correctness of interactive tutoring dialogues
finding.study_size: Tutor-based: n=110 problems; interactive tutoring: n=150 dialogues (30 problems x 5 models)

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: All levels of education (primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional development); no single study population
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities, risks, and implementation challenges of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT, in education. Rather than testing an intervention empirically, the authors synthesize early research and argue for how LLMs could be used for learning, teaching, assessment, and educational content generation, while emphasizing the need for responsible deployment.

The paper discusses potential applications across learner and teacher contexts, including personalized practice, explanation generation, quiz creation, feedback support, lesson planning, and assessment assistance. It also notes possible uses in mathematics education, such as generating math word problems, but does not present head-to-head comparative evidence or original student outcome data.

The main contribution is a conceptual and policy-oriented analysis of benefits and risks. The authors highlight concerns about bias, privacy, plagiarism, overreliance, verification of outputs, and fair access, and recommend human oversight, curriculum integration, and governance safeguards. Overall, the paper concludes that LLMs may be valuable educational tools, but their use should be cautious, ethical, and supported by further research.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models can save teachers time by supporting quiz generation, lesson planning, feedback, grading, and other instructional preparation tasks. However, this is a conceptual claim rather than a measured empirical result, and no study data, sample size, or effect size are reported.
finding.measure: teacher workload / instructional preparation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes institutional-level implications of LLM adoption, including the need for governance, privacy protections, bias mitigation, verification practices, and fair access policies. It discusses how schools and education systems may need new rules, infrastructure, and professional development to integrate these tools responsibly, but provides no empirical institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: policy, governance, privacy, fairness, and implementation considerations

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims LLMs may support critical thinking, problem-solving, and collaboration by generating prompts, explanations, and discussion structures, but also warns that overreliance could weaken students' independent reasoning. These are theoretical assertions supported by cited prior work, not direct empirical findings from the paper itself.
finding.measure: critical thinking / problem-solving / collaboration

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLMs can improve engagement and participation and reduce foreign-language anxiety through conversational support and personalized interaction. These effects are described as potential benefits rather than measured outcomes, and the paper reports no direct sample-based evidence.
finding.measure: engagement, participation, foreign-language anxiety

paper_profiles.title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to scale expert instructional support for novice tutors in K-12 math tutoring, especially in underserved school settings. The authors argue that many tutors lack the real-time pedagogical judgment needed to respond effectively to student misconceptions, and that traditional professional development is too costly and disconnected from live instruction.

The intervention, Tutor CoPilot, is a human-AI system that provides tutors with real-time, expert-like suggestions during live tutoring sessions. It uses a language model adapted with expert reasoning traces and is integrated into a virtual tutoring platform so tutors can request strategies such as hints, guiding questions, or worked examples. The study was preregistered and implemented as a tutor-level randomized controlled trial with 900 tutors and 1,800 K-12 students from Title I schools in a large southern U.S. district, delivering in-school virtual math tutoring across grades 3-8.

The main outcome was whether students mastered lesson topics, operationalized through exit-ticket performance. The authors find that access to Tutor CoPilot increased exit-ticket passing by 4 percentage points overall, with larger gains for lower-rated tutors (9 percentage points) and less-experienced tutors (7 percentage points). Treatment tutors also used more high-quality pedagogical strategies and fewer answer-giving strategies. Survey outcomes and end-of-year math test scores were not significantly improved, suggesting the strongest evidence is for proximal tutoring-session learning rather than longer-term standardized achievement.

finding.finding_summary: In an intent-to-treat analysis, students whose tutors had access to Tutor CoPilot were 4 percentage points more likely to pass their exit tickets than control students (62% to 66%; p<0.01). The main session-level outcome was exit-ticket pass rate, with n=4,136 tutoring sessions; conditional on attempting the exit ticket, students were 3 percentage points more likely to pass (p<0.01).
finding.measure: Exit ticket pass rate / lesson-topic mastery in math tutoring sessions
finding.study_size: n=4136 sessions (students n=1800; tutors n=900 initially, 782 at launch)
finding.effect_size: 4 percentage point increase in exit-ticket passing (intent-to-treat)

finding.finding_summary: Student survey outcomes related to tutor care, confidence, and session ratings showed no statistically significant treatment effects. Across approximately 1,931-1,952 survey responses, estimates were small and nonsignificant (e.g., -0.004 to 0.03), indicating no clear improvement in students' reported engagement, self-efficacy, or perceptions of the tutoring session.
finding.measure: Student post-session survey ratings (e.g., tutor cared about understanding, confidence in learning math, session rating)

finding.finding_summary: Treatment tutors were more likely to use instructional moves that support deeper reasoning and understanding, including prompting students to explain and asking questions to guide thinking. The paper reports these strategies were used about 2 standard deviations more frequently on a log-odds scale in treatment sessions than control sessions, based on analysis of 550,000+ tutor messages classified with NLP models.
finding.measure: Tutor language / pedagogical strategy use in chat messages
finding.effect_size: approximately 2 standard deviations more frequent on a log-odds scale for key high-quality strategies

finding.finding_summary: The system was positioned as a low-cost support tool, with the authors estimating annual cost at $20 per tutor based on observed usage during the study. While not a direct productivity measure, the paper argues Tutor CoPilot can scale expert guidance more cheaply than traditional professional development and can reduce the burden on novice tutors during live instruction.
finding.measure: Estimated annual per-tutor cost of Tutor CoPilot

paper_profiles.title: Retrieval-augmented Generation to Improve Math Question-Answering: Trade-offs Between Groundedness and Human Preference
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS 2023 Workshop on Generative AI for Education (GAIED)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve the quality of large language model responses for middle-school math question answering, and whether increasing grounding in a textbook changes human preference for those responses. The authors focus on conceptual math QA, a use case they distinguish from procedural tutoring, and explore how prompt guidance and retrieval relevance affect groundedness, perceived faithfulness, and user rankings.

The study implements a RAG system using OpenStax Prealgebra as the retrieval corpus and GPT-3.5-turbo-0613 as the response model. The system is evaluated on 51 real student questions drawn from the Math Nation discussion board and on human judgments from 9 educators and education-technology designers. Three linked studies are reported: prompt-guidance manipulation to assess groundedness metrics, a within-subjects preference survey comparing none/low/high guidance responses, and an annotation study of retrieval relevance.

The main conclusion is that RAG can increase groundedness, but there is a trade-off: the most grounded responses are not always the most preferred. Human raters preferred the low-guidance RAG responses over both no-guidance and high-guidance responses, while high guidance produced the most grounded outputs. The authors conclude that math QA systems should balance grounding with conversational usefulness and curriculum fit, and that better notions of faithfulness for educational QA remain an open problem.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies conceptual middle-school math question answering, evaluating whether retrieval-augmented generation improves response groundedness and whether humans prefer those responses. Across 51 student questions, groundedness increased with stronger prompt guidance, but the most preferred condition was low guidance rather than high guidance; for example, low guidance was preferred over high guidance and no guidance, while high guidance had the highest groundedness (mean groundedness 0.90 vs. 0.59 low and 0.52 none).
finding.measure: Human preference rankings and groundedness judgments for generated math QA responses; automated groundedness metrics (K-F1++, BERTScore, BLEURT)
finding.study_size: n=51 queries; n=9 raters; n=153 groundedness judgments

paper_profiles.title: Design and evaluation of ChatGPT-MWPS: an AI-enhanced learning system for improving primary students’ mathematical word problem solving
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of helping primary students solve mathematical word problems, which require students to integrate reading comprehension with quantitative reasoning. The authors argue that conventional digital practice systems often provide static, limited feedback and do not adequately support the step-by-step reasoning needed for word problem solving.

To address this, the study designed and evaluated ChatGPT-MWPS, a generative AI-enhanced learning system built on the ChatGPT API. The system provides adaptive scaffolding, step-by-step hints, and personalized feedback in a classroom and self-directed learning environment for fifth-grade students. The evaluation involved 52 fifth-grade students from one public primary school in Guangdong, China, along with three mathematics teachers who provided usability feedback and interviews.

The study used a quasi-experimental usability evaluation rather than a learning-outcome comparison against another instructional condition. Students completed math word problems in the system and then rated 13 usability dimensions, while teachers were interviewed about technical performance, content quality, and design improvements. Results showed generally favorable usability and strong intention to use, but important weaknesses in information display and design appeal. The authors conclude that generative AI can support primary mathematics learning, but its educational value depends heavily on interface clarity, cognitive flow, and pedagogical fit; they also identify several areas for system refinement before broader classroom use.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that ChatGPT-MWPS was well received as a mathematics word-problem support tool for fifth-grade students, with favorable usability across most dimensions and strong user willingness to continue using it. However, the paper does not report learning gains on standardized math achievement; the evidence is indirect and based on usability, not achievement testing.
finding.measure: Usability scale and student interaction with mathematical word problem solving in the ChatGPT-MWPS environment

finding.finding_summary: Students reported generally positive experiences with the system, especially in intention to use, cognitive engagement, trust, and anthropomorphism. Intention to use showed a very strong correlation with cognitive engagement (r=0.969, p<0.05), suggesting the system supported engagement and motivational acceptance during math problem solving.
finding.measure: Usability dimensions including cognitive engagement, trust, anthropomorphism, and intention to use

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to support step-by-step reasoning and problem-solving, and students’ intention to use was strongly associated with cognitive engagement (r=0.969) and related usability factors such as learnability and information quality. The findings suggest the tool may help scaffold metacognitive engagement and reasoning processes, although no direct measure of problem-solving performance is reported.
finding.measure: Cognitive engagement and usability perceptions during mathematical word problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The system included batch question import, automated worksheet generation, and teacher-facing management tools intended to reduce preparation time and streamline practice creation. Teacher interviews, however, noted technical latency and traffic congestion, indicating that operational efficiency benefits were promising but not yet fully realized in practice.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported workflow features, system performance, and usability-related efficiency concerns

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (literature review; no primary study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a narrative review of artificial intelligence in education, with particular attention to chatbots and ChatGPT. The paper asks what AI tools are, how they are being used in education, what benefits they may offer, and what ethical and practical concerns they raise. Rather than testing an intervention, the authors synthesize prior literature and recent commentary on AI-supported teaching, learning, assessment, and administration.

The review discusses broad educational applications such as intelligent tutoring systems, automated grading, personalized learning platforms, chatbots for student support, and AI-assisted teacher tools. It emphasizes potential gains in personalization, feedback, engagement, motivation, learner confidence, and teacher workload reduction, while also highlighting risks including bias, privacy, academic integrity, overreliance, and lack of human interaction. The paper is not specific to K-12 mathematics and does not present original empirical data or head-to-head comparator evidence.

Overall, the authors conclude that AI and ChatGPT have substantial promise for education but must be implemented responsibly, with attention to ethics, teacher preparation, and governance. They call for further research on effective and equitable use of these technologies and caution that their educational value depends on alignment with pedagogy and learning goals.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: A revolutionary tool for teaching and learning mathematics
paper_profiles.venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.population: Mixed (students and educators; mathematics education stakeholders)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines early perceptions of ChatGPT as a tool for teaching and learning mathematics, with particular attention to how students, educators, and other stakeholders view its usefulness and limitations. The authors ask whether ChatGPT can support mathematics instruction, improve problem solving, and provide useful feedback, while also identifying risks such as errors, overreliance, and weak understanding of mathematical concepts.

The study uses a two-stage qualitative case study design. First, the authors conduct content analysis of 30 publicly available interviews/blog discussions from people using ChatGPT in mathematics. Second, three experienced educators test ChatGPT over a week across several mathematics scenarios, including solving equations, limits, derivatives, and geometry/Pythagorean theorem tasks. The context is early 2023, shortly after ChatGPT’s release, and the paper focuses on mathematics education rather than one specific grade level, though some examples are framed for middle-school learners.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT is viewed as promising and potentially useful for math teaching, especially for quick explanations, examples, and basic problem solving, but it is not reliable enough to replace human teachers or tutoring systems. The paper finds that ChatGPT can produce correct explanations in some geometry cases and simple math tasks, but it also makes substantive mistakes in algebra, calculus, and geometry, sometimes confidently. The authors argue that ChatGPT should be used cautiously as a complementary tool, and they call for guidelines and further research on safe, responsible educational use.

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents mixed evidence on ChatGPT’s mathematics performance. In qualitative user testing, ChatGPT sometimes solved basic equations and explained Pythagorean theorem correctly, but it also produced clear errors on linear equations (e.g., gave 13/20 instead of the correct 13/17), a cubic equation, limits, derivatives, and some geometry prompts. No standardized effect size was reported; evidence comes from 3 educator testers and 30 interviewees rather than a quantitative comparison study.
finding.measure: Qualitative evaluation of ChatGPT responses to mathematics tasks (equations, limits, derivatives, geometry/Pythagorean theorem)
finding.study_size: n=3 educators for user testing; n=30 interviewees for content analysis

finding.finding_summary: Participants generally expressed enthusiasm that ChatGPT could increase educational success by providing instant feedback, personalized support, and quick help with mathematical problems. The paper also reports cautionary views about overreliance and loss of human interaction, so the overall sentiment is positive but qualified. No quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Stakeholder perceptions of usefulness, motivation, and support in mathematics learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests ChatGPT can support problem decomposition and step-by-step reasoning in math, but also shows that it lacks deep understanding and sometimes cannot detect misconceptions or errors in its own outputs. The authors therefore frame its contribution to critical thinking and metacognitive support as limited and inconsistent rather than robust. No quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Ability to provide explanations, step-by-step solutions, and detect/respond to misconceptions
finding.study_size: n=3 educator user-testing cases plus interview data

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly notes that ChatGPT can generate explanations and solutions quickly, sometimes faster than a person could type them manually, which may reduce time spent drafting responses or examples. However, the study also emphasizes that speed does not guarantee correctness, so the efficiency benefit is limited by the need for verification. No quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived speed/efficiency of generating math explanations and solutions
finding.study_size: n=3 educator user-testing cases; interview data

paper_profiles.title: How Does ChatGPT Perform on the United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE)? The Implications of Large Language Models for Medical Education and Knowledge Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether ChatGPT can answer medical multiple-choice questions at a level relevant to medical education and knowledge assessment. The authors test ChatGPT on four question sets spanning USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 content: AMBOSS questions and NBME free questions. They compare ChatGPT’s performance with GPT-3 and InstructGPT, and they also qualitatively assess whether ChatGPT’s answers provide logical justification, internal question information, and external supporting information.

The study is not an intervention trial; instead, it is a benchmarking exercise using curated exam questions. The main context is medical education, with the authors framing ChatGPT as a potential interactive tutor or small-group learning aid for medical students. All testing was done on the December 15, 2022 version of ChatGPT, using text-only prompts and excluding image/table questions.

Results showed that ChatGPT answered 42%-64.4% of questions correctly across the four datasets, outperforming GPT-3 and InstructGPT overall. Performance was higher on NBME free questions than on AMBOSS questions, and accuracy declined significantly as AMBOSS difficulty increased in Step 1 without the attending tip (P=.01). The qualitative review found that ChatGPT always provided a logical explanation, used internal information in nearly all responses, and used external information more often in correct than incorrect answers. The authors conclude that ChatGPT shows promise as an educational tool for medical knowledge review, but they also note the need for further study before educational use can be recommended.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT demonstrated substantial performance on medical knowledge questions drawn from USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 content, answering between 42% and 64.4% of questions correctly depending on dataset. On the NBME free Step 1 set, it achieved 64.4% accuracy (56/87), which the authors interpret as comparable to a passing threshold for a third-year medical student. The study also found that performance declined with increasing AMBOSS difficulty for Step 1 without the attending tip (P=.01).
finding.measure: Accuracy on multiple-choice USMLE Step 1 and Step 2–style questions
finding.study_size: n=389 total questions across 4 datasets; dataset subsamples n=87, n=100, n=100, n=102

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.population: Not population-specific; discusses human learning across educational contexts, with some references to K-12 and higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines the promises, limitations, and ethical challenges of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for human learning. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, it synthesizes recent research across learning sciences, educational technology, and human-computer interaction to argue that GenAI may scale personalized support, diversify learning resources, provide timely feedback, and enable more authentic assessment, while also introducing risks such as hallucinations, bias, privacy concerns, and assessment disruption.

The paper is not specific to one population or one instructional context; it speaks broadly to learners, educators, policymakers, researchers, and technologists, while noting implications for K-12 and higher education. It uses examples such as GenAI tutors (e.g., Khanmigo), automated feedback systems, and AI-supported assessment to illustrate possible use cases. The authors conclude that GenAI should be integrated through human-centered, evidence-based, and methodologically rigorous approaches, with AI literacy as a central need for students and educators.

Because the article is primarily a conceptual perspective, it does not present new empirical findings of its own. Instead, it emphasizes that current evidence for GenAI’s learning effects remains limited, mixed, and context-dependent, and it calls for longitudinal and randomized studies comparing GenAI tutoring with conventional tutoring and other educational technologies.

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses GenAI use in mathematics learning mainly through illustrative examples, especially Khan Academy’s Khanmigo chatbot for fractions and mathematical problem solving. However, it reports no original empirical mathematics outcome data; it only notes that current evidence on learning gains is limited and mixed, including a reference to a lack of gains after removing GenAI supports in prior work.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes prior work suggesting GenAI may affect engagement, motivation, agency, and emotions in learning, but the direction is not uniformly positive. It specifically notes mixed evidence on learning engagement and agency, and cites studies where GenAI support increased exam performance but reduced engagement when the support was removed or when chat was introduced in a coding class.
finding.measure: Engagement, agency, motivation, positive emotions (as discussed across cited studies)

finding.finding_summary: A central theme of the paper is GenAI’s potential to influence critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, creativity, and self-regulation. The authors argue that while GenAI can scaffold deeper thinking and problem solving, overreliance may weaken these durable skills; they cite evidence of a performance paradox where assistance improves performance but removing it lowers performance.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, creativity, self-regulated learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI can increase efficiency by scaling personalized support, automating feedback, and reducing the burden of content creation and assessment. It cites examples where ChatGPT generated more in-depth and fluent feedback than human educators and where AI-generated feedback increased revision, motivation, and positive emotions in secondary students, but these are cited studies rather than new results from this paper.
finding.measure: Feedback generation efficiency, workload reduction, scalable support

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes institutional and policy implications, especially around transparency, privacy, equality, beneficence, AI literacy, and assessment governance. It argues that GenAI can democratize access to support, but may also widen inequities and disrupt existing assessment systems unless institutions adopt evidence-based, ethically grounded governance and regulation.
finding.measure: Transparency, privacy, equality, beneficence, assessment validity, AI literacy adoption

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT in higher education: Considerations for academic integrity and student learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines how ChatGPT was being discussed in mainstream news media in the early months after its release, focusing on higher education in Australia, New Zealand, the United States, and the United Kingdom. The authors ask two related questions: what themes dominate news coverage of ChatGPT in higher education, and whether that coverage frames the tool primarily as an academic integrity threat or as a resource that could support learning.

The study uses content analysis of 100 news articles published between 2020 and February 2023. Articles were coded for themes such as academic integrity, institutional policy responses, avoidance strategies, and opportunities to use ChatGPT in teaching. The population is not students in an intervention study; rather, it is the media discourse surrounding university students, faculty, and institutional leaders in higher education.

The main conclusion is that public discussion is dominated by cheating and academic integrity concerns, with comparatively less attention to learning benefits, equity, or student voice. The authors argue that universities should respond with clearer policy guidance, more thoughtful assessment design, and better student involvement, while also recognizing potential benefits such as plain-language explanations, feedback, brainstorming, and accessibility support. Because the paper is a qualitative media content analysis rather than an outcomes study, it does not provide direct evidence of learning gains or comparative effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: The article found that media coverage and university responses to ChatGPT were dominated by academic integrity concerns, with many institutions banning, reviewing, or delaying policy decisions, while fewer articles described constructive institutional uses. In the 100-article corpus, policy-related codes appeared in 41 articles for explicit institutional policy, 18 for bans, 10 for allowing use, and 22 for undecided policies, indicating active but unsettled governance responses.
finding.measure: Content analysis of media-coded themes related to university policy responses and institutional governance

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly frames ChatGPT as relevant to critical thinking, information literacy, and ethical use of AI, but these are discussed as implications rather than directly measured outcomes. Across the coded articles, only 32 explicitly linked ChatGPT to learning outcomes, and the authors argue that the best-performing students will need to analyze AI outputs critically rather than rely on them unthinkingly.
finding.measure: Content analysis of media discussion of critical thinking, information literacy, and ethical use

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies multiple media-described uses of ChatGPT for writing support, including grammatical feedback, producing first drafts, generating organizational structures, and helping non-native speakers improve writing. However, these are presented as perceived opportunities in media discourse rather than tested effects on writing quality or literacy outcomes.
finding.measure: Content analysis of media mentions of writing support, grammar feedback, and assignment drafting

paper_profiles.title: Generative artificial intelligence empowers educational reform: current status, issues, and prospects
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (no empirical sample; conceptual review focused on education broadly, including K-12 examples)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapid emergence of generative artificial intelligence, especially ChatGPT, and asks how these tools may reshape education. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it offers a macro-level review and logic-based analysis of generative AI’s technical foundations, current educational uses, risks, and future possibilities.

The article surveys generative AI applications in education such as intelligent teaching systems, automated homework grading, intelligent tutoring, and speech interaction systems. It also discusses major challenges including opacity and inexplicability, data privacy and security, personalization and fairness, and effectiveness and reliability. Proposed responses include interpretable algorithms, stronger encryption and access control, anonymization, fairer algorithms, improved datasets, and better regulatory frameworks.

The paper’s context is broad educational practice, with illustrative examples drawn from language learning, tutoring platforms, homework grading, and adaptive systems rather than a focused K-12 mathematics study. Its main conclusion is that generative AI should be treated as a transformative educational resource, but one that requires careful governance, better technical design, and human guidance to support more personalized and effective learning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can improve efficiency in educational tasks such as automated homework grading, intelligent tutoring, speech assessment, and real-time feedback, reducing teacher workload and saving time. However, it provides no primary empirical evaluation, effect sizes, or sample sizes; the claim is conceptual and supported only by illustrative examples.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of task automation, grading efficiency, feedback generation, and teacher time savings

finding.finding_summary: The article contends that generative AI may drive broader educational reform through personalized education, intelligent teaching, collaborative education, and virtual teaching. This is a forward-looking policy and institutional argument rather than an empirical finding, and no sample, effect size, or outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of educational reform, governance, and future institutional uses of generative AI

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a conceptual discussion of how artificial intelligence can be integrated into education, with particular emphasis on AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. The paper responds to the rapid adoption of ChatGPT-like tools in academic settings and the resulting concerns about hallucinations, overreliance, fairness, academic integrity, and the need for educators and students to understand AI’s limitations and possibilities.

The author uses a case study from a Swiss University of Applied Sciences (KFH) combined with a narrative literature review and informal discussions with students and staff. Based on this, the paper describes institutional AI guidelines, discusses the challenges of banning versus permitting AI use, and proposes a “culture of AI” supported by workshops, better training, regular updates, budgets, and dedicated staff roles.

The paper argues that AI literacy should be taught broadly and early, and that prompt engineering can be used pedagogically to promote deeper learning. It also emphasizes that students should learn to critically evaluate AI outputs, not simply accept them. The paper is largely normative and practical rather than empirical; it does not report controlled outcome data or direct evidence of learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and especially critical thinking are essential skills for modern education and for responsible AI use. It does not report an empirical effect size, but it presents these competencies as pedagogically valuable for helping students evaluate AI outputs, avoid hallucinations, and think more independently.
finding.measure: AI literacy, prompt engineering proficiency, and critical thinking skills

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on institutional policy and governance responses to generative AI, including the creation of AI guidelines at a Swiss university, documentation requirements, and recommendations for workshops, regular updates, budgets, and paid AI-support roles. These are presented as practical measures to shape institutional culture and manage AI use rather than as tested interventions.
finding.measure: Institutional AI guidelines, policy adoption, staff support structures, and governance practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that AI tools can help teachers create curricula, generate case studies, and support classroom design more efficiently, but it also notes that prompting can take time and may be less efficient than doing tasks manually in some cases. No quantitative productivity outcomes are reported.
finding.measure: Teacher and instructional task efficiency in curriculum creation and case-study development

paper_profiles.title: AI tutoring can safely and effectively support students: An exploratory RCT in UK classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a generative AI tutor can safely and effectively support secondary school students in real classroom mathematics settings, and how it compares with both static hints and human tutors. The authors argue that while one-to-one tutoring is highly effective, it is difficult to scale; they therefore test LearnLM, a pedagogically fine-tuned generative AI model, integrated into the Eedi mathematics platform.

The study was an exploratory randomized controlled trial with 165 students in Years 9 and 10 (ages 13–15) across five UK secondary schools. Students were randomized either to static, pre-written hints or to interactive tutoring; those in the tutoring arm were further randomized to human tutors alone or to LearnLM sessions supervised by human tutors. The trial focused on short diagnostic math units and measured near-term mistake remediation, misconception resolution, and transfer to the next topic.

Results suggest that supervised LearnLM was safe in the sense that tutors found it reliable: they approved most drafted messages without major edits and found no harmful content, with only five factual errors across 3,617 drafts. On learning outcomes, interactive tutoring outperformed static hints, and LearnLM performed at least as well as human tutors on immediate outcomes. Most notably, LearnLM produced higher knowledge transfer on the next unit than human tutors alone (66.2% vs. 60.7%, a 5.5 percentage-point advantage), suggesting a modest but meaningful benefit for durable math learning in this setting.

The paper also includes qualitative evidence that tutors valued LearnLM’s Socratic questioning and reported increased comfort and efficiency when supervising it, though they still needed to add pacing and social-emotional nuance. Overall, the study concludes that supervised generative AI tutoring may be a promising way to expand access to effective individualized math support at scale, while emphasizing that human oversight remains important.

finding.finding_summary: Students receiving supervised LearnLM tutoring performed at least as well as students tutored by humans on immediate math learning outcomes and better on transfer to the next topic. On knowledge transfer, supervised LearnLM increased correct answers on the first question of the next unit to 66.2% (95% credible interval [61.1%, 71.2%]) versus 60.7% [55.8%, 65.4%] for human tutors, a 5.5 percentage-point advantage [–1.4, +12.4].
finding.measure: Performance on Eedi mathematics study units: mistake remediation, misconception resolution, and knowledge transfer to the next unit

finding.finding_summary: Students reported slightly higher helpfulness ratings for interactive tutoring than for static hints, suggesting a more positive learning experience, though the effect was modest and uncertainty remained. In post-trial surveys, interactive tutoring was rated 3.9/5 [3.1, 4.7] versus 3.6/5 [2.9, 4.2] for static hints (posterior probability of advantage: 74.9%).
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of perceived helpfulness of support

finding.finding_summary: Tutors reported that supervising LearnLM made the tutoring process more fluid and efficient, and 82.4% selected 'supporting multiple students at the same time' as its most useful feature. The paper also reports an average tutor comfort-with-AI increase from 3.4 to 3.9 out of 5 (posterior probability of increase: 90.0%), indicating perceived efficiency and usability gains.
finding.measure: Tutor survey responses and interview themes about workload/efficiency; self-reported comfort with AI

finding.finding_summary: The model’s Socratic prompting appears to have supported deeper reflection and knowledge transfer rather than only immediate correction. Students tutored by LearnLM were 5.5 percentage points more likely than those tutored by humans alone to solve a novel problem on a subsequent topic, indicating better transfer to a fresh challenge.
finding.measure: Knowledge transfer to the first question of the next mathematics study unit

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging LLMs to Assess Tutor Moves in Real-Life Dialogues: A Feasibility Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models can be used to automatically identify and evaluate specific tutor moves in authentic tutoring dialogues. The authors focus on two tutoring practices drawn from learning science and tutoring research: giving effective praise and responding appropriately to student math errors. The motivation is scalability: these judgments are usually made manually, but manual coding is time-consuming and difficult to scale across large corpora of tutoring transcripts.

The study analyzes 50 randomly selected transcript excerpts from remote one-on-one math tutoring sessions in which college students tutored middle school students. The transcripts were lightly processed audio transcriptions from video-conferencing sessions, and the authors tested GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4-turbo, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and LearnLM using a combination of zero-shot, few-shot, rationale-forcing, self-consistency, and prompt-chaining approaches. Human experts coded the same transcripts as a reference standard.

Results show that the LLMs performed strongly on both detecting whether a relevant situation occurred and judging whether the tutor’s response aligned with best practices. Accuracy was high for praise detection (94-98%) and math-error detection (82-88%), with evaluation accuracy at 83-89% for praise quality and 73-77% for error responses. The models were broadly similar in performance, with no single model clearly outperforming the others. The paper concludes that LLMs are promising for scalable assessment of tutoring quality in authentic settings, though the work is a feasibility study rather than an intervention study on student learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: This study did not test an instructional intervention or report student math learning gains; instead, it evaluated how accurately LLMs could code math-tutoring dialogue. On 50 transcript excerpts from middle school math tutoring sessions, GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4-turbo, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and LearnLM identified student math errors with 82-88% accuracy and judged tutor responses with 73-77% accuracy.
finding.measure: Accuracy of LLM classification of math error detection and error-response quality in tutoring transcripts

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Generation of Question Hints for Mathematics Problems using Large Language Models in Educational Technology
paper_profiles.venue: FM-EduAssess at NeurIPS 2024 Workshop / Proceedings of Machine Learning Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can generate useful hints for secondary-level mathematics exercises in an intelligent tutoring system context. The authors focus on a practical educational problem: how to produce hints that help students self-correct without simply giving away the answer, while remaining aligned with pedagogical objectives and cognitive-science-informed exercise design.

The study uses MIA Seconde math remediation exercises for French high-school students and simulates both students and teachers with LLMs. GPT-3.5-turbo, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 play the student role, while GPT-4o and Llama-3-8B-Instruct play the teacher role. The authors compare several prompt types for hint generation, including prompts tailored to specific error types and baseline prompts that ignore the student’s initial response. They also vary sampling temperature to study how it affects error generation, hint revision, and self-correction.

Across four exercises, higher temperatures generally increased the number and diversity of student-model errors. The best specialized hint prompt was one targeted at calculation errors, while the strongest baseline prompt was BaselineTwo, which gives hints based on common mistakes. Hints generated by both GPT-4o and Llama-3-8B-Instruct often improved student-model accuracy, with GPT-3.5-turbo showing the largest gains after hints. The paper concludes that LLMs can support hint generation in mathematics, but prompt design and temperature settings strongly affect performance, and the quality and pedagogical relevance of the generated hints still require further qualitative evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that LLM-generated hints often improved students' math problem-solving accuracy and revision performance. Using the best prompts, especially the calculation-error prompt and BaselineTwo, GPT-3.5-turbo showed notable post-hint gains across four high-school math exercises; the paper reports accuracy improvements after hints, but does not provide a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Accuracy on math exercise solving and answer revision after receiving LLM-generated hints
finding.study_size: n=4 exercises; 3 student models; 40 resolution repetitions per exercise; 10 hint-revision repetitions per incorrect response

paper_profiles.title: Hierarchical Pedagogical Oversight: A Multi-Agent Adversarial Framework for Reliable AI Tutoring
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the reliability problem of large language models used as automated tutors in education, especially their tendency to validate incorrect student reasoning (sycophancy) or provide overly direct answers that are pedagogically unhelpful. The authors argue that current single-agent designs conflate generating feedback with evaluating its educational quality, which can lead to confirmation bias and weak oversight of student misconceptions.

To address this, they introduce Hierarchical Pedagogical Oversight (HPO), a multi-agent framework that separates context distillation, adversarial debate, and final synthesis. The system uses specialist agents to summarize dialogue context, then pits permissive and strict pedagogical critics against each other with a Devil’s Advocate moderator, and finally uses a judge/stress analyst/lead evaluator pipeline to assign labels for mistake identification and guidance quality. The implementation is built on AutoGen with a Llama-3-8B-Instruct backbone and QLoRA fine-tuning.

The empirical evaluation is on MRBench, a dataset of 1,214 middle-school mathematics dialogues. HPO-FT achieves Macro F1 of 0.845, outperforming GPT-4o (0.812) and several multi-agent baselines, including cooperative and unstructured adversarial variants. Ablations show that removing context distillation or the Devil’s Advocate most harms performance, leading the authors to conclude that structured adversarial interaction, more than model scale alone, is key to reliable AI tutoring in this classification setting.

finding.finding_summary: On MRBench’s middle-school mathematics dialogue classification task (n=1,214), the HPO-FT system achieved Macro F1 = 0.845. This outperformed GPT-4o (Macro F1 = 0.812) by 0.033 and also exceeded cooperative and unstructured multi-agent baselines, indicating stronger performance on mathematically grounded tutoring-quality judgments.
finding.measure: Macro F1 on mistake identification and guidance quality classification for middle-school mathematics dialogues

finding.finding_summary: The HPO pipeline improved classification performance but increased inference latency relative to a single model call. The paper reports total HPO-FT inference time of 4.2 seconds per evaluation, compared with 0.4 seconds for a single Llama-3-8B call and 1.2 seconds for GPT-4o, implying a substantial computational overhead for the added deliberative structure.
finding.measure: Inference latency per evaluation

paper_profiles.title: Retrieval-augmented Generation to Improve Math Question-Answering: Trade-offs Between Groundedness and Human Preference
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS 2023 Workshop on Generative AI for Education (GAIED) / arXiv
paper_profiles.population: Middle-school students (grades 8-9; K-12, mainly in Ghana and comparable contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve the quality of generative AI responses for conceptual middle-school math question answering, and whether increasing prompt guidance makes responses more grounded in a retrieved textbook. The authors motivate the work by noting that human tutoring and intelligent tutoring systems are effective for math learning, but that large language models can hallucinate or drift away from curriculum materials.

The intervention studied is a RAG-based chatbot pipeline built on GPT-3.5 that retrieves sections from the OpenStax Prealgebra textbook and generates answers to real student math questions. The authors compare three prompt guidance conditions—no guidance, low guidance, and high guidance—and, in a separate diagnostic condition, an information-retrieval-only prompt. The evaluation uses 51 real middle-school math questions from Math Nation for automated groundedness metrics, plus human judgments from 9 educators/designers who ranked response preference and rated groundedness; a third study had 3 annotators rate retrieval relevance.

The main finding is a trade-off: stronger prompt guidance increases groundedness, but the most preferred responses are produced by the low-guidance condition rather than the highly grounded high-guidance condition. Human raters perceived high-guidance outputs as more grounded, yet low-guidance outputs were preferred overall, suggesting that being closely tied to the textbook is not always what users like best. Retrieval relevance was positively associated with groundedness, but not with preference. The paper concludes that designers of math QA systems should balance faithfulness to educational materials with student preference and conversational usefulness, and that student-centered learning studies are still needed to determine whether these preferences translate into learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure math learning outcomes directly; instead it evaluates middle-school algebra and geometry question answering quality for 51 student queries. Human raters preferred the low-guidance RAG condition over the no-guidance and high-guidance conditions, while high guidance produced the most grounded responses, indicating a trade-off between answer preference and textbook alignment rather than clear evidence of improved math achievement.
finding.measure: Human preference rankings and groundedness ratings for generated math QA responses; automated groundedness metrics (K-F1++, BLEURT, BERTScore) on 51 math questions

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Large Language Models Creation of Interactive Learning Lessons
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models can automatically generate high-quality scenario-based lessons for training novice tutors who teach middle school mathematics online, and whether task decomposition improves the quality of the generated lessons. The authors frame lesson creation as a labor-intensive educational design problem, especially for tutor training programs that need structured scenarios, research-backed instruction, and feedback prompts.

To address this, the study uses GPT-4o with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to produce tutor-training lessons on three topics: encouraging students’ independence, encouraging help-seeking behavior, and turning on cameras. The key methodological comparison is among five prompting configurations, ranging from one-segment generation to five-segment decomposition, and the generated lessons are evaluated by two experienced human coders using a 17-code rubric. The paper also compares the best-performing LLM-generated lessons with human-crafted lessons through written feedback from two lesson designers.

The main finding is that decomposing generation into multiple subtasks improves lesson quality, with the three-segment approach producing the highest average ratings overall. The LLM-generated lessons were judged to be especially strong in producing structured scenarios, practical examples, and time-saving drafts that could support human-AI collaboration. However, the paper also identifies important limitations, including generic feedback for answer choices, unclear learning-objective wording in some configurations, weak pedagogical grounding in some outputs, and unreliable or fabricated references even when RAG was used.

Overall, the study concludes that LLMs can be useful for generating draft tutor-training materials, but they are not yet reliable enough to replace human instructional designers. The authors argue that the strongest use case is a collaborative workflow in which AI speeds up drafting and variation generation while humans refine clarity, pedagogy, and citation accuracy.

finding.finding_summary: Both human lesson designers reported substantial time savings when using the LLM-generated drafts, especially for creating scenario variants and multiple-choice questions. The paper’s qualitative evaluation indicates that AI-assisted drafting reduced repetitive authoring work and cognitive/logistical load, supporting faster lesson development, though no numeric effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Human designer feedback on drafting time, workload, and ease of lesson creation

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on generating tutor-training lessons for middle school mathematics, but it does not measure student math achievement directly. Instead, it evaluates whether LLM-generated math tutoring lessons were judged to be high-quality and pedagogically usable for mathematics tutor training; the best-performing three-segment approach received the highest average rating (14.67) across three lessons, while the one-segment approach was lowest (10.67).
finding.measure: Human ratings of the quality of middle school mathematics tutor-training lessons
finding.study_size: n=3 lessons, rated by n=2 coders

finding.finding_summary: The generated lessons were judged to support instructional skills such as scenario interpretation and pedagogically grounded explanation, but they also showed weaknesses in clarity, logical coherence, and feedback specificity. Human coders and lesson designers noted that decomposition improved some higher-order design features, yet some configurations produced disjointed instruction and generic explanations, indicating mixed effects on metacognitive and instructional reasoning-related quality.
finding.measure: Rubric codes for clarity of writing, pedagogy grounded, alignment with learning objectives, and feedback quality; designer feedback
finding.study_size: n=3 lessons, rated across 5 prompting configurations by n=2 coders; qualitative comparison by n=2 designers

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the LLM-generated lessons were designed around tutoring practices affecting student engagement, independence, and help-seeking, and designers viewed the scenarios as realistic and useful for preparing tutors to respond appropriately. However, the study did not measure student engagement or socio-emotional outcomes directly; the evidence is limited to evaluator judgments that the scenarios and guidance could support these goals.
finding.measure: Human evaluation of scenario realism and alignment with tutoring practices related to engagement/independence/help-seeking
finding.study_size: n=3 lessons, qualitative feedback from n=2 lesson designers

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT-generated help produces learning gains equivalent to human tutor-authored help on mathematics skills
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT-generated worked-solution hints can support mathematics learning as effectively as human tutor-authored hints, and whether such hints are accurate enough for educational use. The authors also test a hallucination-mitigation approach, self-consistency, to reduce the rate of incorrect ChatGPT outputs.

The study used a 3 x 4 randomized design with 274 Mechanical Turk participants assigned to one of three hint conditions (no-hint control, human tutor-authored hints, or ChatGPT-generated hints) and one of four mathematics subject areas drawn from OpenStax textbooks: Elementary Algebra, Intermediate Algebra, College Algebra, and Statistics. Participants completed a three-item pre-test, a five-item acquisition phase, and a three-item repeated post-test. The paper additionally evaluated ChatGPT hint quality by manual screening and by six undergraduate raters, reporting strong inter-rater agreement and substantial error rates in raw ChatGPT output.

Results showed that ChatGPT hints produced statistically significant pre-post learning gains overall and were not statistically significantly different from human tutor-authored hints on learning gains or time-on-task. ChatGPT participants had the largest overall gain (17.00%) compared with human tutor hints (11.62%) and control (1.85%), but the difference between ChatGPT and human tutor hints was not statistically significant. However, raw ChatGPT hints failed quality checks on 32% of problems; self-consistency reduced errors to near zero for algebra topics and 13% for statistics. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can generate effective math help in this setting, but that human oversight or error mitigation is important before classroom deployment.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT-generated hints produced statistically significant learning gains on mathematics skills in the overall sample (n=98 in ChatGPT condition; total analyzed n=274). The overall pre-test average was 43.51% and post-test average was 60.52%, a 17.00% gain; this was significant by Kruskal-Wallis/pre-post analysis (p < .001).
finding.measure: Pre-test to post-test mathematics problem performance across algebra and statistics learning objectives
finding.study_size: n=274 (ChatGPT n=98; human tutor n=86; control n=90)

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT hints were faster to produce than human tutor-authored hint sequences and required only a single generated worked solution per problem, whereas human-authored help required manual authoring and editing. The paper reports that ChatGPT hints were produced in about 1/20th the time of human tutor-authored hints, and that manual quality checking averaged 37.60 seconds per hint.
finding.measure: Hint authoring / generation time and manual quality-check time
finding.study_size: 75 ChatGPT-generated problems for quality checks; study process comparison across 4 subjects

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly measure durable skills such as critical thinking or metacognition, but it does use worked-solution hints and repeated testing to examine whether learners can benefit from example-based support. No direct durable-skill outcome is reported, so this is only a marginal fit and should be interpreted cautiously.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: All educational levels (primary, secondary, tertiary, professional development)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and risks of large language models, especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than testing an intervention, the authors synthesize early research and offer a conceptual overview of how LLMs might be used by students and teachers for content generation, feedback, tutoring, assessment support, and personalized learning across educational settings.

The paper discusses possible uses for elementary, middle, high school, university, and professional learning contexts, including math practice generation, reading/writing support, teacher lesson planning, and automated evaluation. It also reviews early examples of LLM applications in education and argues that these systems could support learning and teaching if used as complements to human instruction.

The core contribution is a balanced discussion of benefits and challenges. The authors emphasize concerns about bias, privacy, cost, sustainability, overreliance, plagiarism, and difficulty distinguishing machine-generated from human-generated work, and recommend human oversight, critical thinking, fact checking, and governance safeguards. Overall, the paper is a forward-looking position piece that proposes mitigation strategies and research directions rather than reporting empirical effects.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models can support middle and high school mathematics learning by generating practice problems, quizzes, and step-by-step explanations, and it cites prior works discussing automatic generation of math word problems. However, it does not report direct empirical evidence on mathematics outcomes for K-12 learners in this paper, so the claim remains conceptual rather than tested.
finding.measure: Math practice problems, quizzes, step-by-step solutions, and math word problem generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating or semi-automating lesson planning, personalized material creation, quiz generation, feedback, and grading support. It cites prior studies suggesting grading effort could be reduced by up to 85% in some NLP-based feedback systems, but these results are from other studies rather than original empirical analysis in this position paper.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, quiz/material generation, feedback production

finding.finding_summary: A central theme is that LLMs may support critical thinking, problem-solving, and fact-checking when used as a complement to instruction. The paper also warns that overreliance could undermine these same skills, making the overall direction mixed, but with a generally positive framing if the tools are used carefully.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, fact-checking, and related higher-order skills

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests LLMs may improve student engagement, curiosity, and participation, especially through interactive dialogue, tailored prompts, and support for remote or group learning. These are presented as anticipated benefits supported by cited prior work, not as outcomes measured in this paper.
finding.measure: Student engagement, curiosity, participation

finding.finding_summary: A substantial portion of the paper addresses institutional issues including governance, privacy, copyright, bias, fairness, access, sustainability, and policy responses for integrating LLMs into education. The overall conclusion is that the technology has promise, but responsible adoption requires strong institutional safeguards and human oversight; no empirical institutional outcome is reported in this paper.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, privacy/security, fairness, access, sustainability, and institutional adoption considerations

paper_profiles.title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a generative-AI system can improve live K-12 tutoring by giving novice tutors expert-like guidance in real time. The motivation is that high-quality expert coaching is expensive and difficult to scale, especially in under-resourced school settings where many tutors are inexperienced.

The intervention, Tutor CoPilot, is a human-AI system integrated into a virtual tutoring platform. When activated during math tutoring sessions, it generates context-sensitive suggestions based on the ongoing chat, lesson topic, and a chosen pedagogical strategy. The system is designed to help tutors provide better prompts, hints, and explanations without taking over the interaction, and it was built using a method that distills expert reasoning from think-aloud data.

The study is a preregistered RCT conducted with 900 tutors and 1,800 K-12 students in grades 3-8 from under-served communities in a southern U.S. school district, in partnership with FEV Tutor. Tutors were randomly assigned to have access to Tutor CoPilot or to continue usual practice. Outcomes included student learning on exit tickets, student survey responses, and automated analysis of tutor language from 550,000+ chat messages.

The main finding is that access to Tutor CoPilot improved proximal math learning: students with treatment tutors were 4 percentage points more likely to pass exit tickets, with especially large gains for students of lower-rated tutors (9 percentage points) and less-experienced tutors (7 percentage points). The tool also shifted tutor behavior toward more high-quality instructional strategies, such as asking guiding questions and prompting students to explain, and away from answer-giving behaviors. The authors report no statistically significant improvement on end-of-year math test scores over the short two-month study window.

finding.finding_summary: In the primary intent-to-treat analysis, students whose tutors had access to Tutor CoPilot were 4 percentage points more likely to pass exit tickets than control students (62% to 66%, p<0.01). The analysis used 4,136 tutoring sessions; conditional on attempting the exit ticket, treatment students were 3 percentage points more likely to pass (p<0.01), and lower-rated tutors saw a 9 percentage point increase in exit-ticket passing.
finding.measure: Math exit ticket pass rate / lesson-topic mastery

finding.finding_summary: Tutor CoPilot changed tutor language toward more expert-like pedagogical strategies that support deeper thinking. Using classifiers trained on 3,000 labeled messages and applied to 550,000+ chat messages, the authors found treatment tutors were more likely to prompt students to explain and ask questions to guide thinking, with these strategies used about 2 standard deviations more often on a log-odds scale than in control sessions.
finding.measure: Tutor message strategy use (e.g., prompting explanation, asking guiding questions, giving away answers)
finding.effect_size: ~2 standard deviations on z-scored log-odds scale for some strategies

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports small positive but statistically non-significant changes on student survey items related to caring, confidence, and preference for understanding over memorization. For example, treatment effects were 0.02 on 'My tutor cared about how well I do in math' and 0.02 on 'Even when math is hard, I know I can learn it,' with no statistically significant differences.
finding.measure: Student post-session survey responses about tutor care, confidence, and attitudes toward math

finding.finding_summary: Tutor CoPilot was positioned as a low-cost scalable support, with the authors estimating an annual cost of about $20 per tutor based on observed usage. The paper also notes the system reduced the need for tutors to craft prompts themselves, but it does not report a formal workload or productivity effect size beyond the cost estimate.
finding.measure: Estimated annual per-tutor cost and implied scalability/workflow support

paper_profiles.title: Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence: Early experiments with GPT-4
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a qualitative exploration of an early, text-only version of GPT-4, arguing that it shows broad, human-like capabilities across language, coding, mathematics, vision-related reasoning, tool use, and social interaction. The authors explicitly position the work as an investigation of an emerging general-purpose AI system rather than a formal benchmark study, and they use a variety of manually designed prompts and side-by-side comparisons with ChatGPT to illustrate strengths and limitations.

The paper focuses on demonstrating cross-domain performance, including writing poetry-style mathematical proofs, generating and editing code, solving mathematical problems, and answering questions about human motives and commonsense reasoning. It also includes informal comparisons where GPT-4 is asked to judge or compare outputs, and it repeatedly emphasizes that the tested model is an early non-multimodal version and that results should be interpreted as illustrative rather than definitive.

The paper does not study K-12 learners, classrooms, or educational interventions directly. Its main conclusion is that GPT-4 represents a substantial step toward more general AI, but it still has important limitations such as hallucinations, arithmetic errors, and weak planning; these capabilities are discussed mainly as evidence about AI progress rather than as educational outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents multiple qualitative demonstrations that GPT-4 can solve mathematical reasoning tasks, including a high-school level problem and other algebraic/logical prompts. No formal educational effect size is reported; the evidence is anecdotal and based on prompt-response examples rather than a controlled study.
finding.measure: Correctness on mathematical reasoning/problem-solving prompts

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 is shown to handle tasks requiring reasoning, abstraction, flexible transfer across domains, and explanation of its own outputs, suggesting strong performance on higher-order cognitive skills. The paper frames these as examples of general reasoning and conceptual synthesis, but provides no controlled measurement of these skills.
finding.measure: Performance on open-ended reasoning, synthesis, and explanation prompts

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights GPT-4’s ability to generate code, assist with technical interviews, create visualizations, and produce structured outputs quickly, implying potential productivity gains for users. For example, it reports that GPT-4 solved LeetCode interview assessments quickly and achieved strong scores, but these are not educational productivity outcomes and no experimental effect size is provided.
finding.measure: Performance on coding/interview-style tasks and generation speed in open-ended workflows

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes examples in writing, literature, history, and interdisciplinary composition, such as Shakespeare-style proofs and Plato-style dialogues. These demonstrations suggest GPT-4 can generate and transform text across non-mathematical academic domains, but the paper does not evaluate learner outcomes or provide quantitative comparisons beyond illustrative examples.
finding.measure: Quality of generated text in literature/humanities-style prompts

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT-Based Simulation Helps to Develop the Pre-Service Mathematics Teachers’ Critical Thinking
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether ChatGPT can be used as a simulation tool in pre-service mathematics teacher preparation, specifically as a digital platform that generates plausible student-like answers with errors that trainees can diagnose and correct. The authors frame this as a way to create quasi-professional practice for teacher candidates, helping them learn to check mathematical reasoning, identify mistakes, and improve their critical thinking.

The experiment was conducted in 2023 at Sumy State Pedagogical University with 32 pre-service mathematics teachers (14 bachelor's and 18 master's students). Participants worked with ChatGPT-generated solutions to inequality proofs, especially tasks based on the method of mathematical induction, and then completed individual work across two time points one month apart. The study qualitatively examined whether students could detect and correct errors in ChatGPT outputs, and it used a Wilcoxon test to compare paired scores over time.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT can produce plausible but mathematically incorrect answers that are useful for teacher training, because students were able to identify errors and often improve with repeated exposure. The authors report a statistically significant increase in critical-thinking-related task scores over time (Wilcoxon T=243; 18 positive changes among 32 participants), and argue that working with ChatGPT improved pre-service teachers' critical thinking. The study is limited to one topic area, one language context (Ukrainian prompts), and a small sample, so the findings are best interpreted as preliminary evidence about simulation-based teacher preparation rather than broad efficacy evidence for ChatGPT in K-12 mathematics instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that repeated work with ChatGPT-generated mathematical proofs improved pre-service mathematics teachers’ critical thinking. Using a paired pre/post design with n=32, the authors reported 18 positive score changes, 4 negative changes, and 10 unchanged pairs; a Wilcoxon test yielded T=243, leading them to reject the null hypothesis that ChatGPT-based tasks do not improve critical thinking.
finding.measure: Critical thinking performance on four task-based indicators: analyzing information critically, identifying logical inconsistencies, rectifying inconsistencies, and seeking the most rational approach to problem-solving

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a PRISMA-based systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education from 2016 to 2022. The authors sought to update the field’s understanding of where AI in education research is being conducted, who the first authors are affiliated with, what academic levels and subject domains are being studied, who the intended users are, and how AI is being used in higher education.

The review included 138 peer-reviewed journal articles identified through database and hand searches. The studies were mostly conducted in Asia and North America, with China emerging as the leading country in recent publications. Undergraduate students were the most frequently studied population, and language learning was the most common subject domain, followed by computer science and engineering.

Using deductive and grounded coding, the authors identified five major uses of AI in higher education: assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. The review concludes that AI in higher education is growing rapidly, but much of the research still focuses on traditional uses such as prediction, feedback, and adaptive support. The authors highlight gaps in research on graduate education, developing-country contexts, and less-explored uses such as managerial support and newer tools like ChatGPT.

finding.finding_summary: This review found that AI in higher education was most commonly used in language learning, computer science, and engineering rather than in a single achievement domain. Across the 138 reviewed studies, language learning was the most common subject domain (17%), with uses including writing, reading, and vocabulary support; however, the paper is descriptive and does not report a pooled effect size or causal comparison.
finding.measure: Subject-domain distribution of included studies; descriptive uses of AI in language learning

finding.finding_summary: The review reports substantial use of AI for literacy-related tasks, especially writing, reading, and vocabulary acquisition. Examples include automatic assessment to improve academic writing skills and AI-based feedback systems, but the paper synthesizes study purposes and trends rather than reporting a pooled estimate of literacy gains.
finding.measure: Writing, reading, vocabulary-related AI applications; descriptive outcomes from included studies

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies used AI to support emotions, persistence, self-regulation, and engagement. The review highlights automatic feedback, AI assistants, and systems that modeled student emotion or supported goal initiation and persistence, indicating that AI was often used to bolster motivational and self-regulatory processes, though no pooled effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student emotion, persistence, self-regulated learning, engagement behaviors

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes AI use for higher-order thinking, reflection, and other durable skills, especially through assessment/evaluation and learning analytics applications. For example, some studies evaluated online reflections and higher-order thinking, but the review does not quantify the magnitude of improvement.
finding.measure: Reflection, higher-order thinking, and related durable-skill outcomes in included studies

finding.finding_summary: A major finding is that AI was frequently used to improve instructional efficiency, particularly through automatic assessment, feedback generation, question creation, learning analytics, and instructional design support. The authors note that automatic assessment can reduce instructor grading time and that AI can help manage large data sets and streamline educational workflows, but the review does not provide a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Instructor workload reduction, automated grading, feedback generation, learning analytics, instructional design support
finding.study_size: n=138 studies (descriptive synthesis); 26 studies for automatic assessment; 19 studies for managing student learning

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies institutional-level uses of AI for managing student learning, predictive analytics, admissions-related decisions, curriculum sequencing, and quality assurance. These applications suggest potential systemic benefits for institutional decision-making, but the paper is a field-mapping review and does not report outcome effects for institutional performance.
finding.measure: Institutional uses of AI for prediction, admissions, curriculum sequencing, and quality assurance

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics appears as a recurring domain in the included studies, especially through college mathematics and online mathematics-course examples. The review notes AI use in an online mathematics course and in mathematics-adjacent tutoring and prediction contexts, but it does not report a synthesized effect on math achievement.
finding.measure: Mathematics course applications and mathematics-related AI uses in included studies

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing healthcare: the role of artificial intelligence in clinical practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review article examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is being applied in healthcare and clinical practice. The paper asks what AI can do across diagnosis, treatment selection, population health management, patient education, and clinician decision support, while also considering the associated technical, ethical, legal, and implementation challenges.

The paper is a narrative review of indexed literature from PubMed/Medline, Scopus, and EMBASE, limited to English-language publications. It synthesizes examples of AI in disease diagnosis, genomic medicine, precision treatment, therapeutic drug monitoring, predictive analytics, virtual health assistants, mental health support, and patient education.
