Across these domains, the authors conclude that AI has substantial potential to improve accuracy, efficiency, cost-effectiveness, and personalization of care, but real-world deployment requires high-quality data, human oversight, privacy protections, and attention to bias and transparency.

The population context is healthcare and clinical practice broadly, not K-12 education. The article does mention intelligent tutoring systems in passing as an example of AI in academia, but it does not study educational outcomes or compare generative AI tools in mathematics instruction. Its main contribution is a broad conceptual and literature-based overview of AI applications in medicine and the conditions needed for responsible implementation.

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses how artificial intelligence is reshaping education, with a particular focus on three competencies the author argues are essential for students and educators: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. The article asks how institutions should respond to generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, especially in academic writing and classroom practice, and it uses a Swiss university case study together with a narrative literature review to motivate a more deliberate institutional approach.

The main empirical context is a university of applied sciences in Zurich, Switzerland, where informal discussions with students, lecturers, and administrators informed the development of internal AI guidelines. The paper describes tensions between banning AI and allowing unrestricted use, and it argues for a middle ground: students may use AI, but must disclose the model, explain the use, critically evaluate outputs, and document where AI was used. The article also surveys classroom uses of AI and proposes workshops, guidelines, and dedicated support to build an AI culture.

The paper does not test an instructional intervention or compare student outcomes experimentally. Instead, it is a conceptual and practice-oriented discussion that synthesizes prior literature on AI literacy and prompting methods, while recommending that schools teach students how to interact responsibly with AI and how to scrutinize its outputs. Its conclusions are normative: institutions should foster transparent, critical, and well-supported AI use rather than prohibit it outright or leave it unregulated.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that institutions should adopt structured AI governance rather than either banning or fully unrestrictedly allowing generative AI. In the Swiss university case, the author describes the creation of internal AI guidelines requiring disclosure of AI use, critical evaluation, and appendix documentation, but no quantitative institutional outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: institutional AI guidelines, governance practices, policy design

finding.finding_summary: Critical thinking is presented as a central educational goal of AI use, especially through prompt engineering and critical evaluation of AI outputs. The paper is conceptual and literature-based rather than empirical, so it reports no measured effect size or sample-based outcome on critical thinking.
finding.measure: critical thinking, prompt engineering skill, critical evaluation of AI outputs

finding.finding_summary: The article suggests that AI tools can improve efficiency in academic tasks such as drafting, brainstorming, curriculum creation, and classroom preparation. These are presented as practical benefits from the case study and discussion, but the paper provides no quantitative measurement of productivity or workload reduction.
finding.measure: workflow efficiency, curriculum creation, academic writing support

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how elementary students and teachers perceive creative mathematical writing activities supported by generative AI. The authors are interested in whether GenAI can support students as they create math stories, represent mathematical ideas visually, and revise AI-generated drafts, as well as what challenges arise when using such tools in real classrooms.

The researchers implemented a GenAI-powered learning environment in six 5th-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools, involving 79 students and six teachers. The activity followed an Ask–Represent–Transform sequence: students first analyzed a provided math story, then represented their thinking on a canvas, and finally used GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 to co-create and revise culturally relevant math stories. Data came from student focus groups, teacher interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations, and were analyzed thematically.

Findings suggest that students and teachers saw several benefits of the GenAI-supported approach, including increased creativity in math writing, improved mathematical understanding, greater AI literacy, and stronger interest, curiosity, and ownership in learning. At the same time, participants identified important challenges: students sometimes failed to critically evaluate AI output, struggled to generate coherent prompts and stories, and wanted more room to create without AI. Teachers and students also wanted better adaptive feedback, more social interaction, and more accessible communication options. Overall, the paper argues that GenAI can support mathematical creative writing, but only when paired with intentional instructional and interface design.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived that GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing strengthened mathematical understanding by helping students break down problems, represent mathematical ideas, and uncover misconceptions. The study is qualitative and does not report test-score effect sizes; evidence comes from interviews and observations with n=79 students and 6 teachers.
finding.measure: Student and teacher perceptions of mathematical understanding, problem representation, and misconception uncovering during story-based math writing

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that the GenAI-supported activity increased interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership in mathematics learning. Students described math as more fun and engaging, and teachers observed heightened attention and motivation during culturally relevant story creation; no quantitative effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership in learning math

finding.finding_summary: The study found that GenAI-supported writing appeared to foster divergent and convergent thinking, flexible thinking, original creation, prompt engineering, and critical evaluation of AI outputs. However, participants also reported difficulties critically evaluating AI-generated content and formulating coherent stories, indicating both skill development and remaining challenges; no quantitative effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Perceived creativity, prompt engineering, critical evaluation, and problem formulation during AI-supported math writing

finding.finding_summary: Because the intervention centers on creative mathematical writing, participants discussed improvements in writing, story drafting, editing, and adding detail to AI-generated drafts. The evidence is qualitative and focused on student/teacher perceptions rather than standardized writing outcomes; no effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions of creative writing, story drafting, and revision in math-story composition

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and students noted that GenAI could help generate story drafts quickly and reduce the effort of starting from scratch, which may improve writing productivity. However, the study did not measure time-on-task or workload quantitatively, so this finding is based on perceptions only and no effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Perceived drafting efficiency and reduced burden in creating math stories

paper_profiles.title: Novice Learner and Expert Tutor: Evaluating Math Reasoning Abilities of Large Language Models with Misconceptions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes a new way to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on grade-school mathematics by testing whether they can behave like a novice learner with specific misconceptions and like an expert tutor who can identify misconceptions behind an incorrect answer. Rather than asking models to simply solve math problems correctly, the authors construct prompts that require the model to produce a particular wrong answer associated with a known misconception, or to infer the misconception from an incorrect response.

The study uses a curated Eedi dataset of 213 multiple-choice grade-school math questions with expert-labeled misconceptions attached to incorrect answer choices. The authors evaluate GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 under zero-shot and few-shot prompting conditions, with and without explanations. GPT-4 performs very well on standard correct-answer math QA (up to 94.8% accuracy), but substantially worse when asked to intentionally answer incorrectly in a specified way (e.g. 61.7% in one zero-shot setting). In the tutor-like task, GPT-4 can identify the correct misconception well when given only a small candidate set (91.9% at n=4), but accuracy falls sharply as the candidate misconception set grows (to 39.8% at n=100). The authors conclude that LLMs remain limited in simulating student misconceptions and in robustly diagnosing them, which has implications for educational applications such as intelligent tutoring systems.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on grade-school math reasoning using 213 multiple-choice questions from Eedi. GPT-4 achieved high correct-answer accuracy (0.948 with explanations; 0.774 without explanations), but performance dropped when the model was asked to produce a specific incorrect answer tied to a misconception (best reported GPT-4 novice-learner accuracy 0.679 in few-shot same-misconception prompting; 0.617 in zero-shot with explanations).
finding.measure: Accuracy on grade-school multiple-choice math questions; accuracy on producing misconception-specific incorrect answers

finding.finding_summary: The study directly tests misconception diagnosis and controllable error generation as a proxy for reasoning about student thinking, which is closely related to metacognition and diagnostic reasoning. GPT-4’s accuracy in identifying the correct misconception was high with a small candidate set (0.919 at n=4) but declined to 0.398 when 100 misconception options were provided, indicating limited robustness in this higher-order reasoning task.
finding.measure: Accuracy in identifying the misconception that explains an incorrect answer
finding.study_size: n=213 questions; n varied by misconception set size

finding.finding_summary: The authors frame the work as relevant to intelligent tutoring systems and educational AI evaluation, arguing that LLMs’ limited ability to simulate misconceptions constrains their usefulness for educational deployment. This is an application-oriented contribution rather than an outcome study, but it provides evidence about the readiness of LLMs for tutoring-system use.
finding.measure: Model suitability for intelligent tutoring system–style student simulation and tutoring support

paper_profiles.title: Educators’ Perceptions of Large Language Models as Tutors: Comparing Human and AI Tutors in a Blind Text-only Setting
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how educators judge the quality of large language model (LLM)-based tutors relative to human tutors in a blind, text-only setting. The authors focus not on learning gains, but on four latent tutoring qualities thought to matter for instruction: engagement, empathy, scaffolding, and conciseness.

To create comparable tutoring interactions, the study uses grade-school math word problem conversations from MathDial as the human-tutor condition and MWPTutor as the LLM-tutor condition. Both were truncated to five turns and then presented in randomized side-by-side pairs to 35 annotators with teaching experience, who selected which tutor performed better on each metric. The paper also had three LLMs perform the same comparisons for contrast.

The main finding is that annotators with teaching experience generally preferred the LLM tutor over the human tutor on all four metrics, with statistically significant differences for conciseness, empathy, and scaffolding, but not engagement. The authors interpret this as evidence that LLMs can match or outperform humans on certain text-only tutoring behaviors in this constrained math setting, while also noting that LLM judgments are more strongly biased toward the LLM-generated tutor than human judgments are. The study does not measure student learning outcomes directly, so its conclusions are limited to perceived tutoring quality rather than efficacy.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly compares tutor quality in grade-school math word problem tutoring dialogs, but it does not measure student math achievement. Instead, 35 annotators with teaching experience judged 210 dialog pairs and generally preferred MWPTutor over MathDial on scaffolding and conciseness, with significant differences on scaffolding (t=3.16, p<0.001) and conciseness (t=3.65, p<0.001).
finding.measure: Teacher-rated quality of tutoring dialogs for grade-school math word problems
finding.study_size: n=210 dialog pairs; n=35 human annotators

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studies engagement and empathy as tutoring qualities, both of which are closely tied to student socio-emotional experience. Human annotators preferred MWPTutor for empathy with a significant difference (mean score 0.65, SD 2.81, t=3.36, p<0.001), while engagement showed a smaller, non-significant advantage for MWPTutor (mean score 0.25, SD 2.72, t=1.32, p=0.09).
finding.measure: Blind pairwise human judgments of tutor engagement and empathy
finding.study_size: n=210 dialog pairs; n=35 human annotators

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats scaffolding as a core tutoring quality because it supports student problem solving and independent reasoning. Across 210 dialog pairs, annotators rated MWPTutor as better at scaffolding than MathDial, with a significant human-annotation result (mean score 0.55, SD 2.51, t=3.16, p<0.001).
finding.measure: Blind pairwise human judgments of scaffolding quality in tutor dialogs
finding.study_size: n=210 dialog pairs; n=35 human annotators

finding.finding_summary: Conciseness is studied as a tutoring-efficiency attribute, with the authors arguing that shorter, more direct dialogue can reduce redundancy and frustration. Human annotators preferred MWPTutor on conciseness in 210 paired comparisons, and the difference was significant (mean score 0.55, SD 2.19, t=3.65, p<0.001).
finding.measure: Blind pairwise human judgments of tutor conciseness
finding.study_size: n=210 dialog pairs; n=35 human annotators

paper_profiles.title: Combining Large Language Models with Tutoring System Intelligence: A Case Study in Caregiver Homework Support
paper_profiles.venue: LAK 2025 (Proceedings of the 15th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how large language models (LLMs) can be combined with an intelligent tutoring system’s instructional model to generate better conversational support for caregivers helping children with math homework. The authors focus on a hybrid tutoring scenario in which caregivers use live chat alongside a middle-school equation-solving tutor, and they explore whether real-time problem-solving context from the tutoring system can improve the relevance and pedagogical quality of LLM-generated message recommendations.

The intervention is the Caregiver Conversational Support Tool (CCST), which embeds an open-source Llama 3 8B Instruct model into the Lynnette equation-solving tutoring system. The prompt includes tutoring-system signals such as correctness, hint use, current equation state, previous chat messages, and suggested next steps from the ITS instructional model, along with few-shot examples and tutoring-practice guidance. The study has two parts: qualitative prompt engineering experiments and a prototyping study with ten middle-school caregivers recruited through a university summer program and remote interviews.

The main findings are that adding tutoring-system context and tutoring-practice examples produced more contextually relevant, pedagogically aligned recommendations than simpler prompts. Caregivers especially valued content-level support and metacognitive prompts that asked students to explain their thinking, while motivational praise was seen as less useful by many participants. The paper concludes that LLMs can be made more useful for caregiver homework support when grounded in ITS data and tutoring principles, though latency, message length, and tone remain design challenges.

finding.finding_summary: The system generated math-help recommendations that caregivers judged to be more contextually relevant and pedagogically useful when grounded in the tutoring system’s equation-solving state. The study did not measure student math achievement directly; instead, it showed that adding problem-solving context (e.g., current equation, correctness, hint use, next steps) improved the quality of generated math support in a ten-caregiver prototyping study.
finding.measure: Caregiver evaluation of LLM-generated math-support messages for equation-solving practice

finding.finding_summary: Caregivers preferred prompts that asked students to explain their reasoning and walk through their thinking, indicating support for metacognition and self-explanation. In the prototype study, five caregivers explicitly favored messages that prompted student explanation of thought processes, and the generated recommendations were designed to encourage reflective problem solving rather than only answer giving.
finding.measure: Caregiver preferences for metacognitive/self-explanation message recommendations

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that caregivers varied in how useful they found motivational support. Some participants valued the encouraging tone and praise, but six caregivers preferred direct content-level help, and several described praise-focused messages as ‘just filler’ or misaligned with their tutoring style. The qualitative evidence suggests motivational support can help, but it was not the primary need for most caregivers in this setting.
finding.measure: Caregiver perceptions of motivational versus content-level message recommendations

paper_profiles.title: AI tutoring can safely and effectively support students: An exploratory RCT in UK classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a generative AI tutor can safely and effectively support secondary students in mathematics when integrated into a real classroom platform. The motivation is the long-standing challenge that one-to-one tutoring is highly effective but difficult and expensive to scale, and the authors test whether LearnLM, a pedagogically fine-tuned genAI model, can help provide scalable tutoring support without sacrificing learning quality or safety.

The study was conducted in five UK secondary schools with N=165 Year 9-10 students using the Eedi mathematics platform. Students who made errors were randomly assigned either to receive static pre-written hints or interactive tutoring; tutoring sessions were further randomized to either a human tutor alone or a human tutor supervising LearnLM drafts. Supervising tutors reviewed every AI-generated message before it was sent, allowing the team to compare human tutoring, supervised AI tutoring, and non-interactive digital hints under classroom conditions.

The main findings suggest that supervised LearnLM tutoring was safe, pedagogically strong, and at least as effective as human tutoring for immediate remediation and misconception resolution. On a transfer measure, students supported by LearnLM were somewhat more likely than those supported by human tutors alone to solve a novel problem on the next topic (66.2% vs. 60.7%, a 5.5 percentage-point difference; credible interval reported as [-1.4%, +12.4%]). The paper also reports that tutors found the system efficient and appreciated its Socratic prompting, though they often edited messages to add pacing and social-emotional nuance.

finding.finding_summary: The RCT found that both interactive tutoring conditions improved mathematics learning outcomes, and supervised LearnLM was at least as effective as human tutoring for immediate remediation and misconception resolution. For durable transfer to a new math topic, students tutored by LearnLM scored 66.2% versus 60.7% for human-tutor-only sessions, a 5.5 percentage-point advantage with a reported 95% credible interval of [-1.4%, +12.4%].
finding.measure: Correctness on diagnostic mathematics questions, including second-attempt remediation, misconception resolution within a study unit, and transfer to the first question of the next study unit

finding.finding_summary: Student survey feedback indicated that interactive tutoring was viewed somewhat more favorably than static hints. Students who received interactive tutoring rated helpfulness at 3.9/5 compared with 3.6/5 for static hints, with posterior probability of an advantage for tutoring of 74.9%.
finding.measure: Post-trial student ratings of helpfulness of the support received

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides evidence that supervised LearnLM improved tutor workflow and perceived efficiency. In post-trial surveys, 82.4% of tutors selected 'supporting multiple students at the same time' as LearnLM’s most useful feature, and tutor comfort with AI rose from 3.4 to 3.9 out of 5 (posterior probability of increase: 90.0%).
finding.measure: Tutor surveys, interviews, and qualitative reports of workload/efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The study’s transfer outcome is also relevant to durable skills because it captures whether students could apply learning to a new problem on a subsequent topic. LearnLM-supported students were more likely than human-tutor-only students to solve the novel next-topic problem (66.2% vs. 60.7%), suggesting stronger knowledge transfer and possibly deeper understanding.
finding.measure: Knowledge transfer to a novel mathematics problem on the next study unit

paper_profiles.title: Elementary Math Word Problem Generation using Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of generating elementary mathematics word problems (MWPs) automatically, with the goal of reducing the manual workload on tutors and providing students with more practice items. The authors argue that existing MWP-generation systems either require substantial manual input (e.g., seeds, equations, or context) or fail to meet curriculum-specific constraints such as grade level and question type.

The study develops an MWP generation system built on open-source large language models, focusing on generating questions for grades 1-6 aligned to the Common Core curriculum. The authors compare candidate LLMs, prompt patterns, decoding settings for diversity, fine-tuning with manually created datasets, few-shot prompting, preference optimization (DPO/KTO/CPO), and a secondary LLM-based solvability checker. Evaluation combines human annotation and LLM-as-judge methods over generated MWPs, including error categories such as grammatical errors, solvability, realism, grade relevance, and section relevance.

The main conclusion is that LLMs can generate mostly fluent and solvable elementary MWPs, but they still struggle to reliably satisfy the requested grade and section requirements. Fine-tuning, few-shot prompting, and solvability filtering improve performance, with the best results coming from the fine-tuned Llama-2 model plus few-shot prompting and solvability checks. The paper’s central contribution is thus a generation pipeline and curated datasets, rather than evidence that generative AI improves student learning outcomes relative to teacher-led instruction or tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that automatic generation of elementary math word problems can reduce manual tutor effort because the system produces MWPs from only grade, section, and count inputs. The authors report that human and automated evaluations confirmed high-quality outputs with minimal spelling and grammar issues, indicating the system is useful for content creation workflows; however, no direct effect size on time savings or productivity is reported.
finding.measure: Human and automated evaluation of generated MWP quality; qualitative claims about tutor workload reduction
finding.study_size: n=4K generated MWPs in the main dataset; n=312 MWPs for evaluation subset; 7 human evaluators

finding.finding_summary: The system is designed to generate practice problems for elementary mathematics across grades 1-6 and multiple curriculum sections (e.g., addition, subtraction, fractions), which can support math practice. The paper does not test student learning gains, but it reports that the generated problems were largely solvable and mathematically appropriate, with the best model achieving 93.08% solvable problems in zero-shot and 84.17% solvable after fine-tuning plus solvability filtering in the summary table.
finding.measure: Solvability, grade relevance, section relevance, and overall human/LLM error evaluations of generated math word problems
finding.study_size: n=312 evaluation MWPs; broader generated corpus n=4K

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that a diverse set of math word problems can help students develop logical thinking and problem-solving practice. Diversity was explicitly optimized and measured using Self-BLEU and Jaccard scores, with the best parameter setting reducing Self-BLEU to 0.003976 and Jaccard to 0.181161, indicating more diverse generated questions.
finding.measure: Output diversity of generated math word problems (Self-BLEU, Jaccard)
finding.study_size: n=generated MWPs under multiple decoding settings

paper_profiles.title: Automated Feedback in Math Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLMs for Open-Ended Responses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can improve automated scoring and feedback generation for middle-school open-ended mathematics responses. The authors compare three systems: a fine-tuned Mistral-based model (GOAT), an existing SBERT-Canberra similarity-based method, and GPT-4 Turbo used zero-shot with a grading rubric. The study asks which approach best predicts teacher scores and which produces the most useful feedback for student math work.

The dataset comes from an online learning platform using Illustrative Mathematics problems. The authors use 50 open-response math problems with 100 student responses each, split into training and test sets, yielding 4,000 training and 1,000 test instances for scoring, plus a human review sample of 100 test responses for feedback evaluation. For scoring, GOAT outperformed SBERT and GPT-4 on AUC, RMSE, and Kappa. For feedback quality, however, GPT-4 was judged best by two experienced teachers on accuracy, relevance, motivation, and overall preference. The paper concludes that fine-tuned open-source LLMs can improve auto-scoring, but stronger general-purpose LLMs still produce better teacher-preferred feedback, and that feedback quality is constrained by the quality of teacher-written training data.

finding.finding_summary: The fine-tuned GOAT model outperformed the SBERT-Canberra baseline and GPT-4 Turbo on automated scoring of middle-school open-response math problems. On the 1,000-item test set, GOAT achieved the best AUC (0.697), lowest RMSE (1.119), and highest Cohen’s kappa (0.422) versus SBERT (AUC=0.662, RMSE=1.364, kappa=0.362) and GPT-4 (AUC=0.639, RMSE=1.160, kappa=0.266).
finding.measure: Automated scoring of student open-ended math responses using AUC, RMSE, and multi-class Cohen’s kappa against teacher-assigned scores
finding.study_size: n=1000 test responses for scoring; 50 problems

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests LLM-based automated scoring and feedback can reduce teacher workload by supporting grading and draft feedback generation for open-ended math items. This conclusion is qualitative rather than based on a direct workload experiment, but the authors explicitly frame the systems as helping teachers by automating scoring and producing feedback drafts, with human raters describing the outputs as potentially useful starting points.
finding.measure: Teacher time/workload implications discussed alongside automated scoring and feedback generation workflow

paper_profiles.title: MathRobust-LV: Evaluation of Large Language Models’ Robustness to Linguistic Variations in Mathematical Reasoning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models that perform well on math benchmarks remain reliable when the same high-school-level math problems are rephrased in linguistically different but mathematically equivalent ways. The authors argue that educational deployments such as tutoring systems, homework help, and assessment tools require robustness to paraphrase, because students and instructors often express the same mathematical structure with different wording.

To test this, the authors create MathRobust-LV, a benchmark built from 130 seed problems drawn from the MATH dataset and scraped AoPS competition problems at difficulty levels 4 and 5. They generate 520 variants using four controlled perturbation types: variable substitution, context substitution, full rewriting with variables fixed, and full rewriting with variable changes. The final benchmark preserves numerical structure, solution logic, and final answer while altering surface language, and the paper evaluates 34 open- and closed-source LLMs in a zero-shot pass@1 setting.

The main conclusion is that linguistic variation consistently reduces accuracy for most models, often by 2-6 points and sometimes by much more for smaller models (e.g., OpenMath-Nemotron-1.5B drops 11.52 points; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B drops 9.59 points). Larger models are generally more stable, and a few frontier models such as Gemini-2.5-pro and GPT-5 show little or no degradation, but the overall pattern suggests substantial brittleness to benign rewordings. The results support the authors’ claim that benchmark performance alone does not demonstrate robust mathematical reasoning in educational settings.

finding.finding_summary: Across 34 models, accuracy generally declined when moving from original high-school math problems to linguistically varied but mathematically equivalent variants. Most open-source models dropped by about 2-6 percentage points, with larger declines for smaller checkpoints such as OpenMath-Nemotron-1.5B (75.36% baseline to 63.84% variant, -11.52) and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (58.44% to 48.85%, -9.59).
finding.measure: Pass@1 accuracy on high-school-level math problem-solving under baseline vs linguistically varied variants

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Auto-Grading and Feedback System for Constructive Geometry Tasks Using Large Language Models on an Online Math Platform
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for scalable, teacher-aligned assessment and formative feedback for open-ended mathematics tasks, especially constructive geometry problems that are difficult to grade with simple answer matching. The authors ask whether a large language model (GPT-4) can support auto-grading and feedback generation for multi-step geometry tasks on an online platform and how closely such automated judgments align with teacher judgments.

The intervention is a personalized auto-grading and feedback system deployed on Algeomath, a Korean dynamic geometry platform. Closed-ended items were graded by rules, while open-ended explanation items used few-shot prompting with teacher-authored exemplars, and constructive geometry tasks used programmatic checks on submitted geometric constructions. Feedback was dynamically adapted to correctness and attempt number, with up to three retries and increasingly explicit guidance across attempts.

The study was piloted in four middle-school classes in South Korea with 79 students and 18 geometry items spanning closed-ended, open-ended, and constructive-geometry formats. Results showed perfect agreement with teachers for rule-based items and substantial agreement for LLM-graded explanations overall (agreement = 0.866, Cohen’s κ = 0.737 across 878 explanation responses), though some items were weaker (e.g., Q15 κ = 0.434). Feedback quality was generally serviceable (pooled mean guidance score 3.98/5, SD = 1.78, n = 754) but sometimes leaked answers or used imprecise terminology. Students often improved after feedback: 36.7% (260/708) of initially incorrect responses were corrected on the next attempt, though evidence for transfer to later questions was not statistically significant. Overall, the paper suggests LLMs can support scalable formative assessment in middle-school geometry, but teacher oversight and better feedback design remain important.

finding.finding_summary: The system supported mathematics task performance in constructive geometry and open-ended explanation items. For rule-based closed-ended and CGT items, grading agreement with teachers was 100%; for seven LLM-graded explanation items, overall agreement was 0.866 with Cohen’s κ = 0.737 across n=878 responses, indicating substantial consistency. Students also corrected 36.7% (260/708) of initially incorrect responses on the next attempt after feedback.
finding.measure: Teacher-agreement on grading accuracy; post-feedback correctness conversion; item-level correctness/learning curves on geometry tasks
finding.study_size: n=79 students; n=878 explanation responses; n=708 feedback-supported incorrect attempts
finding.std_deviation: SD = 1.78 for pooled feedback guidance score

paper_profiles.title: Automated Generation of Curriculum-Aligned Multiple-Choice Questions for Malaysian Secondary Mathematics Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of creating scalable, curriculum-aligned assessment items for Malaysian secondary mathematics, where teachers face substantial workload in producing high-quality multiple-choice questions. The authors argue that generative AI can automate this process, but only if its output is grounded in authoritative curriculum materials rather than relying on unconstrained prompting, which can produce generic or misaligned questions.

The study compares four GPT-4o-based pipelines for generating Form 1 Mathematics MCQs in Bahasa Melayu: two non-grounded prompting methods and two Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) methods, one using LangChain and one manually implemented with custom chunking and retrieval. The system is grounded in official Malaysian curriculum documents, including teacher-prepared notes and the yearly teaching plan (RPT), and the generated questions are evaluated automatically using semantic textual similarity for curriculum alignment and a RAG-based QA check for contextual validity.

The context is Malaysian secondary mathematics (Form 1) and a low-resource language setting (Bahasa Melayu). The paper reports that all methods produced fluent output, but the RAG pipelines were far more aligned with curriculum standards and more likely to be answerable from the curriculum documents. The manual RAG pipeline performed best overall, suggesting that domain-aware chunking can improve quality, while the framework-based LangChain RAG offered a more practical balance of performance and implementation effort. The authors conclude that grounding is essential for trustworthy educational question generation, but they also note that automated metrics cannot fully assess pedagogical depth or cognitive level, so human review remains necessary.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies whether generative AI can reduce the effort required to create curriculum-aligned assessment items. It argues that automated question generation can substantially lessen teacher workload and enables scalable production of question banks, while the RAG-based pipelines produced high-quality output across 100 generated questions per method, making the workflow more practical for educational content creation.
finding.measure: Question generation pipeline performance and discussion of teacher workload / scalability

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on Form 1 mathematics question generation for the topic of rational numbers. RAG-based methods outperformed non-grounded prompting on curriculum alignment, with average STS scores of 0.86 and 0.89 versus 0.58 and 0.55, and validity rates of 92% and 96% versus 15% and 12%, indicating that grounded generation produced more mathematically relevant and curriculum-consistent MCQs.
finding.measure: Curriculum alignment (STS) and RAG-QA validity of generated mathematics MCQs

paper_profiles.title: SMRC: Aligning Large Language Models with Student Reasoning for Mathematical Error Correction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of correcting mathematical reasoning errors in large language models in a way that is more pedagogically appropriate for educational settings. The authors argue that existing self-correction methods are insufficient because they optimize for final-answer correctness but do not preserve the student’s original reasoning path, which is important for teacher-style feedback and cognitive support.

To address this, the paper proposes SMRC (Student Mathematical Reasoning Correction), a framework that combines Monte Carlo Tree Search with a reward model trained on process-level supervision. The method is designed to preserve correct student steps while repairing erroneous ones, using Q-values to guide search and iterative feedback to generate minimally corrected solutions. The authors also introduce MSEB, a new benchmark of 158 authentic high school mathematics solution records with multiple valid solution paths and annotated correct steps.

The empirical evaluation compares SMRC against direct correction, thought-preserving correction, Self-Check, and Self-Refine on ProcessBench, MR-GSM8K, and MSEB. Results show that SMRC generally improves both answer accuracy and correct-step retention, especially on MR-GSM8K and MSEB, and that its search-based approach outperforms simpler generation-based methods in balancing correctness with preservation of student reasoning. The paper is an algorithmic benchmarking study rather than a classroom intervention study.

finding.finding_summary: SMRC improved mathematical error-correction performance compared with baselines, especially on MR-GSM8K and MSEB. On MSEB, SMRC achieved ACC=40.1 and CSRR=73.7 (HM=51.8), outperforming direct correction, thought-preserving correction, Self-Check, and Self-Refine; on MR-GSM8K it reached ACC=91.4 and CSRR=94.5 (HM=92.9).
finding.measure: Mathematical error correction accuracy (ACC), correct step retention rate (CSRR), and harmonic mean (HM) on math reasoning benchmarks

paper_profiles.title: FACET: Teacher-Centred LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems—Towards Personalized Educational Worksheets
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that teachers in heterogeneous classrooms, especially in mathematics, need support to create differentiated instructional materials that account for both students’ knowledge and motivational profiles. The authors argue that most existing AI personalization systems are overly performance-focused and student-facing, leaving a gap in direct teacher support for classroom differentiation.

To address this, they introduce FACET (Framework for Agent-based Classroom Enhancement for Teacher), a teacher-facing, LLM-based multi-agent system that generates personalized worksheets. FACET uses learner agents to simulate student profiles, a teacher agent to generate didactically structured tasks, and an evaluator agent to score the output. The prototype was tested on authentic grade 8 mathematics curriculum content from German secondary education, with four learner profiles varying in mathematical proficiency and intrinsic motivation.

The evaluation combined automated agent-based ratings over ten iterations per learner profile and exploratory feedback from five K–12 in-service teachers. Results suggested the system produced stable outputs that were well aligned with the simulated learner profiles, with particularly strong ratings for task suitability and clarity. Teachers generally found the worksheets useful for differentiating within one topic while reducing overload for lower-motivation students, but they also recommended stronger scaffolding, more explicit worked examples, and richer motivational/narrative elements. The study concludes that multi-agent LLM systems may be promising for scalable, teacher-facing personalization, but it remains a prototype and was not tested in authentic classroom learning trials.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that FACET-generated worksheets were judged to be well aligned with grade 8 mathematics content and learner profiles, suggesting the system can produce personalized math practice materials. Across ten agent-based iterations per worksheet, suitability for learners was high (e.g., M=4.78, SD=0.06 overall in the text; table values often 5.9-6.0) and clarity was also high (M=4.76, SD=0.12), indicating that the generated mathematics tasks were feasible and appropriately matched to the targeted proficiency and motivation levels.
finding.measure: Automated and teacher-rated quality of personalized grade 8 mathematics worksheets (didactical structure, clarity, creativity, suitability)
finding.study_size: n=4 learner profiles; 10 agent iterations per worksheet; n=5 K-12 in-service teachers
finding.std_deviation: 0.06 to 0.26 (agent ratings reported in text); teacher rating ranges reported instead of SD

finding.finding_summary: A central design goal of FACET was to incorporate intrinsic motivation alongside mathematical proficiency, and the resulting worksheets were rated as suitable for different motivational profiles. Teacher feedback indicated that low-motivation learners benefited from reduced task load, motivational comments, and recommendations for narrative and everyday-life relevance, implying that the system can support engagement-related aspects of learning rather than only content mastery.
finding.measure: Intrinsic-motivation-sensitive worksheet design and teacher feedback on motivational suitability/engagement support

finding.finding_summary: The system explicitly operationalizes task sequencing, scaffolding, and alignment to Bloom’s taxonomy, which are intended to support progression, reasoning, and structured problem solving. While not directly measuring durable skills with a learner outcome test, the paper reports that teachers valued the clear progression, hints, and stepwise support, and the agent-based evaluations rated didactical structure favorably (around M=4.12, SD=0.22), indicating potential support for metacognitive and structured reasoning processes.
finding.measure: Didactical structure ratings and task sequencing aligned to Bloom’s taxonomy
finding.study_size: n=4 learner profiles; 10 agent iterations per worksheet; n=5 teachers

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily argues that FACET can reduce teacher workload by automating the generation of individualized worksheets and lowering prompting effort. Teacher feedback described the tool as useful for keeping a whole class on one topic while differentiating difficulty, and the authors explicitly frame the system as reducing manual effort required to tailor materials for heterogeneous classrooms.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of usefulness for worksheet generation and workload reduction; system design claims about reduced prompting overhead
finding.study_size: n=5 K-12 in-service teachers; prototype system evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The paper is not about a non-math subject, but it does evaluate task design quality in general academic instructional terms, including didactical structure and clarity of task presentation. The results show favorable ratings for these broader instructional qualities, with teacher experts rating didactical structure at M=4.95 (range=3-6) and clarity at M=4.68 (range=3-6), suggesting the generated worksheets were pedagogically coherent beyond mere content accuracy.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of didactical structure and clarity of worksheet design

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Large Language Models Creation of Interactive Learning Lessons
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can automatically generate scenario-based tutor training lessons for novice tutors teaching middle school mathematics online. The motivating problem is that high-quality tutor training content is time-consuming and expertise-intensive to author manually, which limits scalability. The authors explore a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) workflow with GPT-4o and compare different levels of task decomposition for lesson generation, ranging from one segment to five segments.

The lessons were designed around an existing tutor-training framework and covered three topics: encouraging student independence, encouraging help-seeking behavior, and turning on cameras. Two human coders with tutoring experience rated the generated lessons using a rubric, and the authors also solicited written feedback from two expert lesson designers who compared LLM-generated lessons with their own hand-crafted lessons. The study found that a three-segment prompting strategy produced the best-rated lessons overall, while single-step generation performed worst and maximal decomposition did not always help. The human reviewers saw strong potential for time savings, realistic scenario generation, and a useful human-AI drafting workflow, but they also identified weaknesses in feedback quality, clarity, and the authenticity of generated references. The paper concludes that LLMs can support lesson creation for tutor training, but human review remains necessary for pedagogical quality and citation verification.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that LLM-assisted lesson generation can substantially reduce the time needed to draft scenario sections and multiple-choice questions for tutor training. Both lesson designers explicitly described the system as saving time and reducing repetitive drafting work, with the generated lessons serving as a foundation for later human refinement rather than a fully finished product.
finding.measure: Human lesson designer feedback on time savings and drafting effort

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that hybrid human-AI lesson generation could help scale tutor-training content development and expand access to structured training materials. The main evidence is qualitative: lesson designers reported that AI-generated drafts can support workflow efficiency and collaborative refinement, but the study did not evaluate institutional adoption, policy, or implementation at scale.
finding.measure: Human lesson designer feedback on scalability and human-AI collaboration

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.population: Not population-specific; discusses human learning broadly across educational contexts including K-12 and higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines the promises, challenges, and research needs associated with using generative AI (GenAI) to support human learning. Rather than testing a specific intervention, the paper synthesizes recent literature and conceptual arguments about how GenAI may affect learning support, learning resources, feedback, and assessment, while also raising concerns about hallucinations, privacy, bias, transparency, and overreliance.

The paper frames GenAI as a potentially transformative tool for education, especially through personalized tutoring, automated content generation, timely feedback, and more authentic assessment. It discusses examples such as ChatGPT, Khanmigo, GPT-4-based feedback systems, and multimodal generative tools, but emphasizes that evidence is still emerging and often mixed. The authors argue that rigorous research, AI literacy, and evidence-based decision-making are necessary before broad adoption.

The article is not an empirical study of one population or grade band; it is a broad conceptual perspective spanning school, higher education, and professional learning contexts. For K-12, it highlights implications for assessment, learner agency, and support tools, but does not report new data or compare outcomes by grade band or mathematics subtype. Its main conclusion is that GenAI should augment, not replace, human learning, and that future work must evaluate its effects carefully across contexts and populations.

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses GenAI tools for mathematics learning, including Khanmigo and a cited study where removing AI assistance lowered performance after improved task performance with assistance. However, this is a narrative synthesis rather than a direct study, and no new mathematics outcome data are reported in the paper itself.
finding.measure: Mathematical learning performance and problem-solving in cited studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights mixed emerging evidence on engagement, agency, and motivation when learners use GenAI. It notes that some studies found reduced engagement or negative effects on agency when AI support was removed, alongside other studies reporting positive experiences and motivation gains in feedback contexts.
finding.measure: Learning engagement, learner agency, motivation, positive emotions

finding.finding_summary: A central argument of the paper is that GenAI may both support and undermine durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, self-regulation, and metacognition. The paper does not report original effect sizes, but it repeatedly cites evidence suggesting better task performance with AI assistance and potential performance loss or skill suppression when support is removed.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, self-regulation, metacognition

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI can increase instructional and feedback efficiency by scaling personalized support, generating learning resources, and providing instant feedback. Examples cited in the paper suggest ChatGPT-generated feedback can be more in-depth and fluent than human feedback, and AI tools can reduce educator workload in resource creation and feedback delivery.
finding.measure: Feedback generation efficiency, resource creation efficiency, workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes broad institutional implications, including ethical risks, transparency gaps, privacy concerns, inequality, and disruption of assessment practices. It argues that schools and education systems will need AI literacy, evidence-based policy, and new assessment approaches to manage GenAI responsibly.
finding.measure: Educational governance, assessment validity, privacy/equality/ethics considerations

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing achievement and interest in mathematics learning through Math-Island
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a long-term game-based learning environment, Math-Island, can improve elementary students’ mathematics achievement and sustain their interest in mathematics. The authors frame the problem around conventional teacher-led instruction in Taiwan, which they argue leaves many low-achieving students behind and reduces motivation and confidence in mathematics.

Math-Island is an online, tablet-based system built around a gamified knowledge map of the elementary mathematics curriculum. Students in the experimental school used the system alongside regular classroom teaching and homework over two years (June 2013 to June 2015), while a comparison school received conventional instruction only. The game incorporated construction-management and sightseeing mechanics: students built and upgraded virtual islands by completing learning tasks, received immediate feedback and hints, and could view one another’s islands to encourage social motivation.

The study included 215 second graders in the experimental school and 125 second graders in the control school, with posttests administered when students were in third/fourth grade as described in the paper. Results showed significant gains for the experimental group in overall mathematics performance, with the clearest advantages in calculating and word problem-solving; conceptual understanding did not differ significantly. For low-achieving students, the strongest effect was on word problem-solving. Interest questionnaire data and teacher interviews suggested that both low-achieving and high-achieving students maintained relatively high interest in mathematics and in the system, indicating that the game-based environment may support sustained engagement rather than only short-term novelty effects.

finding.finding_summary: After two years, the experimental school outperformed the control school on overall mathematics achievement and on two subdomains: calculating and word problem-solving. In the posttest MANOVA, the multivariate effect was significant (Wilks’ λ = 0.946, p < .05), with significant univariate effects for calculating (M=13.84 vs 12.18, p < .001) and word problem-solving (M=7.84 vs 6.39, p < .001), but not conceptual understanding (M=12.00 vs 11.78).
finding.measure: Standardized mathematics achievement assessment covering conceptual understanding, calculating, and word problem-solving
finding.study_size: n=334 (experimental valid tests n=209; control valid tests n=125)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports sustained interest and motivation in mathematics and in Math-Island, including attitude, initiative, confidence, attraction, and satisfaction. Questionnaire results showed low-achieving students scored similarly to other students on mathematics interest dimensions, and teacher interviews described students voluntarily using the system after school and feeling more confident because of immediate feedback.
finding.measure: Interest questionnaire (mathematics attitude, initiative, confidence; system attraction, satisfaction) plus teacher interviews
finding.study_size: n=207 valid questionnaires; teacher interviews n=8

finding.finding_summary: Among low-achieving students, the experimental school significantly outperformed the control school on word problem-solving in the posttest. The MANOVA for low-achieving students showed a significant multivariate effect (Wilks’ λ = 0.934, p < .05), and the only significant univariate difference was for word problems (M=6.29 vs 4.98, p < .01).
finding.measure: Standardized mathematics achievement assessment, low-achieving subgroup; word problem-solving subscale
finding.study_size: n=114 low-achieving students total (experimental n=73; control n=41)

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that the system supported self-directed learning, planning, and self-regulation through the construction mechanism and knowledge map, but these were not directly measured with a separate validated durable-skills instrument. Evidence is mainly inferential, based on students’ ability to choose learning paths, manage pace, and reflect on progress in the game environment.
finding.measure: Behavioral usage/process data and qualitative interpretation of learning-path choice and self-paced progress

paper_profiles.title: Speculative Futures on ChatGPT and Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Collective Reflection from the Educational Landscape
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper explores speculative futures for ChatGPT and generative AI in education rather than testing an intervention or reporting empirical outcomes. The authors use a speculative methodology and collective writing to present a set of fictional narratives imagining both positive and negative educational futures shaped by conversational AI systems. Their aim is to provoke critical reflection on what generative AI might mean for teaching, learning, assessment, academic integrity, ethics, privacy, human agency, and the role of educators.

The paper is situated in a broad educational context, drawing on the authors’ international perspectives and prior AI-in-education literature, but it does not focus on a specific grade band, subject area, or K-12 population. Instead, it discusses possible uses of ChatGPT-like tools across educational settings, including personalized learning, accessibility, feedback, assessment automation, language support, and workload reduction, alongside concerns about bias, dependency, inequity, and dehumanization. Because the paper is explicitly speculative and narrative-based, its conclusions are conceptual: it argues that AI in education is context-dependent and that human educators should remain central while institutions develop ethical, responsible, and critical approaches to adoption.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI such as ChatGPT can support writing and other language-based literacy tasks by providing instant feedback, suggestions, and conversational practice. In the speculative narratives, students use AI for essay writing, story generation, translation, and language development, but no empirical effect sizes or comparative outcomes are reported.
finding.measure: Speculative narrative discussion of writing, translation, and language-support uses

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents multiple speculative examples in which AI tools improve oral and written communication skills, including pronunciation practice, real-time interpretation, and conversational support. One narrative describes learners practicing English oral and written communication with an AI platform and gaining confidence, but the paper provides no empirical effect estimates or sample sizes.
finding.measure: Speculative narrative discussion of oral communication, pronunciation, and translation support

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics is mentioned in a speculative classroom narrative where an AI teacher supports problem solving with visuals, feedback, and easier problems, suggesting potential benefits for math learning. However, this is not evaluated empirically and no comparative data, effect size, or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Speculative discussion of mathematics problem solving and feedback

finding.finding_summary: The narratives describe AI as potentially increasing confidence, reducing frustration, and providing encouragement and emotional support during learning. Examples include soothing feedback, motivational prompts, and personalized interactions that help learners persist, but these are illustrative rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Speculative narrative discussion of confidence, stress reduction, and encouragement

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly frames generative AI as potentially supporting durable skills such as critical thinking, collaboration, and problem solving, while also warning that it may undermine creativity and critical thinking through over-reliance and singularization of knowledge. Because the study is speculative, these claims are conceptual and not accompanied by empirical measures or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Speculative narrative discussion of critical thinking, collaboration, creativity, and problem solving

finding.finding_summary: A major theme is that generative AI can reduce educator workload and increase efficiency by helping with lesson planning, grading, summarizing concepts, and generating assessments. The paper explicitly claims AI could save time and allow teachers to focus more on interpersonal support, but it does not report empirical workload measures or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Speculative discussion of lesson planning, grading, summarization, and assessment generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI could reshape educational systems through curriculum change, assessment redesign, accessibility, and rethinking human-AI roles, while also raising policy concerns around ethics, privacy, equity, bias, and academic integrity. These institutional effects are discussed conceptually across speculative futures, with no empirical institutional outcomes reported.
finding.measure: Speculative discussion of curriculum, policy, governance, ethics, privacy, equity, and academic integrity

paper_profiles.title: A Multimedia Adaptive Tutoring System for Mathematics that Addresses Cognition, Metacognition and Affect
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents Wayang Outpost, later called MathSpring, a multimedia adaptive tutoring system for K-12 mathematics designed to support three intertwined dimensions of learning: cognition, metacognition, and affect. The authors argue that effective math learning requires more than correct answers; it also depends on personalized problem difficulty, fluency with prerequisite skills, self-regulation, persistence, and positive emotional experience.

The system combines several components: adaptive problem selection using an effort-based tutoring algorithm, worked examples and multimedia hints, math facts retrieval training, open student models and progress pages, teacher dashboards, and animated affective learning companions. The paper reports multiple evaluations across years of classroom use, mostly in middle and high school settings in Massachusetts, including controlled comparisons against business-as-usual and other software conditions.

The main findings suggest that Wayang/MathSpring can improve student mathematics outcomes, especially on standardized and curriculum-based assessments, with larger gains in areas emphasized by teachers (notably algebra/patterns). The paper also reports evidence that the system can increase engagement and support metacognitive behaviors such as reflection and help-seeking, although some metacognitive interventions showed mixed or limited effects. Overall, the paper concludes that combining cognitive, metacognitive, and affective scaffolds in one adaptive tutor is feasible and can yield positive learning outcomes for K-12 mathematics.

finding.finding_summary: Across multiple classroom evaluations, students using Wayang Outpost/MathSpring showed improved mathematics performance on researcher-made pre/posttests, state standardized tests, and MAP assessments. In one controlled 2012 study with 198 seventh- and eighth-grade students, 7th graders using Wayang had higher MCAS scores than controls (Mean Wayang n=34=244.82 vs Mean Control n=60=239.50, p=0.14), and combined 7th/8th grade MAP patterns-and-algebra gains were significantly higher for the Wayang group (p<0.01, d=0.38); 8th graders alone showed larger gains in algebra/patterns (d=0.77).
finding.measure: Math achievement: MCAS standardized test scores, MAP patterns-and-algebra scores, and researcher-created pre/post math tests
finding.study_size: n=198 for the 2012 classroom study; additional aggregate samples reported including n=34, n=60, n=65, n=28, n=92, n=186 across subgroup analyses

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to improve engagement, motivation, and affect, and the paper reports evidence that these outcomes improved in classroom use. The authors describe gains in student engagement as reflected in system interaction logs and note that affective supports such as learning companions, progress reports, and effort-based feedback were intended to reduce disengagement and foster perseverance, although not all affective interventions were uniformly successful.
finding.measure: Student engagement logs, behavioral indicators of gaming/effort, and student self-reports/affect measures within the tutor

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies metacognitive support through open student models, progress pages, and help-seeking/self-regulation interventions. The authors argue these tools encourage reflection, goal setting, and informed choice, but one targeted experiment found that the intended boredom-triggered prompt to use the Student Progress Page rarely activated because students reported being almost never bored, so usage did not differ reliably between conditions; a secondary analysis compared high vs. low usage rather than a clear treatment effect.
finding.measure: Student use of the Student Progress Page, reflection/goal-setting behavior, and help-seeking/self-regulation indicators

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-facing reports and dashboards were presented as a major feature, giving real-time summaries of student progress, weakest skills, and challenging problems. The paper describes these tools as helping teachers quickly assess mastery and engagement, but it does not report a formal causal evaluation of workload reduction or productivity gains.
finding.measure: Teacher dashboard/report usage and descriptive teacher feedback on student progress reports

paper_profiles.title: Augmenting large language models with chemistry tools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents ChemCrow, an LLM-powered chemistry agent that integrates GPT-4 with 18 expert-designed tools to help solve chemistry tasks that the base model struggles with, such as retrosynthesis, reaction prediction, molecule search, safety checking, and data analysis. The authors frame the work as a way to overcome hallucination and missing-world-knowledge problems in LLMs by letting the model reason iteratively while calling external tools.

The system is demonstrated on a range of chemistry workflows, including autonomous synthesis of an insect repellent (DEET) and three thiourea organocatalysts, human-AI collaboration to discover and synthesize a novel chromophore, and multiple task-based evaluations comparing ChemCrow with tool-less GPT-4. The evaluation combines expert chemist judgments and LLM-based grading. Expert reviewers generally preferred ChemCrow on chemical factuality and task completion, especially for harder tasks, while the LLM-based evaluator tended to favor GPT-4 because of its more fluent responses.

The paper is not a K-12 education study and does not involve students, teachers, or classroom use. Its context is adult scientific research and laboratory automation, with a focus on chemistry workflows and safety. The main conclusion is that tool augmentation substantially improves the reliability and usefulness of LLMs for chemistry tasks, but that evaluation of such systems still requires expert human assessment rather than relying solely on another LLM.

finding.finding_summary: ChemCrow improved the efficiency and completion of chemistry workflows by automating tool use, planning, and execution across multiple tasks. In expert evaluations (n=4 evaluators; n=56 task-level judgments), expert chemists preferred ChemCrow over tool-less GPT-4 on chemical accuracy and task completeness, especially for more complex tasks, indicating better practical productivity in scientific work.
finding.measure: Expert judgments of chemical accuracy, reasoning quality, and task completion across chemistry tasks; comparative preference between ChemCrow and GPT-4
finding.study_size: n=56 task-level judgments; n=4 expert evaluators

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that tool-augmented LLM agents can change how chemistry research is conducted by lowering barriers to expert tools, supporting laboratory automation, and improving access to chemical reasoning and safety checks. This is framed as a broader workflow and research-infrastructure contribution rather than a measured institutional outcome, so no quantitative institutional effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative assessment of laboratory automation, human-AI collaboration, and safety/risk mitigation implications

paper_profiles.title: Multimodal Learning Analytics and Education Data Mining: Using Computational Technologies to Measure Complex Learning Tasks
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Middle School, High School, Undergraduate
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual review of multimodal learning analytics (MMLA) and educational data mining methods for studying complex learning in settings that are not easily captured by traditional assessments. The authors argue that conventional analytics has focused too heavily on highly structured, screen-based tasks, while many important learning environments involve open-ended, physical, social, and multimodal activity such as making, engineering design, collaborative problem solving, and embodied interaction.

The paper surveys technologies and analytic approaches across multiple modalities, including text, speech, handwriting, sketching, gesture, affect, physiology, EEG, eye gaze, and multimodal fusion. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, it synthesizes prior work to show how these tools can support richer assessment and formative feedback in K-12 and university contexts, especially for project-based and constructionist learning. Its main conclusion is that MMLA can make complex learning processes more observable and measurable, potentially helping researchers and educators better understand student trajectories and improve support in open-ended environments.

finding.finding_summary: The paper cites prior work showing that handwriting recognition in algebra tutoring reduced the time students needed to complete tutoring activities by half for high school and middle school students. This was presented as evidence that low-friction input methods can improve efficiency and support learning in mathematics tasks, but the paper does not report the original study's full statistical details.
finding.measure: Time to complete algebra tutoring activities

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that multimodal sensing and automated analysis can make assessment and formative feedback feasible in complex learning environments, reducing the labor required for teachers and researchers. It also notes one cited study in which handwriting recognition halved task completion time, illustrating improved interaction efficiency in tutoring contexts.
finding.measure: Task completion time; feasibility of assessment and feedback

finding.finding_summary: Across cited studies on affect detection, the paper reports that states such as confusion, boredom, frustration, and surprise relate differently to learning outcomes depending on context and scaffolding. For example, confusion was sometimes associated with good outcomes, while surprise was associated with less favorable outcomes, indicating that affect is an important but context-dependent correlate of learning.
finding.measure: Affective states during tutoring/learning activities

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights several cited studies linking multimodal indicators to collaboration, attention, and problem-solving quality. Examples include eye-gaze and joint visual attention predicting collaboration quality and learning gains, and body-posture/state transitions predicting learning gains in a tangible learning task, suggesting that multimodal analytics can capture durable skills such as collaboration and metacognitive cycles of reflection and action.
finding.measure: Collaboration quality, joint visual attention, posture/state transitions, problem-solving performance

paper_profiles.title: BLOOM: A 176B-Parameter Open-Access Multilingual Language Model
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents BLOOM, a 176-billion-parameter multilingual large language model built by the BigScience collaboration and released as open-access infrastructure for research and downstream applications. The paper’s main question is how to design, train, and release a large-scale language model in a way that is technically competitive while also being transparent, multilingual, and more socially accountable than typical proprietary LLM development.

The approach centers on the ROOTS training corpus, a 1.61TB multilingual and multi-domain dataset assembled from 498 Hugging Face datasets, web sources, code, and curated prompt datasets. The paper describes the data governance process, source selection, filtering, privacy redaction, tokenizer design, model architecture choices, and distributed training stack used to build BLOOM on the Jean Zay supercomputer.

The paper evaluates BLOOM primarily as a general-purpose language model using zero-shot benchmark performance and reports that it is competitive on a wide range of NLP tasks, with better performance after multitask prompted finetuning (BLOOMZ/xP3). Its main conclusions are about model and dataset design, open release, and the feasibility of collaborative multilingual LLM development; it does not study K-12 educational outcomes or mathematics learning.

paper_profiles.title: Personalizing Dialogue Agents: I have a dog, do you have pets too?
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 56th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Long Papers)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of building more engaging, consistent chit-chat dialogue agents by conditioning them on persistent persona information. The authors argue that generic dialogue models often lack specificity, personality, and long-term coherence, and propose a new dataset and modeling framework to address these issues.

The main contribution is the PERSONA-CHAT dataset, a crowd-sourced dialogue corpus collected from Amazon Mechanical Turk. Workers were assigned synthetic personas, asked to chat naturally while asking and answering personal questions, and the resulting dataset included 164,356 utterances across 10,981 dialogues. The paper also introduces several baseline models for next-utterance prediction: retrieval baselines (IR and Starspace), memory-network variants, and generative seq2seq models, each with and without persona conditioning.

Experiments show that conditioning on a speaker's own persona generally improves next-utterance prediction, especially for retrieval/ranking models and for the original personas with overlap. Revised personas, which reduce word overlap, are harder but still provide gains for memory-network models. Human evaluations indicate that PERSONA-CHAT-trained models are more engaging, fluent, and consistent than models trained on Twitter or OpenSubtitles, and that persona-aware models are more detectable by conversation partners while retaining reasonable conversational quality.

finding.finding_summary: Persona-conditioned dialogue models produced more fluent conversational responses in human evaluation than models trained on Twitter or OpenSubtitles, but the paper does not report educational language-learning outcomes. In the human ratings, the best PERSONA-CHAT models received fluency scores around 3.81-4.31/5 depending on condition, with human-human conversations scoring 4.31/5.
finding.measure: Human-rated fluency in dialogue
finding.study_size: n=100 dialogues per model condition (human evaluation); exact number of raters not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The central empirical finding is that persona conditioning improves engagingness and consistency in dialogue, and PERSONA-CHAT-trained models are rated as more engaging than comparable models trained on Twitter or OpenSubtitles. In human evaluation, the best PERSONA-CHAT models achieved engagingness scores of about 3.50-3.88/5 and consistency scores of about 3.36-3.44/5, while human-human dialogues scored 4.25/5 engagingness and 4.36/5 consistency.
finding.measure: Human-rated engagingness and consistency of dialogue
finding.study_size: n=100 dialogues per model condition (human evaluation); human comparison included

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies whether dialogue agents can use profile information to better infer conversational partner interests and maintain coherent, context-sensitive dialogue, which is a form of conversational reasoning rather than a classroom skill outcome. The models with persona access improve next-utterance prediction, and the authors report that profile prediction from dialogue can reach 94.3% accuracy for human speakers and 23% for model dialogue in preliminary experiments.
finding.measure: Next-utterance prediction; preliminary profile prediction from dialogue
finding.study_size: Dataset size: 164,356 utterances across 10,981 dialogues; profile prediction study size not_reported

paper_profiles.title: A Comprehensive Survey of AI-Generated Content (AIGC): A History of Generative AI from GAN to ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of artificial intelligence generated content (AIGC), also referred to as generative AI, tracing the historical development of generative modeling from early approaches such as hidden Markov models and Gaussian mixture models through neural language models, GANs, VAEs, diffusion models, and large language models including GPT-3 and ChatGPT. Its main purpose is to organize the technical landscape of generative AI, explain the major model families and training paradigms, and highlight recent advances in unimodal and multimodal generation.

The survey reviews foundational components such as the transformer architecture, pre-trained language models, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), and the computing infrastructure needed to train large models. It then summarizes generative methods for text, image, and multimodal tasks, including vision-language encoders and decoders, text-to-image generation, and cross-modal prompting. The paper also discusses open problems, risks, and future directions for AIGC.

Although the paper notes that AIGC has applications in education, it does not study any educational intervention, learner population, or K-12 mathematics outcome. It is a technical review paper rather than an empirical study of student learning or school implementation.

paper_profiles.title: A Multitask, Multilingual, Multimodal Evaluation of ChatGPT on Reasoning, Hallucination, and Interactivity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates ChatGPT across a broad suite of publicly available benchmarks to characterize its strengths and limitations in multitask NLP, multilingual understanding and generation, multimodal code-mediated image generation, reasoning, hallucination, and multi-turn interactivity. The central question is not whether ChatGPT improves learning outcomes in an educational setting, but what kinds of language and reasoning tasks the model can or cannot perform reliably.
