The authors use a benchmarking framework with 23 datasets spanning 8 NLP tasks, plus additional reasoning, factuality, and multimodal experiments. They compare ChatGPT against prior zero-shot and fine-tuned systems using small test subsets (typically 30-200 samples per task), and they also test whether multi-turn prompting improves outputs. Overall, ChatGPT is strong on many standard NLP tasks and can benefit from interaction, but it remains unreliable on complex reasoning, low-resource language generation, and hallucination-prone outputs. In reasoning experiments, the model is especially weak on mathematical, spatial, and inductive reasoning, while it performs better on commonsense and some temporal reasoning. The paper is a broad capability evaluation of a general-purpose LLM, not a K-12 instructional study.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT showed weak mathematical reasoning performance in the paper’s reasoning benchmark suite. On the MATH dataset, it answered 7/30 items correctly (23.33%), indicating substantial limitations on mathematical problem solving rather than instructional benefit.
finding.measure: Accuracy on MATH mathematical reasoning questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates reasoning-related durable skills such as inductive, deductive, abductive, analogical, causal, multi-hop, temporal, and spatial reasoning. ChatGPT performed unevenly: it was stronger on deduction and commonsense reasoning but weak on induction, spatial reasoning, and multi-hop reasoning, showing inconsistent reasoning capability overall.
finding.measure: Accuracy across reasoning QA benchmarks (e.g., bAbI, CLUTRR, EntailmentBank, StepGame, hotpotQA, CommonsenseQA)
finding.study_size: varies by task; total reasoning sample size reported as n=634 across 10 reasoning categories

paper_profiles.title: A Benchmark for Math Misconceptions: Bridging Gaps in Middle School Algebra with AI-Supported Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of identifying and responding to students’ algebra misconceptions in middle school, especially for learners in underserved contexts. The authors argue that accurate misconception diagnosis is important for supporting conceptual understanding and for helping teachers provide targeted instruction, but that existing AI systems struggle to recognize the specific kinds of errors students make in algebra.

To address this, the paper introduces a benchmark dataset of 55 middle-school algebra misconceptions and common errors, each paired with four diagnostic examples (220 total), assembled from 145 peer-reviewed and scholarly sources. The authors then evaluate GPT-4-turbo using in-context learning on this benchmark in two experimental settings: one with random examples from the full dataset and one constrained by topic. They also collect feedback from five middle school math educators on clarity, classroom relevance, and potential classroom use of the benchmark, combining model evaluation with human judgment.

Results show that GPT-4-turbo performs substantially better when examples are constrained by topic, reaching 0.753 precision and 0.748 recall per misconception in the topic-matched setting, compared with 0.526 precision and 0.529 recall in the unconstrained setting. Performance varies by topic, with ratios and proportional thinking being the hardest area and algebraic representations the easiest under topic-constrained testing. Educators largely validated the dataset’s classroom relevance: most reported encountering these misconceptions, and four of five expressed interest in using the dataset with AI tools for diagnosis or teacher training. The paper concludes that topic-constrained prompting and educator feedback improve AI’s usefulness for misconception diagnosis, while also highlighting the importance of multimodal inputs and domain expertise.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark and GPT-4-turbo evaluation focus directly on middle school algebra misconception diagnosis, a core mathematics learning task. In the topic-constrained setting, the model reached 0.753 precision and 0.748 recall per misconception (n=1,100 iterations), and educator review suggested the benchmark captured real classroom misconceptions relevant to algebra instruction.
finding.measure: Precision and recall for diagnosing algebra misconceptions/errors (MaEs) in student responses
finding.study_size: n=5,500 iterations in Experiment 1; n=1,100 iterations in Experiment 2; 55 misconceptions; 220 examples

paper_profiles.title: Improving Student Learning with Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring: A Three-Study Quasi-Experimental Investigation
paper_profiles.venue: LAK '24: Proceedings of the 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether hybrid human-AI tutoring—where remote human tutors work alongside adaptive math software—improves students’ learning processes and intermediate outcomes relative to software alone. The motivation is equity and scalability: many low-income students have limited access to high-quality tutoring, and AI-supported tutoring might extend individualized support at lower cost. The authors focus on whether adding human tutoring to edtech increases engagement, software usage, and lesson completion, and whether benefits differ by students’ baseline performance.

The study reports three quasi-experimental field studies in urban, low-income U.S. middle schools. Site 1 involved 125 seventh graders in Pennsylvania using IXL and compared software-only support to conditions that added a math teacher and then remote tutoring. Site 2 involved 385 seventh graders in California using i-Ready and examined lesson completion and time-on-task before versus during a short hybrid tutoring period. Site 3 involved 75 grades 6-8 students in a Pennsylvania charter school using MATHia and compared two phases of tutoring implementation, including a shift from roughly 1:8 to 1:4 tutor-to-student ratios and the introduction of a live dashboard.

Across sites, the authors find positive effects on process outcomes: hybrid human-AI tutoring increased time on task, questions answered, skills proficient, and lessons completed, with especially strong benefits for lower-pretest or below-grade-level students. A math teacher present during edtech use also improved engagement, but the benefit was larger for higher-pretest students. The paper concludes that hybrid tutoring can improve access to learning opportunities and may be especially valuable for students with greater academic need, while lower tutor-to-student ratios and dashboard-guided support appear promising for future scaling.

finding.finding_summary: Across three quasi-experimental studies in middle school math contexts, hybrid human-AI tutoring improved math learning-process outcomes compared with software alone. In Site 1 (n=125), the mixed-effects model found a positive effect on time spent practicing with IXL (β=0.202, 95% CI [0.057, 0.347], p=0.006), and significant gains in questions answered and skills proficient relative to EdTech only. In Site 2 (n=385), students completed more lessons during the tutoring period, and in Site 3 (n=75) students completed an additional 0.36 workspaces per hour after tutor-to-student ratios improved from about 1:8 to 1:4 (95% CI [0.02, 0.70], p=.03).
finding.measure: Math software learning-process outcomes: time spent, questions answered, skills proficient, lessons passed/completed, and MATHia workspaces completed per hour

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats engagement and participation as central intermediate outcomes and finds that hybrid human-AI tutoring increased student engagement with math software. In Site 1, time spent and questions answered increased significantly when tutoring was added; in Site 2, average weekly time-on-task rose from 24 to 33 minutes during the tutoring period. The authors interpret these changes as evidence that the intervention improved students’ engagement and willingness to persist with practice, especially for students with greater need.
finding.measure: Engagement / participation indicators such as time on task, time spent, and questions answered

finding.finding_summary: The intervention is also studied as a scalable tutoring model that can improve tutor utilization and lower cost per student. The paper reports that hybrid human-AI tutoring allowed a single tutor to work with more students, with tutor-to-student ratios ranging from 1:8 to 1:4, and states that annual marginal cost averaged about $700 per student (range $597–$1170), substantially below other high-dosage tutoring models. These are presented as evidence of improved operational efficiency rather than a direct learner outcome.
finding.measure: Tutor-to-student ratio and marginal cost per student

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation Report on Large Language Models Solving High School Mathematics Questions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report evaluates how multiple large language models (LLMs) perform on high school mathematics exam questions and asks whether they can be useful in educational settings. The paper uses mathematics questions drawn from college entrance examinations from 2019 to 2023, including pre- and post-reform papers, and assesses model outputs using several criteria: accuracy, response time, logical reasoning, guidance sensitivity, and creativity/multi-solution generation.

The study compares eight LLM APIs/models, including GLM-4-Flash, ERNIE-Speed-128K, Spark-lite, Hunyuan-lite, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, gemma-2-9b-it, Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Yi-34B. Questions were categorized by format (multiple choice, fill-in-the-blank, comprehensive) and by difficulty level, and the authors also tested different prompting styles to see how guidance affected performance. The report finds substantial variation across models: some are faster on simpler tasks, some achieve higher accuracy on comprehensive or multi-solution tasks, and others show stronger logical guidance performance. Overall, the paper concludes that LLMs have promise for high school mathematics support, but their reasoning, creativity, and efficiency are uneven and still need improvement.

finding.finding_summary: Across eight LLMs, performance on high school mathematics questions varied substantially by model, question type, and difficulty. The report shows that Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and ERNIE-Speed-128K had the highest single-solution accuracy on comprehensive questions (0.850 and 0.950 reported for comprehensive questions in Table 12), while Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct also led multi-solution accuracy at 0.64 and was ranked first overall in the weighted creativity/efficiency summary. No effect size or confidence interval was reported; the evidence is descriptive and based on model-level accuracy and timing comparisons rather than inferential statistics.
finding.measure: Accuracy on high school mathematics exam questions; response time; logical reasoning/guidance; multi-solution creativity metrics

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly evaluates logical reasoning using chain-of-thought prompting, guidance attempts, and success rate, treating these as indicators of reasoning quality. Models differed meaningfully: Hunyuan-lite performed best on guiding incorrect answers, requiring an average of only 3 attempts, while other models required 4-6 attempts; the reported composite logic scores also varied across models (e.g., 0.42 for Hunyuan-lite, 0.406 for Spark-lite, 0.39 for GLM-4-Flash). No inferential statistics were reported, and the findings are model-comparison summaries rather than student outcomes.
finding.measure: Logical reasoning / chain-of-thought guidance performance; number of guidance attempts; success rate; composite logic score

finding.finding_summary: The report measures model response time on high school math questions and finds large differences in efficiency across models and task types. In single-solution settings, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and gemma-2-9b-it were fastest on simple/intermediate items, while Yi-34B and GLM-4-Flash were slower on several categories; in multi-solution settings, Spark-lite was fastest overall (688 seconds) and GLM-4-Flash slowest (7400 seconds). The paper reports timing averages and a weighted efficiency score but no confidence intervals or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Response time on multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, and comprehensive/high school mathematics questions; weighted efficiency score

finding.finding_summary: The paper also evaluates creativity in generating multiple solutions, which is not a core mathematics achievement outcome but is directly studied as a model capability. GLM-4-Flash produced the most solutions overall (472 total; 4.5 average solutions per question) and had the highest complexity score (68), while Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ranked first in the final weighted score because it balanced accuracy, complexity, richness, and efficiency. These are descriptive model-comparison results rather than human-learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Number of generated solutions; solution richness; solution complexity; weighted creativity score

paper_profiles.title: AMO-Bench: Large Language Models Still Struggle in High School Math Competitions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces AMO-Bench, a new benchmark for evaluating advanced mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs). The benchmark contains 50 original, human-crafted problems designed to meet at least International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) difficulty standards, with an emphasis on avoiding contamination from existing contest items and ensuring automatic grading through final-answer formats.

The study evaluates 26 LLMs on the benchmark and analyzes their accuracy under repeated sampling, output length, and test-time scaling. The authors report that even the best model reaches only 52.4% average accuracy on AMO-Bench, with most models below 40%, indicating that current LLMs still struggle with Olympiad-level high school mathematics. The paper also finds that higher-performing models tend to generate longer outputs and that performance improves with increased test-time compute, suggesting substantial remaining room for reasoning improvements.

Although the benchmark is framed around high school mathematics competitions, it is not a student learning study and does not test educational interventions with K-12 learners. Instead, it is an AI evaluation paper focused on model capability on competition-style mathematics tasks, using expert-created items and automated/LLM-based grading. The main contribution is a harder and less contaminated benchmark for future assessment of advanced math reasoning in LLMs.

finding.finding_summary: Across 26 LLMs on 50 Olympiad-level math problems, the best model (GPT-5-Thinking (High)) achieved 52.4% AVG@32 accuracy, while most models scored below 40%. The benchmark is intentionally difficult, and the paper shows that performance improves with increased test-time compute, with top-tier models exceeding 70% pass@32 on some settings, indicating both current weakness and scaling potential in advanced mathematical reasoning.
finding.measure: Accuracy / AVG@32 on AMO-Bench; pass@k across repeated samples
finding.study_size: n=26 models; benchmark size n=50 problems

paper_profiles.title: The Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence for Upper Secondary Mathematics Education Through the Lens of Technology Acceptance
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 40th ACM/SIGAPP Symposium on Applied Computing (SAC ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Finnish upper secondary school students perceive the use of generative AI tools, specifically Copilot, in mathematics learning. The study is framed by the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and asks which factors drive students’ intention to use GenAI, while also comparing the Finnish results to a prior Hong Kong study on ChatGPT adoption in higher education.

The authors conducted four teaching experiments in a Finnish general upper secondary school during 2023–2024, spanning first-, second-, and third-year students (n=135 total). Students used GenAI in several advanced mathematics topics, including equations and systems of equations, normal distribution, logic and programming, and congruence and Diophantine equations. Data were analyzed with PLS-SEM and CB-SEM to test paths among perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, perceived enjoyment, intention to use, and an added compatibility construct.

The main finding is that perceived usefulness was the strongest predictor of intention to use GenAI in this context, while perceived enjoyment mainly influenced usefulness and ease of use rather than intention directly. Perceived ease of use had weak, non-significant direct effects on intention, and compatibility significantly improved prediction of perceived usefulness but did not directly drive intention. The study concludes that in Finnish upper secondary mathematics, students value the practical utility of GenAI more than enjoyment, and that fit with existing digital learning practices matters for adoption.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that students’ intention to use GenAI in upper secondary mathematics was strongly driven by perceived usefulness, with PU predicting ITU at β=0.737 (p<.001) in the baseline model and β=0.694 (p<.001) in the extended model. The sample included Finnish high school students using Copilot across mathematics topics (n=135 across teaching experiments; final SEM sample n=102), but the paper did not measure mathematics achievement or test scores—rather, it measured adoption-related perceptions tied to mathematics learning.
finding.measure: Technology acceptance constructs in mathematics education context (perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, perceived enjoyment, compatibility, intention to use)

finding.finding_summary: Perceived enjoyment was an important driver of students’ acceptance beliefs, especially its strong effect on perceived usefulness (β=0.652, p<.001) and perceived ease of use (β=0.715, p<.001) in the baseline model. However, enjoyment did not directly predict intention to use (β=0.126, p=.162), suggesting that it mattered indirectly rather than as a direct adoption driver. The study measured enjoyment through TAM survey items rather than behavioral engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceived enjoyment survey scale within the extended TAM

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally examines perceived ease of use and compatibility as acceptance-related constructs that relate to students’ ability to work effectively with GenAI, but these are not direct measures of durable skills. Perceived ease of use did not significantly predict intention to use (β=0.085, p=.201 in the baseline model; β=0.095, p=.318 in the extended model), while compatibility significantly predicted perceived usefulness (β=0.602, p<.001). The evidence is about students’ perceptions of technology fit and usability, not direct gains in metacognition or critical thinking.
finding.measure: Perceived ease of use and compatibility survey scales

finding.finding_summary: The study repeatedly frames GenAI as a tool that may improve efficiency in mathematics learning by helping students solve tasks and by fitting smoothly into a digitized school environment. In the extended model, compatibility significantly increased perceived usefulness (β=0.602, p<.001), and usefulness strongly predicted intention to use, indicating that students saw GenAI as practically efficient for their coursework. The paper does not report a direct efficiency outcome such as time saved or teacher workload, so the evidence is attitudinal rather than behavioral.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness and compatibility as proxies for practical efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Generation of Question Hints for Mathematics Problems using Large Language Models in Educational Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can generate pedagogically useful hints for mathematics problems and whether those hints help simulated students self-correct. The authors focus on the challenge of producing hints that are relevant, do not reveal the answer, and align with the cognitive approach embedded in the exercise design.

The study uses a pipeline in which several LLMs act as students (GPT-3.5-turbo, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3) and other LLMs act as teachers (GPT-4o or Llama-3-8B-Instruct). The exercises come from MIA Seconde, a French high-school remediation platform, and the paper evaluates different prompt strategies for hint generation, including specialized prompts tied to specific error types and baseline prompts that ignore the student’s response.

Across four high-school math exercises, the authors find that higher sampling temperatures generally increase error rates in student model solutions, and that hint effectiveness depends strongly on prompt design and the teacher model. The best prompt among specialized prompts was the calculation-error prompt, while the best baseline prompt was BaselineTwo. Llama-3-8B-Instruct often outperformed GPT-4o as a teacher in terms of student accuracy after hints, though the paper does not provide human validation of hint quality and notes that the results are limited by the small number of exercises and the use of simulated rather than real students.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that LLM-generated hints can improve performance on high-school mathematics problem solving and answer revision, especially when using the best prompt designs. For example, GPT-3.5-turbo showed a substantial increase in accuracy after receiving hints, and some prompt/model combinations achieved mean revision error rates of 0 across repeated trials on specific exercises (n=40 repetitions per exercise for solution generation; 10 repetitions per error type/prompt in hint testing).
finding.measure: Accuracy on math exercise solving and answer revision; mean revision error rate after hints

paper_profiles.title: Assessment of Evolving Large Language Models in Upper Secondary Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates how several large language models (LLMs) perform on high-stakes upper secondary mathematics tasks using the Finnish matriculation examination. The authors are interested in the rapid evolution of generative AI systems and ask how different model versions perform on a standardized, human-administered mathematics exam that is used for university admission in Finland.

The study compares multiple model releases across four time periods: August 2023, November 2023, April 2024, and January 2025. The models were tested on versions of the advanced-level Finnish matriculation exam in mathematics, and answers were graded using the official national grading scheme. Performance improved substantially over time: earlier models such as GPT-4 and Bard achieved mid-to-high grades, while later models such as GPT-4-turbo, Gemini 2.0, o1, o3, and DeepSeek R1 reached near-perfect or perfect scores on the exam.

The paper concludes that state-of-the-art LLMs now have mathematical problem-solving performance at or above the top range of the Finnish grading scale for upper secondary mathematics. The authors argue that these tools are already strong enough to qualify for higher education admissions in competitive fields, but they note that instructional and pedagogical uses remain an open question and should be the focus of future research. The work is primarily a benchmark-style observational evaluation of model performance rather than a study of classroom implementation or learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: LLM mathematical performance improved sharply over time on the Finnish upper secondary advanced mathematics matriculation examination (max 120 points). GPT-4 scored 64/120 (grade E) in August 2023, GPT-4-turbo scored 92/120 (L) in April 2024, and by January 2025 Gemini 2.0 scored 115/120, ChatGPT o1 118/120, and both DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT o3 achieved perfect scores of 120/120. The paper also reports item-level January 2025 totals on an expanded 13-task version, where DeepSeek R1 and ChatGPT o3 each scored 156/156.
finding.measure: Scores and grades on the Finnish matriculation examination in advanced mathematics

paper_profiles.title: VNHSGE: VietNamese High School Graduation Examination Dataset for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces the VNHSGE dataset, a benchmark built from Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination questions and similar exams to evaluate large language models (LLMs). The dataset spans nine subjects and includes both multiple-choice and essay items, along with images, formulas, and step-by-step explanations, enabling evaluation of tasks such as question answering, reading comprehension, text generation, and visual question answering.

The main goal is to assess how well LLMs handle high school-level content in Vietnamese and English, with particular attention to the models’ strengths and limitations across subjects and difficulty levels. The authors evaluate ChatGPT and BingChat on the dataset and compare their performance with Vietnamese students’ score distributions. They report that both models reach human-level performance in some humanities and language areas, but remain weaker in mathematics and the natural sciences, especially on higher-difficulty, multi-step reasoning items.

The paper is primarily a dataset and benchmark paper rather than an intervention study. Its evidence is based on comparative model evaluation against exam questions, with no experimental manipulation in an education setting. It is most relevant for understanding where current LLMs succeed or fail on authentic high school exam content, and it aims to inform future educational use of generative AI by highlighting risks and limitations.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT and BingChat handled knowledge- and comprehension-level mathematics questions, but they struggled with complex calculations and logical reasoning requiring multi-step deduction. The paper reports that the models often produced inaccurate explanations and answers on higher application-level math problems, although no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Vietnamese high school graduation examination mathematics questions, stratified by difficulty level

finding.finding_summary: On literature, English, history, geography, and civics, ChatGPT and BingChat sometimes performed at a human level, but performance varied by subject and task. The paper summarizes this as strong performance in several humanities areas while still leaving room for improvement on some exam items; no effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Vietnamese high school graduation examination questions in literature, English, history, geography, and civic education

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly emphasizes the models’ strengths and weaknesses in reasoning, inference, and multi-step problem solving across subjects, especially mathematics and physics. These are not measured as standalone durable-skill outcomes, but the benchmark is explicitly used to probe deductive reasoning and complex reasoning ability; no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Performance on multi-step reasoning and inference-demanding exam questions across subjects

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Final Answers: Evaluating Large Language Models for Math Tutoring
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) are suitable for mathematics tutoring, focusing on two related questions: how accurately they solve algebra problems and how well they provide step-by-step tutoring support. The authors argue that benchmark-style evaluations that check only final answers are insufficient for educational use because tutoring also depends on the correctness and pedagogical quality of intermediate steps, hints, and feedback.

To study this, the authors used two complementary evaluation methods on college algebra problems drawn from the Apprentice Tutors intelligent tutoring platform. First, they generated 110 algebra problems across 22 problem types and asked several ChatGPT-family models (GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4o, o1-mini, and o1-preview) to solve them; the tutor’s expert answers were used as a reference. Second, they had human evaluators interact with the same models as if they were students seeking tutoring help, and then rated the resulting dialogues for quality and correctness using a rubric plus thematic analysis.

The results show that LLMs can often produce correct final answers, but their tutoring performance is less reliable when the entire dialogue is considered. In the automated problem-solving evaluation, the overall accuracy was 85.5%, with GPT-4o performing best at 97.3%. In the interactive tutoring evaluation, reviewers judged 90% of dialogues to be high quality, but only 56.6% were entirely correct overall; GPT-4o again performed best on dialogue correctness at 75% on average across reviewers. The authors conclude that current LLMs are not yet safe as standalone math tutors without human oversight, although they may still be useful for generating hints, alternative explanations, and positive reinforcement.

finding.finding_summary: Across 110 college algebra problems generated from an intelligent tutoring system, the evaluated LLMs produced correct final answers for 85.5% of problems overall. Performance varied by model, with GPT-4o reaching 97.3% accuracy (107/110 correct), while GPT-3.5 Turbo and GPT-4 were lower at 77.3% and 74.5%, respectively.
finding.measure: Final-answer accuracy on college algebra problems

finding.finding_summary: In the interactive tutoring evaluation, reviewers found that LLMs frequently provided encouraging feedback, positive reinforcement, and motivational nudges that could support learner persistence and well-being. Table 4 identified 7 positive occurrences of encouraging reinforcement, including statements intended to maintain a supportive atmosphere.
finding.measure: Qualitative rubric/thematic analysis of tutoring dialogue behaviors

finding.finding_summary: The paper assessed whether LLMs modeled effective problem-solving strategies, scaffolding, and step-by-step reasoning during tutoring interactions. Reviewers found that dialogues were often high quality pedagogically, but many contained incorrect or miscalibrated sub-steps, overgeneralized hints, or failures to teach specialized methods, indicating mixed support for deeper reasoning and metacognitive skill development.
finding.measure: Rubric-based quality ratings and correctness coding of tutoring dialogues

paper_profiles.title: The Invalsi Benchmarks: measuring the Linguistic and Mathematical understanding of Large Language Models in Italian
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces three Italian-language benchmarks for evaluating large language models (LLMs): Invalsi MATE for mathematical understanding, Invalsi ITA for language understanding, and Olimpiadi MATE for more advanced mathematical reasoning. The motivation is that, despite the growing number of open and instruction-tuned LLMs, there are few native Italian benchmarks for assessing whether models can handle school-level mathematical and linguistic tasks in Italian.

The authors construct the benchmarks from publicly available INVALSI tests used in the Italian school system and from Italian math olympiad problems. They evaluate 10 LLMs across model families (English-pretrained, multilingual, and Italian fine-tuned) using likelihood-based accuracy, and in some cases manual/human evaluation. They also stratify results by grade band and compare model performance against aggregated student results from INVALSI.

The main conclusions are that Llama 3.1 70B/405B instruct models are strongest overall, multilingual pretraining tends to outperform English-only pretraining on Italian tasks, and Italian fine-tuning alone does not close the gap. Models transfer mathematical reasoning across languages better than language understanding, but they struggle more on later-grade language items and on the harder Olimpiadi MATE benchmark. Compared with students, most models are near or below student performance on mathematics, while many outperform students on Italian language items.

finding.finding_summary: On Invalsi MATE (420 questions), the best model was Llama 3.1 70B instruct with 0.71 accuracy, followed by Llama 3.1 405B instruct at 0.70; many multilingual models outperformed English-only and Italian-fine-tuned models. On the harder Olimpiadi MATE benchmark (619 questions), performance dropped substantially, with only Llama 3.1 405B instruct exceeding 0.45 accuracy; grade-stratified results varied by at most about 10 percentage points on Invalsi MATE.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Italian mathematics benchmarks (Invalsi MATE, Olimpiadi MATE), including question-type and grade-stratified accuracy
finding.confidence_interval: ±0.01 to ±0.04 reported for model accuracies in tables; not a single effect size

finding.finding_summary: On Invalsi ITA (1117 or 1264 questions depending on the table/description in the paper), the strongest model was again Llama 3.1 70B instruct with 0.88 accuracy, and most evaluated models exceeded student performance on many Italian language items. The paper reports that language-understanding performance shows a smaller gap than mathematics for top models, but still degrades on later-grade questions.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Italian language-understanding benchmark (Invalsi ITA), including question-type and grade-stratified accuracy
finding.confidence_interval: ±0.01 to ±0.04 reported for model accuracies in tables; not a single effect size

paper_profiles.title: BanglaMATH : A Bangla benchmark dataset for testing LLM mathematical reasoning at grades 6, 7, and 8
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces BanglaMATH, a new benchmark dataset of 1.7k Bangla math word problems collected from elementary school workbooks and exam materials in Bangladesh. The authors ask whether large language models can perform mathematical reasoning in Bangla, a low-resource language, and whether performance varies by grade level, problem complexity, distractor presence, and translation into English.

The benchmark includes problems from grades 6, 7, and 8, annotated with grade level, answer, number of reasoning steps, and digit count. The authors evaluate several LLMs in a zero-shot setting, including GPT-4, LLaMA 4 Maverick, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Grok 3, and DeepSeek-V3. Performance is reported by accuracy across grades and by arithmetic/reasoning complexity. Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek-V3 are the strongest models overall, exceeding 80% accuracy on all three grades, while performance generally drops as grade level, digit count, and reasoning steps increase.

The paper also tests robustness by adding irrelevant distractors and examines language bias by comparing Bangla problems with English translations. Both top models degrade substantially when distractors are added, and both perform better on English translations by about 6.5% or more, suggesting a clear language bias favoring English. Overall, the paper concludes that current general-purpose LLMs still struggle with elementary math reasoning in Bangla, especially under distraction and when problem complexity increases.

finding.finding_summary: Across grades 6-8, model accuracy declined as grade level, digit count, and reasoning-step complexity increased. Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek-V3 were the strongest systems, reaching at least 80% accuracy across all three grades, while GPT-4 remained below 70% on all grades and accuracy fell below 50% for problems requiring four or more reasoning steps.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Bangla math word problems stratified by grade level, digit count, and number of reasoning steps
finding.study_size: n=1,703 total problems (grade 6 n=508, grade 7 n=679, grade 8 n=516)

paper_profiles.title: Aligning Tutor Discourse Supporting Rigorous Thinking with Tutee Content Mastery for Predicting Math Achievement
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether the interaction between human tutor discourse and students’ proximal math content mastery can predict students’ math achievement. The authors focus on two feature sources: tutor talk moves from small-group tutoring sessions and students’ performance metrics on an Intelligent Tutoring System (MATHia). They use interpretable machine-learning models to identify which combinations of discourse and ITS mastery best separate high- versus low-performing assessment outcomes.

The study was conducted with 1,080 9th-grade students in a large urban Midwestern district during the 2022–23 school year. Students participated in high-dosage, small-group tutoring with human tutors and alternated with individual work on the MATHia ITS. The authors analyzed five rounds of math skills assessments and built random forest classifiers, then extracted decision trees to improve interpretability. They compared tutor talk moves alone, ITS metrics alone, and combined features.

Results showed that the combined model performed best for predicting both assessment scores and changes in scores, with AUCs around 0.77–0.79 on the whole dataset. The most informative patterns suggested that tutor revoicing was more predictive for students with lower ITS mastery, whereas pressing for reasoning was more predictive for students with higher mastery. The paper concludes that discourse and content mastery interact in meaningful, but correlational, ways and that these relationships may help explain when certain tutoring talk moves are associated with better math outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that a combined model of tutor talk moves and MATHia ITS mastery best predicted math assessment performance, with an AUC of 0.79 on the whole dataset and 0.77 in cross-validation for changes in scores. In the best combined decision tree, Revoicing was associated with higher assessment scores for students with lower ITS mastery (mean scores improved from 15.2 to 22.8), while Press for Reasoning was associated with higher scores for students with higher ITS mastery (from 15.7 to 22.7).
finding.measure: Math skills assessment scores and changes in assessment scores
finding.effect_size: AUC=0.79; AUC=0.77; score differences reported as mean changes

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examined discourse features tied to rigorous thinking, including Press for Reasoning and Revoicing, and how these interacted with students’ content mastery. The findings indicate that these talk moves differentially predicted achievement depending on mastery level, suggesting a relationship between instructional discourse and students’ reasoning-related learning processes rather than a causal intervention effect.
finding.measure: Tutor talk moves related to rigorous thinking and reasoning
finding.effect_size: AUC=0.79 (combined features); AUC=0.64–0.68 for single-source models

paper_profiles.title: Novice Learner and Expert Tutor: Evaluating Math Reasoning Abilities of Large Language Models with Misconceptions
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th) and Middle School and High School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks a different question from standard math-benchmark evaluations of large language models (LLMs): instead of measuring whether models can solve problems correctly, it tests whether they can intentionally answer incorrectly in ways that match specific student misconceptions, and whether they can identify the misconception behind an incorrect answer. The authors frame these as two educationally motivated tasks: simulating a novice learner and simulating an expert tutor.

The study uses an Eedi dataset of multiple-choice grade-school mathematics questions paired with expert-curated misconception labels for incorrect choices. After preprocessing, the dataset contains 213 questions, 482 answer choices, and 319 misconceptions. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 are evaluated under multiple prompting strategies for both tasks. The paper reports that both models can answer the questions correctly at high rates, especially GPT-4 (94.8% with explanation), but they struggle substantially when asked to imitate a novice learner or diagnose misconceptions. For novice-learner simulation, GPT-4 reaches 61.7% in zero-shot with explanations and 67.9% with few-shot same-misconception examples. For expert-tutor simulation, GPT-4 performs well when only four misconceptions are provided (91.9%), but accuracy falls as the misconception set grows, dropping to 39.8% at 100 misconceptions.

Overall, the paper concludes that current LLMs are much weaker at controlled erroneous generation and misconception diagnosis than at standard correct-answer math solving. The results suggest that educational uses such as intelligent tutoring systems may require stronger student-simulation and misconception-understanding capabilities than current general-purpose LLMs provide. The paper is a preprint and focuses on model evaluation rather than measuring learning outcomes for human students.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates LLM mathematical reasoning on grade-school multiple-choice math problems, but with two nonstandard tasks: producing a specified incorrect answer and identifying misconceptions behind errors. GPT-4 performed very well on ordinary correct-answering (94.8% with explanation on the 213-question dataset), but substantially worse on novice-learner simulation (61.7% zero-shot with explanation; 67.9% few-shot same-misconception) and expert-tutor misconception identification (91.9% with 4 misconceptions, falling to 39.8% with 100 misconceptions).
finding.measure: Accuracy on correct-answer math questions; accuracy on specified incorrect-answer generation; accuracy on misconception identification
finding.std_deviation: 0.009-0.031 (reported as mean ± SD for accuracies across four trials)

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats misconception diagnosis, counterfactual reasoning, and explanation of student errors as indicators of deeper reasoning and metacognitive-like capability. LLMs showed clear weaknesses in these durable-skill-adjacent tasks: they struggled to intentionally produce specific erroneous responses and to infer the misconception that explains a wrong answer, especially as the number of candidate misconceptions increased.
finding.measure: Accuracy on novice-learner simulation and expert-tutor misconception identification

paper_profiles.title: SCIBENCH: Evaluating College-Level Scientific Problem-Solving Abilities of Large Language Models
paper_profiles.venue: ICML (Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces SCIBENCH, a benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on college-level scientific problem solving. The authors argue that prior benchmarks overemphasize high-school or basic algebra tasks and do not adequately test complex scientific reasoning, advanced mathematics, multimodal understanding, or precise numerical computation.

SCIBENCH contains 869 free-response problems drawn from college textbooks in mathematics, physics, and chemistry, plus a closed exam subset of 103 problems from computer science and math courses. The benchmark includes both text-only and multimodal items, with detailed solutions and a focus on problems requiring multi-step reasoning, calculus/differential equations, and scientific knowledge retrieval.

The paper evaluates several open-source and proprietary LLMs under zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, and tool-augmented settings. Results show that even the strongest models remain far from robust on these college-level tasks; GPT-4 performs best in many settings, but overall scores are still modest. The authors also perform an error analysis that identifies ten essential scientific problem-solving skills and shows that prompting strategies often improve some skills while degrading others, rather than providing universal gains.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark directly evaluates college-level mathematical problem solving and finds that even top LLMs perform only modestly on these tasks. On the textbook math subset, the best reported score was 54.76% for GPT-4-Turbo in zero-shot learning on the calculus book and 68.00% for GPT-4 in few-shot + Python on the calculus book, while the overall best weighted average on the full textbook set was 43.22% for GPT-4 with few-shot + Python (n=869 total problems across math, physics, and chemistry; math subset drawn from 3 textbooks).
finding.measure: Accuracy on college-level mathematics problems (textbook benchmark; includes calculus, differential equations, statistics, and math textbook subsets)
finding.study_size: n=869 total problems; math textbooks n=309 (calc n=161, stat n=93, diff n=55)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies scientific reasoning across mathematics, physics, and chemistry, showing that current LLMs struggle with complex scientific problem solving that requires conceptual understanding, multi-step reasoning, and numerical computation. Across the full textbook dataset, the best overall average score was 43.22% (GPT-4 with few-shot + Python), and the authors report that CoT and external tools improve some skills but do not produce universally strong scientific reasoning performance.
finding.measure: Accuracy on college-level scientific problem-solving benchmark questions spanning mathematics, physics, and chemistry
finding.study_size: n=869 textbook problems; additional n=103 closed exam problems and n=177 multimodal problems

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s error analysis explicitly targets underlying problem-solving skills such as logical decomposition, assumption identification, abstract reasoning, logical reasoning, and calculation. It finds mixed effects: chain-of-thought reduces calculation-related errors, but can increase errors in other skills such as causal reasoning and logical decomposition; few-shot prompting similarly helps some skills while hurting others.
finding.measure: LLM error profiles over ten essential scientific problem-solving skills
finding.study_size: Error analysis based on 112 manually annotated incorrect GPT-3.5 solutions plus benchmark-wide automated classification

paper_profiles.title: CMM-Math: A Chinese Multimodal Math Dataset To Evaluate and Enhance the Mathematics Reasoning of Large Multimodal Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of Chinese multimodal mathematics benchmarks for evaluating large multimodal models (LMMs). The authors argue that existing math benchmarks are either text-only or English-only and do not adequately test visual mathematical reasoning across school grades. To fill this gap, they introduce CMM-Math, a dataset of over 28,000 Chinese math problems spanning 12 grade levels from elementary school through high school, with multiple problem types and many items containing images.

The paper describes the construction of both evaluation and training splits for CMM-Math, including data collection from real exam papers, automated extraction, cleaning, and manual checking/subject labeling. The benchmark is used to compare a range of open-source and closed-source LMMs on accuracy and GPT-4o-scored solution quality across grade levels and subject areas. The authors also propose Math-LMM, a three-stage trained multimodal model, and report that it improves performance relative to several open-source baselines, especially on harder levels and some multimodal math tasks.

The main contribution is benchmark creation and model evaluation rather than a causal study in schools. The results show that current LMMs still struggle with Chinese multimodal math reasoning, with performance generally decreasing at higher grade levels and varying by subject. Because the paper evaluates AI systems on a math dataset rather than studying student learning outcomes, it is best characterized as an observational benchmark study centered on academic mathematical numeracy.

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily evaluates large multimodal models on Chinese mathematics problems and finds substantial performance limitations overall. On CMM-Math, average accuracy across models is 35.66%, with better performance on elementary-grade items and weaker performance on higher-grade and geometry-heavy items; the best reported accuracy is 65.98 for GPT-4o (3-shot), while mean GPT-4o score across models is 4.62/10. The proposed Math-LMM improves over many open-source baselines, but the study does not measure student outcomes.
finding.measure: Accuracy on CMM-Math; GPT-4o scored solution quality; subject- and grade-level math problem performance

paper_profiles.title: MathChat: Converse to Tackle Challenging Math Problems with LLM Agents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces MathChat, a conversational framework for solving mathematical problems with large language model (LLM) agents. The system pairs an LLM-based solver with a user proxy agent that extracts code, executes Python or other tool queries, returns results, and prompts the model to continue until a final boxed answer is produced.

The main question is whether a dialogue-based, tool-augmented agent setup can improve math problem solving compared with standard zero-shot prompting approaches. The authors evaluate GPT-4 on level-5 problems from the MATH benchmark, focusing on challenging competition-style problems that are primarily high school level, and compare MathChat against vanilla prompting, Program of Thoughts (PoT), and Program Synthesis (PS). They also test simplified prompts using Python alone or Python plus Wolfram Alpha.

Results show that MathChat improves overall accuracy over PoT and PS, with the paper reporting about a 6 percentage point gain over previous tool-using prompting methods and 44.71% total accuracy on the six evaluated categories. Performance is strongest in Algebra, Number Theory, Prealgebra, and Counting & Probability, while Intermediate Algebra and Precalculus remain difficult. The paper concludes that conversational tool use can improve performance and error correction, but challenging math problems still remain hard for current LLMs even with external tools.

finding.finding_summary: MathChat improved GPT-4’s performance on level-5 MATH problems relative to vanilla prompting, PoT, and PS. Across six categories, MathChat achieved 44.71% total accuracy (n=1192), compared with 37.67% for PoT, 39.60% for PS, and 28.69% for vanilla prompting; the paper describes this as about a 6 percentage point improvement over previous tool-using prompting methods.
finding.measure: Problem-solving accuracy on level-5 MATH benchmark problems across algebra, counting & probability, intermediate algebra, number theory, prealgebra, and precalculus

paper_profiles.title: FineMath: A Fine-Grained Mathematical Evaluation Benchmark for Chinese Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces FineMath, a fine-grained benchmark for evaluating the mathematical reasoning abilities of Chinese large language models (LLMs). The benchmark was designed around elementary-school mathematics concepts and organized into 17 categories of math word problems, each annotated by difficulty level according to the number of reasoning steps required.

The paper’s core contribution is not an instructional intervention, but a dataset and evaluation framework. The authors collected and manually standardized 1,584 Chinese math word problems from textbooks, workbooks, and the internet, then transformed them into both open-ended and multiple-choice evaluation formats. They evaluated GPT-4, GPT-3.5-Turbo, and several Chinese LLMs, comparing performance across math concept categories, reasoning-step difficulty levels, prompt formats, and answer-selection methods.

The main findings are that GPT-4 and GPT-3.5-Turbo substantially outperform the other models, but performance varies strongly by problem type and reasoning depth. Models generally perform better on simpler one-step problems and worse as reasoning steps increase. The authors also show that prompt wording and evaluation format can materially change measured accuracy, and that contamination from overlapping training data can inflate performance for some models. Overall, the paper concludes that fine-grained, contamination-aware evaluation is necessary for fairly assessing LLM mathematical capability.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates mathematical problem-solving accuracy on FineMath, a 1,584-item Chinese elementary-school math word-problem benchmark spanning 17 categories and three reasoning-depth levels. GPT-4 achieved 0.73 overall accuracy under Prompt 0, GPT-3.5-Turbo 0.62, and several Chinese LLMs performed lower (e.g., ChatGLM2-6B 0.42, Baichuan-7B 0.08). Performance varied substantially by concept and reasoning depth, with GPT-4 reaching 0.83 on level-1 items and 0.62 on level-3 items; counting and some geometry/proportion categories were notably harder.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Chinese elementary-school math word problems across 17 categories and reasoning-step levels

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (position paper; broad education stakeholders across K-12, tertiary, and professional learning)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the potential opportunities and risks of large language models, especially ChatGPT-like systems, for education. Rather than testing a specific intervention, the authors synthesize early research and propose use cases for learners and teachers, including generating practice materials, providing explanations and feedback, supporting writing and assessment, and enabling more interactive or personalized learning experiences.

The paper discusses these possibilities across educational levels, with examples for elementary, middle, and high school, as well as university and professional training. It also emphasizes major risks such as bias, privacy, copyright, overreliance, difficulty distinguishing AI-generated from student-generated work, and unequal access. The conclusion is that large language models may be valuable in education if used carefully with human oversight, critical thinking, responsible governance, and pedagogical guidance.

Because this is a conceptual and review-oriented position paper, it does not report original quantitative outcomes or experimental effects. Its main contribution is a structured discussion of applications, challenges, and mitigation strategies for integrating LLMs into educational practice.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models can support reading and writing development by suggesting syntactic and grammatical corrections, generating summaries and explanations of complex texts, and assisting with writing style. These claims are illustrative rather than based on a single empirical study, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension, writing support, grammar/style assistance

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that LLMs can generate practice problems, quizzes, explanations, and step-by-step solutions for mathematics learning, especially for middle and high school students. However, it provides no direct quantitative evidence for math outcomes, effect sizes, or sample sizes.
finding.measure: Math practice problems, explanations, and step-by-step solution support

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly emphasizes potential support for critical thinking, problem-solving, and analytical thinking through question prompting, explanation generation, and fact-checking-oriented use of LLMs. These are conceptual claims grounded in proposed educational uses rather than measured effects, so no empirical statistics are reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, analytical thinking, fact-checking

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLMs can improve student engagement, interaction, and curiosity, for example by prompting questions and supporting conversational practice. These outcomes are discussed as opportunities rather than results of a controlled study, and no effect sizes or sample sizes are provided.
finding.measure: Student engagement, interaction, curiosity

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims LLMs can reduce teacher workload by generating quizzes, practice problems, feedback, summaries, lesson plans, and by semi-automating grading and text feedback. It also cites prior work suggesting grading effort could be reduced by up to 85% in large courses, but this position paper itself does not present original efficiency data.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, automated feedback, grading effort, lesson planning efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally addresses institutional and policy issues around responsible adoption of LLMs in education, including governance, privacy, fairness, copyright, oversight, and access. Its conclusion is that benefits are possible only with clear strategies, human monitoring, and ethical/regulatory safeguards; this is a conceptual position rather than an empirical institutional study.
finding.measure: Governance, privacy, fairness, access, integrity, institutional adoption strategies

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that the rapid rise of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT requires a new educational emphasis on AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. The author frames AI as a transformative but risky force in education: it can personalize learning and support diverse learners, but it can also encourage uncritical dependence, hallucinated outputs, and academic integrity problems.

The paper is not an intervention study. Instead, it combines the author’s experience at Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich with a narrative literature review to discuss how an institution can respond to student use of AI in academic work and classroom settings. The main context is higher education, especially student writing and classroom pedagogy, though the author suggests the ideas may also be useful for children.

The article proposes a middle-ground institutional policy that allows AI use with transparency, documentation, and critical reflection, rather than outright bans or unrestricted use. It also recommends a broader AI culture through workshops, updated guidance, budgeting, and dedicated staffing. In the classroom, the paper highlights AI literacy instruction and prompt engineering as ways to improve student understanding, critical thinking, and responsible use of AI tools.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that institutions should adopt formal AI guidelines, transparency requirements, workshops, staff development, and dedicated AI support roles rather than banning or fully unrestricted use. The evidence is conceptual and case-based from one Swiss university (KFH), so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Institutional AI policy and governance practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that prompt engineering and AI literacy can strengthen students’ critical thinking by encouraging them to evaluate outputs, compare alternatives, and reflect on hallucinations and limitations. This is presented as a pedagogical argument rather than a measured outcome, so no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking / critical reflection in AI use

finding.finding_summary: The article suggests that AI can improve efficiency in academic tasks such as drafting, brainstorming, curriculum design, and creating case studies, but it also notes tradeoffs such as time spent prompting and evaluating outputs. These claims are illustrative and not supported by empirical estimates in the paper.
finding.measure: Perceived productivity / workflow efficiency in academic tasks

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle school students want generative AI to function as a peer collaborator during collaborative mathematical problem solving (CPS), rather than as a tutor or answer-giver. The authors ask what students perceive as helpful or frustrating when AI is embedded in small-group math work, and what features, behaviors, and controls students want from such a system.

To explore this, the researchers ran a five-day summer camp with 24 rising grades 6–8 students. Students completed human-only CPS and AI-involved CPS using a custom web-based AI peer technology probe with two AI peers, then participated in reflections, interviews, participatory design poster activities, and a preference survey. The math tasks were grade-aligned middle-school problems in ratios/proportional reasoning, expressions/equations, and early functions/geometry.

The study finds that students preferred AI peers that were scaffold-first, deferential, and under explicit student control. They wanted hints, checks, concept refreshers, and error detection before direct answers, and they strongly rejected behavior that felt teachery, repetitive, inattentive, or emotionally unresponsive. Quantitatively, AI peers reduced perceived temporal demand (lower NASA-TLX temporal demand, d=1.15) but increased physical demand and reduced social/task cohesion, indicating a trade-off between procedural efficiency and the lived quality of collaboration. The paper concludes with design recommendations for AI peers in middle-school mathematics that emphasize co-agency, social attunement, and controllable help delivery.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies middle-school mathematics CPS with AI peers, but the evidence is about students’ experiences and collaboration rather than learning gains on math achievement. Students wanted math help to be scaffold-first (hints, checks, concept refreshers) and rejected direct-answer or over-scripted help; the technology probe was designed around grade-aligned math tasks in ratios/proportional reasoning, expressions/equations, and early functions/geometry. No posttest math learning outcome or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Grade-aligned middle-school mathematics collaborative problem-solving tasks; student perceptions of math help quality
finding.study_size: n=24 (design study); paired survey analyses n=22

finding.finding_summary: Students’ affective experience changed in both positive and negative ways when working with AI peers. On the negative side, AI peers significantly reduced perceived social attractiveness of the group (GEQ ATGS: M=5.21, SD=1.81 vs. 6.50, SD=2.05; p=0.029; d=0.94), and students described frustration, self-blame, and reduced trust when the AI failed to recognize emotional states. At the same time, students valued encouragement and emotional scaffolding from human peers, implying that affective support was an important missing feature in the AI design.
finding.measure: GEQ Attractions to Group-Social; interview/reflection themes on frustration, trust, encouragement, and emotional support
finding.study_size: n=22 for GEQ; interview sample n=18 plus whole-class reflections
finding.std_deviation: GEQ ATGS SDs: 1.81 (AI peer) vs 2.05 (human CPS)

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines collaboration, co-agency, and problem-solving coordination in middle-school CPS. AI peers lowered perceived task coordination on GEQ Group Integration-Task (M=4.76, SD=1.58 vs. 5.54, SD=1.52; p=0.047; d=0.81) even while students reported lower temporal demand, suggesting a trade-off between efficiency and collaborative quality. Qualitative data show students wanted the AI to negotiate methods, listen, and support shared reasoning rather than impose procedures or repeat itself.
finding.measure: GEQ Group Integration-Task; qualitative reflections/interviews about collaboration, co-agency, and turn-taking
finding.study_size: n=22 for GEQ; interview sample n=18 plus whole-class reflections
finding.std_deviation: GEQ GIT SDs: 1.58 (AI peer) vs 1.52 (human CPS)

finding.finding_summary: AI peers reduced students’ perceived temporal demand during collaborative mathematics work, indicating faster or less time-pressured task progress. On the NASA-TLX temporal demand subscale, the AI-peer condition scored lower than human-only CPS (M=5.67, SD=4.38 vs. 9.62, SD=4.13; p=0.002; d=1.15) for n=22 paired participants. However, this benefit came with higher physical demand and lower social/task cohesion, so the efficiency gain was not uniformly positive across the collaboration experience.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX Temporal Demand

finding.finding_summary: The study also addresses metacognitive and strategic aspects of collaborative problem solving, especially students’ desire for co-agency, checking, and method negotiation. Qualitative findings indicate that students wanted the AI to ask what they thought should happen next, provide examples rather than one fixed procedure, and support shared reasoning; these are durable-skill processes central to collaboration and metacognition. No direct performance-based measure of critical thinking or metacognition was reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview/reflection themes on co-agency, method negotiation, and checking work
finding.study_size: n=18 interview participants; whole-class reflections across 5 sessions

paper_profiles.title: Students' Perceived Roles, Opportunities, and Challenges of a Generative AI-powered Teachable Agent: A Case of Middle School Math Class
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how middle school students perceived a generative AI-powered teachable agent (TA) used in an authentic mathematics classroom. The paper asks what roles students expected the TA to play, what benefits they experienced from learning with it, and what barriers they encountered.

The intervention was a GenAI-powered TA built for secondary math learning using GPT-4-Turbo, retrieval-augmented generation, and a dynamically updated knowledge graph drawn from authentic math Q&A. The design combined learning-by-teaching with personalized learning, contrast cases, gamification, and psychological supports. Students in a public laboratory research middle school in the southeastern United States interacted with the TA during a two-session classroom study while solving rates-and-ratio problems.

The sample included 108 sixth-grade students across six classes, with 14 additionally participating in focus-group interviews. Data came from classroom observations, open-ended surveys, and semi-structured interviews, and were analyzed thematically. The findings indicate that students saw the TA as a learning companion, facilitator, and collaborative problem-solver.

Students reported several perceived benefits: a more student-centered learning climate, greater autonomy, improved cognitive/social/emotional capacities, stronger math understanding, better application of knowledge, increased enjoyment of math, higher self-efficacy, stronger intrinsic motivation, interdisciplinary connections, and a more positive attitude toward AI. They also identified barriers, including weak problem presentation, surface-level questioning, poor accommodation of learning styles, disorganized sequencing, limited socio-emotional skill, students’ own lack of domain and pedagogical knowledge, technical issues, lack of multimodal input, poor interoperability, a non-intuitive interface, and the need for teacher facilitation. Because the study is qualitative and perception-based, it does not provide causal estimates of learning gains, but it offers design implications for future GenAI-powered TAs in K-12 mathematics.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that interacting with the GenAI-powered TA improved their understanding of the unit content (rates and ratio) and helped them apply mathematical knowledge in new contexts. The paper is based on a qualitative classroom study with 108 sixth-grade students; the evidence is students’ self-reported perceptions rather than a measured achievement gain, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of math understanding and application of knowledge from open-ended surveys, focus groups, and classroom observations

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived increased enjoyment of math, self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, and emotional resilience when learning with the TA. The study used qualitative data from 108 sixth-grade students and 14 interviews; no quantitative effect size or confidence interval was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived enjoyment of math, self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, and emotional responses during TA-supported math learning

finding.finding_summary: Students said the TA encouraged cognitive reflection, communication, perspective-taking, and collaborative problem-solving. These were reported as perceived gains from a qualitative classroom study of 108 sixth-grade students, with no quantitative effect estimates reported.
finding.measure: Perceived cognitive, social, and collaborative skills developed through teaching the TA and co-solving problems

paper_profiles.title: Improving Student Learning with Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring: A Three-Study Quasi-Experimental Investigation
paper_profiles.venue: LAK '24 (The 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether hybrid human-AI tutoring can improve student learning processes in middle school mathematics, and whether those effects are larger for students with lower baseline achievement. The motivation is that AI-based math software can personalize practice at scale, but many students—especially those from low-income backgrounds—need the relational, motivational, and content support that human tutors provide.

The authors report results from three quasi-experimental studies conducted in urban, low-income U.S. middle schools. Across the sites, students used math software during the school day (IXL, i-Ready, or MATHia), and the intervention added remote human tutoring in different formats: round-robin tutor support without a dashboard at two sites, and dashboard-guided tutoring at one site. The sites included a 7th-grade Pennsylvania school with delayed treatment, a 7th-grade California school with a late-semester tutoring period, and a Pennsylvania charter school in grades 6-8 that compared two tutor-to-student ratios (about 1:8 vs 1:4).

finding.finding_summary: Across the three studies, hybrid human-AI tutoring improved mathematics-related learning process outcomes relative to math software alone or earlier lower-intensity tutoring. In Site 1 (n=125), mixed-effects models showed significant gains in time spent on IXL (β=0.202, 95% CI [0.057, 0.347]) and in skills proficient, and Site 2 (n=385) showed increased lesson completion and time on task during the tutoring period. In Site 3 (n=75), moving from a 1:8 to a 1:4 tutor-to-student ratio increased MATHia progress by 0.36 workspaces per hour (95% CI [0.02, 0.70]).
finding.measure: Math software engagement and progress measures: IXL time spent/questions answered/skills proficient; i-Ready minutes on task and lessons passed; MATHia workspaces completed per hour

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines engagement and participation as intermediate outcomes, finding that hybrid human-AI tutoring increased time on task and usage of the math software. In Site 2, average time on task rose from 24 to 33 minutes per week during tutoring, and in Site 1 tutoring significantly increased time spent practicing with IXL (β=0.202, 95% CI [0.057, 0.347]). These results are interpreted by the authors as improved student engagement and learning opportunities.
finding.measure: Time on task, time spent practicing, usage/proficiency logs, lesson completion
finding.effect_size: β=0.202; increase from 24 to 33 minutes/week; 0.36 more workspaces/hour

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved productive use of software time and tutor allocation, especially when dashboard-guided tutoring increased tutor access from about 1:8 to 1:4. In Site 3, students completed 0.36 more workspaces per hour after the shift, suggesting greater output per unit of software time with improved tutoring intensity. The authors also frame the model as scalable and lower-cost than conventional high-dosage tutoring, but they do not provide a formal efficiency effect size beyond the workspace-completion rate.
finding.measure: Workspaces completed per hour of MATHia engagement; tutor-to-student ratio

paper_profiles.title: AI tutoring can safely and effectively support students: An exploratory RCT in UK classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a generative AI tutor can safely and effectively support students in real classroom mathematics instruction. The authors evaluate LearnLM, a pedagogy-fine-tuned generative model, inside the Eedi platform and compare it against static, pre-written hints and against interactive tutoring delivered by expert human tutors.

The study was conducted as an exploratory randomized controlled trial in five UK secondary schools with N=165 students in Years 9 and 10 (ages 13–15). Students were randomized to either static hints or interactive tutoring, and tutoring sessions were then randomized to human tutor only versus human-supervised LearnLM. The platform measured three math-learning outcomes: immediate mistake remediation, misconception resolution, and transfer to the next study unit.

Results show that LearnLM was generally safe and pedagogically sound under human supervision: tutors approved most drafted messages with no or minimal edits, and the audit found no harmful content and only five factual errors across 3,617 drafts. For learning, LearnLM performed at least as well as human tutoring on immediate outcomes and outperformed human tutoring on knowledge transfer to a new topic (66.2% vs 60.7%, a 5.5 percentage-point gain; credible interval for the difference [-1.4, +12.4]). The authors conclude that supervised genAI tutoring may be a promising way to scale individualized mathematics support, while noting that longer-term and broader subject-area evidence is still needed.

finding.finding_summary: The trial found that supervised LearnLM tutoring was at least as effective as human tutoring for immediate mathematics learning and better for transfer. Students tutored by LearnLM were more likely to solve a novel problem on the next topic (66.2%) than students receiving human tutoring alone (60.7%), a difference of 5.5 percentage points with a reported credible interval of [-1.4, +12.4].
finding.measure: Performance on Eedi mathematics study-unit outcomes: mistake remediation, misconception resolution, and especially knowledge transfer to the first question in the next unit

finding.finding_summary: The paper also reports evidence that LearnLM improved tutor workflow efficiency, though this was not measured as a primary experimental outcome. Supervising tutors overwhelmingly reported that the system made it possible to support multiple students at the same time, and their comfort with AI tools increased from 3.4 to 3.9 out of 5 (posterior probability of increase: 90.0%).
finding.measure: Tutor surveys and interviews on workload, comfort with AI, and perceived ability to support multiple students simultaneously
finding.study_size: n=17 tutors; survey responses from 17 tutors

finding.finding_summary: Student experience was generally positive, but the paper also notes that LearnLM’s Socratic style sometimes risked frustrating students if it persisted too long. In post-trial surveys, students rated interactive tutoring as slightly more helpful than static hints (3.9 vs 3.6 out of 5), but tutors frequently intervened to moderate pacing and tone to preserve engagement.
finding.measure: Post-trial student helpfulness ratings and qualitative interview evidence about engagement/frustration
finding.study_size: n=27 student survey responses; n=5 tutor interviews

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Generation of Question Hints for Mathematics Problems using Large Language Models in Educational Technology
paper_profiles.venue: FM-EduAssess at NeurIPS 2024 Workshop / Proceedings of Machine Learning Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can generate pedagogically useful hints for mathematics exercises and whether those hints help simulated students self-correct. The authors focus on a problem that is central to intelligent tutoring systems: producing hints that are relevant, do not reveal the answer, and align with a cognitive-science-informed instructional design.

The study uses four French high-school mathematics exercises from the MIA Seconde educational platform. Three LLMs are used as simulated students (GPT-3.5-turbo, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3), while GPT-4o and Llama-3-8B-Instruct are used as teacher models to generate hints. The authors compare several hint-generation prompt types, including specialized prompts tied to specific error types and baseline prompts that ignore the student response. They also vary temperature settings to study how randomness affects error patterns and revision behavior.

Results suggest that higher temperatures increase the diversity and frequency of student-model errors. Among prompt types, calculation-error prompts and a baseline prompt labeled BaselineTwo performed best overall for enabling revision. When hints were generated with either GPT-4o or Llama-3-8B-Instruct, student models often improved after receiving hints, with the strongest gains seen for GPT-3.5-turbo. The paper concludes that LLMs can support hint generation in math, but that prompt design, teacher model choice, and temperature all materially affect performance; the authors also note that Llama-3-8B-Instruct often outperformed GPT-4o in their setup, though they caution that hint quality still needs qualitative validation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that LLM-generated hints can improve math problem-solving and answer revision on four high-school exercises, but the effect depends strongly on prompt type, teacher model, student model, and temperature. The strongest gains were observed for GPT-3.5-turbo after receiving hints; for example, with the best prompts, accuracy improved after hinting, while higher temperatures generally increased error rates and reduced performance.
finding.measure: Accuracy on solving math exercises before and after hints; mean revision error rate after hint generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames and evaluates hint generation as support for self-correction, problem-solving, and response revision, which are durable skills closely tied to metacognition and reasoning.
