Simulated students often improved their answers after receiving hints, especially when the hint aligned with the error type, indicating that the prompts could scaffold self-correction rather than simply provide answers.
finding.measure: Ability of simulated student models to revise incorrect answers after receiving hints

paper_profiles.title: Automated Feedback in Math Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLMs for Open-Ended Responses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can improve automated scoring and feedback generation for open-ended mathematics responses on an online learning platform. The authors compare three approaches: a fine-tuned Llama/Mistral-based model called GOAT, the prior SBERT-Canberra similarity-based method, and GPT-4 used zero-shot with a math grading rubric.

The study uses a dataset of roughly 50 middle-school math problems, each with about 100 student responses, teacher-assigned scores, and teacher-written feedback. Models are evaluated on score prediction using AUC, RMSE, and Cohen’s kappa, and on feedback quality using two human raters with teaching experience who judge accuracy, relevance, motivation, and preference.

For scoring, GOAT performs best (AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, Kappa=0.422), outperforming SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4. For feedback quality, GPT-4 is preferred by human raters and scores highest on accuracy (86% consensus), relevance (91% consensus), and preference (77.5% of selections), though GOAT is generally better than SBERT-Canberra. The paper concludes that fine-tuned LLMs can improve automated math scoring, while GPT-4 currently produces the most useful feedback.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the fine-tuned GOAT model improved automated scoring of middle-school open-ended math responses relative to SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4. On the held-out test set (n=1,000 responses), GOAT achieved AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, and Kappa=0.422, compared with SBERT-Canberra (AUC=0.662, RMSE=1.364, Kappa=0.362) and GPT-4 (AUC=0.639, RMSE=1.16, Kappa=0.266).
finding.measure: Teacher score prediction for open-ended math responses; AUC, RMSE, and multi-class Cohen’s kappa

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central focus is automated scoring and feedback generation intended to reduce teacher workload on open-ended mathematics items. Although it does not directly measure time saved, the authors argue that both GOAT and GPT-4 can support scalable assessment; teacher raters also preferred GPT-4 feedback, suggesting practical usefulness for reducing grading and feedback burdens.
finding.measure: Human-rated feedback quality and model-based automated scoring for open-ended responses
finding.study_size: n=100 sampled feedback cases for human evaluation; n=1,000 scored responses

paper_profiles.title: Automated Generation of Curriculum-Aligned Multiple-Choice Questions for Malaysian Secondary Mathematics Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of generating high-quality, curriculum-aligned assessment items at scale for Malaysian secondary mathematics. The authors argue that while generative AI can reduce teacher workload and support personalized learning, unconstrained prompting risks producing generic or misaligned questions, especially in a low-resource language setting such as Bahasa Melayu.

To test this, the paper compares four GPT-4o-based pipelines for generating Form 1 Mathematics multiple-choice questions: two non-grounded prompting methods and two Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) methods. The RAG pipelines ground generation in official curriculum documents and teacher notes, with one implemented using LangChain and the other via a custom manual retrieval pipeline that better preserves document structure. The generated questions are evaluated with two automated checks: semantic textual similarity (STS) to curriculum standards and a RAG-based QA validity test.

The study uses 100 generated questions per method and finds that both RAG approaches substantially outperform non-grounded prompting on alignment and validity. The manual RAG pipeline performs best overall (STS=0.89, validity=96%), followed closely by LangChain RAG (STS=0.86, validity=92%), while non-grounded prompting lags far behind (STS=0.55-0.58, validity=12%-15%). The authors conclude that grounding is essential for curriculum-specific question generation and that custom, domain-aware retrieval can offer a small but meaningful advantage over off-the-shelf RAG, though automated metrics still cannot fully assess cognitive level or pedagogical quality.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that generative AI, especially RAG-based pipelines, can automate curriculum-aligned MCQ creation and thereby reduce the burden of question development for teachers. While it does not measure teacher time directly, the study explicitly frames the approach as a scalable assessment-generation workflow and reports that 100 questions per method could be generated and evaluated automatically.
finding.measure: Automated generation of curriculum-aligned multiple-choice questions; discussion of teacher workload and scalability

finding.finding_summary: The generated items focus on Form 1 Mathematics content, specifically rational numbers/integer operations in the Malaysian secondary curriculum. RAG-based methods produced questions that were much more tightly aligned to the relevant mathematics standards than non-grounded prompting, with STS alignment scores of 0.86 and 0.89 versus 0.55 and 0.58, and validity rates of 92% and 96% versus 12% and 15%.
finding.measure: Curriculum alignment of generated mathematics MCQs; STS score against RPT Bab 1 and RAG-QA validity

paper_profiles.title: GPT takes the SAT: Tracing changes in Test Difficulty and Students’ Math Performance
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether the SAT Math section has become easier over time and whether observed changes in student SAT Math scores reflect changes in exam difficulty, student performance, or both. The authors frame the work as a comparison of historical SAT Math exams from 2008–2023 using GPT-4 as a fixed benchmark, then compare GPT-4’s score trajectory with population SAT Math performance for U.S. students, state-level aggregates, and Massachusetts district-level data.

The core methodological contribution is a “Transformed Control” approach: GPT-4 (via OpenAI API) takes sampled SAT Math exams from each year under a constant zero-shot prompt, and its score changes are treated as a counterfactual benchmark for changes in test difficulty. The paper then uses difference-in-differences-style logic and Bayesian comparisons of means to estimate the change in student math performance relative to baseline year 2008, controlling for exam difficulty shifts inferred from GPT-4.

The study focuses on high school students and the SAT Math assessment context in the United States, with supplementary analyses at the state aggregate level and in Massachusetts school districts. The authors report that GPT-4’s performance improved over time, suggesting the SAT Math section became less rigorous, while student performance declined more sharply. Their main conclusion is that from 2008 to 2023, SAT Math difficulty fell and student math performance also declined, with an estimated 107-point divergence relative to 2008 on the SAT Math scale. The paper also reports heterogeneity by race and gender, finding larger declines for White students and for male students, though it is not an intervention study and does not make causal claims about student outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds a substantial decline in high school students’ SAT Math performance relative to the GPT-4 benchmark over 2008–2023. Using the authors’ transformed-control and Bayesian comparison approach, student performance is reported to have fallen by about 36 points net of a 71-point decline in exam rigor, yielding a 107-point divergence from the 2008 baseline.
finding.measure: SAT Math scaled scores / Average Difference in Scores (ADS) relative to baseline year 2008
finding.study_size: national population reports across 2008-2023; state-aggregated annual reports; Massachusetts district-level sample of 228 districts
finding.std_deviation: reported in source for population and state reports but exact values not extracted

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that SAT Math has become less rigorous over time, which has implications for the SAT’s usefulness as a college admissions sorting tool. It also reports heterogeneous declines by demographic group and discusses broader institutional mechanisms such as test-optional policies, selection pressure, grade inflation, screen time, and adolescent mental health.
finding.measure: Change in SAT Math rigor/difficulty over time; policy-relevant interpretation of admissions utility
finding.study_size: SAT exams from 2008-2023; GPT-4 evaluated on 50 sampled exams per year

paper_profiles.title: EZYer: A simulacrum of high school with generative agent
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents EZYer, a generative educational agent designed to support high school mathematics teaching and learning. The system has three main components: a Teacher Module that generates structured teaching materials and LaTeX Beamer courseware from uploaded text or documents, a Student Module that simulates classroom interaction through five roles (Teacher, Assistant, Top Student, Struggling Student, and Note Taker), and a Controller that filters content and checks quality for pedagogical appropriateness and LaTeX correctness.

The paper’s central question is whether an LLM-powered agent can reliably generate high-quality high school mathematics instructional materials and notes while simulating interactive classroom behavior. The authors evaluate 100 generated Beamer presentations and Notes using five large language models as judges, scoring content accuracy, knowledge coverage, usability, formatting correctness, and visual design/appeal. The results indicate strong performance on content accuracy and knowledge coverage, with somewhat weaker scores for usability and visual design, suggesting EZYer is promising for high school math lesson preparation and note generation.

The study is explicitly scoped to ordinary high school mathematics and does not report student learning outcomes, controlled comparisons, or direct classroom effectiveness measures. Its evidence is therefore limited to system/output quality evaluation rather than causal educational impact.

finding.finding_summary: EZYer-generated high school mathematics materials were rated highly on content accuracy and knowledge coverage by five large language models. Across 100 generated Beamer presentations and Notes, the average scores were reported as 4.74 for Beamer content accuracy and 4.70 for Notes knowledge/content quality, suggesting the system can produce mathematically relevant instructional content that is largely accurate and comprehensive.
finding.measure: LLM-rated quality of generated high school mathematics Beamer courseware and Notes; dimensions included content accuracy and knowledge coverage
finding.study_size: n=100 generated Beamer and Notes documents

finding.finding_summary: The system is designed to automate lesson material creation, exercise generation, note taking, and LaTeX Beamer compilation for high school mathematics teachers and students. The authors conclude that EZYer can raise teacher lesson-preparation efficiency and reduce manual formatting work, and the evaluation results support that the generated outputs are usable for high school classroom preparation, though usability scored lower than accuracy/coverage on some models (average as low as 4.1).
finding.measure: LLM-rated usability plus system capability for automated generation of teaching materials, exercises, notes, and Beamer PDFs
finding.study_size: n=100 generated Beamer and Notes documents

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Models in Numberland: A Quick Test of Their Numerical Reasoning Abilities
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how well large language models can handle low-level numerical reasoning, a capability the author argues is foundational to broader mathematical reasoning but has been less studied than high-level benchmark performance. The study introduces a custom 100-problem test called “Numberland,” designed to probe elementary arithmetic, advanced operations, primality checking, and the 24 game as increasingly complex numerical tasks.

Five LLM-based agents were tested over multiple trials: OpenAI o1-mini, OpenAI o1, Google Gemini 1.5, Anthropic Claude Sonnet 3.7, and Microsoft Copilot. The paper reports that all models performed reasonably well on deterministic tasks such as basic arithmetic, advanced calculations, and primality checking, but accuracy dropped sharply on the 24 game, especially when trial-and-error search was required. The best model, o1, scored 73% on the easier 24-game set but fell to 27% on a harder follow-up set, with common errors including incorrectly claiming no solution existed, breaking game rules, and miscalculating expressions.

The main conclusion is that current LLMs exhibit a fragile form of number sense: they can execute straightforward numerical procedures, but their performance degrades when they must search, self-monitor, or manage multi-step reasoning under higher cognitive load. The paper frames this as a limitation in LLM numerical reasoning rather than a general failure on all math tasks, and suggests that targeted tests like Numberland can help diagnose specific reasoning bottlenecks and inform future interpretability work.

finding.finding_summary: Across 100 hand-picked tasks, five LLM-based agents performed well on deterministic numerical problems but much worse on the 24 game. On the first three sets (basic operations, advanced operations, primality checking), reported accuracies ranged from 74% to 95%, while performance on the 24-game set dropped to 11% to 73%; the best model (o1) scored 73% on the easier set and 27% on a harder follow-up set (n=25 harder games).
finding.measure: Accuracy on numerical reasoning tasks in Numberland (basic operations, advanced operations, primality checking, and 24 game)
finding.study_size: n=5 models; 100 initial problems; 25 harder follow-up problems

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Multimodal Feedback Using Multiple External Representations: Strategy Profiles and Learning in High School Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether students’ voluntary use of elaborated, multimodal feedback is associated with improved learning in high school physics. The authors focus on a computer-based environment that provides standard verification feedback plus optional elaborated feedback in three multiple external representations (MERs): verbal/textual, graphical/pictorial, and mathematical.

The study follows 661 German 10th- and 11th-grade students across 26 schools and 66 classes over 16–24 weeks. Students completed pre- and post-tests on kinematics and worked through 43 optional exercises on the KI4SCool platform. The authors analyzed associations between feedback use and post-test performance using linear mixed-effects models, and they also used clustering to identify common feedback-selection strategies over time and across representation types.

Results showed a small positive association between elaborated feedback use and post-test performance after controlling for prior knowledge, platform performance, number of exercises solved, and response confidence. This association was significant in Cohort 1 and positive but marginal in Cohort 2. The paper did not find strong evidence that students’ initial representational competence explained which feedback strategy they used, nor that baseline competence robustly moderated the relationship between feedback strategy and learning. Overall, the authors conclude that using elaborated multimodal feedback is associated with better learning, but the observational design does not support causal claims.

finding.finding_summary: Across two high-school cohorts (n=351 and n=310), greater use of elaborated feedback was associated with higher post-test performance on kinematics assessments after controlling for pre-test score, platform score, exercises solved, and confidence. In Cohort 1 the standardized effect was β=0.13, 95% CI [0.05, 0.22]; in Cohort 2 it was positive but only marginally significant, β=0.08, 95% CI [0.00, 0.16].
finding.measure: Post-test score on kinematics concept tests (percent correct)

finding.finding_summary: The paper examined average response confidence and response time as related student characteristics, but the central social-emotional result was that elaborated feedback use was not strongly explained by confidence, prior knowledge, or number of exercises solved. Feedback frequency was essentially uncorrelated with average confidence in both cohorts (r≈0.00 and r=0.10), while it was moderately correlated with average response time (r=0.43 and r=0.34), suggesting more reflective students tended to use feedback more.
finding.measure: Average response confidence; average response time; correlations with feedback frequency

paper_profiles.title: MATH-BEYOND: A Benchmark for RL to Expand Beyond the Base Model
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint introduces MATH-Beyond (MATH-B), a benchmark designed to test whether reinforcement learning and related post-training methods can expand a language model’s mathematical reasoning beyond what its base model can already solve. The authors argue that many existing math benchmarks are saturated because strong open-source models can solve them with enough sampling, so improvements from RL often reflect sharpening of existing solution paths rather than discovering new ones.

To build MATH-B, the authors filter problems from DAPO-Math-17K and DeepScaleR, remove ambiguous or poorly verifiable items, verify ground-truth answers with frontier models, deduplicate against standard benchmarks, and then keep only problems that remain unsolved by a suite of open-source models at pass@1024. The resulting benchmark contains a union set of 181 high-school competition math problems and a harder intersection set of 41 problems unsolved by all considered base models.

The paper then evaluates several post-trained models on MATH-B and reports that current RL methods achieve only modest expansion beyond their base models, while some supervised distillation approaches achieve substantially higher expansion rates. The main conclusion is that current open-source RL methods often fail to discover genuinely new reasoning pathways, and that benchmarks like MATH-B can better measure and encourage true boundary expansion in mathematical reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is centered on mathematical reasoning performance as measured by pass@1024 on the MATH-B benchmark. RL-finetuned models showed limited expansion beyond their base models, with reported expansion rates of 7.83% (nemotron_v1, n=115 base-unsolved), 9.57% (nemotron_v2, n=115), 5.22% (DeepScaleR, n=115), and 21.21% (Skywork-OR1-7B, n=99), whereas Qwen3 distilled models showed much larger gains (58.93% for Qwen3-4B and 66.38% for Qwen3-8B). These results indicate that current RL methods only modestly improve mathematical reasoning on a benchmark specifically constructed to be unsolved by the base model.
finding.measure: Expansion rate / pass@1024 on high-school math benchmark (MATH-B-U and model-specific unsolved subsets)
finding.study_size: n=181 benchmark problems overall; model-specific subsets n=99-115 base-unsolved problems

paper_profiles.title: Teaching Arithmetic to Small Transformers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how small decoder-only transformer models learn arithmetic from scratch, focusing on whether data formatting, sampling strategy, model scale, and chain-of-thought-style intermediate steps can accelerate learning. The authors study addition, subtraction, multiplication, square root, and sine in controlled synthetic settings using NanoGPT and related GPT-family models trained with next-token prediction.

The central contribution is not an educational intervention in a classroom, but an analysis of how different training formats affect arithmetic learning in language models. They compare plain output formatting against reversed-output formats and scratchpad/chain-of-thought formats that include intermediate steps, and they also test balanced sampling, noisy intermediate labels, and fine-tuning from pretrained models. Across experiments, more instructive formats substantially improve sample efficiency and accuracy, with detailed scratchpad formatting often learning fastest; however, the models still show weak length generalization beyond trained digit ranges.

The work is entirely in a synthetic modeling context rather than with K-12 learners, teachers, or schools. Its main conclusion is that arithmetic abilities in small transformers can emerge rapidly when training data is structured to match the next-token prediction objective, but these models learn more as constrained mappings than as fully general arithmetic algorithms. The paper also shows that chain-of-thought-style intermediate supervision can improve learning, while poor formatting or noisy intermediate steps can slow learning or harm performance.

finding.finding_summary: Across a series of synthetic arithmetic experiments, structured training formats substantially improved model performance on addition and related operations. Reversing the output order, using simplified scratchpad data, and using detailed scratchpad data all increased sample efficiency and often produced 100% test accuracy on addition; for 3-digit addition, reverse formatting reached perfect accuracy after roughly 1,000–4,000 training examples, simplified scratchpad after about 2,000 examples, and detailed scratchpad after about 1,000 examples.
finding.measure: Test accuracy on synthetic arithmetic tasks (addition primarily; also subtraction, multiplication, square root, sine)

paper_profiles.title: Learning Elementary Cellular Automata with Transformers
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS 2024 Workshop on Mathematical Reasoning and AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether Transformer models can learn and generalize the rules governing elementary cellular automata (ECA), a simplified discrete dynamical system used here as a toy benchmark for mathematical reasoning and planning. The motivation is to probe a core question in LLM research: whether failures in reasoning and planning stem from training data, objective design, or architectural limits.

The study trains a small encoder-only Transformer on sequences of binary ECA states generated from random initial conditions and randomly sampled local rules of fixed arity. Several training tasks are compared: predicting the next state from an orbit (O-S), predicting multiple future states (O-O), predicting the next state plus the latent rule (O-SR), and predicting the next state when the rule is provided (RO-S). The dataset uses lattice size 20, radius 2, about 9.5e5 training samples and 1e5 test samples, with test rules excluded from training rules to assess generalization to unseen rules rather than memorization.

Results show that the Transformer can learn next-state prediction well and can generalize across unseen Boolean rules of fixed arity, indicating rule abstraction. However, performance drops sharply for multi-step planning without intermediate context, especially for look-ahead horizons of 2 or more steps. Adding future-state prediction or explicit rule prediction improves longer-horizon performance, and deeper models are better able to carry out the sequential computations needed for longer rollouts. The paper concludes that longer-horizon loss design, recurrence, and adaptive computation time may help improve Transformer reasoning and planning, but it does not study educational settings or student learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies mathematical reasoning in the form of learning and generalizing rules of elementary cellular automata with a Transformer. The model achieved high next-state prediction accuracy (about 0.96 for the O-S task) on sequences of binary states, but performance declined sharply on multi-step planning, dropping to about 0.80 for 1-step look-ahead and below 0.75 for 2- and 3-step look-ahead tasks.
finding.measure: Per-bit prediction accuracy on ECA state-sequence tasks (next-state prediction, multi-step look-ahead, autoregressive rollout)

paper_profiles.title: Examining the Behavior of LLM Architectures Within the Framework of Standardized National Exams in Brazil
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how large language models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and MariTalk) behave on Brazil’s ENEM standardized exam, with a focus on whether their answer patterns resemble different socioeconomic groups of human test takers. The authors use 2022 ENEM microdata to compare model and human multiple-choice answer distributions across subjects and socioeconomic status (SES) strata, and they also compare LLM-generated essays with human-written ENEM essays using syntactic complexity metrics and bag-of-words classification.

The main question is whether apparent similarity between LLM outputs and humans reflects genuine socioeconomic bias or simply differences in accuracy. For the objective questions, the authors find that all models perform best in Languages and Humanities and worst in Math and Natural Sciences; however, the decreasing distance between model and human answer distributions for higher-SES groups is largely explained by human accuracy rather than SES itself. In regression analyses, SES adds little explanatory power beyond accuracy, suggesting no strong evidence that these LLMs mirror privileged human groups on the multiple-choice test.

For essays, the models’ writing differs substantially from human writing. Human and LLM essays are easily separable (mean accuracy 0.98 ± 0.02), and several syntactic metrics differ significantly, with GPT-4 generally closest to humans and MariTalk often farthest. Overall, the paper concludes that these LLMs do not closely represent Brazilian students’ behavior in ENEM, either in their multiple-choice responses or their essay writing, and that apparent demographic similarity on the objective items is mostly driven by performance rather than socioeconomic bias.

finding.finding_summary: The math section was the weakest area for all three models. GPT-3.5 reached 0.29 accuracy, GPT-4 0.23, and MariTalk 0.29 on 44 Math items, all substantially below their performance in Languages and Humanities. The authors also report that human-model answer distance in Math is smaller partly because both humans and models perform relatively poorly, not because the models specifically emulate any socioeconomic group.
finding.measure: ENEM Math multiple-choice accuracy and human-model Jensen-Shannon distance/answer overlap on Math items
finding.study_size: n=44 Math questions (model evaluation); human microdata used for all ENEM takers answering those items

finding.finding_summary: The Natural Sciences section was another weak area for the models. GPT-3.5 achieved 0.58 accuracy, GPT-4 0.71, and MariTalk 0.72 on 45 items, with the authors noting that these items often require multi-step reasoning that LLMs struggle with. As with Math, the model-human distance patterns are interpreted as reflecting confidence/accuracy characteristics more than socioeconomic bias.
finding.measure: ENEM Natural Sciences multiple-choice accuracy and human-model Jensen-Shannon distance/answer overlap on Natural Sciences items

finding.finding_summary: For the writing task, the models produced essays with language patterns that differed markedly from human ENEM essays. Compared with human essays (mean length 517 ± 40.45 words), GPT-3.5 essays averaged 481 ± 13.27 words, GPT-4 532 ± 11.50 words, and MariTalk 382 ± 3.17 words; syntactic metrics also differed significantly for all but MLT. The authors conclude that model-written essays are structurally distinct from human writing, although GPT-4 is generally closest to humans across several metrics.
finding.measure: ENEM essay syntactic complexity metrics (MLC, CPC, MLT, MLS, TS), essay length, and bag-of-words separability
finding.study_size: n=61 human essays; n=100 essays per LLM
finding.std_deviation: Human essay length SD=40.45; GPT-3.5 SD=13.27; GPT-4 SD=11.50; MariTalk SD=3.17

finding.finding_summary: The paper also studies ENEM performance in Languages and Humanities, which are not direct literacy or numeracy outcomes in the paper’s framing. GPT-3.5 scored 0.76 in Languages and 0.87 in Humanities, GPT-4 scored 0.84 and 0.93, and MariTalk scored 0.82 and 0.95, respectively. The authors describe these as the strongest sections for the models and note that GPT-4 and MariTalk outperform GPT-3.5 in Humanities, while Languages performance is also relatively high.
finding.measure: ENEM Languages and Humanities multiple-choice accuracy
finding.study_size: n=50 Languages questions; n=45 Humanities questions

finding.finding_summary: The core institutional finding is that the apparent resemblance between LLM outputs and higher-SES human answer distributions is not evidence of socioeconomic bias. Linear regression shows that human accuracy explains most of the overlap with model answers, while SES contributes little additional explanatory power (e.g., for GPT-3.5, R2=0.889 with human accuracy and SES; SES-only R2=0.174). The authors conclude that the models do not systematically represent any Brazilian SES group on the multiple-choice ENEM tests.
finding.measure: Jensen-Shannon distance, answer-overlap metric, and linear regression predicting overlap from human accuracy and SES
finding.study_size: Human microdata across ENEM 2022; regression analyses over all question responses and SES strata

paper_profiles.title: VGBench: Evaluating Large Language Models on Vector Graphics Understanding and Generation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces VGBench, a benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on vector graphics understanding and generation. The authors argue that vector graphics offer a useful alternative to raster images because they preserve geometric structure and can represent visual content in a compact textual form, making them a natural testbed for LLMs' ability to reason over code-like visual representations.

The benchmark covers three vector graphics formats: SVG, TikZ, and Graphviz. For understanding, the authors create 4,279 multiple-choice question-answer pairs spanning format-specific question types such as color, category, usage, concept, counting, relation, domain, and layout. For generation, they collect 5,845 caption-to-vector-graphics pairs and evaluate generated outputs with CLIP Score and FID after rasterization. GPT-4V is used to help generate captions and questions, with human filtering for quality control.

The main findings are that LLMs, especially GPT-4, perform substantially better on higher-level semantic formats such as TikZ and Graphviz than on low-level SVG, and that chain-of-thought and in-context prompting can improve performance mainly on SVG. The paper also finds that GPT-4 is strongest overall, open-source models such as Llama-3-70B and Qwen2-72B are competitive on some understanding tasks, and both GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 show strong vector graphics generation performance by CLIP/FID criteria. This is a benchmark/evaluation paper rather than a study of educational intervention or K-12 learning outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Responsible AI in Construction Safety: Systematic Evaluation of Large Language Models and Prompt Engineering
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates how well two large language models, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o, answer standardized construction-safety certification questions. The authors frame the work as a responsible-AI assessment, asking whether LLMs can support safety professionals and where human oversight remains necessary, especially in domains that require factual recall, reasoning, and calculation.

The study uses 385 multiple-choice questions drawn from three BCSP certification exams (ASP, CSP, and CHST), spanning seven safety knowledge areas. The models were tested under multiple prompt-engineering conditions: direct prompting, chain-of-thought prompting, and few-shot prompting, plus variations in reasoning inclusion, reasoning order, and answer format. The authors also evaluated reliability across repeated attempts and consistency via an entropy-based response metric. GPT-4o outperformed GPT-3.5 overall (84.6% vs. 73.8%), and both exceeded the BCSP passing threshold, but both struggled most in science-and-math items and emergency response/fire prevention. Prompting choices did not significantly change aggregate accuracy, though some configurations helped specific knowledge areas. Reliability was high across repeated trials, and response consistency was generally strong. The authors conclude that LLMs show promise for construction safety support tasks, but calculation-heavy and some domain-specific questions still require human oversight and/or more specialized tools.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates mathematics-related safety questions as part of the BCSP Science and Math knowledge area, but the models performed relatively poorly compared with other domains. The authors report that both GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o struggled with calculation-heavy items and identify calculation errors as one of the four main error types (7% of 42 analyzed errors), indicating limited but present competence rather than robust mathematical performance.
finding.measure: Accuracy on BCSP Science and Math multiple-choice questions; error analysis of calculation-related responses
finding.study_size: n=385 questions total; 55 science-and-math questions in the full test bank; 42 low-performing outputs in error analysis

finding.finding_summary: Science-and-math items were among the weakest areas for both models, and the paper explicitly notes difficulty with concepts in physics, chemistry, anatomy, physiology, and statistics relevant to safety. At the same time, the models still exceeded the passing benchmark overall, so the result is mixed: acceptable overall test performance, but clear weakness on scientific reasoning tasks compared with other safety knowledge areas.
finding.measure: Accuracy on BCSP Science and Math knowledge area questions
finding.study_size: n=385 questions total; 55 questions per knowledge area

finding.finding_summary: The study tests step-by-step reasoning performance through chain-of-thought prompting and analyzes reasoning flaws as a key failure mode. Prompt configurations that included reasoning were sometimes beneficial in the science-and-math domain, and reasoning flaws accounted for 31% of analyzed errors, showing that the models can engage in and sometimes improve with structured reasoning, but remain unreliable at it.
finding.measure: Accuracy under reasoning-oriented prompt configurations; qualitative error analysis of reasoning failures
finding.study_size: n=385 questions total; 42 outputs analyzed for error types

finding.finding_summary: Although not an education study, the paper substantively examines whether LLMs can support routine professional work more efficiently by answering safety certification questions accurately and consistently. The authors suggest the models could help with explanatory support, second opinions, and administrative extraction tasks, and they find strong reliability across five repeated attempts (p=0.957), indicating stable performance under controlled settings.
finding.measure: Repeated-measures accuracy across five attempts; overall MCQ accuracy as a proxy for task support
finding.study_size: n=385 questions; 16 configurations retested five times

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can contribute to safety management systems and responsible AI deployment in a high-stakes professional domain, but should be used with human oversight in weaker knowledge areas. Both models exceeded the BCSP passing benchmark, and the study concludes that LLMs could support safety practices while informing governance around prompt design, oversight, and countermeasures such as RAG or fine-tuning.
finding.measure: BCSP exam pass benchmark and domain-area performance across safety knowledge areas
finding.study_size: n=385 questions across three certification exams

paper_profiles.title: When the robotic Maths tutor is wrong - can children identify mistakes generated by ChatGPT?
paper_profiles.venue: 2023 UK Robotics Week / conference paper (venue not explicitly stated in text)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether primary school children can detect mistakes made by a ChatGPT-powered robotic maths tutor, and whether that ability is related to their own correctness on the maths question, their school year, or gender. The study is motivated by concerns that LLM-generated answers can be wrong but appear authoritative, potentially misleading young learners in classroom settings.

The intervention/approach was a user study in a primary school classroom using a Pepper robot connected to OpenAI’s gpt-3.5-turbo via custom Python code. Seventy-seven students in Years 3–5 answered 20 maths questions drawn from a pool of 29 UK Year 3 curriculum questions; each session mixed 10 correct and 10 incorrect robot answers in random order. After each item, students rated Pepper’s answer on a 5-point Likert scale. The authors then analyzed whether ratings differed by answer correctness and by student factors (their own question correctness, year group, and gender) using chi-square tests.

The main findings were that students could distinguish correct from incorrect robot answers at better-than-chance levels: 76.5% identified correct answers and 72% identified incorrect answers, with partial correctness causing some confusion. Students who answered the maths question correctly were more likely to spot the robot’s error (81% vs. 72% overall error detection), while year group was not a significant moderator. Gender was significant, with female students tending to identify errors more often than male students in this sample. The paper concludes that LLM-powered educational robots can be used cautiously as maths tutors, but only with gradual integration, human verification, and attention to prior knowledge and potential confounds.

finding.finding_summary: Primary school students were able to judge the correctness of robot-generated maths answers with statistically significant accuracy. Across 1,540 ratings from 77 students, 76.5% identified correct answers and 72% identified incorrect answers; the study reports χ2 = 504.7, df = 4, p < .001, indicating that students discriminated between correct, incorrect, and partially correct responses.
finding.measure: Student ratings of Pepper’s ChatGPT-generated maths answers on a 5-point Likert scale, analyzed against answer correctness

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines students’ ability to detect errors in AI-generated answers, which is a form of verification and critical evaluation. Students who solved the maths question correctly were significantly more likely to identify the robot’s error (81% detected incorrect LLM answers when they were correct on the item; χ2 = 374.95, df = 8, p < .001), suggesting prior knowledge supports error checking and metacognitive monitoring.
finding.measure: Error detection / judgment of correctness of AI-generated answers, split by whether students answered the maths question correctly

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that students were engaged enough to participate in the classroom robot activity and could make judgments about the robot’s answers, with discussion used to clarify mistakes and avoid misinformation. While engagement was not measured with a validated scale, the authors interpret the observed participation and rating behavior as evidence of engagement and confidence in responding to AI output.
finding.measure: Observed participation and Likert-scale judgments of robot answers

paper_profiles.title: War of the chatbots: Bard, Bing Chat, ChatGPT, Ernie and beyond. The new AI gold rush and its impact on higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines the rapid emergence of generative AI chatbots—especially ChatGPT, Bing Chat, Bard, and Ernie—and their implications for higher education. The paper is primarily a critical review and comparative commentary, situating the chatbot boom within the broader AI race between major U.S. and Chinese technology companies and discussing risks such as hallucination, plagiarism, academic integrity concerns, and the disruption of assessment practices.

The authors review English- and Chinese-language scholarship published up to mid-April 2023, then describe a comparative test of selected chatbots on higher-education-relevant tasks. The intervention or approach is not an educational treatment study but a set of benchmark-style comparisons of bot performance on academic tasks. The context is higher education, with special attention to how instructors and institutions may need to redesign assessment, teaching, and policy in response to generative AI.

The main conclusion is that current LLM-based chatbots are promising but unreliable, with GPT-4 and earlier ChatGPT versions performing better than Bing Chat and Bard, though still far from perfect. The article argues that universities should not rely on simple bans alone; instead, they should adapt assessment and teaching practices, improve academic integrity policies, and encourage thoughtful, bounded uses of AI in learning. Because the paper is a narrative review with illustrative comparative testing rather than a controlled empirical study, its evidence is preliminary and interpretive rather than causal.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 performed best among the tested chatbots on higher-education-relevant academic tasks, but even these systems remained unreliable and inconsistent. The authors emphasize failures in factual accuracy, reasoning, and source reliability, and conclude that current generative chatbots are not yet dependable for academic work.
finding.measure: Comparative performance on higher-education-relevant academic tasks and exam-like prompts

finding.finding_summary: A central argument is that generative AI can support or undermine higher-order thinking depending on how it is used, but the paper’s own comparisons show inconsistent reasoning and frequent hallucinations. The authors specifically note weaknesses in logic, problem solving, and the ability to handle complex academic prompts, which limits claims about durable-skill support.
finding.measure: Reasoning quality, problem-solving performance, and susceptibility to hallucination in chatbot outputs

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that generative AI is already forcing universities to reconsider assessment design, academic integrity policies, and classroom teaching practices. It concludes that outright bans are problematic and that institutions should instead adapt policies, redesign assessments, and support responsible AI use.
finding.measure: Institutional recommendations regarding assessment, integrity policy, and teaching practice

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that chatbots and related AI tools can reduce workload by helping with drafting, summarizing, brainstorming, and other routine academic tasks, but it does not provide a formal efficiency trial. Its evidence is illustrative and based on examples and cited claims rather than measured productivity outcomes.
finding.measure: Illustrative use cases for drafting, summarizing, and task support

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines the emerging role of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in human learning, focusing on both its promise and its risks. The authors frame GenAI as a potentially transformative tool for learning support, learning resource creation, feedback delivery, and assessment, while also highlighting major concerns including hallucinations, privacy, equity, and disruption to conventional assessment practices.

Rather than reporting a single empirical study, the paper synthesizes evidence and examples from recent educational technology, learning sciences, and human-computer interaction research. It argues that GenAI could scale personalized tutoring, diversify learning materials, and provide timely feedback and adaptive assessments, but that these benefits depend on human-centered design, teacher expertise, AI literacy, and rigorous validation. The paper also stresses that future research must evaluate GenAI’s cognitive, metacognitive, and creative effects over time, including in K-12 contexts where assessment of human learning remains especially important.

Overall, the article is a forward-looking conceptual review and research agenda rather than a comparative intervention study. It does not provide primary experimental evidence on K-12 mathematics or other student outcomes; instead, it uses cited studies and examples to motivate methodological rigor, evidence-based decision-making, and ethical governance for GenAI in education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI could substantially reshape educational assessment, resource creation, feedback practices, and institutional decision-making, but these changes carry serious governance, privacy, equity, and validity risks. The conclusion is that institutional impacts are likely to be significant but depend on regulation, AI literacy, and evidence-based implementation rather than on any single measured intervention effect.
finding.measure: Conceptual synthesis of educational system-level issues (assessment, governance, ethics, policy, institutional practice)

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly emphasizes potential effects of GenAI on critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, and self-regulation, but it does not present original quantitative estimates. It notes that GenAI may support deeper inquiry and problem solving when used as a scaffold, yet may also weaken these skills through overreliance and performance illusions.
finding.measure: Conceptual synthesis of critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, and self-regulation

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses learner engagement, motivation, agency, and emotional responses as plausible outcomes of GenAI-enabled learning, citing prior studies showing both positive experiences and reduced engagement in some settings. No new empirical data are reported, but the overall message is that social-emotional impacts are context dependent and may be positive or negative depending on implementation.
finding.measure: Conceptual synthesis of engagement, motivation, agency, and emotions

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI can reduce educator workload and improve efficiency by scaling personalized feedback, generating resources, and automating parts of assessment. These benefits are described qualitatively rather than through a new experiment, but the central claim is that GenAI can improve productivity and lower the burden of time-intensive instructional tasks.
finding.measure: Conceptual synthesis of teacher workload, content generation efficiency, feedback scalability, and assessment automation

paper_profiles.title: MizAR 60 for Mizar 50
paper_profiles.venue: 14th International Conference on Interactive Theorem Proving (ITP 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates a large collection of AI-guided automated theorem proving methods on the Mizar Mathematical Library (MML) to measure how far automated proving and premise selection have advanced since the earlier Mizar40 evaluation. The authors study learning-guided theorem proving systems, including ENIGMA and Deepire, together with premise selection methods based on k-nearest neighbors, Naive Bayes, LightGBM, graph neural networks, and ensemble portfolios.

The intervention/approach is not a classroom or instructional treatment but a large-scale comparative systems evaluation over formal mathematics problems. The context is the Mizar Mathematical Library and multiple versions of it, with training/dev/holdout splits and iterative prove-learn feedback loops using millions of ATP proofs. The paper reports that the strongest systems can now prove about 75% of Mizar theorems in the bushy setting and about 58% in hammering mode, with stronger transfer to a newer MML version than prior methods.

The paper’s main contribution is methodological and empirical: it shows that internal guidance, premise selection, multi-phase ENIGMA, leapfrogging, and robust portfolio construction substantially improve automated proving performance. It also documents how premise selection benefits from larger proof corpora and subproblem-based premise minimization, and it demonstrates that anonymous, logic-aware ML methods generalize well to new mathematical terminology.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows substantial efficiency gains for automated theorem proving workflows. The strongest single 3-phase ENIGMA strategy proved 40% of lemmas in 30 s in hammering mode, and the final 420 s portfolio solved 58.36% of holdout problems (1690/2896), indicating improved proof-search productivity and better portfolio efficiency than earlier Mizar40 baselines.
finding.measure: Automated theorem proving success rate, number of problems solved, runtime per problem, portfolio coverage
finding.study_size: n=57,897 theorems in MML 1147; holdout n=2,896; development n=2,896

paper_profiles.title: Learning gain differences between ChatGPT and human tutor generated algebra hints
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether algebra hints generated by ChatGPT can support learning as effectively as pre-authored human tutor hints in an intelligent tutoring system. The authors frame the work as an initial learning-gain evaluation of large language model (LLM)-generated educational content, focusing on whether ChatGPT-produced worked-solution hints are usable, how often they fail quality checks, and how they compare to human-written hints for student learning.

The study used Open Adaptive Tutor (OATutor) with 77 Amazon Mechanical Turk participants, who were randomly assigned in a 2 x 2 design to either ChatGPT-generated hints or human-authored control hints and to either an Elementary Algebra or Intermediate Algebra lesson. Each condition included a three-item pre-test, a five-item acquisition phase, and a three-item post-test with the same items as the pre-test. ChatGPT hints were generated from problem text using the December 15, 2022 version of ChatGPT and then manually screened for correctness and appropriateness; 70% of generated hints passed quality checks, with failures due to incorrect answers or solution steps. Human hints came from the existing OATutor content authored by undergraduate tutors and editor-checked.

Results showed positive learning gains in all conditions, but statistically significant pre/post gains occurred only for the human-hint conditions, not for the ChatGPT-hint conditions. In both algebra lessons, human hints produced substantially higher learning gains than ChatGPT hints, and the differences between conditions were statistically significant. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can generate some usable algebra hint content, but in this setting it did not match the learning effectiveness of human-authored hints and still required human supervision for quality control.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates algebra learning gains from human-authored versus ChatGPT-generated hints. All four experimental cells showed positive pre-to-post learning gains, but only the human-hint conditions were statistically significant; ChatGPT conditions were not. For Elementary Algebra, learning gain was 24.63% (n=19) for control vs 11.14% (n=21) for experiment, and for Intermediate Algebra it was 23.65% (n=17) vs 1.7% (n=20), with human hints significantly outperforming ChatGPT hints in both lessons (p=0.038).
finding.measure: Pre-test to post-test algebra performance in OATutor lessons (percent correct / learning gain)

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual discussion of how artificial intelligence should be integrated into education, with a focus on higher education. It argues that the rapid spread of tools such as ChatGPT creates both opportunities and risks, especially if students and teachers use them without sufficient understanding of AI’s limitations.

The paper combines the author’s observations from a Swiss University of Applied Sciences with a narrative literature review. From this, it proposes that three competencies are especially important for responsible AI use in education: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. It also discusses institutional responses such as AI-use guidelines, workshops, and AI-focused curriculum changes.

The paper does not evaluate a formal intervention or report quantitative outcomes. Instead, it offers practical recommendations for building a campus culture of responsible AI use, including transparency requirements for students, staff development, and embedding AI literacy across courses. Its main conclusion is that policies alone are insufficient; sustained training and critical engagement are needed to make AI use educationally beneficial.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that institutional AI guidelines, workshops, dedicated budgets, and paid expert roles would improve responsible AI use and help build a campus-wide AI culture. This is a conceptual recommendation rather than an empirical estimate; no effect size, sample size, or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Institutional policy and governance recommendations; campus AI-use practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally emphasizes critical thinking as a core educational goal when using AI tools, arguing that students should critically evaluate AI outputs rather than accept them uncritically. No quantitative study, sample size, effect size, or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking and critical evaluation of AI outputs

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests AI tools may help teachers create curricula, case studies, and classroom materials more efficiently, but also notes that prompting can be time-consuming and that benefits depend on user skill. These are illustrative examples and recommendations, not measured outcomes; no effect size or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / curriculum and lesson-material creation

paper_profiles.title: The effect of ChatGPT on students’ learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking: insights from a meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This meta-analysis examines whether ChatGPT improves student learning outcomes, addressing the mixed findings in early empirical studies of generative AI in education. The authors synthesized 51 quasi-experimental/experimental studies published from November 2022 to February 2025, yielding 72 independent effect sizes across three outcome areas: learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking.

The review focused on studies where an experimental group used ChatGPT and a control group did not, and where sufficient quantitative data were available to compute Hedges’s g. Included studies spanned primarily college settings, with some secondary-level studies, and covered STEM-related courses, language/academic writing, and skills/competencies development. The authors also coded moderators such as course type, grade level, learning model, duration, ChatGPT role, and application area.

Overall, ChatGPT showed a large positive effect on learning performance (g=0.867, 95% CI 0.683 to 1.052) and moderate positive effects on learning perception (g=0.456, 95% CI 0.287 to 0.625) and higher-order thinking (g=0.457, 95% CI 0.255 to 0.650). Effects were heterogeneous, but the authors reported the results were robust in sensitivity analyses and suggested stronger benefits for 4–8 week interventions, problem-based learning, and certain course types. The paper concludes that ChatGPT can support learning, especially when used with appropriate scaffolds and instructional design, but notes that evidence for perception and higher-order thinking is based on fewer studies.

finding.finding_summary: Across 44 independent studies, ChatGPT had a large positive effect on learning performance (Hedges’s g=0.867, 95% CI 0.683 to 1.052; Z=8.458, p<0.001). The authors describe this as a substantial improvement on post-test learning outcomes, with high heterogeneity (I²=89.243%).
finding.measure: Learning performance (tests/exams; standardized mean difference on post-test or pre-post data)

finding.finding_summary: Across 19 independent studies, ChatGPT had a moderate positive effect on learning perception (Hedges’s g=0.456, 95% CI 0.287 to 0.625; Z=5.289, p<0.001). The paper reports this as a beneficial effect on learner perceptions, with moderate heterogeneity (I²=72.580%).
finding.measure: Learning perception (scale/questionnaire outcomes such as attitudes, motivation, or perceived learning support)

finding.finding_summary: Across 9 independent studies, ChatGPT had a moderate positive effect on higher-order thinking (Hedges’s g=0.457, 95% CI 0.255 to 0.650; Z=4.471, p<0.001). The authors summarize this as evidence that ChatGPT can foster higher-order thinking, though the evidence base was relatively small and moderately heterogeneous (I²=55.813%).
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking (scales/questionnaires assessing critical thinking, creative thinking, and related constructs)

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.population: Not directly studied; perspective on learning contexts spanning K-12, higher education, and adult learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a perspective article that examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may reshape human learning. It is organized around three main themes: the promises of GenAI for learning support, learning resources, feedback, and assessment; the challenges posed by hallucinations, ethical concerns, and assessment disruption; and the research and policy needs for responsible adoption, including AI literacy, evidence-based decision-making, and methodological rigor.

The article does not report a new empirical study. Instead, it synthesizes recent literature and examples of GenAI applications in education, including chatbot tutoring, AI-generated learning materials, automated feedback, and adaptive assessment systems. The authors argue that GenAI could improve personalization, efficiency, and access, but only if educators and researchers carefully validate outputs, protect privacy, and account for bias and overreliance.

The paper’s core conclusion is that GenAI should be used as a tool to augment, not replace, human learning and instruction. It emphasizes the need for rigorous, context-sensitive evaluation of GenAI tools across educational settings, along with stronger AI literacy and governance frameworks to ensure that these technologies support rather than undermine deep learning, critical thinking, and equitable access.

paper_profiles.title: War of the chatbots: Bard, Bing Chat, ChatGPT, Ernie and beyond. The new AI gold rush and its impact on higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines the rapid emergence of generative AI chatbots—especially ChatGPT, Bing Chat, Bard, and Baidu’s Ernie—and argues that they are reshaping higher education, particularly assessment, academic integrity, and teaching practice. The paper is primarily a narrative review and comparative analysis of chatbot capabilities, situated in the broader context of the AI industry, corporate competition, and policy responses in higher education.

The authors review English-language and Chinese-language literature on LLM-based chatbots and then describe a small comparative test of major chatbots on tasks relevant to higher education. Their central conclusion is that, despite substantial hype, these systems remain unreliable: GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 performed best, while Bing Chat and Bard performed poorly relative to academic expectations. The paper recommends that instructors, students, and institutions adapt assessment and teaching practices in response to the risks posed by generative AI, but it does not report a formal experimental design or robust quantitative outcome analysis.

Although the article discusses K-12 bans and broader educational implications, its substantive focus is higher education rather than school-age learners. The piece is best characterized as a scholarly commentary/narrative review with illustrative comparisons, not a controlled empirical study. As such, it offers contextual and policy insights more than extractable effect estimates.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports a qualitative comparative test showing that GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 performed better than Bing Chat and Bard on tasks relevant to higher education, but it does not provide standardized effect sizes or a formal statistical analysis. The authors conclude that the bots are not yet reliably capable of meeting academic performance expectations, with no direct quantitative estimate reported.
finding.measure: Comparative performance on higher-education-relevant tasks and prompts

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that generative AI can speed up writing, summarization, coding, and other academic tasks, citing examples such as GPT-4 rapidly generating a working website from a sketch. However, these efficiency gains are presented as illustrative claims rather than being measured in a controlled study, so no quantitative productivity estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Task completion speed / productivity in generating educational and work products

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI is already affecting institutional assessment policies, academic integrity rules, and university responses such as bans and renewed emphasis on in-class or closed-book assessment. This is a policy and governance discussion rather than a measured institutional outcome, and no effect size or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Institutional policy responses, academic integrity concerns, and assessment redesign

finding.finding_summary: The authors suggest that reliance on chatbots may weaken students’ critical engagement and create risks of plagiarism, misinformation, and demotivation, but these claims are not tested with direct learner outcome measures. No quantitative evidence on critical thinking or metacognition is reported.
finding.measure: Critical evaluation, academic integrity, and student judgment in using AI outputs

paper_profiles.title: A large-scale comparison of human-written versus ChatGPT-generated essays
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether ChatGPT can produce argumentative essays comparable to or better than human-written student essays, and how the linguistic properties of AI-generated essays differ from human writing. The authors frame the work as an independent, large-scale assessment of generative AI in an educational writing task that is common in upper secondary schooling.

The study uses 90 essay topics drawn from an argumentative essay corpus associated with high-school-level writing. For each topic, the authors compare one human-written essay from an online forum frequented by German high-school students with essays generated by ChatGPT-3 and ChatGPT-4 using a simple zero-shot prompt. A group of 111 secondary-school teachers rated six essays each on seven rubric categories (topic completeness, logic/composition, expressiveness/comprehensiveness, language mastery, complexity, vocabulary/text linking, and language constructs), and the paper also computed several linguistic markers such as lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, nominalization, modal use, epistemic markers, and discourse markers.

Results show that both ChatGPT models were rated significantly higher than the human essays across all rubric criteria, with ChatGPT-4 outperforming ChatGPT-3 and showing especially strong gains in logic/composition, vocabulary/text linking, and complexity. Reported effect sizes for human vs. ChatGPT-3 ranged from d=0.52 to 1.15, and for human vs. ChatGPT-4 from d=0.88 to 1.43; differences between ChatGPT-3 and ChatGPT-4 were smaller (roughly d=0.45 to 0.50) and significant only for a subset of criteria. The study concludes that generative AI can already write highly persuasive argumentative essays, implying that educators should rethink homework, writing assessment, and the role of AI tools in teaching writing.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT-generated argumentative essays were rated higher than human-written essays on all seven writing-quality rubric criteria. For human vs. ChatGPT-3, effect sizes ranged from d=0.52 to d=1.15; for human vs. ChatGPT-4, effect sizes ranged from d=0.88 to d=1.43, indicating medium to very large advantages for the AI-generated texts.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of essay quality on seven criteria (topic completeness, logic/composition, expressiveness/comprehensiveness, language mastery, complexity, vocabulary/text linking, language constructs)
finding.std_deviation: Human essay ratings SD ranged 1.15 to 1.37; ChatGPT-3 SD ranged 1.02 to 1.19; ChatGPT-4 SD ranged 1.01 to 1.12 depending on criterion

paper_profiles.title: Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of hallucinations in large language models (LLMs), focusing specifically on a subset the authors call confabulations: fluent but arbitrary and incorrect answers that vary with irrelevant factors such as random seed. The core research question is whether an uncertainty measure based on meaning, rather than surface form, can identify when an LLM is likely to produce such errors.

The authors introduce semantic entropy, which clusters multiple sampled model outputs by bidirectional entailment and then computes entropy over semantic meaning classes. They also propose a discrete version that uses only sampled outputs, enabling black-box use when token probabilities are unavailable. The approach is evaluated on question-answering datasets (TriviaQA, SQuAD 1.1, BioASQ, NQ-Open), a mathematical word-problem dataset (SVAMP), and a biography-generation dataset constructed for this paper, using LLaMA 2 Chat, Falcon Instruct, Mistral Instruct, and GPT-4.

Across datasets and models, semantic entropy generally outperforms naive entropy, a supervised embedding-regression baseline, and P(True) in detecting incorrect answers, as measured by AUROC and AURAC. The paper reports averaged AUROC of 0.790 for semantic entropy versus 0.691 for naive entropy, 0.698 for P(True), and 0.687 for embedding regression, with similar patterns in the biography setting. The main conclusion is that semantic uncertainty is a promising general method for detecting a major class of LLM failures, but it does not solve systematic errors or guarantee factuality.

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes SVAMP, a math word-problem dataset using elementary-school mathematical reasoning tasks, but it evaluates error detection rather than math learning or performance improvement per se. Semantic entropy is reported to outperform baseline uncertainty methods in predicting incorrect model answers on this dataset, contributing to better rejection accuracy when refusing likely-wrong responses; however, no direct educational effect size on student math outcomes is reported.
finding.measure: AUROC and AURAC for detecting incorrect answers on the SVAMP mathematical word-problem dataset
finding.study_size: n=400 train, n=400 test (sampled per dataset); model outputs evaluated across 30 task-model combinations

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary school students and teachers perceive a generative AI–supported activity for creative mathematical writing. The authors are interested in whether GenAI can help students engage in math story creation, mathematical reasoning, and revision, and what challenges arise when AI is used as a writing and learning partner in the classroom.

The study was conducted in six 5th-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools with 79 students and 6 teachers. Students used a GenAI-powered platform built with GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 in a three-step workflow: Ask, Represent, and Transform. In the Ask step, students analyzed a story problem; in Represent, they modeled ideas visually; and in Transform, they supplied prompts and generated/corrected their own math stories with AI assistance. Data came from focus-group interviews with 10 students, one-on-one interviews with all 6 teachers, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations.

Thematic analysis produced six themes: four benefits and two challenge categories. Participants perceived the tool as supporting creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and interest/ownership in learning. At the same time, they identified limitations including weak critical evaluation skills, difficulty generating coherent stories, overly “perfect” AI output, lack of adaptive feedback, reduced autonomy, limited social connection, and limited accessibility features. Because the study is qualitative and perception-based, it does not report quantitative learning effects, confidence intervals, or risk-of-bias metrics; instead, it offers design implications for how GenAI tools in elementary mathematics should balance support with student agency and pedagogical scaffolding.

finding.finding_summary: Participants perceived the GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing activity as helping students understand math problems, represent mathematical ideas, and uncover misconceptions. The study is qualitative and reports thematic findings from 79 5th-grade students across 6 classrooms, rather than numeric achievement gains; no effect size or confidence interval was reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions of mathematical understanding, problem comprehension, and mathematical knowledge representation gathered through interviews, open-ended surveys, and classroom observations
finding.study_size: n=79 students (with 10 student interviewees and 6 teachers interviewed)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies creative mathematical writing as an academic writing task and finds that students and teachers perceived GenAI as supporting divergent/convergent thinking, originality, and story development in math writing. The evidence is thematic rather than quantitative; no effect size, confidence interval, or dispersion statistic was reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions of creative mathematical writing performance and story generation quality
finding.study_size: n=79 students (with 10 student interviewees and 6 teachers interviewed)

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers reported that GenAI-made math writing more interesting, enjoyable, and curiosity-provoking, and that it increased feelings of ownership over learning. These findings come from qualitative thematic analysis of interviews, surveys, and observations; no quantitative effect estimate was reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions of interest, enjoyment, curiosity, and ownership in math learning
finding.study_size: n=79 students (with 10 student interviewees and 6 teachers interviewed)

finding.finding_summary: The study found that working with GenAI was perceived to promote AI literacy and prompt engineering strategies, as students learned to refine prompts and evaluate AI strengths and weaknesses. This is based on qualitative reports from 5th-grade students and teachers, with no numeric effect size or confidence interval provided.
finding.measure: Perceptions of AI literacy and prompt engineering skill use
finding.study_size: n=79 students (with 10 student interviewees and 6 teachers interviewed)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and students also described gains in flexible thinking, divergent thinking, and convergent thinking during the math story-writing process. The paper frames these as creativity-related durable skills supported by the tool, but reports no quantitative test scores, effect size, or follow-up measurement.
finding.measure: Perceptions of divergent thinking, convergent thinking, originality, and flexible thinking
finding.study_size: n=79 students (with 10 student interviewees and 6 teachers interviewed)

paper_profiles.title: Improving Student Learning with Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring: A Three-Study Quasi-Experimental Investigation
paper_profiles.venue: LAK '24: The 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether hybrid human-AI tutoring can improve middle-school mathematics learning more than using math software alone. The motivation is that many low-income students have limited access to high-quality tutoring, while AI-enabled software may scale individualized practice but does not provide the relational and motivational support that human tutors can supply.

The authors report three quasi-experimental studies conducted in urban, low-income U.S. middle schools using different math platforms: IXL, i-Ready, and MATHia. Across sites, students received varying versions of hybrid support during the school day, including remote human tutors, a math teacher, and in one site a live tutor dashboard. Outcomes focused mainly on software-based learning process measures such as time spent, questions answered, skills proficient, lessons passed, and workspaces completed per hour.

Results suggest hybrid human-AI tutoring improved engagement and intermediate learning outcomes relative to software-only or earlier lower-intensity conditions. In Site 1, adding a math teacher and then a tutor significantly increased time spent and skills proficient, with stronger benefits for lower-pretest students. In Site 2, tutoring increased time on task and lesson completion, especially for students below grade level. In Site 3, improving tutor access from a 1:8 to a 1:4 ratio increased MATHia workspace completion rate. The paper concludes that hybrid tutoring shows promise for improving learning opportunities and that dashboards and better targeting of tutor attention may further strengthen effects.

finding.finding_summary: Across three quasi-experimental site studies in middle-school math, hybrid human-AI tutoring improved intermediate math learning measures relative to software-only or lower-intensity conditions. In Site 1, adding a math teacher and then remote tutoring increased skills proficient and time spent; in Site 2, tutoring increased lessons passed; and in Site 3, improving tutor access from 1:8 to 1:4 increased workspace completion rate by 0.36 per hour (95% CI [0.02, 0.70]).
finding.measure: IXL skills proficient and time spent; i-Ready lessons passed and time on task; MATHia workspaces completed per hour

finding.finding_summary: The intervention increased student engagement with math software, which the paper treats as an important learning-process outcome. In Site 1, time spent rose significantly with math teacher support and further with tutoring (tutoring effect β=0.202, 95% CI [0.057, 0.347]); in Site 2, average weekly time on task increased from 24 to 33 minutes during tutoring.
finding.measure: Time spent on task / time spent practicing with software

finding.finding_summary: The paper also studies whether tutors can be used more efficiently via hybrid AI-supported models and dashboards. Site 3 reports that increasing tutor availability from about 1:8 to 1:4 improved student progress rate, with 0.36 additional workspaces completed per hour, suggesting a more productive use of tutor time and a potentially more efficient intervention structure.
finding.measure: Workspaces completed per hour; tutor-to-student ratio

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether teachers should remain “in the loop” when using generative AI to personalize mathematics problems for students, and what the implications are for task quality, student response, and teacher efficiency. The study is grounded in context personalization theory, especially the ideas of depth, grain size, and ownership in how students’ interests are represented in math problems.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers worked with ChatGPT/GPT-4o to revise existing Illustrative Mathematics problems for Units 4 and 6, producing 143 personalized problems for 521 students across 6 U.S. schools. Teachers participated in training, used recorded Zoom sessions while prompting ChatGPT, and their prompts/time were coded. Students then rated problems for interestingness and closeness to their interests, and a subset gave open-ended feedback. The study found that teachers most often used prompts to adjust broad or specific popular-culture references and to improve realism; students preferred finer-grained references that matched their own interests. Personalizing a problem took about 4 minutes on average, did not become clearly faster over time, and using 3-5 prompts was associated with higher student ratings than fewer or more prompts. From Unit 4 to Unit 6, teachers used more prompts and spent more time, and student ratings increased modestly, suggesting improvement in task quality but not efficiency.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined middle school mathematics task personalization, but it did not measure student achievement or learning gains. Instead, it reported student ratings of personalized math problems: ratings of interestingness averaged 2.46/5 and closeness to interests averaged 2.53/5 across 53 problems, and a mixed-effects model found that using 3-5 prompts was associated with higher ratings by about 0.24 points on a 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073).
finding.measure: Student ratings of math problem interestingness and closeness to interests on 1-5 scales
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 143 problems; 53 problems with closed-ended ratings

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studied student interest/engagement reactions to personalized math problems. Across 454 responses to the interest question, 163 were positive and 243 negative; across 449 responses to the closeness question, students often preferred specific popular-culture references that matched their interests, but disliked mismatched references.
