This suggests personalization can support interest, but effects depend strongly on whether the reference aligns with individual preferences.
finding.measure: Student survey ratings and open-ended feedback on problem interestingness and closeness to interests

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluated teacher efficiency in creating GenAI-personalized mathematics problems and found the process was time-consuming. Teachers used 558 prompts to create 143 problems (3.2 prompts/problem, SD=2.6), and each problem took about 246 seconds on average (SD=165.7), with no clear evidence that time efficiency improved over time. Compared with Unit 4, Unit 6 required more prompts (B=1.26, SE=0.41, t=3.08, p=0.0025) and more time (B=70.4 seconds, SE=29.6, t=2.38, p=0.0189).
finding.measure: Number of prompts per problem; seconds spent per problem; comparisons across Unit 4 vs Unit 6
finding.std_deviation: SD=2.6 prompts/problem; SD=165.7 seconds/problem; Unit 4 SD=2.6 and 153 seconds; Unit 6 SD=2.6 and 169 seconds

finding.finding_summary: The study also touched on teacher prompting as a form of iterative problem-solving and reflection, but it did not directly measure durable skills outcomes with validated instruments. Evidence was indirect: teachers improved their ability to craft interesting problems over time, yet this came with higher prompting and longer time, indicating iterative refinement rather than clear gains in generalizable efficiency or metacognitive skill.
finding.measure: Teacher prompting patterns and iterative revision across units

paper_profiles.title: Investigating Students’ Preferences for AI Roles in Mathematical Modelling: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks how students perceive different generative AI roles during mathematical modelling, and whether those preferences vary by students’ baseline design thinking (DT), computational thinking (CT), and mathematical modelling self-efficacy (MMSE). The paper is motivated by a gap in AI-in-education research: while large language models are increasingly used in mathematics learning, little direct comparative evidence exists on which pedagogical persona is most preferred or supportive during the modelling process.

The authors ran an online within-subjects randomized controlled trial with 26 university students in non-STEM majors who had not taken university-level mathematics courses, using six modelling tasks: one baseline task without AI and five tasks with AI configured as Tutor, Teaching Assistant (TA), Peer Student, Struggling Student, or Excellent Student. Participants also completed pre-task scales measuring DT, CT, and MMSE, plus post-task ratings of task confidence, helpfulness, and ease of interaction. Quantitative analyses used correlations, PLS-SEM, Friedman tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and Mann-Whitney U tests; qualitative comments were thematically analyzed.

The main findings were that DT and CT were positively associated with MMSE, with DT a particularly strong predictor. For AI role preferences and user experience, the competent roles (Tutor, TA, Peer, Excellent Student) were all rated similarly and much more favorably than the Struggling Student role across rankings, helpfulness, confidence, and ease of interaction. Baseline competency groups generally did not differ in role preferences, except that students with higher DT rated the TA role more favorably than those with lower DT. The study concludes that students value competent, supportive AI personas in mathematical modelling, and that design thinking may shape preference for more scaffolded AI support.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies mathematical modelling outcomes through students’ preferences for five AI roles and their task confidence in modelling tasks. In a within-subjects RCT with n=26, the Tutor role received the best overall preference ranking (M=2.35, SD=1.02 on a 1=best to 5=worst scale), but the four competent roles did not differ significantly from one another; the Struggling Student role was consistently rated worst. The study also found a significant positive relation between DT and MMSE (β=0.730, p<.001) and CT and MMSE (β=0.300, p<.001), but it did not report achievement gains on a mathematics test.
finding.measure: Mathematical modelling role preference rankings; modelling task confidence; mathematical modelling self-efficacy (MMSE)

finding.finding_summary: AI role significantly affected task confidence, perceived helpfulness, and ease of interaction in the modelling tasks. In the n=26 within-subjects trial, the constructive roles were rated substantially better than the Struggling Student role: for example, task confidence was highest for Excellent Student (M=3.69, SD=1.19) and Tutor (M=3.65, SD=1.16) and lowest for Struggling Student (M=1.88, SD=1.24), with Friedman χ2(4)=24.85, p<.001. Similar patterns appeared for helpfulness (χ2(4)=32.63, p<.001) and ease of interaction (χ2(4)=36.43, p<.001).
finding.measure: Task confidence, perceived AI helpfulness, ease of interaction
finding.std_deviation: SDs reported in-study; not_reported as a single summary statistic

finding.finding_summary: The study directly measured design thinking and computational thinking as learner competencies related to mathematical modelling, and examined how these shaped AI role preferences. In the n=26 sample, DT and CT were both positively associated with MMSE (DT: β=0.730, p<.001; CT: β=0.300, p<.001), and several subdimensions showed significant positive correlations with MMSE (e.g., DT subscales and CT creativity/critical thinking). A between-group comparison found one significant difference: the high-DT group preferred the TA role more than the low-DT group (Mhigh=2.38 vs. Mlow=3.46, p=.049).
finding.measure: Design thinking, computational thinking, and their relations to MMSE; AI role rankings by high/low DT, CT, and MMSE groups
finding.effect_size: β=0.730; β=0.300; specific rank differences not reported as effect size

paper_profiles.title: Machine Learning Assisted Adjustment Boosts Efficiency of Exact Inference in Randomized Controlled Trials
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes a machine-learning-assisted covariate adjustment procedure for exact inference in randomized controlled trials. The main goal is to improve statistical efficiency—especially power and sample-size requirements—while preserving valid type I error control under Rosenbaum’s randomization-based framework.

The method uses random forests to generate out-of-bag predictions from baseline covariates, then analyzes residuals rather than raw outcomes. The authors compare this approach against unadjusted two-sample tests, linear-regression adjustment, and a cross-estimation method across simulation studies with nonlinear, linear, and interaction-based outcome-generating processes. They report that the proposed random-forest adjustment usually improves power, particularly when covariate-outcome relationships are nonlinear, and remains robust under non-Gaussian errors and treatment-by-covariate interactions.

A real-world diet intervention example with 76 young adults illustrates the approach on post-intervention fatigue. In that example, the random-forest Wilcoxon test found a statistically significant difference between groups (p=0.0451), with an estimated treatment effect of -1.57 and 95% CI (-3.01, -0.05), whereas several alternative methods were non-significant. The paper concludes that machine-learning adjustment can yield substantial efficiency gains for RCT inference, though the study is methodological rather than an education intervention study.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central contribution is a random-forest-assisted adjustment method that improves inferential efficiency in RCTs. In simulations across N=50, 100, 200, and 400 with 10,000 Monte Carlo replications, the adjusted tests generally showed higher power than unadjusted or linear-adjusted alternatives; in one nonlinear setting, the RF tests reached >80% power at about N=170, roughly 80 fewer subjects than competing methods.
finding.measure: Statistical power and sample-size efficiency for exact inference in randomized trials

paper_profiles.title: AI Instructional Agent Improves Student’s Perceived Learner Control and Learning Outcome: Empirical Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether an AI instructional agent that can deliver lecture content and respond to student questions in real time improves students’ perceived learner control and academic performance relative to a human lecturer and a self-paced MOOC with chatbot support. The motivation is to test whether a more integrated AI teaching role can do more than automate content delivery and instead support learner autonomy during instruction.

The study was conducted in a university general-education course in Beijing with 140 undergraduates randomly assigned to three conditions: a human teacher, a MOOC-style video lecture with chatbot support, or an AI instructional agent within the MAIC platform. After excluding 15 invalid self-report cases, analyses used 125 students (41 human teacher, 43 MOOC, 41 AI teacher). The AI condition allowed learners to pause, interrupt, and ask questions in real time, while keeping content and audio largely constant across conditions.

Results from one-way ANOVAs showed that the AI instructional agent significantly increased perceived learner control, reduced learning duration, increased interaction frequency, and produced higher post-test scores than the other conditions. Regression and correlational analyses further indicated that perceived learner control was positively associated with post-test performance and with more efficient learning behaviors. The paper concludes that AI agents designed as interactive instructional systems, rather than passive content tools, can enhance both learning experience and immediate learning outcomes; however, the study measured only immediate post-test performance and was conducted in a single university course context.

finding.finding_summary: Students in the AI instructional agent condition reported significantly higher perceived learner control than students taught by a human teacher or using the MOOC condition. The ANOVA showed a significant group effect, F(2,122)=12.155, p<.001, with Tukey post-hoc differences favoring AI over human (M difference=0.732, p<.001) and AI over MOOC (M difference=0.416, p<.05).
finding.measure: Perceived learner control scale (4-item self-report)

finding.finding_summary: Perceived learner control was positively associated with post-test performance and negatively associated with learning duration, suggesting gains in self-regulation/time management during the task. Correlations reported were r=0.23 with post-test scores, r=-0.30 with learning duration, and r=0.23 with self-regulated learning.
finding.measure: Correlations among perceived learner control, learning duration, self-regulated learning, and post-test scores

finding.finding_summary: The AI instructional agent group completed the learning task more efficiently than the human teacher group, and the MOOC and AI conditions both required less time than the human teacher condition. Learning duration differed significantly across groups, F(2,122)=265.168, p<.001, with reductions of approximately 30 minutes for AI-human and MOOC-human comparisons.
finding.measure: Learning duration / task completion time

finding.finding_summary: Academic performance on the post-test was higher in the AI instructional agent condition than in both comparison conditions. The ANOVA found a significant group effect, F(2,122)=7.673, p<.01; Tukey comparisons showed AI exceeded the human teacher group by M difference=0.128 (p<.01) and the MOOC group by M difference=0.112 (p<.01).
finding.measure: Post-test score (16-item multiple-choice test; proportion correct)

finding.finding_summary: The AI instructional agent also increased behavioral engagement and interaction frequency, both of which are process-oriented indicators of student involvement. Interaction frequency differed significantly by group, F(2,122)=21.755, p<.001, with AI-human difference=5.410 and AI-MOOC difference=7.015; behavioral engagement correlated with post-test performance at r=0.34 (p<.001).
finding.measure: Interaction frequency; behavioral engagement scale

paper_profiles.title: Testing for Reviewer Anchoring in Peer Review: A Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether peer reviewers anchor to their initial scores when they are later shown corrected information, which is relevant to understanding whether rebuttals in conference peer review meaningfully change reviews. The authors frame anchoring as a possible explanation for the limited effect of rebuttals on final scores and decisions in academic peer review.

To test this, they ran a randomized controlled trial with 108 participants who were PhD students or PhD holders with recent computer science publications. Participants acted as reviewers for a mock conference paper; the control group saw a version of the paper with an animated GIF showing stronger results, while the experimental group initially saw a frozen frame showing weaker results and then, after submitting an initial review, saw the corrected animated version and could revise their scores.

The main analysis compared initial experimental scores to control scores to verify that the manipulation changed perceived paper quality, and compared revised experimental scores to control scores to test for anchoring. The manipulation worked: initial experimental scores were lower than control scores for Evaluation (A=0.6375, adjusted p=0.0096) and somewhat lower for Overall (A=0.5857, adjusted p=0.0575). However, the revised scores were not significantly different from control scores for either Overall (A=0.5048, adjusted p=0.6064) or Evaluation (A=0.4863, adjusted p=0.6064), so the authors conclude they found no evidence of anchoring in this peer-review setting.

The study is a controlled mock peer-review experiment in a computer science context, not a K-12 or classroom study. It provides evidence about reviewer behavior and the rebuttal process rather than student learning outcomes, and its exploratory subgroup analyses suggest possible heterogeneity by reviewer confidence and seniority, though these were not the primary findings.

finding.finding_summary: In the primary anchoring test, revised reviewer scores after exposure to the corrected paper were not significantly different from control scores. For Overall score, Vargha-Delaney A=0.5048 with adjusted p=0.6064; for Evaluation score, A=0.4863 with adjusted p=0.6064, indicating no evidence that the rebuttal-like correction shifted reviewer judgments toward the corrected version.
finding.measure: Mock conference peer-review scores (Overall score and Evaluation category score) compared between revised experimental reviews and control reviews

paper_profiles.title: AI for Proactive Mental Health: A Multi-Institutional, Longitudinal, Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a generative AI-powered mobile app can proactively improve well-being, rather than simply treat symptoms after they emerge. The authors argue that most AI mental health tools are deficit-focused and reactive, and they instead test a strengths-based approach intended to build positive affect, resilience, belonging, mindfulness, and flourishing through brief, personalized interactions.

The intervention was Flourish, a mobile app featuring an AI chatbot (“Sunnie”) that delivered emotionally intelligent conversations, science-based activities, weekly insights, and gamified reinforcement. In a six-week randomized controlled trial during Fall 2024, 486 undergraduate students from Chapman University, the University of Washington, and Foothill College were assigned either to app access or to a waitlist control condition. Outcomes were measured across four waves (Weeks 0, 2, 4, and 6) using validated well-being instruments, with longitudinal mixed-effects models estimated under an intent-to-treat framework.

The main results show that the treatment group improved relative to control on several well-being outcomes: positive affect, calm, well-being, loneliness, belonging, closeness to school, resilience, mindfulness, and flourishing. Effects on negative affect, depression, anxiety, stress, and academic self-efficacy were not statistically significant. The paper concludes that a purpose-built generative AI system can produce measurable, scalable benefits for student well-being, but also notes important limitations, especially the lack of an active control group and the short duration of follow-up.

finding.finding_summary: The intervention produced significant improvements in several well-being and adjustment outcomes, including positive affect (b=0.22, p=.020), calm (b=0.10, p=.013), loneliness (b=-0.05, p=.038), belonging (b=0.06, p=.030), resilience (b=0.11, p=.047), mindfulness (b=0.19, p=.045), and flourishing (b=0.19, p=.032). It did not significantly change negative affect (b=0.008, p=.933) or its subcomponents, and the authors interpreted the pattern as both boosting and buffering of well-being across the six-week trial.
finding.measure: Validated self-report well-being measures: Subcomponents of Affect Scale, UCLA 3-item Loneliness Scale, Perceived Cohesion single item, Inclusion of Other in the Self scale, Brief Resilience Scale, Mindful Attention Awareness Scale, and Flourishing Scale
finding.std_deviation: reported in Extended Data Table 3; not_reported here

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports no statistically significant effect on academic self-efficacy, which was included as an additional outcome beyond the core well-being measures. The authors note that this null finding may reflect the short intervention duration and the intervention’s preventive, strengths-based design rather than direct academic skill development.
finding.measure: Academic self-efficacy (self-report; details in Supplementary Materials)

paper_profiles.title: Learning From Failure: Integrating Negative Examples when Fine-tuning Large Language Models as Agents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models can learn from failed interaction trajectories when fine-tuned as agents, rather than training only on successful examples. The authors argue that discarded negative trajectories contain useful information, but that naively mixing them with positive examples can also teach the model errors.

They propose negative-aware training (NAT), which re-formats training data by explicitly tagging whether a trajectory is correct or incorrect using simple prompt suffixes/prefixes. The method is evaluated on agent-style math reasoning, multi-hop question answering, strategic question answering, and a preliminary chain-of-thought setup, using LLaMA-2-Chat 7B and 13B models fine-tuned on GPT-3.5-generated trajectories. Across experiments, NAT usually outperforms a positive-only baseline and a naive positive+negative baseline, with the largest gains in low-resource settings and when negative samples are of higher quality.

The study is not about K-12 education or classroom use; it is a machine learning methods paper about LLM agent training. Its main conclusion is that negative trajectories are useful if the model is told how to interpret them, and that the quality of negative data matters substantially more than simply adding more negative examples.

finding.finding_summary: On math reasoning tasks, negative-aware training (NAT) consistently improved accuracy over both the positive-only baseline (Vanilla) and naive positive+negative training (NUT). For LLaMA-2-7B with 2k positive examples, average accuracy rose from 55.90 (Vanilla) to 64.64 (NAT), a +8.74 point gain; with 5k positives, it rose from 64.17 to 67.42 (+3.25). The paper reports task-level results on GSM8K, ASDiv, SVAMP, and MultiArith, but does not provide confidence intervals or standard deviations for these main math results.
finding.measure: Accuracy on GSM8K, ASDiv, SVAMP, and MultiArith math word problem test sets

finding.finding_summary: The paper also reports preliminary chain-of-thought results on GSM8K, showing that NAT improves performance beyond positive-only training and naive positive+negative training. With LLaMA-2-7B and 2k positive samples, average accuracy improved from 29.04 (Vanilla) to 36.24 (NAT), a +7.20 point gain, indicating that the method transfers beyond the agent/ReAct setting to CoT reasoning. No confidence intervals or standard deviations are reported.
finding.measure: Accuracy on GSM8K under chain-of-thought prompting

paper_profiles.title: Search for stable hadronising squarks and gluinos with the ATLAS experiment at the LHC
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports a high-energy physics search for long-lived, massive particles predicted by supersymmetry, specifically stable or metastable squarks and gluinos that hadronize into so-called R-hadrons. The ATLAS Collaboration uses proton-proton collision data at 7 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 34 pb−1 to look for slow-moving, highly ionizing candidates using detector signatures based on pixel-detector dE/dx and tile-calorimeter time-of-flight.

The analysis combines kinematic selection, data-driven background estimation, and reconstructed mass estimates from two independent subsystems to define signal regions for different mass hypotheses. No statistically significant excess over the Standard Model is observed. The study sets 95% CL lower mass limits of 294 GeV for sbottom R-hadrons, 309 GeV for stop R-hadrons, and 562 GeV for gluino R-hadrons under the most conservative model assumptions; alternative gluino interaction models give limits of 566 and 562 GeV. This is a collider search paper rather than an education study, so it does not address any K-12 instructional outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: AI and the EU Digital Markets Act: Addressing the Risks of Bigness in Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether the European Union’s Digital Markets Act (DMA) should be extended to generative AI services. The central problem is regulatory: the authors argue that generative AI platforms may develop gatekeeper power similar to large digital platforms, creating risks of concentrated control, reduced contestability, and unfair practices in AI markets.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or any learner population. Instead, it analyzes how generative AI products and platform architectures could fit within the DMA’s definitions of core platform services and gatekeepers. The discussion focuses on mechanisms such as computing-power concentration, early-mover advantage, data advantages, and integration across services.

The authors conclude that some generative AI systems already exhibit gatekeeper-like characteristics and that the DMA should be amended to explicitly cover them. They argue this would help preserve diversity, openness, contestability, and fairness in the emerging generative AI industry. The paper is normative/legal-analytical rather than empirical, and it contains no quantitative outcome evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that extending the DMA to generative AI would improve contestability and fairness in the AI market by limiting gatekeeper behavior and preventing entrenched dominance. This is a conceptual legal proposal rather than an empirical test, so no effect size or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Policy and regulatory analysis of Digital Markets Act coverage and obligations

paper_profiles.title: E-EVAL: A Comprehensive Chinese K-12 Education Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces E-EVAL, a benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on Chinese K-12 education content. The authors argue that existing LLM benchmarks do not adequately cover the Chinese primary, middle, and high school curriculum, especially elementary-level content, and they propose E-EVAL as a comprehensive multiple-choice benchmark spanning 23 subjects across arts and science domains.

The benchmark contains 4,351 questions collected from homework, practice sets, and mock exams, with manual cleaning and answer balancing. The study evaluates 15 LLMs, including proprietary and open-source models such as Qwen, ERNIE-Bot, GPT-4, ChatGPT, Yi, ChatGLM3, Baichuan2, and EduChat, under zero-shot, five-shot answer-only, and five-shot chain-of-thought prompting. Accuracy is the sole evaluation metric. The paper reports that Chinese-dominant models outperform English-dominant models overall, but all models struggle more on science than arts, and especially on mathematics. It also finds that few-shot prompting tends to help modestly overall, while chain-of-thought prompting often hurts average performance but can help on harder science subjects such as mathematics.

The paper’s primary contribution is methodological and evaluative rather than instructional: it does not test an educational intervention with students, but instead provides a benchmark and comparative model analysis for future AI-in-education work. The findings suggest that current LLMs still have weaknesses in elementary-level and mathematical reasoning despite strong performance on broader Chinese language tasks.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates mathematics performance across primary, middle, and high school questions and finds that all models generally perform worse on science than arts, with mathematics being one of the weakest areas. The best overall model (Qwen-72B-Chat) achieved 84.0% on science and 88.9% average accuracy, but even top models showed errors on simple arithmetic comparison items; the authors note that chain-of-thought prompting can improve performance on complex science subjects such as mathematics while sometimes reducing average accuracy overall.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on primary, middle, and high school mathematics questions
finding.study_size: n=102 primary math, n=172 middle math, n=251 high school math (subset of 4351 total questions)

finding.finding_summary: Science subjects as a group were harder than arts subjects, and the paper reports that all models performed worse on science than arts. The authors also find that chain-of-thought prompting improved performance on complex science subjects, indicating some benefit for structured reasoning tasks, though no inferential statistics or effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on science-subject questions and prompt-condition comparisons (zero-shot vs five-shot-ao vs five-shot-cot)

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark shows that LLM performance is substantially higher on arts subjects than on science subjects, and that Chinese-dominant models outperform English-dominant models on Chinese K-12 content overall. For the top model, Qwen-72B-Chat, accuracy was 92.5% on arts and 84.0% on science, with 88.9% average accuracy across prompt settings.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy across Chinese K-12 subjects outside math and science, especially language, history, geography, politics, and ethics

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses reasoning behavior, including whether few-shot prompting and chain-of-thought prompting improve model reasoning. Few-shot prompting slightly improves performance for most models, but chain-of-thought often reduces average accuracy, suggesting that added reasoning steps are not uniformly beneficial. However, the paper does not measure durable skills in humans; this is a model capability analysis only.
finding.measure: Accuracy under zero-shot, five-shot-answer-only, and five-shot-chain-of-thought prompting

paper_profiles.title: Using Large Language Models to Assess Tutors’ Performance in Reacting to Students Making Math Errors
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Machine Learning Research (AAAI 2024 Workshop AI4ED)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models can accurately evaluate how human tutors respond when middle school students make math errors. The authors focus on a specific tutoring skill from an online tutor lesson, Reacting to Errors, which teaches tutors to respond indirectly, motivationally, and accurately when students struggle in mathematics.

The study first uses GPT-4 to generate 50 synthetic tutor-student dialogues to calibrate two human annotators and establish inter-rater reliability on five criteria: process-focused, motivating, indirect, immediate, and accurate. The main analysis then applies GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 to 50 real-world tutoring dialogues from remote middle school tutoring in which college-student tutors worked with 6th-8th graders. Performance is compared against human graders using precision, recall, and F1 for the five criteria, and the models are also evaluated on whether a student actually made an error.

The results suggest both GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 can reasonably score several tutor-response criteria, especially immediate and accurate, but both struggle to determine whether an error occurred in the first place. GPT-4 performs slightly better overall than GPT-3.5-Turbo, particularly on the easier criteria, but it also tends to infer errors when human raters judged there were none. The authors conclude that GPT-3.5-Turbo may be sufficiently cost-effective for scalable dialogue assessment, though improvements in prompting and error detection are needed before LLMs can be relied on alone for tutor evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that LLMs can be used to automate aspects of tutor-performance assessment, reducing the need for fully manual human grading. Across 50 real tutoring dialogues, GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 achieved useful F1 scores on several criteria (e.g., immediate: 0.80 and 0.93; accurate: 0.80 and 0.95), suggesting potential for scalable and lower-cost tutor feedback workflows.
finding.measure: Precision, recall, and F1 for automated scoring of tutor dialogue criteria; comparison of model outputs with human graders

finding.finding_summary: The study is centered on mathematics tutoring interactions, but it evaluates AI's ability to judge tutor responses rather than student math achievement. The models performed well on mathematically grounded criteria such as accurate (F1=0.80 for GPT-3.5-Turbo and 0.95 for GPT-4), but they struggled to determine when a student had actually made a math error, correctly identifying no-error dialogues only 54% of the time for GPT-3.5-Turbo and 63% for GPT-4.
finding.measure: Model classification accuracy and F1 on math-tutoring dialogue annotations; no student achievement outcome was measured

paper_profiles.title: Towards Evaluation Guidelines for Empirical Studies involving LLMs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses a methodological problem: how to conduct and report rigorous empirical studies involving large language models (LLMs) in software engineering research. The authors argue that LLM-based studies are vulnerable to reproducibility problems because model behavior can vary by version, configuration, prompts, hidden system components, and time of access, making traditional empirical-study guidance incomplete.

The paper does not evaluate an educational intervention or a learner-facing tool. Instead, it synthesizes concerns from existing literature and a discussion session with empiricism experts at the 2024 ISERN meeting to propose a preliminary taxonomy of LLM study types and a set of reporting guidelines. These guidelines emphasize declaring LLM use and role, reporting model version/date and configuration, sharing prompts and prompt-development procedures, using open-model baselines, and validating LLM outputs with humans.

The intended context is empirical research in software engineering, not K-12 education. The main conclusion is that LLM studies need specialized methodological standards to support validity, reproducibility, and transparent reporting, and that the proposed framework is a starting point for broader community consensus rather than a tested intervention.

paper_profiles.title: Improving Student Learning with Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring: A Three-Study Quasi-Experimental Investigation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a hybrid human-AI tutoring model improves K-12 mathematics learning compared with math software alone. The core question is whether adding human tutoring to AI-driven math practice increases students’ engagement and learning processes, and whether those effects differ by students’ prior achievement. The authors frame the work as an early-stage, rapid-cycle evaluation of a scalable tutoring model intended to support low-income middle school students during the school day.

The intervention combines adaptive math software with remote human tutors who provide motivational, relational, and content support. Across three separate urban middle-school sites in Pennsylvania and California, students used different platforms (IXL, i-Ready, and MATHia) under different tutoring structures, including round-robin tutor assignment and a prototype dashboard-guided model. The study uses quasi-experimental comparisons, interrupted time-series logic, and mixed-effects regression to compare software-only periods with periods including a math teacher and/or human tutoring.

The main findings are that hybrid human-AI tutoring increased intermediate learning-process outcomes such as time on task, questions answered, skills proficient, lessons passed, and workspaces completed. Effects were generally stronger for students with lower baseline achievement, while math teacher support appeared beneficial but more advantageous for higher-pretest students in some analyses. The paper does not report direct standardized achievement gains on external tests; instead, it argues that the observed increases in software use and lesson progress are promising proxies that may translate into later achievement gains based on prior correlations from the software vendors and prior studies.

finding.finding_summary: Across three quasi-experimental site studies, hybrid human-AI tutoring improved math learning-process outcomes relative to software-only or earlier tutoring conditions. In Site 1, mixed-effects models showed positive effects on time spent practicing with IXL (β=0.202, 95% CI [0.057, 0.347], p=0.006) and on skills proficient in the descriptive comparisons; in Site 2, students passed more i-Ready lessons during tutoring (β=0.244, 95% CI [0.106, 0.381], p<0.001); and in Site 3, students completed 0.36 more MATHia workspaces per hour after the tutor:student ratio improved from 1:8 to 1:4 (95% CI [0.02, 0.70], p=0.03).
finding.measure: IXL time spent/questions answered/skills proficient; i-Ready lessons passed and time on task; MATHia workspaces completed per hour

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports increased student engagement with math software when human tutoring was added, which the authors interpret as improved participation and motivation-related engagement. In Site 2, average weekly time on task increased from 24 minutes before tutoring to 33 minutes during tutoring, and in Site 1 tutoring produced a positive effect on time spent with IXL (β=0.202, 95% CI [0.057, 0.347]). These findings are consistent with stronger engagement, though no validated motivation or self-regulation scale was used.
finding.measure: Time on task / time spent using math software

finding.finding_summary: The intervention appears to improve the efficiency of student use of math software, especially when tutors and dashboards are better aligned to student need. Site 1 showed increases in time spent and questions answered under teacher-plus-tutor support relative to software only, Site 2 showed increased lesson completion during tutoring, and Site 3 showed higher workspace completion after moving from a 1:8 to 1:4 tutor:student ratio, suggesting more productive use of tutor time and software time. The paper does not report a direct workload measure for tutors or teachers, but it explicitly argues the model is scalable and low-cost relative to traditional high-dosage tutoring.
finding.measure: Time spent, questions answered, lessons passed, workspaces completed per hour, tutor:student ratio

paper_profiles.title: Advancing Education through Tutoring Systems: A Systematic Literature Review
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Middle School, High School, Undergraduate
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how tutoring systems in education have evolved from early computer-assisted instruction to modern AI-driven intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), robot tutoring systems (RTS), and multimodal hybrids. It also examines how these systems differ in artificial intelligence methods, system behavior, engagement affordances, and ethical implications, with a particular interest in their educational effectiveness and responsible use.

The authors conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review of 86 representative studies published from 1972 through 2024. They coded study features such as adaptability, feedback modality, appearance, interaction tools, AI techniques, and ethical concerns, then used latent class analysis to group systems into three classes: computer-based ITS, verbal robot-based systems, and multimodal systems.

The review concludes that software-based ITS tend to offer stronger cognitive adaptability and scalability, especially when using Bayesian Knowledge Tracing and large language models, while robot-based systems are stronger for social-emotional engagement. The paper also argues that ethical issues such as data privacy, transparency, fairness, and hallucination risk are increasingly important, and that future work should integrate the cognitive strengths of ITS with the relational benefits of RTS while improving governance and responsible AI safeguards.

finding.finding_summary: The review substantially focuses on mathematics-focused tutoring systems as one of its core exemplars, including middle-school and primary-school math ITS studies. It reports that AI-driven tutoring systems, especially those using Bayesian Knowledge Tracing and adaptive content adjustment, were associated with improved learning outcomes in mathematics, but the paper does not provide a pooled effect size, confidence interval, or standardized outcome estimate because it is a narrative/systematic review rather than a meta-analysis of these studies.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning outcomes / student performance in math tutoring studies

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that robot-based and multimodal tutoring systems improve engagement, motivation, and social-emotional involvement through gestures, verbal praise, physical presence, and human-like interaction. The paper synthesizes prior studies as showing that these affordances help sustain student interest, particularly for younger learners, but it does not report a pooled quantitative effect size or confidence interval.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, and social-emotional engagement

finding.finding_summary: The review discusses tutoring systems as supporting cognitive engagement, personalization, and problem-solving through adaptive feedback and conversational interaction. However, durable skills are not a primary focus and the paper does not report direct quantitative estimates for critical thinking, metacognition, or collaboration outcomes.
finding.measure: Problem-solving / cognitive engagement indicators discussed across reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that tutoring systems raise important institutional issues around privacy, fairness, scalability, transparency, and governance, and it recommends encryption, audits, access controls, and oversight committees. These are synthesized conclusions from the reviewed literature rather than an original institutional-outcome study, so no effect sizes or confidence intervals are reported.
finding.measure: Ethical, governance, and scalability considerations in tutoring system deployment

paper_profiles.title: LLM Performance Predictors: Learning When to Escalate in Hybrid Human-AI Moderation Systems
paper_profiles.venue: Proc. of the 25th International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems (AAMAS 2026)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of deciding when to trust large language model (LLM) outputs versus escalating cases to human reviewers in hybrid human-AI content moderation systems. The authors argue that the key operational challenge is not just prediction accuracy, but uncertainty-aware routing that can reduce the cost of moderation failures while preserving scalability.

To solve this, they propose LLM Performance Predictors (LPPs), a supervised meta-model that uses gray-box and black-box signals derived from LLM outputs, including token probabilities, entropy, self-reported confidence, and novel uncertainty-attribution indicators. The meta-model is trained with ridge regression and evaluated as a cost-aware selective classification system across several proprietary and open-source LLMs (e.g., GPT, Gemini, Llama, Qwen) on two moderation datasets: an OpenAI text moderation dataset and a multimodal moderation dataset spanning video, transcript, thumbnail, and frame inputs.

The study reports that the LPP-based meta-model generally improves error-prediction performance and lowers expected moderation cost relative to baseline uncertainty heuristics such as MSP, entropy, and top-2 margin. Gains are strongest for some models and settings, but not universal: performance is more mixed under multimodal distribution shift, and some models do not benefit or show trade-offs. Overall, the paper concludes that uncertainty-attributed selective escalation can improve operational efficiency in real-world moderation workflows, though generalization depends on the base model and task distribution.

finding.finding_summary: The LPP meta-model reduced expected moderation cost and escalation volume relative to baseline uncertainty heuristics across multiple LLMs. For example, on the OpenAI Moderation Dataset, cost dropped from $132 to $38 for gpt-4o-mini (331 to 148 escalations), from $122 to $77 for gemini-2.5-flash-lite (315 to 227 escalations), and from $74 to $41 for gemini-2.0-flash-lite (248 to 162 escalations).
finding.measure: Expected cost ($) and escalation count / escalation ratio in selective human-review routing

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates a human-AI moderation workflow and argues that uncertainty-aware routing can improve production moderation systems by directing ambiguous or high-risk cases to humans and reducing unnecessary reviews. It reports lower operational cost and describes implications for scalable, responsible moderation pipelines and policy-update loops.
finding.measure: Moderation workflow cost, escalation policy behavior, and routing of cases to human reviewers

paper_profiles.title: Case Study of GAI for Generating Novel Images for Real-World Embroidery
paper_profiles.venue: GenAICHI: CHI 2024 Workshop on Generative AI and HCI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents an auto-ethnographic case study of using generative AI to create images that can be converted into real-world embroidery patterns. The authors are motivated by accessibility concerns: creating original embroidery designs can be difficult for disabled makers, especially when designs require fine detail control, centering, simple outlines, and other constraints needed for successful machine embroidery.

The study examines two phases of use. First, one disabled researcher explored DALL-E 2 in fall 2023 to generate embroiderable images, documenting how repeated prompt refinement was required to avoid outputs with too much detail, jagged lines, off-center compositions, or other features that caused embroidery failures. Second, a five-person disabled-led team iteratively developed custom GPTs in winter 2024 using few-shot learning, training files, and prompt engineering to better produce embroidery-suitable SVG images of motifs such as monstera leaves, lotus flowers, paisleys, and mountain scenery.

The paper concludes that generative AI can sometimes improve accessibility and creativity in embroidery design, but performance is inconsistent and highly sensitive to prompt specificity. The authors report fewer conversion and embroidery problems with the custom GPT approach than with the initial DALL-E 2 exploration, but they emphasize that the tools still frequently ignored constraints or produced overly complex outputs. The paper is explicitly qualitative and exploratory, and it ends by proposing future quantitative evaluation and more accessible embroidery-generation tools for disabled creators.

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that custom GPTs reduced some of the user burden compared with the initial DALL-E 2 exploration, including fewer off-center images, fewer SVGs with excessive paths, and fewer back-and-forth prompt adjustments. However, the process still required extensive prompt engineering and iterative refinement, so the efficiency gains were partial rather than robustly demonstrated.
finding.measure: Qualitative comparison of prompt iterations, image alignment, SVG path complexity, and number of back-and-forth conversations needed to obtain embroiderable outputs
finding.study_size: n=6 researchers total; one end-user evaluator (A1) in the second phase and one evaluator in the initial exploration

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that generative AI can support creative problem solving and design iteration by helping users prototype embroidery images under real-world constraints. The authors describe the process as enabling experimentation and serendipity, although the evidence is purely qualitative and not measured with standardized outcomes.
finding.measure: Qualitative observations of iterative design, prompt engineering, and creative ideation during embroidery pattern generation
finding.study_size: n=6 researchers total; auto-ethnographic case study

finding.finding_summary: This paper centrally studies embroidery as a creative and technical making activity, not formal academic attainment. The authors found that GAI sometimes facilitated the creation of culturally relevant and novel embroidery designs, but also frequently generated unusable outputs with too much detail, incorrect centering, or unwanted textures, making the overall effect mixed.
finding.measure: Qualitative success/failure of generated embroidery motifs and their conversion into machine-embroiderable files

paper_profiles.title: Consensus Sampling for Safer Generative AI
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (no human participants; theoretical generative AI models)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a theoretical safety problem in generative AI: how to aggregate outputs from multiple models so that the combined system is safer than any single model, even when some models may be adversarial or unreliable. The authors focus on risks that are difficult or impossible to detect by output inspection alone, such as steganography and hidden vulnerabilities in generated code.

The main contribution is a consensus sampling algorithm that samples from multiple generative models and accepts outputs only when the models sufficiently agree. The paper proves formal guarantees: the algorithm’s risk is bounded relative to the safest subset of models, and its abstention rate depends on the overlap among safe models. It also shows a leakage bound, demonstrating that the method can limit information leakage to at most O(log R) bits under the stated assumptions.

The work is purely theoretical and does not study K-12 learners, classrooms, or educational outcomes. Its context is AI safety and cryptographic-style robustness analysis for language and multimodal models. The conclusions are that consensus sampling can provide provable safety/robustness tradeoffs, but only under assumptions such as having multiple safe models with enough distributional overlap; it is not an end-to-end safety solution.

paper_profiles.title: Competing Visions of Ethical AI: A Case Study of OpenAI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how OpenAI publicly frames AI ethics over time, asking how the company deploys terms such as "ethics," "safety," "alignment," and related concepts in its public communications and what that discourse signals about ethical practice. The study is motivated by concerns that AI ethics may function rhetorically or as "ethics-washing" rather than as a substantive constraint on organizational behavior.

Using a mixed-methods case study design, the authors assembled a corpus of 454 OpenAI-authored or co-authored documents from OpenAI.com and arXiv spanning December 2015 to July 2025. They combined keyword-frequency analysis, topic modeling, PCA-based clustering, and a manual qualitative audit of ethics-related language in web articles and publications. The analysis shows that explicit ethics language is rare in OpenAI’s public web articles and relatively limited even in publications, while safety, risk, responsibility, and alignment become increasingly prominent over time.

The main conclusion is that OpenAI’s public discourse systematically narrows from broader ethics language toward safety-, risk-, and governance-adjacent framing. The authors argue that ethics appears mainly in peripheral or rhetorical contexts, whereas safety and compliance language dominate and help structure the organization’s public narrative. They interpret this as evidence of ethics-washing and discuss implications for AI governance, transparency, and accountability in industry.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that OpenAI’s public discourse shifted from sparse use of explicit ethics language toward much heavier use of safety, risk, responsibility, and alignment framing. Across 424 web articles, only 16 (3.8%) contained an ethics variant, while safe/safety peaked at 687 mentions and risk at 386 mentions in 2024; in the 30-publication corpus, 31 of 180 reviewed texts (17.2%) used ethic language, but usually only a few times and often in peripheral contexts. The authors conclude that ethics is used more rhetorically than substantively and that discourse functions as a form of ethics-washing.
finding.measure: Keyword frequencies, document tagging, and qualitative discourse audit of OpenAI public communications
finding.study_size: n=454 documents total (424 web articles; 30 publications in final corpus; 180 publications reviewed for screening)

paper_profiles.title: What Should Developers Be Aware Of? An Empirical Study on the Directives of API Documentation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates the content of API documentation in object-oriented Java libraries, asking what kinds of natural-language directives appear in API docs and how those directives can be classified. The authors argue that API documentation contains implicit constraints and usage guidelines that are important for developers, but that the structure of these directives had not been thoroughly studied.

To address this, the authors conducted a large exploratory empirical study over more than 6,000 Java API documentation items drawn from the JDK, Eclipse JFace, and Apache Commons Collections. They searched for syntactic patterns such as must, should, may, override, and related terms, then manually reviewed occurrences to determine whether they expressed directives and how they should be categorized. The result is a taxonomy of 23 API directive kinds, grouped into method call directives, subclassing directives, and state directives.

The study is descriptive rather than intervention-based: it does not test a tool or educational treatment, but instead characterizes real documentation practice and reports the relative abundance of directive types. The main conclusion is that API directives are common, varied, and often subtle; many encode constraints that are hard to represent in programming language types alone. The paper also argues that the taxonomy and corpus can support future tool-building work for documentation analysis and checking.

paper_profiles.title: Calculation of sample size guaranteeing the required width of the empirical confidence interval with predeﬁned probability
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a statistical design problem: how to calculate sample size so that an empirical confidence interval will have a required width with a pre-specified probability. The author argues that conventional sample-size methods often use expected parameter values and therefore underestimate the sample size needed to actually achieve the desired precision in the realized sample.

The paper presents a general approach for precision-based sample-size planning and illustrates it for Normal, Poisson, and Binomial settings. For each case, the author compares the traditional “expected-value” sample size to an “exact” sample size based on the distribution of the interval width, showing that the exact approach can require substantially larger samples—often more than 20% larger, and in some cases around 50% larger for the settings examined.

The context is methodological and statistical rather than educational: the paper is written for researchers planning estimation studies, not for K-12 learners or educators. It includes formulas, numerical tables, and R code to demonstrate implementation, but it does not evaluate an intervention or educational outcome.

paper_profiles.title: Locally Private Mean Estimation: Z-test and Tight Confidence Intervals
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2019 Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies the problem of estimating the mean of a Gaussian distribution under local differential privacy (LDP), with an emphasis on constructing valid confidence intervals and a private Z-test. The authors analyze several settings: known variance, unknown but bounded variance, and very large unknown variance. Across these settings, they design LDP algorithms that use randomized response, bit-flipping, binary search over quantiles, and Gaussian perturbation to produce confidence intervals for the population mean.

The paper is methodological rather than educational: it does not study students, teachers, classrooms, or any AI-in-education intervention. Its main contribution is theoretical, giving upper and lower bounds on the length of private confidence intervals and sample complexity for one-shot LDP mean estimation. The paper also includes a small simulation study of the proposed Z-test to illustrate behavior under different privacy levels and sample sizes, showing that stronger privacy generally requires substantially more data to reject a false null hypothesis.

Because the work is about privacy-preserving statistical inference and not about learning outcomes or educational implementation, there is no K-12 population or instructional context. The empirical component is limited to synthetic Gaussian simulations used to assess the private Z-test, and the strongest claims are asymptotic theoretical guarantees rather than educational effects.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (position paper; discusses elementary through professional education contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper asks what opportunities and challenges large language models, especially ChatGPT-style systems, present for education. Rather than testing an intervention, the authors synthesize early research and provide a conceptual overview of how large language models might support learning, teaching, assessment, and educational technology design.

The paper discusses use cases across educational levels, with examples for elementary, middle/high school, university, and professional learning. For students, it highlights potential uses such as reading and writing support, quiz generation, curiosity prompting, code explanation, language learning, and math word problem generation; for teachers, it emphasizes lesson planning, personalized feedback, assessment support, and content generation. The paper also surveys key risks including bias, privacy, overreliance, copyright, academic integrity, sustainability, and unequal access.

Its main conclusion is that large language models may become powerful educational tools, but only if integrated with human oversight, critical thinking, transparency, governance, and careful pedagogical design. Because the article is a position paper grounded in prior studies and argumentation rather than original empirical data, it does not provide outcome-level effects for K-12 mathematics or other student outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: A Careful Examination of Large Language Model Performance on Grade School Arithmetic
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS 2024 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks / arXiv
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models’ strong performance on the GSM8k elementary math benchmark reflects genuine arithmetic reasoning or contamination from benchmark data. To test this, the authors create GSM1k, a new set of 1,205 grade-school arithmetic problems written by human annotators to closely match GSM8k in style, difficulty, solve rate, and answer magnitude, while avoiding any LLM-assisted generation.

They then evaluate a range of open- and closed-source models on both GSM8k and GSM1k using a standardized evaluation harness. Across models, they find accuracy drops of up to 8 percentage points on GSM1k, with several model families (notably Phi and Mistral) showing consistent overfitting patterns, while frontier models such as Gemini, GPT, and Claude show little to no gap. The paper also reports a positive relationship between a model’s GSM8k memorization proxy and its GSM8k-to-GSM1k performance gap, suggesting partial memorization contributes to overfitting, though it is not the whole explanation; importantly, all models still generalize to novel grade-school math problems to some extent.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates elementary arithmetic performance of LLMs on GSM8k versus the newly created GSM1k benchmark (n=1,205). The main finding is mixed: several model families show clear overfitting, with accuracy drops of up to 8 percentage points on GSM1k, but frontier models show little to no drop and all models still generalize to new grade-school math problems.
finding.measure: Accuracy on grade-school arithmetic word problems (GSM8k and GSM1k)
finding.study_size: n=1205 (GSM1k); GSM8k comparison benchmark size not reported in the paper text

paper_profiles.title: Design and evaluation of ChatGPT-MWPS: an AI-enhanced learning system for improving primary students’ mathematical word problem solving
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge that primary students face in solving mathematical word problems, especially the need to translate text into mathematical representations and follow multi-step reasoning. The authors propose ChatGPT-MWPS, a generative AI-enhanced learning system that provides adaptive scaffolding, step-by-step hints, and real-time feedback within a digital test-paper environment.

The system was designed for fifth-grade mathematics and evaluated in a public primary school in Guangdong, China with 52 fifth-grade students and 3 mathematics teachers. Students used the system in a 40-minute task and then completed a 13-dimension usability scale; teachers provided follow-up interviews about system performance and instructional fit.

The main findings concern usability and perceived educational value rather than learning gains on math achievement tests. Students generally rated the system favorably, with especially strong associations between intention to use and cognitive engagement, learnability, design attraction, and trust. However, information display and design appeal were weaker areas, and teachers reported issues with latency, content filtering, and the sequencing of hints. Overall, the paper concludes that ChatGPT-MWPS is promising for supporting primary mathematics word problem solving, but it needs interface and functionality refinements before broader classroom use.

finding.finding_summary: The system was evaluated specifically for fifth-grade mathematical word problem solving, and results suggest promising support for students’ mathematics learning process. However, the paper did not report post-test achievement gains or effect sizes; the empirical evidence is primarily that students and teachers perceived the system as useful for step-by-step math problem solving.
finding.measure: Usability scale and teacher interviews focused on mathematical word problem solving support

finding.finding_summary: Students reported generally favorable usability perceptions, and intention to use was strongly associated with cognitive engagement. The paper reports a very strong correlation between intention to use and cognitive engagement (r=0.969, p<0.05), suggesting the system may support engagement with mathematics tasks, although this is not an outcome test of achievement.
finding.measure: Usability scale dimensions, especially cognitive engagement and intention to use

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to externalize problem-solving strategies and support step-by-step reasoning, and the study found strong positive relations between intention to use and dimensions such as learnability and cognitive engagement. This suggests potential support for metacognitive and problem-solving processes, but the paper does not report direct measures of critical thinking or metacognitive gains.
finding.measure: Usability scale dimensions and teacher interview feedback on reasoning flow
finding.effect_size: r=0.720 (intention to use with learnability); r=0.541 (intention to use with cognitive engagement)

finding.finding_summary: The system was intended to reduce instructional preparation time through batch question import and automated worksheet generation, but teachers reported limitations including latency during peak usage and problems with content filtering. The paper does not quantify time savings, but it provides qualitative evidence that the system could improve efficiency while also introducing technical bottlenecks.
finding.measure: Teacher interviews on system performance and workflow; system functionality description

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a conceptual discussion of how artificial intelligence should be integrated into education, with a particular emphasis on AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. Rather than testing an intervention with students, the paper uses an informal case study from a Swiss University of Applied Sciences combined with a narrative literature review to argue that AI is becoming unavoidable in academic work and classroom practice.

The paper focuses on higher education, especially the experiences of lecturers, supervisors, and students at Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich. It describes institutional concerns around ChatGPT and other large language models, including academic integrity, hallucinations, student overreliance, and unclear expectations about acceptable use. In response, the university created internal AI guidelines requiring transparency about model use, purpose, critical evaluation, and manuscript locations where AI was used.

The main conclusion is that banning AI outright or allowing it without restrictions are both inadequate. The author argues for a middle-ground approach built around a stronger AI culture, regular workshops, updated guidance, dedicated support, and explicit instruction in AI literacy and prompt engineering. The paper also contends that critical thinking is essential because students and educators must learn to evaluate AI outputs rather than accept them uncritically. Although the paper is framed around higher education, it suggests the ideas may also be useful for children and K-12 settings, but it does not empirically study those populations.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking are important learner capabilities, but it does not test a student intervention or report outcome data. Its claims are conceptual: students who learn to prompt effectively may better evaluate AI limitations and avoid uncritical reliance, but no empirical effect sizes or sample-based results are reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of critical thinking, AI literacy, and prompt engineering; no empirical outcome measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that AI tools can improve teaching and curriculum-design efficiency, for example by helping educators create case studies, recommend curricula, and generate classroom materials. These claims are illustrative and based on the author’s institutional experience and examples rather than measured productivity outcomes, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Illustrative discussion of curriculum creation, classroom preparation, and AI-assisted teaching workflows

finding.finding_summary: A central contribution of the paper is its description and justification of institutional AI guidelines at Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences. The paper argues that transparent documentation, clear permitted/prohibited uses, and staff/student support structures are preferable to total bans or unrestricted use, but these recommendations are not evaluated with outcome data.
finding.measure: Institutional AI guidelines and governance practices; no empirical effect measure reported

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This catchword article provides a conceptual and research-agenda-oriented overview of generative AI, with a focus on its role in business and information systems engineering. Rather than evaluating a specific educational intervention, the paper explains what generative AI is, how it works at the model, system, and application levels, and why it matters for organizations and society.

The article discusses core technical foundations such as generative models, large language models, diffusion models, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and prompt learning. It then outlines key limitations of current generative AI, including incorrect outputs/hallucinations, bias and fairness issues, copyright risks, and environmental costs, and argues that these constraints shape how systems should be designed and governed.

A substantial portion of the paper lays out future research directions for the BISE community across business process management, decision analytics, digital leadership, economics of information systems, enterprise engineering, human-computer interaction, and information systems engineering. Education is mentioned as one area of future application, but the paper does not empirically study K-12 classrooms, student outcomes, or mathematics learning; instead, it is a conceptual perspective piece aimed at researchers and practitioners in organizations.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI will have broad systemic and institutional effects on organizations, governance, and work practices, but these are presented as projected implications rather than empirical results. It highlights issues such as shadow IT, policy and licensing needs, knowledge management changes, and the need for governance frameworks, but reports no study-level effect sizes or samples.
finding.measure: Conceptual implications for organizational governance, policy, and institutional practices

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (conceptual perspective; no study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a perspective on how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may reshape human learning, with particular attention to educational uses in support, resource creation, feedback, and assessment. Rather than reporting a new empirical study, the authors synthesize prior research from learning sciences, educational technology, and human-computer interaction to argue that GenAI could personalize learning support, diversify materials, provide timely feedback, and enable more adaptive assessments.

The paper also emphasizes the major risks and constraints of GenAI in education, including hallucinations, bias, privacy concerns, inequity in access, and the possibility that AI assistance can undermine assessment validity and learner agency. It argues for a human-centered approach in which AI literacy, evidence-based decision-making, and methodological rigor guide future research and implementation. The discussion repeatedly notes that empirical evidence in K-12 settings is still limited and mixed, and calls for rigorous longitudinal and randomized studies before strong claims about learning benefits can be made.

Because this is a conceptual viewpoint article, it does not test a specific intervention on a defined K-12 sample. Instead, it frames a research agenda for educators, researchers, policymakers, and technologists, with some examples drawn from existing studies in writing, programming, language learning, feedback, and assessment. Its main conclusion is that GenAI should be treated as a potentially powerful but imperfect tool that must augment, not replace, human learning and human judgment.

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses GenAI for mathematics tutoring and assessment mainly through illustrative examples such as Khanmigo, but it does not report original mathematics outcome data. It notes that GenAI-driven math support may improve problem solving and conceptual understanding, yet also stresses that current empirical evidence on short- and long-term math learning gains is limited and mixed.
finding.measure: mathematics learning support, problem-solving, and conceptual understanding (illustrative, not newly measured in this paper)

paper_profiles.title: E-EVAL: A Comprehensive Chinese K-12 Education Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces E-EVAL, a new benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on Chinese K-12 educational content. The authors argue that existing benchmarks do not adequately cover the full K-12 spectrum in China, especially primary school content, so they assemble 4,351 multiple-choice questions spanning primary, middle, and high school across 23 subjects. The benchmark is split into arts and science domains, and the paper evaluates 15 open-source and proprietary LLMs using zero-shot, few-shot-answer-only, and few-shot chain-of-thought prompting.

The study is not an intervention study in schools; rather, it is a model evaluation study using exam-style questions drawn from homework, practice sets, and mock exams. The paper reports overall accuracy patterns by subject, grade band, and prompting method. Chinese-dominant models generally outperform English-dominant models on Chinese K-12 tasks, but all models struggle with science and especially mathematics. The authors also find that top models often do better on middle school than primary school questions, suggesting that mastery of higher-level knowledge does not imply mastery of simpler content.

The paper’s main conclusions are that E-EVAL provides a useful benchmark for tracking Chinese K-12 LLM capability, that arts subjects are easier for current LLMs than science subjects, and that few-shot prompting helps more on arts than science while chain-of-thought helps mainly on harder science subjects. Because the work evaluates model performance rather than learner outcomes, its educational significance is primarily about the capability and limitations of AI systems that might be used in educational contexts.

finding.finding_summary: All evaluated models performed relatively poorly on mathematics compared with arts subjects, and the paper explicitly notes that 'almost all models perform poorly in complex subjects such as mathematics.' In the category results, math-containing science performance was substantially below arts performance (e.g., Qwen-72B-Chat science 84.0 vs arts 92.5; GPT 4.0 science 64.2 vs arts 75.4). No effect size is reported because the study reports accuracy only.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on E-EVAL mathematics questions / science category containing mathematics

finding.finding_summary: Models performed better on arts than science overall, indicating weaker performance on science reasoning tasks. The paper reports that CoT prompting improved performance on science subjects, especially middle and high school mathematics and other science items, but the overall science-category accuracy remained below arts-category accuracy for all models. Sample size is the benchmark’s science subset (10 subjects; 1,652 questions) and reported metric is accuracy.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on E-EVAL science subjects (physics, chemistry, biology, mathematics, primary science) under zero-shot and few-shot prompting
finding.study_size: n=1652 questions in science across 10 subjects

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds consistently higher performance on arts/humanities-style subjects than on science. This is shown in the aggregate arts results (e.g., Qwen-72B-Chat 92.5, ERNIE-Bot 4.0 90.8) and in the discussion that 'all models perform better in arts subjects than in science subjects.' The study measures accuracy on Chinese-language arts subjects such as Chinese, English, politics, history, and geography.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on E-EVAL arts subjects (Chinese, English, politics, history, geography, ethics)
finding.study_size: n=2699 questions in arts across 13 subjects

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark analysis suggests limits in model reasoning and transfer, including the observation that higher-order knowledge mastery does not ensure mastery of lower-order knowledge. The paper also states that CoT can help structured science reasoning but can hurt on many arts items, implying that step-by-step reasoning is not uniformly beneficial. The measured outcome is performance on reasoning-intensive benchmark questions rather than a direct durable-skills test.
finding.measure: Accuracy on benchmark questions requiring reasoning and multi-step problem solving, especially under CoT prompting

finding.finding_summary: The paper contributes a new evaluation infrastructure for Chinese K-12 LLM assessment and positions it as a public benchmark for tracking model progress. While not an institutional outcome study in the schooling sense, it directly impacts the AI-in-education research ecosystem by creating a benchmark, leaderboard, and dataset intended for future evaluation and development.
finding.measure: Creation and release of the E-EVAL benchmark, dataset, and public leaderboard

paper_profiles.title: PATCH! Psychometrics-AssisTed benCHmarking of Large Language Models against Human Populations: A Case Study of Proficiency in 8th Grade Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a measurement problem in benchmarking large language models (LLMs): many existing academic benchmarks compare model scores to human performance without strong evidence that the items are high quality, well targeted, or comparable across human populations. The authors argue that psychometric methods, especially item response theory (IRT) and test development principles, can make LLM benchmarking more valid and informative.

They propose PATCH (Psychometrics-AssisTed benCHmarking), a framework that uses validated psychometric tests to compare LLM responses against representative human samples. In the demonstration study, they use TIMSS 2011 8th-grade mathematics items and human response data from 56 participating regions, then evaluate four vision-language models (GPT-4V, Gemini-Pro-Vision, Qwen-VL-Plus, and Qwen-VL-Max). Human and model responses are scored using the official TIMSS rubrics and analyzed with IRT models matched to item type.

The main conclusion is that IRT-based proficiency estimates can differ meaningfully from simple percent-correct benchmarking, especially in human-vs-model comparisons. While GPT-4V remains the top-performing model, the estimated rank ordering of some regions and the statistical interpretation of “super-human” performance change under IRT; the paper reports that the apparent GPT-4V advantage over the top human groups disappears when uncertainty is modeled appropriately. The authors conclude that psychometric benchmarking can yield more valid and precise comparisons, and they release several math/science datasets to support future work.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central finding is that proficiency estimates for 8th-grade mathematics depend on whether benchmarking uses raw percent-correct scores or IRT-based psychometric modeling. Using TIMSS 2011 mathematics items (88 items; 56 human populations; four vision-language models), GPT-4V ranked highest under both approaches, but some regional rankings shifted and the interpretation of super-human performance changed: GPT-4V’s apparent advantage over the top human groups disappeared under IRT when 95% confidence intervals were considered.
finding.measure: 8th-grade mathematics proficiency on TIMSS 2011 items, estimated via percent-correct and item response theory (3PL/2PL/GPC) models
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CIs reported; exact pooled intervals not_reported

paper_profiles.title: A Careful Examination of Large Language Model Performance on Grade School Arithmetic
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS 2024 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models’ strong scores on grade-school math benchmarks reflect true reasoning or contamination from benchmark exposure. The authors introduce GSM1k, a newly created set of 1,205 elementary arithmetic word problems intended to closely mirror GSM8k in difficulty, answer magnitude, and human solve rates while avoiding contamination by using only human annotators and no LLM assistance.

The study evaluates a broad set of open- and closed-source LLMs on both GSM8k and GSM1k using a standardized evaluation harness. Many model families, especially Phi, Mistral, Yi, Xwin, Gemma, and CodeLlama, show lower accuracy on GSM1k than GSM8k, with drops of up to 8 percentage points, suggesting systematic overfitting or memorization of benchmark-like data. Frontier models such as GPT, Gemini, Claude, and Mistral Large show little to no overfitting.
