The authors also find a positive association between a model’s likelihood of generating GSM8k examples and its GSM8k–GSM1k performance gap (Spearman’s r² = 0.36, p = 0.03), supporting contamination as one contributor, but not the sole explanation, for benchmark overperformance.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates elementary mathematics performance of LLMs on grade-school arithmetic word problems. Across models, accuracy on GSM1k was up to 8 percentage points lower than on GSM8k, but many frontier models showed minimal differences and all models still generalized to novel problems, indicating mixed evidence of strong but uneven math reasoning performance.
finding.measure: Accuracy on GSM8k vs. GSM1k grade-school arithmetic word problems
finding.effect_size: up to 8 percentage point accuracy drop

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates the usefulness of LLMs as benchmarked math solvers in an evaluation pipeline, showing that the standardized harness can identify likely overfitting and contamination issues. The main operational contribution is a more reliable method for testing model performance on elementary math tasks, rather than a direct productivity intervention.
finding.measure: Benchmark evaluation procedure and comparison of model outputs across two datasets

paper_profiles.title: BanglaMATH: A Bangla benchmark dataset for testing LLM mathematical reasoning at grades 6, 7, and 8
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces BanglaMATH, a benchmark dataset of 1.7k elementary-school math word problems in Bangla designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on mathematical reasoning in a low-resource language. The authors argue that most math benchmarks are English-centric and therefore do not adequately assess Bangla-language performance, especially for educational use cases.

The dataset is compiled from Bangla elementary-school workbooks, quizzes, and exam materials and is annotated with grade level, number of reasoning steps, number of digits, and answer type. The paper evaluates several commercial and open-source LLMs in a zero-shot setting, including GPT-4, Llama 4 Maverick, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Grok 3, and DeepSeek-V3, and reports accuracy by grade, arithmetic complexity, reasoning complexity, and robustness to distractors.

The main conclusion is that even strong general-purpose LLMs struggle with elementary math reasoning in Bangla, with performance declining as grade level, arithmetic complexity, and reasoning complexity increase. Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek-V3 perform best overall, but both are vulnerable to irrelevant information and show clear language bias, scoring better on English translations than on the original Bangla problems. The study is primarily a benchmark/evaluation paper rather than an intervention study in classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: Across 1.7k Bangla elementary math word problems, model performance varied substantially by grade and problem complexity. Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek-V3 were the strongest systems, reaching at least 80% accuracy across grades 6-8, but accuracy dropped as grade level, number of digits, and reasoning steps increased; GPT-4 stayed below 70% across grades, and all models struggled on harder items.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Bangla math word problems, stratified by grade level, number of digits, and number of reasoning steps

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly tests whether LLMs can sustain correct mathematical reasoning when problem complexity rises and when distractors are added. Accuracy fell sharply with more reasoning steps, and the best models were frequently misled by irrelevant information, indicating weak robustness and limited problem-structuring skill in this setting.
finding.measure: Accuracy under varying reasoning-step complexity and distractor-augmented problems
finding.study_size: n=1700 for complexity analyses; n=60 for distractor subset

finding.finding_summary: The authors compare performance on original Bangla problems versus English translations to assess language sensitivity. Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek-V3 improved by about 6.5% to 6.9% when problems were translated into English, showing that these models reasoned more effectively in English than in Bangla.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Bangla problems versus English-translated versions

paper_profiles.title: AMO-Bench: Large Language Models Still Struggle in High School Math Competitions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces AMO-Bench, a new benchmark of 50 original, human-crafted advanced mathematics problems designed to be at least International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) level in difficulty. The authors argue that existing high-school competition benchmarks such as AIME and HMMT are becoming saturated for top language models, and that many prior benchmarks may also be vulnerable to memorization or leakage. AMO-Bench is built to be original, difficult, and amenable to automatic grading by requiring final answers rather than proof-style solutions.

The benchmark covers five math categories: algebraic equations and inequalities, functions and sequences, geometry, number theory, and combinatorics. The paper evaluates 26 large language models using 32-sample average accuracy (AVG@32), with a best score of 52.4% for GPT-5-Thinking (High) and most models below 40%. The authors also report that models consume substantially more output tokens on AMO-Bench than on easier math benchmarks, and that performance improves with greater test-time compute, suggesting the benchmark remains challenging even for frontier models.

Although the paper is not an educational intervention study, it is relevant to K-12 mathematics benchmarking because it focuses on high-school-level and Olympiad-level mathematical reasoning tasks. The main conclusion is that current LLMs still struggle on very difficult high school math competition problems, and that AMO-Bench may serve as a stronger evaluation set for future reasoning-model research.

finding.finding_summary: Across 26 LLMs on 50 Olympiad-level math problems, even the best-performing model achieved only 52.4% AVG@32 accuracy, and most models scored below 40%. The benchmark therefore shows that current models still struggle substantially with advanced mathematical problem solving in a high-school competition context.
finding.measure: Accuracy on AMO-Bench math problems (AVG@32)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that performance increases as test-time compute/output length increases, with a near-linear growth trend between AVG@32 and the logarithm of average output length for GPT-5, o4-mini, and o3-mini. This suggests that more reasoning effort is associated with better performance on difficult mathematical tasks, a proxy for reasoning persistence and extended problem solving.
finding.measure: Relationship between AVG@32 performance and output length / test-time compute
finding.study_size: n=3 model families analyzed in depth

paper_profiles.title: Seeing the Big Picture: Evaluating Multimodal LLMs’ Ability to Interpret and Grade Handwritten Student Work
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Educational Data Mining Conference
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can interpret and grade handwritten student mathematics work, with a particular focus on the difference between routine arithmetic and more visually complex mathematical illustrations. The authors frame the problem as one of both visual interpretation (reading what the student wrote) and grading (judging correctness), arguing that these tasks are important for learning analytics and teacher workload reduction because much K-12 math work remains handwritten.

The study uses two experiments. Experiment A analyzes 288 handwritten arithmetic responses from Ghanaian middle school students on fractions, percentages, and basic algebra. Four frontier MLLMs are prompted to transcribe the student answer and judge correctness; Gemini 2.5 Pro performs best, reaching 89% vision accuracy and 95% grading accuracy with linear weighted kappa of 0.90. Experiment B uses 150 student-drawn mathematical illustrations from DrawEDU, split into an image-only condition and a human-description condition. All models perform much worse on direct image interpretation (about 61-64% accuracy; kappa 0.15-0.38) but improve substantially when given human descriptions (about 72-75% accuracy; kappa 0.43-0.47), suggesting that visual interpretation is a major bottleneck.

Overall, the paper concludes that current MLLMs may be useful for routine handwritten arithmetic grading, but they are not yet reliable for more ambiguous mathematical illustrations that require contextual pedagogical judgment. The results highlight a gap between generic visual-language capability and the tacit knowledge educators use when interpreting student mathematical thinking. The authors recommend hybrid human-in-the-loop workflows rather than autonomous deployment for complex student work.

finding.finding_summary: On 288 handwritten middle-school arithmetic responses from Ghana, the best-performing model (Gemini 2.5 Pro) achieved 95% grading accuracy and linear weighted kappa of 0.90, approaching human performance. Across the four models, grading accuracy ranged from 77% to 95%, indicating strong capability on routine objective mathematics tasks.
finding.measure: Grading accuracy and linear weighted kappa on handwritten arithmetic responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central practical claim is that MLLMs could reduce teacher workload by grading routine handwritten arithmetic work more efficiently. The authors note that such systems may support automated data collection, flag struggling students, and pre-sort work for educator review, but the measured evidence is model performance on grading tasks rather than direct workload reduction.
finding.measure: Potential for automated grading / screening of handwritten math work
finding.study_size: n=288 for arithmetic; n=150 for illustrations

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Auto-Grading and Feedback System for Constructive Geometry Tasks Using Large Language Models on an Online Math Platform
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of assessing and supporting student learning on open-ended constructive geometry tasks in K-12 mathematics, where answer-only grading is insufficient. The authors argue that such tasks require systems that can judge diverse student constructions and written explanations while also giving individualized, timely formative feedback.

To address this, they developed and deployed a hybrid auto-grading and feedback system on the Korean online geometry platform Algeomath. The system combines rule-based grading for closed-ended and geometric construction tasks with GPT-4-based few-shot grading and feedback generation for open-ended explanations, using teacher-authored exemplars and attempt-aware prompting. The study was piloted in four middle-school classes in South Korea with 79 students across 18 math problems, including closed-ended, constructive geometry, and open-ended explanation items.

The main findings are that the system matched teacher grading perfectly on closed-ended and construction tasks, and showed substantial agreement on open-ended explanation tasks overall (agreement rate 0.866, Cohen’s κ=0.737 across 878 responses). Expert review of feedback quality suggested the generated feedback was generally serviceable but variable by item (pooled mean guidance score 3.98/5, SD=1.78), with issues including answer leakage, imprecise terminology, and overly generic or harsh prompts. Student response data showed that feedback often helped learners revise errors quickly: 36.7% of initially incorrect responses were corrected on the next attempt, with the highest conversion for closed-ended items (55.1%), followed by CGT (35.6%) and open-ended tasks (33.9%). However, evidence for longer-term transfer to later questions was not statistically significant.

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed and evaluated primarily for middle-school geometry learning, including constructive geometry tasks and open-ended explanations about the circumcenter. Rule-based grading achieved 100% agreement with teacher judgments on the closed-ended and CGT items, while LLM grading on seven explanatory items reached 0.866 agreement overall (Cohen’s κ=0.737, n=878 responses).
finding.measure: Grading agreement with teacher judgments on mathematics responses; feedback-supported correctness on geometry tasks
finding.study_size: n=79 students; 18 questions; 878 open-ended explanatory responses for LLM grading analysis

finding.finding_summary: The platform’s iterative feedback was associated with frequent immediate correction after errors, suggesting support for persistence and engagement in problem solving. Across all questions, 36.7% (260/708) of initially incorrect responses were converted to correct answers on the next attempt, and the authors report that the feedback was designed to encourage retrying and sustained effort.
finding.measure: Post-feedback correctness conversion rate; attempt-by-attempt revisions
finding.study_size: n=79 students; 708 initially incorrect feedback-supported attempts

finding.finding_summary: The feedback system appears to support iterative refinement of mathematical explanations and conceptual reasoning, though longer-term transfer was not clearly demonstrated. Examples showed students moving from vague answers to more precise, conceptually grounded explanations across attempts, but analyses of carry-over to later target questions were not statistically significant.
finding.measure: Iterative answer refinement; transfer/carry-over to subsequent questions; attempt-level learning curves

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents the system as a scalable way to reduce teacher workload by automating grading and feedback for complex geometry tasks. The tool achieved perfect agreement on rule-based items and substantial agreement on open-ended items, while providing immediate feedback and allowing up to three retries per item, demonstrating practical automation of formative assessment processes.
finding.measure: Automated grading agreement and automated feedback delivery on K-12 math tasks

paper_profiles.title: Learning to Love Edge Cases in Formative Math Assessment: Using the AMMORE Dataset and Chain-of-Thought Prompting to Improve Grading Accuracy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatic grading for open-response mathematics questions in K-12 settings, especially when student answers are mathematically correct but formatted in unexpected ways. The authors introduce AMMORE, a dataset of more than 53,000 open-response math answers from 2,508 at-home users of the Rori WhatsApp math tutor in several African countries, and use it to study how different grading strategies perform on difficult-to-score answers.

The paper compares six grading approaches: naive string matching, text processing, zero-shot prompting, few-shot prompting, chain-of-thought prompting, and a hybrid text-processing-plus-zero-shot pipeline. Using a curated difficult subset of 4,463 answers, the authors find that chain-of-thought prompting with GPT-4o performed best overall, reaching 97% accuracy and a linear weighted kappa of 0.93 on the binary correct/wrong task. The paper also shows that improved answer-level grading can materially change downstream Bayesian Knowledge Tracing estimates: misclassification of lesson mastery fell from 6.9% of students under string matching to 2.6% under chain-of-thought grading.

The context is middle-school mathematics practice delivered through an AI tutor used in low-resource, real-world settings across West Africa. The dataset spans grades 6-9 and focuses on algebra and number/operations questions. The main conclusion is that LLMs can be useful for grading open-ended math responses in K-12 settings, but prompt design matters, chain-of-thought reasoning can introduce inconsistency and occasional mathematical errors, and improved grading accuracy has important consequences for student mastery estimation in intelligent tutoring systems.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates LLM-based grading of open-response math answers and finds that chain-of-thought prompting achieved the best performance on the difficult AMMORE-hard set. On 4,463 answers, chain-of-thought reached 97% accuracy and linear weighted kappa of 0.93 against human labels, improving overall grading accuracy from 98.7% to 99.9% when used to recover the 1% of cases that the rules-based system failed to grade accurately.
finding.measure: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and linear weighted kappa for binary correct/wrong grading of student math responses
finding.study_size: n=4,463 (AMMORE-hard); n=53,031 in the full dataset

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that LLM-based grading can reduce human workload by automating evaluation of open-response math answers, though with latency tradeoffs. Chain-of-thought grading was substantially slower than text processing (average 2.79 seconds vs 0.006 seconds), but it improved grading reliability and reduced the need for manual correction of edge cases.
finding.measure: Processing time / latency for grading approaches; automated grading accuracy as a proxy for grading efficiency
finding.study_size: n=4,463 for accuracy evaluation; n=100 for repeated-run reliability checks

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that more accurate automated grading can improve Bayesian Knowledge Tracing estimates, which in turn affect intelligent tutoring system decisions such as lesson progression and feedback. Using human labels as gold standard, chain-of-thought grading reduced the share of students whose mastery was misestimated from 6.9% (165/2,388) under string matching to 2.6% (61/2,388).
finding.measure: Student mastery estimates from Bayesian Knowledge Tracing; misclassification rate of mastery status across completed lessons

paper_profiles.title: GSM-PLUS: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating the Robustness of LLMs as Mathematical Problem Solvers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models (LLMs) that perform well on standard grade-school math benchmarks are truly robust mathematical reasoners, or whether their performance collapses when the wording, numbers, or reasoning structure of a problem changes. To study this, the authors introduce GSM-PLUS, an adversarial extension of GSM8K that generates eight perturbation types across five reasoning perspectives, including numerical substitutions, arithmetic changes, distractor insertion, and critical-thinking variants that remove essential information.

The study evaluates 25 LLMs spanning closed-source foundation models, open-source foundation models, and math-focused supervised fine-tuned models, plus several prompting strategies. The main finding is that accuracy drops substantially from GSM8K to GSM-PLUS for nearly all models, with especially large declines on critical thinking, arithmetic variation, distractors, and integer-decimal-fraction conversion. GPT-4 is the most robust among the tested models, but even it shows a notable drop; humans remain far more stable. The paper concludes that high benchmark accuracy does not reliably indicate robust math reasoning and that compositional prompting can help but does not close the gap.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates math word-problem solving accuracy and robustness for 25 LLMs on GSM8K and the adversarial GSM-PLUS benchmark. Performance drops markedly under perturbations: for example, GPT-4 falls from 93.25% on GSM8K to 85.58% on GSM-PLUS (PDR 8.23%), and GPT-3.5-Turbo falls from 73.62% to 61.19% (PDR 16.88%). Some perturbations preserve or slightly improve performance (e.g., numerical substitution, problem understanding), while others sharply reduce it, especially critical thinking and arithmetic variation.
finding.measure: Accuracy on GSM8K and GSM-PLUS math word-problem benchmarks; performance drop rate (PDR); accurately solved pairs (ASP)
finding.study_size: n=25 models; GSM8K n=1,319 seed questions; GSM-PLUS n=10,552 question variations

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Models and Mathematical Reasoning Failures
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how well several state-of-the-art large language models solve newly constructed high-school-level mathematics word problems. The authors focus not only on whether the final answer is correct, but also on whether the solution steps are logically sound, because a model can sometimes reach the right answer via flawed reasoning.

The study uses a set of 50 original problems spanning arithmetic, algebra, counting, geometry, strategy, and spatial reasoning. Eight models are queried once each through their APIs, and the first author manually evaluates both final answers and solution explanations. The paper finds that newer reasoning-oriented models generally outperform earlier general-purpose models, but all systems still make serious errors, especially on problems requiring spatial intuition, multi-step deduction, or strategic planning. Several models also show a tendency to fit problems into familiar templates, ignore constraints, or produce correct answers with incorrect justifications.

The paper is best understood as a descriptive benchmark study of LLM mathematical reasoning in a K-12-adjacent high-school setting rather than an instructional intervention. Its main conclusion is that answer accuracy alone substantially overstates model competence, and that evaluation of reasoning traces is necessary to identify failure modes. The study does not test students or educational outcomes directly; instead it analyzes model performance on educationally relevant math tasks.

finding.finding_summary: Across 50 newly constructed high-school-level word problems, models ranged from 0/50 correct solutions (Mixtral 8x7B) to 40/50 correct solutions (o3-mini), with several intermediate results such as gpt-4o at 14/50 and o1 at 37/50. The paper also reports 21 cases where a model gave the correct answer but an incorrect solution, showing that answer accuracy alone overstates mathematical reasoning competence.
finding.measure: Manual correctness assessment on 50 high-school-level math word problems; both final answer and solution steps were scored

paper_profiles.title: SKYLENAGE Technical Report: Mathematical Reasoning and Contest-Innovation Benchmarks for Multi-Level Math Evaluation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This technical report introduces two new math evaluation benchmarks for large language models: SKYLENAGE-REASONINGMATH and SKYLENAGE-MATH. The paper addresses a central problem in AI math evaluation: existing benchmarks are increasingly saturated by frontier models, making it hard to distinguish strong systems or diagnose where they fail. To address this, the authors build harder, structure-aware, and grade-stratified benchmarks that emphasize multi-step reasoning, symbolic manipulation, and contest-style problem solving.

SKYLENAGE-REASONINGMATH contains 100 reasoning-focused items with metadata for length, numeric density, symbolic complexity, and other structural features. SKYLENAGE-MATH contains 150 contest-style problems spanning high school through doctoral level and covering seven math subjects. The study evaluates 15 contemporary LLM variants under a unified prompting and grading protocol, then analyzes performance by subject, grade band, answer type, and structural difficulty. The work is not an intervention study in K-12 classrooms; it is a benchmark evaluation of model performance on mathematics tasks that include high-school-level content and extend beyond K-12 into advanced levels.

The main conclusion is that benchmark design strongly affects how well frontier models can be separated. On the contest-style set, the best model reaches 44.0% accuracy and performance declines steadily from high school to doctoral items, with notable subject specialization and leader rotation across models. On the reasoning set, the best model reaches 81% overall, but hardest-slice performance exposes larger gaps than overall accuracy alone. The authors conclude that single aggregate scores hide important differences, and that grade-band, subject-specific, and structure-aware evaluation is more informative for judging mathematical reasoning systems.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates mathematical problem-solving accuracy across two benchmarks rather than an educational intervention. On SKYLENAGE-MATH (n=150), the top model reached 44.0% accuracy and performance declined from high school to doctoral items (HS 26.3% vs. PhD 14.1%), while on SKYLENAGE-REASONINGMATH (n=100) the best model reached 81% overall. Results show strong subject- and grade-band variation, with discrete domains and numeric-dense items producing the clearest separations among models.
finding.measure: Exact-match accuracy on contest-style and reasoning-focused math benchmark items, stratified by subject and grade band
finding.study_size: n=150 and n=100 benchmark items; 15 models evaluated

paper_profiles.title: CMM-Math: A Chinese Multimodal Math Dataset To Evaluate and Enhance the Mathematics Reasoning of Large Multimodal Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces CMM-Math, a large Chinese multimodal mathematics dataset intended to evaluate and improve large multimodal models (LMMs) on math reasoning tasks. The authors argue that prior benchmarks are mostly English and often focus on text-only problems, leaving a gap for Chinese, visually grounded math problems drawn from real school exams.

The dataset contains 28,069 problems spanning 12 grade levels from primary school through high school, 13 subjects, and four problem types (choice, fill-in-the-blank, yes-no, and analysis). The authors describe a construction pipeline involving data collection from more than 10,000 exam papers, cleaning with OCR/image extraction tools, and human/model-based annotation to organize problems by grade and subject. They also split the corpus into evaluation and training sets and propose a three-stage Math-LMM training approach using multimodal pretraining, instruction tuning, and math-specific fine-tuning.

The main experimental contribution is a benchmark evaluation of several open- and closed-source LMMs on CMM-Math, with breakdowns by grade level and mathematical subject. Results show that current models struggle substantially on the dataset overall, with performance declining at higher grade levels and on geometry-related subjects; closed-source systems generally outperform open-source ones, and few-shot prompting often improves accuracy. The paper concludes that multimodal mathematical reasoning remains challenging and that CMM-Math can support both evaluation and model improvement for K-12 math reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: Across 28,069 Chinese multimodal math problems, current large multimodal models showed substantial variation in mathematical reasoning performance. Mean accuracy across models was 35.66%, with GPT-4o (3-shot) reaching the best overall accuracy at 65.98% and Qwen-VL-Max (3-shot) also performing strongly; however, performance dropped notably on harder grade levels and geometry-heavy subjects. The study is benchmark-based rather than an intervention trial, so the findings primarily describe model capability rather than student learning gains.
finding.measure: Accuracy on choice/yes-no math questions; GPT-4o score on fill-in-the-blank and analysis questions; subject- and grade-level performance

paper_profiles.title: GSM-SYMBOLIC: Understanding the Limitations of Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how well large language models (LLMs) solve grade-school math word problems and whether standard benchmark scores on GSM8K are a reliable indicator of mathematical reasoning. The authors introduce GSM-Symbolic, a template-based benchmark that generates many controlled variants of GSM8K problems by changing names, numerical values, and the number of clauses, allowing them to study model performance as a distribution rather than a single score.

Using more than 20 open and closed models, the paper reports that performance varies substantially across semantically equivalent problem instances. Models are generally more robust to changing proper names than to changing numerical values, and accuracy declines as problems become more complex with additional clauses. The authors also introduce GSM-NoOp, where irrelevant but seemingly relevant information is added, and show large performance drops, suggesting models often rely on pattern matching rather than formal reasoning.

The population/context is K-12 grade-school mathematics, but the study evaluates LLMs rather than human learners. The work is primarily a benchmark and robustness analysis, not an educational intervention. Its main conclusion is that current LLM math benchmarks may overstate reasoning ability and that LLMs are fragile to small perturbations, especially in arithmetic word problems.

finding.finding_summary: Across more than 20 evaluated LLMs, accuracy on GSM-Symbolic is lower than on GSM8K and varies substantially across controlled problem instantiations. For example, the paper reports drops such as Gemma2-9B from 87.0% on GSM8K to 79.1% on GSM-Symbolic (about -7.9 points) and Phi-3.5-mini from 88.0% to 82.1% (-5.9 points), with notable variance across 50 generated datasets (e.g., ±3.0 to ±3.5 points depending on model).
finding.measure: Accuracy on grade-school math word problems (GSM8K, GSM-Symbolic, GSM-M1/P1/P2, GSM-NoOp)
finding.study_size: n=100 templates per benchmark, 50 samples per template (5000 examples per benchmark); 25 models evaluated
finding.std_deviation: ±3.0, ±3.4, ±3.5, and similar model-specific SDs reported across benchmark variants

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the models do not exhibit robust logical reasoning or reliable discrimination of relevant versus irrelevant information, which is central to durable skills such as reasoning and problem decomposition. On GSM-NoOp, adding irrelevant but plausible clauses caused dramatic drops, with the paper reporting decreases up to 65.7% (e.g., Phi-3-mini-128k-instruct), and performance did not recover even when given 8-shot examples that included the correct reasoning chain.
finding.measure: Robustness to irrelevant clauses and reasoning sensitivity in math word problems
finding.study_size: n=25 models; 5000 examples per benchmark variant

paper_profiles.title: Can LLMs Solve Longer Math Word Problems Better?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) become less capable when math word problems are lengthened with additional narrative context. The authors frame this as a study of Context Length Generalizability (CoLeG): whether a model can solve the same math problem reliably across progressively longer versions of the prompt. To test this, they create E-GSM, an extended version of GSM8K generated by iteratively rewriting grade-school math problems into longer forms while keeping the conditions, order of conditions, and ground-truth answer unchanged.

The paper evaluates four proprietary LLMs and four open-source LLMs on the extended benchmark using zero-shot prompting methods, and it also tests two mitigation strategies: a condition-retrieving instruction prompt (CoRe) for proprietary models and extension-based fine-tuning for open-source models. The population is grade-school math word problems, so the relevant educational context is elementary-level mathematics, though the actual study subjects are LLMs rather than students. The results show that all tested models generally degrade as context length increases, with accuracy dropping from earlier to later extension rounds even though problem difficulty was intended to remain constant.

The authors also report that CoRe and extension-based fine-tuning improve performance, especially on longer problems, and that these gains appear to come primarily from improved mathematical reasoning rather than improved semantic understanding. They conclude that current LLMs are sensitive to long contexts in math reasoning and that targeted prompting or training on extended problems can improve robustness. The work further argues that standard GSM8K accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize model quality, motivating additional metrics for efficacy and robustness across lengthened variants.

finding.finding_summary: Across four proprietary and four open-source LLMs, accuracy consistently declined as math word problems were extended in length, indicating weaker performance on longer grade-school math problems. For example, average accuracy dropped from Q0 to Q4 by 15.33% for proprietary models under zero-shot prompting and by 17.41% for open-source models trained without extension. The paper also shows that CoRe and extension-based fine-tuning improved accuracy on the long-context benchmark, with stronger gains in later rounds.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Extended Grade-School Math (E-GSM) round-by-round; CoLeG-E and CoLeG-R; GSM8K accuracy

paper_profiles.title: Findings of MEGA: Maths Explanation with LLMs using the Socratic Method for Active Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a novel generative-AI tutoring approach called MEGA (Mathematics Explanations through Games by AI LLMs) improves the learning experience of math explanations compared with a standard chain-of-thought (CoT) explanation. MEGA combines the Socratic method, chain-of-thought reasoning, simplified gamification with two answer choices at each step, and formative feedback delivered by large language models.

The study was conducted in a university context with master’s students who evaluated math solutions generated for two benchmark datasets: GSM8K (easier word problems) and MATH (more difficult problems). Students performed blind pairwise comparisons between MEGA and CoT explanations, and the authors also analyzed model accuracy across datasets, difficulty levels, and problem types. The central conclusion is that students generally preferred MEGA, especially for harder MATH problems, where MEGA was rated substantially better than CoT. However, the paper also shows that model hallucinations still occur, including at intermediate Socratic steps, and that MEGA does not fully eliminate these errors.

finding.finding_summary: Students judged MEGA explanations to be better for understanding math problems than standard CoT explanations, with the effect being much stronger on the harder MATH dataset than on GSM8K. In the human evaluation, MEGA was preferred in 47.5% of MATH cases versus 26.67% for CoT (n=60 sampled MATH problems), while on GSM8K the difference was small (26.67% vs 24.17%; n=60).
finding.measure: Student pairwise preference for explanation quality on math problem solutions; dataset-specific agreement percentages
finding.study_size: n=120 total sampled problems (n=60 GSM8K, n=60 MATH); 34 student evaluators
finding.confidence_interval: p=0.0201 for MATH; p=0.6731 for GSM8K

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that MEGA was often experienced as more engaging and interactive, which students linked to easier understanding on harder problems, but some students found the interaction tedious or unnecessary for easier questions. The survey also found that 77.78% of evaluators preferred interactive learning overall, yet 22.22% preferred non-interactive learning, indicating mixed learner responses to the intervention.
finding.measure: Student preference for interactive vs non-interactive learning; free-text feedback on engagement and usability

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests MEGA can support active learning and stepwise reasoning by forcing learners to engage with each sub-question before proceeding. Student comments indicated that this structure helped them understand complex problems more deeply, especially when compared with a direct CoT explanation.
finding.measure: Student qualitative feedback about clarity, step-by-step reasoning, and engagement with explanations

finding.finding_summary: The intervention changed the efficiency of explanation delivery: several students reported that MEGA was slower and more tedious for simple problems, while others found it more efficient for complex problems because it broke explanations into manageable steps. The paper frames this as a tradeoff between efficiency and pedagogical support rather than a uniform productivity gain.
finding.measure: Student qualitative feedback on time/effort required to use MEGA versus CoT

paper_profiles.title: Novice Learner and Expert Tutor: Evaluating Math Reasoning Abilities of Large Language Models with Misconceptions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models (LLMs) can go beyond simply solving grade-school math problems correctly and instead behave like students with specific misconceptions or like tutors who can diagnose those misconceptions. The authors frame two evaluation tasks: a “novice learner” task, where the model must intentionally choose an incorrect answer that matches a given misconception, and an “expert tutor” task, where the model must identify which misconception explains a student’s wrong answer.

The study uses multiple-choice grade-school mathematics questions drawn from Eedi’s platform, filtered to 213 questions with expert-curated misconceptions attached to incorrect options. The authors evaluate GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 under several prompting conditions, including zero-shot and few-shot settings, and report mean accuracy over four independent trials. While GPT-4 performs very well on ordinary correct-answering (up to 94.8% with explanation prompting), it performs substantially worse when asked to simulate a novice learner (e.g., 61.7% in zero-shot with explanation; 67.9% in few-shot with same-misconception examples) and its expert-tutor accuracy declines as the number of candidate misconceptions increases (91.9% with 4 misconceptions, dropping to 39.8% at 100 misconceptions).

The main conclusion is that LLMs can answer standard elementary math questions well, but they are much less reliable at modeling misconception-based errors or diagnosing those errors, even in a relatively simple grade-school setting. The paper argues that this reveals an important limitation for educational applications such as intelligent tutoring systems, where robust student-simulation and misconception-diagnosis capabilities are needed.

finding.finding_summary: The models performed strongly on ordinary math problem answering but much more weakly on misconception-based math reasoning tasks. GPT-4 reached 94.8% accuracy on correct-answering with explanation prompting, but only 61.7% accuracy when asked to choose the specific incorrect answer matching a misconception, and expert-tutor accuracy fell from 91.9% with 4 misconceptions to 39.8% with 100 misconceptions.
finding.measure: Accuracy on multiple-choice grade-school math questions, novice-learner incorrect-answer selection accuracy, and expert-tutor misconception-identification accuracy
finding.confidence_interval: w/o exp: 0.948 ± 0.009; novice zero with exp: 0.617 ± 0.005; expert tutor at n=4 misconceptions: 0.919; at n=100 misconceptions: 0.398
finding.std_deviation: w/o exp: 0.009; novice zero with exp: 0.005

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that LLMs struggle with misconception-based reasoning tasks that require identifying, representing, and counterfactually applying specific error patterns. This suggests weaker performance on metacognitive and analytical reasoning tasks relevant to durable skills, even though the paper is not a direct human-subject study of students.
finding.measure: Performance on misconception simulation and misconception diagnosis tasks

paper_profiles.title: CMMaTH: A Chinese Multi-modal Math Skill Evaluation Benchmark for Foundation Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces CMMaTH, a large Chinese multimodal mathematics benchmark designed to evaluate foundation models on K-12 math problems that require interpreting both images and text. The authors argue that existing multimodal math benchmarks are insufficient for Chinese K-12 settings because they lack fine-grained grade-level coverage, diverse visual question types, and detailed knowledge-point annotations.

To address this, the paper constructs a 23,856-question dataset spanning elementary, junior high, and senior high school levels, with 13 visual subject categories, 5 difficulty levels, and detailed K-12 knowledge annotations. The authors also build GradeGPT, an open-source answer-comparison tool for judging whether model outputs match reference answers, and use it to evaluate several multimodal and text-only large models. Their evaluation shows that current models, including GPT-4V and open-source multimodal systems, still struggle substantially on Chinese multimodal math reasoning, especially on diverse visual formats and free-form answer types.

The study is primarily a benchmark and model-evaluation paper rather than an intervention study. It provides descriptive performance comparisons across models, visual subject areas, answer formats, and grade bands, and concludes that stronger multimodal OCR, diagram reasoning, and Chinese-language reasoning capabilities are still needed for K-12 math applications.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark results show large performance variation across model families and math subtypes, with even strong models struggling on K-12 multimodal math. GPT-4V achieved 27.0% overall accuracy on the benchmark, while GPT-4o reached 35.2%; open-source multimodal models were much lower (e.g., LLaVA-v1.5 5.5%, InternLM-XComposer2-VL 3.4%, Yi-VL-34B 8.3%, CogAgent-Chat 10.6%). The paper also reports grade-band and subject-specific results, showing that performance differs substantially by visual subject and by elementary/junior/senior school levels, but no causal intervention effect is tested.
finding.measure: Accuracy on CMMaTH multimodal math benchmark overall, by visual subject, and by grade-level question sets
finding.study_size: n=23,856 questions (testmini n=1,000; human testmini n=not_reported)

paper_profiles.title: FACET: Teacher-Centred LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems—Towards Personalized Educational Worksheets
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of teacher workload and classroom heterogeneity in mathematics education by asking whether a multi-agent large language model system can generate teaching materials that are adapted to individual learner needs. The authors argue that existing AI personalization tools are often too focused on performance alone and do not adequately support teachers in designing instruction that reflects both cognitive and motivational differences among students.

To address this, the paper introduces FACET, a teacher-facing LLM-based multi-agent framework with three roles: learner agents that simulate students with different knowledge and motivation profiles, a teacher agent that generates personalized worksheets aligned to didactical principles and Bloom’s taxonomy, and an evaluator agent that scores output quality. The system was tested on authentic grade 8 mathematics curriculum content in German secondary education, using four learner profiles defined by combinations of high/low knowledge and high/low motivation. Evaluation combined automated agent-based ratings across 10 iterations per profile with exploratory feedback from five K–12 in-service teachers.

The results indicate that FACET can reliably produce worksheets that are judged as structurally sound, clear, and suitable for the modeled learners. Internal agent-based scores were consistently high, especially for task suitability and clarity, and teacher feedback was also positive, with educators noting the usefulness of differentiation, scaffolding, and reduced overload for less motivated learners. The study concludes that multi-agent LLM systems may be a promising way to support personalized worksheet generation, though the authors emphasize that the current evidence is preliminary and that real classroom trials are still needed.

finding.finding_summary: The system generated grade 8 mathematics worksheets that were rated as highly suitable and clear for the intended learner profiles. Across 10 iterations per worksheet, the agent-based evaluation gave suitability scores near the top of the 6-point scale (e.g., M=4.78 overall; Table 1 shows suitability means of 5.9–6.0 for the four profiles), indicating that the math tasks were successfully adapted to the learner’s cognitive level.
finding.measure: Quality ratings of generated grade 8 mathematics worksheets (didactical structure, clarity, creativity, suitability for learners)
finding.study_size: n=4 learner profiles, 10 iterations per profile
finding.std_deviation: SD reported for agent ratings (e.g., suitability SD=0.06 overall; profile-level SDs 0.0–0.3)

finding.finding_summary: The framework explicitly modeled and adapted to intrinsic motivation, and teacher feedback suggested that motivational tailoring improved engagement, especially for low-motivation learners. Teachers recommended narrative elements and everyday-life relevance to foster problem-solving motivation and noted that the reduced number of tasks for low-motivation students helped prevent cognitive overload.
finding.measure: Teacher feedback on motivational suitability and qualitative comments; learner profile dimensions included intrinsic motivation
finding.study_size: n=5 K-12 in-service teachers; 4 learner profiles

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that FACET can reduce teacher effort by generating reusable personalized worksheets and lowering prompt-engineering burden. Teachers valued the ability to differentiate within one topic without manually creating many versions, indicating potential efficiency gains in planning and material preparation.
finding.measure: Exploratory teacher feedback on usefulness/workload reduction and system design features related to reusable agent profiles

finding.finding_summary: The framework incorporates Bloom’s taxonomy and stratified task selection intended to scaffold progression from recall to abstraction, which directly targets reasoning and metacognitive progression rather than only procedural practice. However, this outcome is evaluated indirectly through worksheet design and suitability ratings rather than through student performance on durable-skill measures.
finding.measure: Bloom-aligned task sequencing and evaluator ratings of didactical structure

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education (broad, not a single sampled population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models, especially ChatGPT/GPT-3–style systems, for education. Rather than testing an intervention, it synthesizes early use cases and research examples to argue that these models may support learning content creation, feedback, tutoring, assessment, and teacher productivity, while also introducing risks related to bias, privacy, integrity, overreliance, and unequal access.

The paper discusses applications across elementary, middle/high school, university, and professional learning contexts, with particular attention to how language models could be used by both students and teachers. Examples include quiz generation, reading comprehension support, curiosity prompting, code explanations, adaptive feedback, and automated grading or content creation. It also highlights design and governance considerations for responsible deployment, such as human oversight, fact-checking, copyright compliance, and data protection.

The main conclusion is that large language models have substantial educational promise, but their adoption should be cautious, human-centered, and grounded in pedagogical goals. The paper does not report original empirical results; instead, it provides a conceptual framework and mitigation strategies for integrating LLMs into education responsibly.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models can support reading and writing development through summaries, explanations, grammar/style feedback, and reading-comprehension quiz generation, but it presents no original empirical effect estimates. Claims are based on illustrative prior work and conceptual reasoning rather than a controlled study.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLMs can support language learning, pronunciation practice, conversational practice, and reducing foreign-language anxiety, but these are discussed as potential applications rather than measured outcomes. No empirical effect size or study sample is reported in this paper.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that LLMs can generate practice problems, quizzes, explanations, and step-by-step solutions for middle and high school mathematics learning. However, this is a position-paper claim supported by examples and citations, not by direct evaluation of math achievement in this paper.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes use cases in science and STEM education, including supporting scientific argumentation and science-related problem solving through explanations and feedback. It mentions prior work in high school climate activity tasks, but this paper itself reports no new scientific-reasoning outcome data.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights broader subject-area uses such as computer science, data science, and medical education, including code explanations, assessment question generation, and exam preparation support. These are presented as promising applications, but the paper provides no direct empirical outcome estimates.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs may increase student engagement, curiosity, and participation, and may reduce foreign-language anxiety or willingness-to-communicate barriers. These claims are descriptive and based on cited prior studies; no new engagement or motivation data are reported here.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: A central theme is that LLMs can support critical thinking, problem solving, collaboration, and metacognition, but may also undermine these skills if learners over-rely on generated answers. The paper offers no quantitative estimate; it frames durable skills as both a key opportunity and a key risk in LLM-supported education.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by assisting with lesson planning, quiz generation, adaptive feedback, summarization, and automated assessment. One cited example notes grading effort could be reduced by up to 85% in a related NLP-based feedback study, but that result is not newly produced in this paper.
finding.measure: teacher workload / grading effort / content-generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper devotes substantial attention to institutional governance, including copyright, bias, privacy, sustainability, access, and policy responses such as school bans and responsible-use frameworks. Its overall conclusion is that institutional adoption is promising but requires clear governance, human oversight, and equitable access; no empirical institutional outcome is tested.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the sudden emergence of ChatGPT and asks how such generative AI tools may affect higher education, especially assessment, learning, and teaching. The authors frame the discussion around OpenAI’s history, the technical capabilities and limitations of GPT-3/ChatGPT, and the broader context of Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd).

Methodologically, the paper is a desktop analysis and literature review supplemented by the authors’ own exploratory prompting of ChatGPT. They test the system with a few illustrative prompts, including conceptual explanations, statistical concepts, a short essay request, and a Chinese composition task, to show where the tool performs well and where it fails. Their examples suggest ChatGPT is useful for quick explanations, simple calculations, and draft generation, but weak on higher-order reasoning, citation accuracy, and some non-English language production.

The paper’s main contribution is interpretive rather than empirical: it situates ChatGPT within student-facing, teacher-facing, and system-facing AIEd categories and argues that educators should treat it as both a challenge and an opportunity. The authors conclude that ChatGPT may undermine traditional take-home writing assessments, but it can also motivate assessment redesign, more in-class and oral work, and better use of feedback and active learning. They recommend adapting higher education practices rather than trying to ignore or ban the technology.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT can rapidly produce short essays and conceptual explanations, but its output is often generic, descriptive, and weak in breadth, depth, and citation quality. In the authors' test prompt for a 2000-word essay on schizophrenia, ChatGPT produced only about 500 words within 120 seconds and failed to supply reliable in-text/end-of-text references, suggesting limited usefulness for high-quality academic writing.
finding.measure: ChatGPT-generated essay quality, breadth/depth, and citation support in a prompted writing task

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that ChatGPT can communicate in multiple languages, but its performance is uneven outside English. In the authors' Chinese composition prompt, the bot produced a scenario aligned with the prompt but the writing lacked structure, was grammatically poor, and appeared to be directly translated from English, indicating weaker performance in low-resource languages.
finding.measure: Quality of a generated Chinese composition

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that ChatGPT could clearly explain statistical concepts such as mean, standard deviation, and z-scores, and it also generated a real-world example with step-by-step calculations. This is presented as a successful demonstration of basic mathematical explanation rather than a controlled test, with no formal effect size reported.
finding.measure: ChatGPT explanation of mean, standard deviation, z-scores, and an applied calculation example

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT is less competent when tasks require higher-order thinking, especially critical and analytical reasoning. In the essay prompt example, the model produced generic, largely descriptive prose with limited evidence and weak argumentation, which the authors interpret as a limitation for durable-skill development and for assessments targeting deeper thinking.
finding.measure: Quality of higher-order reasoning in a prompted essay task

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly emphasizes that ChatGPT can generate responses within roughly 60-120 seconds, making it useful for rapid drafting, quick explanations, and brainstorming. The authors also argue that such tools may reduce workload for teachers in feedback and assessment redesign contexts, although they do not report formal efficiency metrics.
finding.measure: Speed of generating answers and potential workload reduction in teaching/assessment workflows

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that ChatGPT may threaten traditional take-home essay assessments and plagiarism-detection regimes, but also create pressure and opportunity for institutions to redesign assessment policies. The authors note that institutions may need to adapt quickly because AI-generated text may become mainstream and harder to regulate through conventional anti-plagiarism tools.
finding.measure: Implications for assessment policy, plagiarism detection, and institutional response

paper_profiles.title: When the robotic Maths tutor is wrong - can children identify mistakes generated by ChatGPT?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether primary school children can detect errors in answers generated by a ChatGPT-powered robot acting as a maths tutor. The authors are motivated by concerns that LLM-based educational tools may present incorrect information convincingly, and they test whether children can recognize those mistakes and what factors influence that ability.

The intervention was a classroom user study with a Pepper robot in a UK primary school. Seventy-seven students in Years 3 to 5 (roughly ages 7 to 11) answered 20 maths questions drawn from the Year 3 UK curriculum; the robot then presented either correct or incorrect LLM-generated answers and explanations, and students rated the correctness on a 5-point Likert scale. The study also examined whether students’ own correctness on the maths questions, school year, and gender were associated with their ability to identify robot errors.

The results showed that children were generally able to distinguish correct from incorrect AI answers: 76.5% identified correct answers and 72% identified incorrect answers, with statistical evidence that ratings differed by answer correctness (chi-square test, χ2=504.7, df=4, N=1540, p<.001). Students were better at spotting errors when they themselves answered the maths question correctly (81% identified incorrect LLM answers in that case; χ2=374.95, df=8, N=1540, p<.001), suggesting prior knowledge matters for verification. School year was not significantly associated with error detection (χ2=19.68, df=16, N=1540, p>.05), while gender was significant (χ2=37.88, df=8, N=1540, p<.001), with female students observed to be more accurate than male students in this task.

Overall, the paper argues for cautious, gradual integration of LLM-powered educational robots under teacher/domain-expert supervision. It concludes that even young children can notice AI mistakes in a maths setting, but that prior knowledge is important and implementation should avoid over-reliance on autonomous AI in education.

finding.finding_summary: Primary school students could detect both correct and incorrect ChatGPT-generated maths answers at statistically significant rates, but performance varied by response type and by students’ own correctness on the questions. Across 1,540 student ratings from 77 pupils (Years 3-5), 76.5% identified correct answers and 72% identified incorrect answers; when students answered the maths item correctly themselves, they identified incorrect LLM answers more often (81%).
finding.measure: Student ratings of Pepper robot's maths answers on a 5-point Likert scale, alongside whether students' own maths answers were correct

finding.finding_summary: The study provides evidence for children’s error-detection and verification skills when using AI-generated content, which the authors frame as prior knowledge-based checking and critical evaluation. Statistically significant associations showed that students were better at identifying LLM mistakes when they had solved the maths item correctly themselves (χ2=374.95, df=8, N=1540, p<.001), indicating that domain knowledge supported more accurate verification of AI output.
finding.measure: Ability to judge the correctness of AI-generated answers and detect mistakes

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual discussion of how AI should be integrated into education, with a focus on higher education. It argues that the rise of ChatGPT and similar large language models requires students and educators to develop three core capacities: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. The paper is motivated by the author’s experience with AI adoption at a Swiss University of Applied Sciences, where students and staff were rapidly encountering generative AI in academic work.

The article combines an informal case study from the author’s institution with a narrative literature review. It describes the university’s response to student use of AI in academic writing, including internal guidelines requiring transparency about what AI tools were used, how they were used, and how outputs were critically evaluated. The paper also surveys emerging AI literacy components and recent prompting methods such as chain-of-thought, self-consistency, automatic prompt engineering, generated knowledge prompting, and tree-of-thought prompting.

The paper’s main conclusion is that bans or unrestricted use of AI are both problematic; instead, institutions should build an AI culture supported by workshops, guidelines, dedicated budgets, and staff expertise. It argues that AI can support classroom learning and task creation, but only if students learn to use it as a sparring partner rather than a ghostwriter. The discussion is primarily aimed at higher education, though the author suggests the ideas may also be useful for children and K-12 settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and especially critical thinking are essential skills for responsible AI use in education. It does not report original effect sizes or experimental results, but it synthesizes literature and institutional practice to claim that prompt engineering and reflective evaluation can strengthen students’ critical thinking and awareness of AI limitations.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, AI literacy, and prompt engineering skills discussed conceptually; no quantitative measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on institutional responses to generative AI, especially the development of AI guidelines at a Swiss university and recommendations for workshops, budgeting, dedicated positions, and governance structures. It presents these as necessary institutional measures to manage AI use transparently and responsibly, but does not provide quantitative evaluation of policy effects.
finding.measure: Institutional AI guidelines, governance practices, workshops, and implementation recommendations

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that AI tools can improve efficiency in tasks such as curriculum design, creating case studies, and supporting classroom preparation. These claims are presented as practical recommendations and examples rather than measured outcomes, with no quantitative evidence of workload reduction reported.
finding.measure: Teacher/curriculum preparation efficiency and task support

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary students and teachers perceive a generative AI–supported environment for creative mathematical writing. The authors focus on whether GenAI can support students in constructing math stories, representing mathematical ideas, and revising AI-generated drafts, while also identifying barriers and design challenges in classroom use.

The study was conducted in six 5th-grade classrooms across two U.S. elementary schools with 79 students and six teachers. Students used a custom GenAI-powered tool built with GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 through a three-step process: Ask, Represent, and Transform. The tool prompted students to analyze math story problems, visually represent their thinking, and then co-create culturally relevant math stories with AI, followed by self-review using a checklist.

Using interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations, the authors conducted thematic analysis and identified six themes: four benefits and two challenge categories. Perceived benefits included fostering creativity in mathematics, improving mathematical understanding, promoting AI literacy, and increasing interest, curiosity, and ownership of learning. Reported challenges included students’ difficulty critically evaluating AI output and generating coherent stories, as well as AI-side limitations such as being too perfect, lacking pedagogical feedback, reducing autonomy, limiting social interaction, and not supporting multiple communication modes. The paper concludes that GenAI can support mathematical creative writing and related learning processes, but only when intentionally designed to preserve meaningful student cognition, agency, and interaction.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing was perceived to improve students’ mathematical understanding, including breaking down problems, representing mathematical ideas, and uncovering misconceptions. At the same time, participants noted challenges when students struggled to generate coherent math stories or when AI output was too complete, suggesting the tool supports numeracy-related learning processes but also requires careful instructional design.
finding.measure: student and teacher perceptions from interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations about mathematical understanding, problem decomposition, and representation
finding.study_size: n=79 students; 6 teachers (10 students interviewed in focus groups)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention directly targeted creative writing, with students co-authoring and revising math stories generated by GenAI. Participants reported that the system helped them draft, expand, correct, and make stories more original and interesting, indicating perceived gains in writing productivity and quality within the math-story writing task.
finding.measure: perceived creative mathematical writing quality, originality, and revision of AI-generated story drafts

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived that the GenAI-supported activity increased interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning. The authors describe these as affective-domain benefits, with students reporting that math became more fun and that they felt more responsible for their own learning when acting as authors of math stories.
finding.measure: interview and survey themes on interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies AI literacy and prompt engineering as a substantive learning outcome, along with flexible thinking and critical evaluation of AI strengths and weaknesses. Students reportedly learned to refine prompts through trial and error and to judge AI output, indicating growth in metacognitive and critical-thinking skills tied to human-AI collaboration.
finding.measure: perceived prompt engineering ability, evaluation of AI strengths/weaknesses, and flexible/divergent thinking in thematic interviews

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 (Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how middle school students want generative AI to participate in collaborative mathematical problem solving (CPS). The authors ask how students perceive an AI peer in group mathematics work and what behaviors, controls, and features they want from such a system.

To address this, the researchers ran a five-day participatory design summer camp with 24 rising grades 6–8 students. Students completed human-only math CPS tasks and then worked with two text-based AI peers in a technology-probe sandbox designed to simulate peer collaboration. They also reviewed dialogue excerpts, redesigned the AI peers through posters and example scripts, and completed feature-preference surveys and interviews.

The main findings are that students did not want an AI peer that simply delivers correct answers or follows a rigid instructional script. Instead, they preferred an AI that offers scaffold-first support—hints, checks, error detection, concept refreshers, and follow-up practice—while staying under student control and using a friendly, peer-like tone. Students also strongly valued co-agency, emotional attunement, and clear turn-taking; they criticized AI behaviors that felt overly didactic, repetitive, inattentive, or emotionally flat. Overall, the paper argues that youth-centered design should treat AI peers as collaborative partners that support student thinking and social norms rather than as tutors or automated answer engines.

finding.finding_summary: The study centers on middle-school mathematics collaborative problem solving and shows that AI peers changed students' mathematical work in both positive and negative ways. Quantitatively, students reported lower temporal demand during CPS with AI peers (M=5.67, SD=4.38) than human-only CPS (M=9.62, SD=4.13), d=1.15, but they also reported higher physical demand (M=8.48 vs. 4.90, d=1.14) and lower task coordination on GEQ (GIT M=4.76 vs. 5.54, d=0.81).
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal and physical demand; GEQ Group Integration-Task during collaborative mathematics problem solving
finding.study_size: n=22 paired survey participants for the quantitative comparisons; N=24 enrolled
finding.std_deviation: Temporal demand SD=4.38 vs 4.13; physical demand SD=4.65 vs 2.41; GIT SD=1.58 vs 1.52

finding.finding_summary: Students experienced lower social cohesion and affective engagement when working with AI peers, but they also valued emotional support in principle. On the GEQ, Attractions to Group-Social was lower in the AI-peer condition (M=5.21, SD=1.81) than human-only CPS (M=6.50, SD=2.05), d=0.94, indicating reduced social warmth. Qualitative data further showed that students became frustrated, self-blaming, or less trusting when the AI failed to recognize confusion or frustration.
finding.measure: GEQ Attractions to Group-Social; interview and reflection accounts of frustration, trust, and emotional attunement
finding.study_size: n=22 paired survey participants; interviews N=18; whole-class reflections across 5 sessions

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines collaboration, co-agency, and turn-taking during mathematical CPS, showing that students wanted an AI peer to support rather than replace joint reasoning. Quantitatively, perceived coordination declined in the AI condition (GEQ GIT M=4.76, SD=1.58) versus human-only CPS (M=5.54, SD=1.52), d=0.81, while qualitative findings showed students disliked repetitive, non-responsive, or overly directive AI turns that undermined teamwork. Students preferred explicit prompting for shared reasoning, method negotiation, and clear conversational pacing.
finding.measure: GEQ Group Integration-Task; qualitative reflections on collaboration, co-agency, listening, and turn-taking
finding.study_size: n=22 paired survey participants; interviews N=18; whole-class reflections across 5 sessions

finding.finding_summary: AI peers improved perceived time efficiency but increased operational burden. Students reported significantly lower temporal demand with AI peers (M=5.67, SD=4.38) than with human-only CPS (M=9.62, SD=4.13), d=1.15, suggesting the system reduced time pressure and accelerated progress. However, the text-based interface added physical/interactional effort (M=8.48 vs 4.90, d=1.14), meaning efficiency gains came with higher mediation overhead.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand and physical demand
finding.std_deviation: Temporal demand SD=4.38 vs 4.13; physical demand SD=4.65 vs 2.41

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination (VNHSGE), a high-stakes high school exit exam covering mathematics, literature, English, physics, chemistry, biology, history, geography, and civic education. The authors use the VNHSGE evaluation dataset and prompt ChatGPT in a zero-shot format to answer multiple-choice questions, with literature represented by essays and the other subjects by multiple-choice items.

The study evaluates ChatGPT’s responses by comparing them to human-labeled ground truth answers and reports subject-level scores from 2019 to 2023, as well as combined scores for natural-science and social-science groupings. Across subjects, ChatGPT generally performs in the mid-to-high range, with stronger results in English and literature and weaker results in chemistry and some higher-order/problem-solving tasks. The authors conclude that ChatGPT would pass the exam overall, with combined scores above the passing threshold each year.

The paper is situated in a K-12/high-school assessment context and is primarily a performance-analysis study of a generative AI system rather than an intervention study with students or teachers. It offers descriptive evidence that ChatGPT can answer many exam questions at a level comparable to passing the exam, while also noting limitations on more complex questions, visual/chart-based items, and subject-specific reasoning demands.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT achieved passing-level mathematics scores on the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination dataset, with yearly scores ranging from 5.2 to 6.6 and an average of 5.88/10 across 2019-2023. The authors report that these scores were generally lower than most Vietnamese students, but still sufficient to contribute to an overall passing result.
finding.measure: Mathematics exam score on VNHSGE (10-point scale)

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT showed strong performance on non-mathematics academic subjects, especially English and literature, but weaker performance in chemistry and some geography/civic education tasks. For the VNHSGE overall, its combined natural and social science scores ranged from 6.30 to 6.94, indicating it would pass the exam in every year studied.
finding.measure: Subject exam scores and combined natural/social science scores on VNHSGE

finding.finding_summary: Across physics, chemistry, and biology, ChatGPT’s performance was uneven: physics scores ranged from 5.75 to 6.5, biology from 5.25 to 6.0, and chemistry from 4.0 to 6.25. The paper concludes that chemistry was the weakest subject overall, while physics and biology were more competitive, but still often below the majority of Vietnamese students.
finding.measure: Physics, chemistry, and biology exam scores on VNHSGE

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT performed well on literacy-related tasks, particularly literature, where scores ranged from 5.63 to 7.5 with an average of 6.8/10. The authors report that it usually outperformed the majority of Vietnamese students in literature, except in 2022 when it was slightly lower.
finding.measure: Literature exam score on VNHSGE (10-point scale)

paper_profiles.title: MathVC: An LLM-Simulated Multi-Persona Virtual Classroom for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of Make sure to enter the correct conference title from your rights confirmation email (Conference acronym ’XX)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of supporting collaborative mathematical problem solving in middle school settings, where students often lack sufficient peers, time, or balanced participation for productive group work. The authors ask whether large language models can be used to simulate multiple student peers in a virtual classroom that promotes collaborative problem solving rather than one-on-one tutoring.

To explore this, they built MathVC, a multi-persona LLM-based virtual classroom in which one student interacts with two simulated classmates: one with limited math proficiency and one with advanced proficiency. The system uses a meta-planning layer to manage collaborative problem-solving stages and next-speaker turns, plus persona schemas that inject common mathematical misconceptions and are updated during dialogue. The study deployed MathVC with 14 U.S. middle school students (grades 6–8, plus one advanced student below grade 6) across 40 dialogue sessions and collected interaction logs, exit surveys, and semi-structured interviews.

The main findings were broadly positive. Students reported that MathVC supported constructive interaction, helped them reach shared solutions, and improved their engagement, motivation, and confidence. Qualitative data suggested that students found the virtual peers believable when they made mistakes, offered critiques, and behaved like classmates, though some felt the language was too formal or adult-like. Overall, the paper concludes that LLM-simulated peers can create a productive collaborative math environment and offers design insights for future educational LLM systems, especially those intended to mimic peer collaboration rather than teacher-student tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: The study focused on collaborative mathematical problem solving with MathVC and found that students perceived the system as helping them understand and solve math problems. On the exit survey (n=14), students strongly agreed that they and the group reached a shared understanding or solution (Mean=4.43/5) and that they could understand the math problem and work effectively in the virtual classroom (Mean=4.21/5).
finding.measure: Exit survey ratings of shared understanding/solution and ability to understand and work on math problems; interaction logs during mathematical problem solving

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that MathVC increased engagement, motivation, persistence, and confidence during mathematical problem solving. The paper describes participants valuing immediate scaffolding, diverse perspectives, and reduced cognitive burden, and the exit survey showed high ratings for constructive interaction (Mean=4.36/5) and responsible contribution (Mean=4.29/5).
finding.measure: Interview themes, conversational logs, and exit survey ratings of interaction, responsibility, and planning

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examined collaborative problem solving and related metacognitive processes, including planning, shared understanding, and critique. Exit survey responses were high for planning steps and understanding how each action contributed to solving the problem (Mean=4.36/5), and qualitative results indicated that students experienced collaborative dialogue, justification, and error correction with the virtual peers.
finding.measure: Exit survey rating of planning and contribution; conversational interaction patterns and interview themes related to collaboration and metacognition

paper_profiles.title: Short-term AI literacy intervention does not reduce over-reliance on incorrect ChatGPT recommendations
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a brief AI literacy intervention can reduce students’ tendency to over-rely on incorrect ChatGPT outputs.
