The authors focus on whether explaining ChatGPT’s working mechanism, limitations, and proper use changes how often students accept wrong AI recommendations while solving math puzzles.

The study was conducted with 12th-grade Estonian high school students. Participants were randomly assigned to read either a short educational text about ChatGPT’s limitations and responsible use or a control text with only general information about ChatGPT. After reading, students solved eight math puzzles with ChatGPT recommendations, half of which were deliberately incorrect. The primary outcome was over-reliance: accepting incorrect ChatGPT advice. The intervention did not significantly reduce over-reliance, but it did significantly increase under-reliance, meaning students became more likely to ignore correct ChatGPT recommendations.

Overall, students showed substantial over-reliance, adopting incorrect suggestions in 52.1% of cases and most participants exhibiting at least one instance of over-reliance. The intervention improved self-reported knowledge about ChatGPT’s working mechanism and usage, but not perceived knowledge of its limitations. The authors conclude that brief AI literacy texts may be insufficient to reduce over-reliance on LLM outputs and may even encourage excessive caution toward correct advice.

finding.finding_summary: Students solved math puzzles with ChatGPT assistance and showed widespread reliance behavior. Across all participants, over-reliance occurred on 52.1% of incorrect recommendations (SD = 28.90; n = 36), and the intervention did not significantly reduce over-reliance compared with control (M = 48.68% vs 55.88%, Welch’s t(28.78) = -0.73, p = .236, d = -0.25).
finding.measure: Adoption of ChatGPT recommendations while solving Kangaroo math puzzles; over-reliance rate on incorrect recommendations

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined over-reliance, under-reliance, and initial decision time as indicators of critical thinking / analytical reasoning and metacognitive control. The intervention did not significantly change initial decision time (M = 1.56 vs 1.64 minutes, U = 179.5, p = .560), but longer decision time on incorrect items was associated with lower over-reliance (rs = -0.41, p = .013), and longer decision time on correct items was associated with higher under-reliance (rs = 0.35, p = .038).
finding.measure: Initial decision time and reliance behavior (over-reliance, under-reliance)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention affected self-reported confidence and reliance behavior, but not in a beneficial way for appropriate trust calibration. Confidence in using ChatGPT recommendations was slightly lower in the intervention group than control, but not significantly so (M = 3.58 vs 3.67, U = 188.50, p = .400, rrb = 0.17). The intervention also significantly increased under-reliance (M = 36.84% vs 19.12%, t(34) = 2.35, p = .025, d = 0.78), suggesting a shift toward aversion rather than calibrated engagement.
finding.measure: Self-reported confidence and reliance behavior

finding.finding_summary: The task context was mathematics, but the paper’s substantive contribution was not about math achievement or mathematical learning outcomes; it used math puzzles as a vehicle to measure AI reliance. There was no reported improvement in puzzle-solving performance attributable to the intervention, and the paper did not analyze mathematics learning gains beyond reliance/error behavior.
finding.measure: Performance on Kangaroo-style math puzzles

paper_profiles.title: How GenAI Mentor Configurations Shape Early Collaborative Dynamics: A Classroom Comparison of Individual and Shared Agents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks how the access structure of generative AI in a collaborative classroom shapes students’ interaction patterns and socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL). Rather than comparing AI versus no AI, the authors compare two configurations of the same GenAI mentor: a shared-agent condition in which each small group interacted with one common AI instance, and an individual-agent condition in which each student had a personal AI instance.

The study was conducted in two Grade 8 classes in a public middle school in China during a multi-week creative problem-solving project (“Smart Garden”), focusing on the problem-framing phase. Students worked in small groups of three to four, and the researchers collected classroom video/audio, screen recordings, interaction logs, teacher notes, and brief post-activity interviews. They analyzed transcripts with multi-layer discourse coding, lag sequential analysis, ordered network analysis, and Markov transition analysis to compare interaction distribution, AI-student coupling, cognitive progression, teacher orchestration, and shared regulation across conditions.

The main finding is that AI access configuration meaningfully reorganized collaborative dynamics. Shared AI access supported more peer-to-peer interaction, stronger alignment around common AI outputs, more coordinated group-level reasoning, and more cohesive SSRL cycles. Individual AI access produced more distributed student-AI exchanges, more evaluative and exploratory but also more fragmented interaction patterns, and greater teacher intervention to reconcile divergent outputs. Overall, the paper argues that AI configuration is a structural design variable that shapes the regulatory ecology of classroom collaboration, not just a technical implementation detail.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined collaborative regulation and group interaction in Grade 8 creative problem solving (N=38). Shared AI access produced more coordinated peer collaboration, stronger alignment around common AI outputs, and more cohesive socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL), while individual AI access produced more exploratory but fragmented interaction cycles. The evidence is process-focused rather than outcome-focused, so no standardized effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Interaction distribution, lag sequential analysis (LSA), ordered network analysis (ONA), and SSRL transition patterns

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that the individual-AI configuration increased teacher intervention and orchestration demand, whereas shared AI reduced the need for teacher help during group work. In the shared condition, teacher activity was mainly whole-class guidance; in the individual condition, teachers more often intervened to address divergent AI outputs and help students interpret responses. No workload scales or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-initiated and responsive orchestration moves; classroom interaction logs and coded transcripts

finding.finding_summary: The study reports differences in engagement-related and affective regulatory dynamics across configurations. Shared AI access more often elicited a positive group climate and motivational alignment after AI-generated ideas or feedback, while individual AI access was associated with more off-task behavior and more fragmented engagement. These findings come from coded interaction data rather than self-report measures.
finding.measure: Student affect codes, off-task/non-task-related cognition, and SSRL affective regulation transitions

paper_profiles.title: From Individual Prompts to Collective Intelligence: Mainstreaming Generative AI in the Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that common classroom uses of generative AI are too individualistic and may undermine deeper learning, collaboration, and equity. The authors propose a Generative Collective Intelligence (GCI) approach in which AI is used to amplify peer-to-peer sense-making rather than replace it, drawing on thinking routines from Harvard Project Zero and ideas from collective intelligence and interactionalism.

The empirical component is an exploratory classroom implementation in two undergraduate engineering courses at Qatar University: Data Communications and Computer Networks I and Signals and Systems. Across two 50-minute sessions, 140 students participated in structured activities including Question Sorts, Peel the Fruit, and two strategically timed AI consultations. Data came from surveys, open-ended reflections, and instructor observations.

Findings suggest students generally valued combining human collaboration with AI, recognized risks of over-reliance and bias, and believed the timing of AI consultation matters for learning. Group work plus AI was the most preferred modality overall, and students’ qualitative comments emphasized that collaborative reasoning supported deeper understanding and more critical evaluation of AI outputs. However, the study is explicitly exploratory, relies on self-report and observation, includes no control group, and does not measure objective learning gains, so it is best read as proof-of-concept rather than causal evidence.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that group-based reasoning combined with strategic AI consultation supported deeper understanding, creative problem-solving, and critical evaluation of outputs. In the survey, 50% of students overall preferred group work + AI, and qualitative responses repeatedly described collaboration as helping them think more critically and understand others’ ideas better; however, these are perception-based findings rather than objective skill gains.
finding.measure: Student preference survey items; open-ended reflections; instructor observations of collaboration, question quality, and critical evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports increased engagement, motivation, and perceived value of collaborative learning during the structured GCI activities. Instructor observations noted energy levels that exceeded typical lecture-based sessions, and students indicated that group work made learning more engaging and supported shared ownership of knowledge.
finding.measure: Student survey preferences; instructor observational notes on engagement

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived AI as speeding up work, and many described AI consultation as improving the efficiency of idea generation and analysis when used strategically within group work. The paper does not measure time savings directly, but student responses show that AI was seen as a useful productivity aid when combined with collaboration.
finding.measure: Open-ended student reflections; preference survey items about learning modalities

paper_profiles.title: Learning gain differences between ChatGPT and human tutor generated algebra hints
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether hints generated by ChatGPT can support algebra learning as effectively as human-authored tutor hints in an adaptive tutoring environment. The motivation is to test whether large language models can automate the labor-intensive creation of worked-solution style hints used in computer tutoring systems.

The authors ran a 2×2 online experiment with 77 Amazon Mechanical Turk participants assigned to either human-authored hints or ChatGPT-generated hints, and to one of two algebra lesson topics: Elementary Algebra or Intermediate Algebra. Each condition included a three-item pre-test, a five-item practice/acquisition phase, and a three-item post-test. ChatGPT hints were generated by prompting the model with each problem and then manually quality-checked; 30% of generated hints were rejected because they contained incorrect answers or incorrect work.

Results showed positive learning gains in all conditions, but only the human-hint conditions had statistically significant pre-to-post gains. In both algebra topics, human-authored hints produced substantially higher learning gains than ChatGPT hints, and the difference between conditions was statistically significant. The study also found that the Intermediate Algebra experiment group began near ceiling on the pre-test, limiting room for improvement. The authors conclude that ChatGPT-generated worked-solution hints were not yet comparable to human-authored hints for this task and that human oversight remains necessary.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized comparison of algebra hint sources, human-authored hints outperformed ChatGPT-generated hints on learning gains in both Elementary Algebra and Intermediate Algebra. All groups showed positive pre-to-post gains, but only the control (human-hint) conditions were statistically significant (Elementary: p=0.0219; Intermediate: p=0.0213), while ChatGPT conditions were not (Elementary: p=0.1427; Intermediate: p=0.7912).
finding.measure: Algebra pre-test and post-test scores; learning gain defined as post-test average minus pre-test average

finding.finding_summary: The paper also evaluates the feasibility of using ChatGPT to automate hint creation. ChatGPT produced usable hints for 70% of problems after manual quality checking, but 30% were rejected due to wrong answers or incorrect work, indicating that human supervision is still required. The study does not report a direct time-saving advantage; average session times were similar across conditions despite fewer hints requested in the ChatGPT condition.
finding.measure: Hint quality rejection rate; number of hints requested; average time spent in lesson
finding.study_size: Elementary n=24 hints checked; Intermediate n=16 hints checked; participant sessions n=77

paper_profiles.title: Novice Learner and Expert Tutor: Evaluating Math Reasoning Abilities of Large Language Models with Misconceptions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks a different question from standard math benchmark evaluations: instead of only measuring whether large language models (LLMs) can solve grade-school math problems correctly, it tests whether they can behave like a novice learner who makes a specific misconception-driven mistake, and like an expert tutor who can identify the misconception behind an incorrect answer. The motivation is to evaluate mathematical reasoning in a way that better reflects educational settings, especially intelligent tutoring systems that need to model student errors and diagnose misconceptions.

The authors use a dataset of multiple-choice grade-school math questions from Eedi that includes expert-curated student misconceptions linked to incorrect answer choices. They evaluate GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 under several prompting strategies for two tasks: (1) generating the incorrect answer associated with a given misconception, and (2) selecting the misconception that explains a wrong answer from a candidate set. The work is not an intervention study with learners; it is a benchmark-style evaluation of LLM behavior on educational math items.

Results show a strong gap between correct-answer performance and misconception-aware performance. GPT-4 answers the math questions correctly at high rates (up to 94.8% with explanation prompting), but performs much worse when asked to deliberately produce misconception-consistent wrong answers (up to 67.9% on the novice-learner task) and when asked to identify misconceptions among many candidates (dropping to 39.8% accuracy when 100 misconceptions are provided). The authors conclude that current LLMs still struggle with controlled error generation and robust misconception diagnosis, indicating opportunities for improved student simulation and expert tutoring models in educational applications.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on grade-school multiple-choice math problems and misconception-aware variants of those problems. On standard correct-answer math solving, GPT-4 reached 0.948 accuracy with explanations (n=213 questions), but performance was substantially lower when models were asked to answer incorrectly in a misconception-specific way (best GPT-4 accuracy 0.679) or to identify the correct misconception among many candidates (GPT-4 declined from 0.919 at n=4 misconceptions to 0.398 at n=100).
finding.measure: Accuracy on correct-answer math questions; accuracy on misconception-consistent wrong-answer generation; accuracy on misconception identification

paper_profiles.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 2.1, Grade-School Math and the Hidden Reasoning Process
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This paper studies how language models solve grade-school math problems in a fully controlled synthetic setting. The authors create the iGSM dataset, which generates diverse K-12-style math word problems from dependency graphs over hierarchical objects and parameters, with difficulty controlled by the number of instance parameters and solution operations. They train GPT2-style transformers from scratch on this synthetic data and evaluate both in-distribution and out-of-distribution generalization.

finding.finding_summary: A GPT2-style model pretrained from scratch on iGSM achieved very high accuracy on grade-school math problems, reaching about 99% accuracy on in-distribution settings and strong out-of-distribution generalization to longer reasoning lengths than seen in training. The paper reports that a 16-layer, 576-dim transformer can solve harder reasoning-length problems than a 4-layer, 1920-dim model, indicating that the model learned actual mathematical reasoning rather than memorizing templates.
finding.measure: Exact-answer accuracy on synthetic grade-school math problem solving (iGSM; including mod-23 arithmetic and chain-of-thought solution parsing)

paper_profiles.title: Elementary Math Word Problem Generation using Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically generating elementary-level math word problems (MWPs) that align with specified grade and question-type requirements. The authors argue that manually writing MWPs is time-consuming for tutors and that prior automated approaches often require extra inputs such as seed text, equations, or context, and do not reliably control grade or question type.

To tackle this, the study develops an LLM-based MWP generation system and compares open-source models (notably Llama-2, Mistral, and Zephyr) under different prompts, decoding settings, fine-tuning regimes, few-shot prompting, human-feedback methods (DPO, KTO, CPO), and a solvability-checking pipeline using a secondary LLM. The paper also creates two datasets: a 4K MWP curriculum-aligned dataset covering grades 1–6 and a 1,005-item preference dataset for selected grade-section pairs.

The population/context is elementary mathematics curriculum content aligned to U.S. Common Core standards, and the target users are educators or tutors generating practice problems. Human and LLM-based evaluation found that generated problems were generally fluent, grammatical, and solvable, but the models still struggled to consistently satisfy grade and section requirements. The best reported configuration combined few-shot prompting and solvability filtering, improving grade and section relevance relative to the zero-shot baseline, though overall performance remained imperfect.

finding.finding_summary: The system can generate elementary math word problems of generally high surface quality, but it struggles to consistently satisfy the intended mathematical grade and section requirements. In the best reported configuration (fine-tuned Llama-2 with 5-shot prompting plus solvability filtering), average accuracy reached 92.28%, with grade relevance at 74.52% and section relevance at 78.76%; the zero-shot baseline was 90.64% average accuracy with 65% grade relevance and 54.62% section relevance.
finding.measure: Human and LLM-based evaluation of generated math word problems on solvability, realism, grade relevance, section relevance, and language-quality error categories

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central practical contribution is an automated system intended to reduce educator/tutor workload in creating math practice items. The authors report that the model can generate batches of MWPs from minimal input (grade, section, and question count), and that the released datasets and pipeline support scalable problem generation with human-feedback and solvability filtering.
finding.measure: System capability to generate curriculum-aligned MWPs from user-specified inputs and produce a 4K corpus plus 1,005-item preference dataset

paper_profiles.title: Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models: Assessing Logical and Arithmetic Errors across Wide Numerical Ranges
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how large language models (LLMs) perform on mathematical word problems when the numerical values are systematically expanded beyond the narrow ranges commonly used in benchmarks. The authors argue that standard evaluations obscure important distinctions between logical reasoning errors and arithmetic/computational errors, so they introduce two tools: GSM-Ranges, a perturbation-based dataset generator built from GSM8K, and an automated grading method that uses GPT-4o to convert model responses into executable Python code in order to separate logical from non-logical errors.

The study samples 100 GSM8K questions and generates six perturbation levels that replace numbers with values from increasingly large ranges while preserving problem structure. Nine models are evaluated on 5,000 perturbed problems per level, plus the original GSM8K items; the paper also includes additional analyses of sampling-based recall, o3-mini reasoning behavior, and standalone arithmetic performance. Results show that both logical and arithmetic errors generally increase as numbers grow, with logical error rates rising by as much as 14 percentage points at the highest perturbation level, while arithmetic accuracy also deteriorates when operations are embedded in word problems rather than posed standalone.

Overall, the paper concludes that LLM math performance is highly sensitive to numerical scale and that conventional answer-only scoring can miss important failure modes. It does not study K-12 learners directly; rather, it evaluates AI models as math solvers. The main contribution is methodological, offering a finer-grained evaluation framework for mathematical reasoning under out-of-distribution numeric conditions.

finding.finding_summary: Across nine LLMs, increasing numerical perturbation levels generally worsened mathematical performance. Logical error rates rose by up to 14 percentage points from level 1 to level 6, and non-logical (mostly arithmetic) errors also increased substantially as numbers became larger; for example, Gemma 2 2B logical errors rose from 24.3% at level 1 to 38.5% at level 6, and non-logical errors rose from 3.6% to 37.2%.
finding.measure: Logical error rate and non-logical error rate on GSM-Ranges mathematical word problems
finding.study_size: n=5,000 problems per perturbation level; 9 models; 100 base GSM8K questions
finding.confidence_interval: reported in tables as level-wise CIs, but no single effect size reported

paper_profiles.title: Adaptable Logical Control for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of controllable generation in large language models (LLMs): how to make an LLM reliably satisfy logical constraints at inference time without task-specific retraining. The authors propose Ctrl-G, a framework that combines a frozen production LLM with a distilled Hidden Markov Model (HMM) and a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) encoding of user-specified constraints. The method estimates the probability that a partial generation will eventually satisfy the constraint and uses that signal to guide token selection.

The paper evaluates Ctrl-G on several constrained generation tasks, including commonsense generation, text infilling, and interactive text editing. In these settings, Ctrl-G is compared against constrained decoding baselines and strong LLMs such as GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Results show that Ctrl-G often achieves perfect or near-perfect constraint satisfaction while maintaining competitive or better generation quality; for example, in interactive text editing it substantially outperforms GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 in overall satisfaction. The paper also reports runtime analysis consistent with the proposed algorithmic complexity and includes a proof-of-concept study on GSM math reasoning, where adding keyphrase constraints modestly improves accuracy. Overall, the work argues that inference-time logical control can improve both controllability and downstream performance of LLMs.

finding.finding_summary: As a proof-of-concept on the Grade School Math (GSM) benchmark, Ctrl-G was used to encourage the model to include all numbers from the problem statement in chain-of-thought reasoning. On the 293 GSM items where the baseline model failed to use all provided numbers, accuracy increased from 14.6% without Ctrl-G to 28.3% with Ctrl-G after sampling 16 outputs and majority voting; this is a +3.4 percentage-point gain relative to the no-Ctrl-G condition on that subset.
finding.measure: GSM benchmark accuracy on a subset of 293 items where the base model omitted some numbers from the prompt
finding.study_size: n=293 (subset of GSM); full GSM benchmark n=1319 referenced

paper_profiles.title: The LLM as a Network Operator: A Vision for Generative AI in the 6G Radio Access Network
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes a formal vision for using large language models (LLMs) as network operators inside future 6G/Open RAN architectures. The central problem is that next-generation radio access networks (RANs) are too complex for traditional automation, so the authors argue for embedding LLMs into the control loop to translate human intent into network policies and actions.

Rather than presenting a user study or experiment, the paper develops a mathematical framework for an "LLM-RAN operator". It defines state, intent, and action spaces, proposes an O-RAN-grounded architecture that separates strategic reasoning in the Non-RT RIC from fast execution in the Near-RT RIC, and states propositions about expressiveness, monotonic improvement, and convergence to a fixed point. The paper also discusses practical challenges such as latency, hallucinated commands, formal verification, and physical grounding.

The context is wireless systems engineering and NextG standardization, not K-12 education. The paper is aimed at researchers and network operators exploring generative AI for telecom control. Its main conclusion is that LLMs may serve as cognitively capable agents for intent-driven RAN management, but substantial research is still needed before such systems can be safely deployed.

paper_profiles.title: Speculative Futures on ChatGPT and Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Collective Reflection from the Educational Landscape
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a speculative, collectively authored reflection on the promises and pitfalls of ChatGPT and related generative AI tools in education. Rather than testing an intervention or estimating causal effects, the authors use fictional future narratives and speculative methodology to explore how generative AI might reshape teaching, learning, assessment, access, and the human roles in education.

The paper’s purpose is to provoke critical thought about possible educational futures, including both optimistic and cautionary scenarios. Positive narratives imagine AI supporting personalized learning, collaboration, accessibility, language development, and teacher workload reduction; negative narratives emphasize risks such as bias, privacy loss, academic integrity problems, dependence on technology, and dehumanization.

The paper is not an empirical study of K-12 mathematics achievement or any student outcome. Its conclusions are conceptual and normative: educators should approach AI critically, attend to ethics and equity, and avoid over-exaggerating technology’s role relative to human educators. Because it is a speculative/qualitative piece, it provides no comparative evidence about true generative AI versus standard instruction or non-AI digital tools.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can save educator time by automating routine tasks such as grading, drafting emails, summarizing concepts, and generating quiz questions. These claims are presented as speculative benefits in future narratives, but no empirical study or measured effect is reported.
finding.measure: Speculative educator workload / task automation benefits

finding.finding_summary: The narratives suggest AI could increase learner motivation, engagement, confidence, and support through personalized feedback and encouragement, but they also warn about anxiety, dependence, and dehumanization. No quantitative measure or sample is reported; the claims are interpretive rather than empirical.
finding.measure: Speculative engagement, motivation, and confidence

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly discusses critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, and problem-solving as outcomes that AI might support or undermine. It argues that AI can facilitate collaboration and idea generation, but may also reduce originality and critical thinking if over-relied upon; no direct measurement is reported.
finding.measure: Speculative critical thinking, creativity, and collaboration

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses heavily on institutional implications such as ethics, privacy, equity, academic integrity, policy, and redefining human versus AI roles in education. It concludes that adoption is context-dependent and requires new literacies, updated assessment practices, and governance, but it provides no empirical institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Speculative policy, ethics, equity, and institutional change

paper_profiles.title: Text Data Augmentation for Deep Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a survey of text data augmentation methods for deep learning, not an empirical study of K-12 education. It reviews why data augmentation is useful for supervised learning in NLP, focusing on reducing overfitting, improving generalization, and enabling learning with limited labeled data.

The paper organizes augmentation approaches into symbolic methods (for example, rule-based augmentation, graph-structured augmentation, and MixUp) and neural methods (for example, back-translation, style augmentation, and generative data augmentation). It also discusses label augmentation and practical implementation issues such as consistency regularization, prompt-based generation, and augmentation controllers. The context is machine learning and natural language processing broadly, including examples from translation, question answering, summarization, and text classification.

Because the paper is a survey, it does not study K-12 students, mathematics instruction, or educational outcomes directly. It synthesizes prior NLP research and highlights promising directions for generative modeling and augmentation, but it does not provide comparative evidence about generative AI improving math achievement relative to standard instruction or non-AI digital tools.

paper_profiles.title: Interpreting Black-Box Models: A Review on Explainable Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (review paper; no K-12 study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), focused on why black-box machine learning and deep learning models need interpretability and how XAI methods attempt to provide it. The paper synthesizes conceptual foundations, design principles, and evaluation frameworks for explaining AI predictions, emphasizing transparency, trust, accountability, regulatory compliance, and human-centered design.

Rather than evaluating a single educational intervention or an instructional AI system, the article surveys XAI methods such as LIME, SHAP, model extraction, rule extraction, distillation, and feature-importance approaches across domains like healthcare, finance, and autonomous systems. It does not study K-12 learners, teachers, or mathematics instruction, and it does not compare generative AI with standard instruction or non-AI digital tools.

The main conclusion is that explainability is important for trustworthy deployment of AI in high-stakes settings, but the field lacks a single universally effective method. The paper argues that explanation methods should be designed with user behavior, context, and multiple stakeholders in mind, and that rigorous evaluation is needed because many current XAI approaches trade off interpretability, fidelity, and usability.

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary students and teachers perceive a generative-AI-powered tool for creative mathematical writing. The authors are interested in whether and how GenAI can support students as they create math stories, especially for young learners who may struggle with open-ended writing and mathematical expression.

The study implemented a three-step classroom activity framework—Ask, Represent, Transform—in six 5th-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools, involving 79 students and 6 teachers. The GenAI system used GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 to generate and illustrate math stories from student prompts, while students also reviewed and revised AI output. Data came from student focus groups, teacher interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations, and were analyzed thematically.

The paper reports perceived benefits in four areas: creativity in math, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and affective engagement (interest, curiosity, ownership). It also identifies challenges, including weak student critical evaluation of AI output, difficulty generating coherent prompts, AI being perceived as too perfect, limited pedagogical feedback, reduced opportunities for independent work, weaker social connection, and limited communication modes. The study does not measure math achievement with a comparison group; its contribution is qualitative and design-oriented rather than causal.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived that GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing helped students understand math problems, represent mathematical ideas, and uncover misconceptions, but the paper did not test math achievement with standardized or comparative outcome measures. The evidence is based on thematic analysis of interviews and classroom observations with n=79 5th-grade students and 6 teachers, so the study supports perceived mathematical understanding rather than measured gains.
finding.measure: Student and teacher perceptions of mathematical understanding, problem representation, and misconception detection from interviews, surveys, and observations

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that the GenAI-supported activity increased interest in mathematics, sparked curiosity, and strengthened students’ sense of ownership over learning. These benefits were identified qualitatively through thematic analysis of interview, survey, and observation data in six classrooms.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership in learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports perceived growth in creativity, flexible/divergent thinking, prompt engineering, and evaluation of AI strengths and weaknesses, all framed as durable skills or AI literacy-related competencies. These findings come from qualitative themes rather than performance tests, so the study indicates skill development in a descriptive sense but does not provide comparative effect estimates.
finding.measure: Perceived creativity, divergent/convergent thinking, prompt engineering, and AI evaluation skills

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was designed to support creative mathematical writing, and participants reported that the tool helped them generate and refine math stories with text and images. However, the paper focuses on perceptions of writing support and classroom experience rather than literacy outcomes measured with writing rubrics or achievement tests.
finding.measure: Perceived support for creative mathematical writing and story creation

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how middle school mathematics teachers use generative AI, specifically ChatGPT/GPT-4o, to personalize existing curriculum problems to students’ interests. The central question is whether a teacher should remain “in the loop” when using GenAI for context personalization, and what that means for the quality, realism, and efficiency of the personalized tasks.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers in six U.S. schools participated after training on personalization, bias, readability, and cultural relevance. Across two units of the Illustrative Mathematics curriculum, teachers modified 143 problems using ChatGPT and assigned them to 521 students through ASSISTments. The study combined qualitative coding of teacher prompts and student open-ended feedback with quantitative analyses of prompt counts, time spent, and student ratings of interestingness and closeness to students’ interests.

The main conclusions are that teachers used GenAI in varied ways to control grain size, depth, and ownership of personalization, but the process was not especially time efficient: on average, each problem took about 246 seconds and 3.2 prompts to create. Student feedback suggested a preference for fine-grained, specific popular-culture references, while teachers often had to intervene to improve realism and appropriateness. A “Goldilocks zone” emerged in which 3–5 prompts was associated with slightly better student ratings, but overall the study found no evidence that teachers became more efficient over time; in fact, they spent more time and used more prompts in the second unit. The study did not measure mathematics achievement or learning outcomes, so it does not provide comparative evidence that GenAI personalized tasks improve K-12 math achievement relative to standard instruction or non-AI tools.

finding.finding_summary: The study did not measure student mathematics achievement or learning outcomes, so it provides no direct evidence that GenAI-personalized tasks improved mathematical numeracy relative to standard instruction or non-AI digital tools. The authors explicitly note that the study was exploratory and lacked a control group for performance outcomes.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement / performance outcomes
finding.study_size: n=521 students (assigned personalized problems), but achievement not measured

finding.finding_summary: Students generally found the personalized problems only modestly interesting, but ratings improved in Unit 6 relative to Unit 4. Average interestingness rose from 2.27 to 2.56 and closeness from 2.28 to 2.66 on 5-point scales, with the regression analysis showing a significant combined increase (B=0.33, SE=0.095, t=3.49, p=0.0012).
finding.measure: Student ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests on 1-5 scales
finding.study_size: n=521 students; ratings collected for 52-53 problems

finding.finding_summary: Personalizing problems with GenAI was time-consuming for teachers. Across 143 problems, teachers used an average of 3.2 prompts per problem and took about 246 seconds per problem (SD=165.7), and the authors conclude there was no clear evidence that efficiency improved over time. In fact, from Unit 4 to Unit 6, teachers spent significantly more time per problem (204 to 286 seconds; B=70.4, SE=29.6, p=0.0189) and used more prompts (3.2 to 4.6; B=1.26, SE=0.41, p=0.0025).
finding.measure: Teacher time per problem and number of ChatGPT prompts per problem
finding.effect_size: B=70.4 seconds; B=1.26 prompts; B=0.33 for student ratings linked to prompt zone

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how middle school students perceive an AI peer during collaborative mathematical problem solving and what features they want from such a peer. The authors argue that most GenAI tools in education are designed as tutors or teacher aids, and that much less is known about AI positioned as a fellow student collaborator in small-group math work.

To explore this, the researchers ran a five-day participatory design summer camp with 24 rising grades 6-8 students. Students completed human-only collaborative math tasks and then worked with a technology probe featuring two text-based AI peers (Alice and Bob) that participated in mathematics CPS using GPT-4o, after which students reflected on the experience, redesigned ideal AI peers, and completed preference surveys. The study collected GEQ and NASA-TLX ratings, interviews, reflections, and design artifacts; however, the primary purpose was design inquiry rather than a causal test of learning gains.

The main conclusion is that students preferred an AI peer that provides scaffold-first help, such as hints, checks, and concept refreshers, while staying deferential, emotionally attuned, and under student control. Quantitatively, compared with human-only CPS, AI-peer sessions reduced temporal demand (M=5.67 vs. 9.62, SD=4.38 vs. 4.13, p=0.002, d=1.15) but increased physical demand (M=8.48 vs. 4.90, p=0.014, d=1.14) and lowered social/task collaboration ratings on the GEQ (ATGS: M=5.21 vs. 6.50, p=0.029, d=0.94; GIT: M=4.76 vs. 5.54, p=0.047, d=0.81). The paper does not test mathematics achievement outcomes, so it provides design and perception evidence rather than evidence that generative AI improves K-12 math performance.

finding.finding_summary: The study included grade-aligned middle-school mathematics collaborative problem-solving tasks, but it did not measure math achievement or learning gains. Instead, it examined students’ reactions to AI peers while solving mathematics problems, finding that AI involvement changed the collaboration experience but providing no direct evidence that it improved mathematical numeracy outcomes.
finding.measure: Mathematics collaborative problem-solving tasks; no achievement outcome measured
finding.study_size: n=24 (qualitative/participatory design camp); paired quantitative comparisons on n=22

finding.finding_summary: Students reported lower social cohesion and task coordination in AI-peer sessions than in human-only CPS, but they also valued the reduced time pressure. On the GEQ, Attractions to Group-Social decreased (M=5.21 vs. 6.50, p=0.029, d=0.94) and Group Integration-Task also decreased (M=4.76 vs. 5.54, p=0.047, d=0.81), suggesting weaker perceived engagement and coordination despite faster progress.
finding.measure: Group Environment Questionnaire (ATGS, GIT) and qualitative reflections on frustration/engagement
finding.study_size: n=22 paired survey comparisons; n=18 individual interviews; 5 whole-class reflection sessions
finding.std_deviation: ATGS SD=1.81 vs. 2.05; GIT SD=1.58 vs. 1.52

finding.finding_summary: The paper centered on collaborative problem solving, co-agency, and negotiation of methods, which are durable skills, but it did not directly measure skill gains. Qualitative evidence showed students wanted AI peers that supported shared reasoning, asked questions, and negotiated approaches rather than taking over, indicating that the intervention shaped perceptions of collaboration rather than demonstrating improved collaboration skill.
finding.measure: Qualitative interviews, reflections, and participatory design artifacts about collaboration/co-agency

finding.finding_summary: AI peers reduced perceived time pressure during mathematical CPS, indicating improved task efficiency. On NASA-TLX temporal demand, students in AI-peer sessions scored lower than in human-only CPS (M=5.67, SD=4.38 vs. M=9.62, SD=4.13; p=0.002; Cohen’s d=1.15), a large effect; however, students also reported higher physical demand from typing and navigating the interface (M=8.48 vs. 4.90; p=0.014; d=1.14), so the efficiency benefit came with notable interaction overhead.
finding.measure: NASA Task Load Index temporal demand and physical demand subscales
finding.std_deviation: Temporal demand SD=4.38 vs. 4.13; physical demand SD=4.65 vs. 2.41

paper_profiles.title: A Benchmark for Math Misconceptions: Bridging Gaps in Middle School Algebra with AI-Supported Instruction
paper_profiles.population: Middle School (4th-8th grade algebra context); educators teaching grades 6-10
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of identifying and responding to middle-school algebra misconceptions, especially for low-income and minoritized students. The authors argue that misconceptions and common errors are important instructional targets, but that educators and AI systems need better structured resources to diagnose them accurately.

To address this, the paper introduces a benchmark dataset of 55 algebra misconceptions/common errors with 220 diagnostic examples drawn from 145 prior sources. The benchmark is intended for use with large language models (LLMs) and AI-supported educational tools. The study evaluates GPT-4 turbo on the benchmark using repeated random subsampling validation and also gathers feedback from five middle-school math educators via survey/interview about clarity, prevalence, and possible classroom use of the misconceptions.

The main empirical result is that GPT-4 turbo can identify misconceptions with moderate accuracy, but performance depends strongly on topic constraint. In the unrestricted condition, precision and recall were about 0.526 and 0.529 per misconception, while topic-constrained testing improved performance to 0.753 precision and 0.748 recall. After expert educator relabeling of some ambiguous cases, accuracy rose to 65.45% in the unrestricted setting and 83.91% in the topic-constrained setting. Educators generally found the benchmark relevant and were interested in using it for diagnosis, but the paper does not test whether AI improves student mathematics achievement relative to standard instruction or non-AI tools.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure student achievement directly; instead it evaluates GPT-4 turbo’s ability to diagnose middle-school algebra misconceptions, which is a math-learning support task. In repeated subsampling experiments over 55 misconception categories and 220 diagnostic examples, performance was moderate in the unrestricted condition (precision=0.526, recall=0.529 per MaE) and stronger when testing was constrained within topic (precision=0.753, recall=0.748 per MaE). Expert educator relabeling raised reported accuracy to 65.45% in experiment 1 and 83.91% in experiment 2, suggesting the model can support misconception identification but with substantial topic dependence.
finding.measure: Misconception diagnosis accuracy in middle school algebra (precision, recall, and expert-adjusted accuracy)
finding.study_size: n=5500 iterations in experiment 1; n=1100 iterations in experiment 2; 5 educators surveyed; 2 additional expert educators for relabeling

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports educator feedback on the utility of the benchmark for classroom use and teacher support. Four of five surveyed teachers expressed interest in using the dataset with AI to diagnose student misconceptions or train teachers, and at least 80% indicated that the surveyed misconceptions were encountered among their students, suggesting the resource has practical institutional relevance.
finding.measure: Educator survey/interview responses on relevance, clarity, and intended classroom use

paper_profiles.title: Students' Perceived Roles, Opportunities, and Challenges of a Generative AI-powered Teachable Agent: A Case of Middle School Math Class
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle school students perceived a generative AI-powered teachable agent (TA) used in a 6th-grade mathematics classroom. The study asks what roles students assign to the TA, what benefits they perceive from learning with it, and what challenges they encounter while using it. The motivation is to understand how generative AI might strengthen the long-standing learning-by-teaching approach in K-12 education.

The intervention was an in-class, two-session use of a GenAI-powered TA for rate-and-ratio math problems. The system used GPT-4-Turbo, retrieval-augmented generation, and a dynamically updated knowledge graph, and it was designed with personalized learning, contrasting cases, gamification, and psychological supports. The participants were 108 sixth-grade students in a public laboratory middle school in the southeastern United States, with 14 also participating in focus-group interviews; data came from classroom observation, open-ended surveys, and interviews.

The study is qualitative and does not test achievement impacts against a comparison condition. Instead, it shows that students viewed the TA as a learning companion, facilitator, and collaborative problem-solver, and perceived benefits for autonomy, engagement, self-efficacy, motivation, communication, and math understanding. Students also identified important barriers, including weak problem presentation, surface-level questioning, mismatch with learning styles, technical issues, and a strong need for teacher facilitation. Overall, the paper suggests promise for GenAI-powered TAs in math learning, but provides no comparative evidence that they improve K-12 mathematics achievement relative to standard instruction or non-AI tools.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported perceived improvements in rate-and-ratio understanding, application of knowledge, and clarity of common math concepts after interacting with the GenAI-powered teachable agent, but the study did not measure achievement with pre/post tests or a control group. Evidence is based on qualitative reports from 108 sixth-grade students and 14 interviewees in an in-class math activity.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of math learning, understanding, and application from open-ended surveys, focus groups, and observations

finding.finding_summary: Students described the GenAI-powered TA as increasing enjoyment of math, self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, confidence, and resilience. These were self-reported perceptions gathered through classroom observations, interviews, and open-ended surveys rather than quantified outcome measures.
finding.measure: Self-reported joy of math, self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, and emotional responses

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived gains in cognitive, social, and collaborative capacities, including reasoning, elaboration, perspective-taking, communication, and collaborative problem-solving. The paper’s evidence is qualitative and based on thematic analysis of students’ explanations of their learning experience with the TA.
finding.measure: Self-reported cognitive, social, and collaborative skill development

paper_profiles.title: GPT takes the SAT: Tracing changes in Test Difficulty and Students’ Math Performance
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether SAT Math has become easier over time and whether observed changes in average SAT Math scores reflect changes in the test itself versus changes in students’ mathematical performance. The authors use OpenAI’s GPT-4 Turbo as a benchmark counterfactual, treating the model’s year-by-year SAT Math performance as a “Transformed Control” to estimate changes in test difficulty from 2008 to 2023.

The study compiles SAT Math exams from online sources, excludes image- and table-based questions, and administers sampled exams to GPT-4 under zero-shot, zero-temperature prompting. The paper then compares GPT-4’s performance across years and against College Board population-level SAT data, state-level averages, and Massachusetts district-level data. The central empirical claim is that SAT Math became less rigorous over time, with an estimated 71-point decline in test rigor from 2008 to 2023.

Using the GPT-based control to adjust for changing test difficulty, the authors estimate that average student math performance declined more than the test became easier, with an overall divergence of 107 points relative to the 2008 baseline. They report similar patterns in national, state-aggregated, and Massachusetts district-level analyses, as well as heterogeneous declines across demographic groups. The paper is methodological and descriptive rather than an evaluation of an instructional intervention, and it does not study K-12 classroom AI use or true generative AI tutoring effects on achievement.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that SAT Math rigor declined over time while observed student math performance also fell relative to the 2008 baseline. Using GPT-4 Turbo as a transformed control, the authors estimate a 71-point drop in test rigor and a 36-point decline in student performance, producing a 107-point divergence from 2008 to 2023.
finding.measure: SAT Math scaled scores, raw correct answers, and Average Difference in Scores (ADS) using GPT-4 as a transformed control

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that declining SAT Math rigor may weaken the SAT’s usefulness as a college admissions sorting tool and raises concerns about the broader educational ecosystem. It frames the results as evidence relevant to admissions policy, test-optional policies, and institutional selection practices rather than classroom-level instruction.
finding.measure: Changes in SAT Math difficulty over time and comparative score trends across national, state, district, and demographic aggregates

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.population: K-12 mathematics educators (elementary, middle, and high school contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how K-12 mathematics educators evaluate lesson plans produced by generative AI models compared with human curriculum designers. The authors focus on whether a customized GPT-4 model and a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model can generate lesson plans that educators prefer over human-authored plans, and they examine preferences across lesson-plan components (warm-up, main task, cool-down, overall quality) and grade bands (elementary, middle, high school).

The study used a controlled pairwise preference task with 20 experienced K-12 math educators. Participants compared 529 complete lesson-plan pairs (2,116 total judgments) drawn from human-designed plans and AI-generated plans, and they also provided qualitative comments. The study was restricted to mathematics lesson plans aligned to Common Core standards. The analysis combined descriptive quantitative comparisons, bootstrapped preference estimates, and thematic analysis/topic modeling of educator comments.

The main conclusion is that human-authored lesson plans were generally preferred overall, especially for elementary grades and for pedagogically rich components such as warm-ups, main tasks, student discourse, and scaffolding. However, GenAI plans were more competitive in cool-down activities and, in some high-school comparisons, the fine-tuned LLaMA model outperformed human plans. The authors conclude that GenAI is best viewed as an assistive planning tool rather than a replacement for educator expertise, with the strongest promise in structured lesson components rather than deeper pedagogical design.

finding.finding_summary: This study directly examined K-12 mathematics lesson plans, but the outcome was educator preference for lesson-plan quality rather than student math achievement. Across 529 lesson-plan pairs judged by 16 educators, human-created plans were preferred overall, while the GenAI models were more competitive in cool-down activities and some high-school contexts.
finding.measure: Educator binary preferences for K-12 mathematics lesson plans across warm-up, main task, cool-down, and overall quality
finding.study_size: n=16 educators; 529 lesson-plan pairs; 2,116 total evaluations

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI can reduce educator workload in lesson planning, positioning it as an assistive tool. Although it does not measure time savings experimentally, the discussion and conclusion explicitly frame AI-generated lesson plans as a way to streamline planning and reduce cognitive load for teachers.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness of AI for lesson planning and workload reduction; qualitative educator feedback

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination (VNHSGE), a high-stakes exam covering mathematics, literature, English, physics, chemistry, biology, history, geography, and civic education. The authors evaluate ChatGPT in a zero-shot setting using the VNHSGE evaluation set, prompting the model to answer multiple-choice questions and one essay-based literature task, then grading outputs against human-verified ground truth answers.

The study analyzes ChatGPT performance across years 2019-2023 and compares its scores to Vietnamese students’ score distributions from 2019-2022. The results indicate that ChatGPT can achieve passing-level combined scores for the graduation formula, with natural and social combination scores ranging from 6.30 to 6.94. Subject performance is uneven: the model does relatively well in English and literature, but performs less consistently in mathematics, physics, chemistry, geography, and civic education, often scoring below the majority of students in those subjects.

Overall, the paper concludes that ChatGPT has enough knowledge and comprehension capacity to pass this specific exam under the study’s conditions, but it still needs improvement on harder, more reasoning-heavy, and visually grounded questions. Because the paper is a single-model benchmark evaluation without an instructional intervention or learner outcome comparison, it provides evidence about model capability rather than direct evidence that generative AI improves K-12 achievement relative to standard instruction or other digital tools.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT achieved passing-level mathematics scores on the VNHSGE, with scores ranging from 5.2 to 6.6 across 2019-2023 and an average of 5.88. However, when compared with Vietnamese students, the paper reports that ChatGPT mathematics performance was generally lower than the majority of students, suggesting only moderate competence rather than superior achievement.
finding.measure: VNHSGE mathematics exam score (10-point scale) and comparison to Vietnamese student score distributions

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT performed comparatively well in literacy-related tasks, especially literature and English. Literature scores ranged from 5.63 to 7.5 (avg. 6.8), and English scores ranged from 7.6 to 8.6 (avg. 7.92), with the paper stating that ChatGPT generally outperformed the majority of Vietnamese students in English and was at or above many student results in literature.
finding.measure: VNHSGE literature essay score and English multiple-choice exam score (10-point scale) compared with Vietnamese student distributions

finding.finding_summary: In science subjects, ChatGPT showed uneven performance: physics scores ranged from 5.75 to 6.5 (avg. 6.1), chemistry from 4.0 to 6.25 (avg. 4.8), and biology from 5.25 to 6.0 (avg. 5.8). The paper reports that ChatGPT was generally below the majority of Vietnamese students in physics and chemistry, while biology results were comparatively better and sometimes above most students.
finding.measure: VNHSGE physics, chemistry, and biology exam scores (10-point scale) compared with Vietnamese student score distributions

finding.finding_summary: For non-core subjects, ChatGPT’s performance varied substantially. History scores ranged from 4.25 to 7.75, geography from 5.0 to 7.5, and civic education from 6.0 to 8.25; the authors report that history could be above most students in many cases, geography was often below most students, and civic education remained below most students despite high raw scores.
finding.measure: VNHSGE history, geography, and civic education exam scores (10-point scale) compared with Vietnamese student score distributions

paper_profiles.title: Automated Feedback in Math Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLMs for Open-Ended Responses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can improve automated scoring and feedback generation for open-ended middle-school mathematics responses. The central comparison is between a fine-tuned open-source LLM based on Mistral 7B (called GOAT), a prior non-generative similarity-based system (SBERT-Canberra), and GPT-4 used in a zero-shot prompting setup.

The study uses a dataset of 50 open-response math problems from an online learning platform, with 100 student responses per problem and teacher-provided scores and feedback. Models were trained on 4,000 responses and tested on 1,000 responses; scoring performance was evaluated with AUC, RMSE, and Cohen’s kappa, while feedback quality was judged by two human raters with teaching experience on accuracy, relevancy, motivation, and preference.

For scoring, GOAT performed best overall (AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, Kappa=0.422), outperforming SBERT-Canberra (AUC=0.662, RMSE=1.364, Kappa=0.362) and GPT-4 (AUC=0.639, RMSE=1.16, Kappa=0.266). For feedback quality, however, GPT-4 was preferred by teachers and achieved the highest consensus on accuracy (86%) and relevance (91%), while GOAT was generally better than SBERT but still lagged GPT-4. The paper concludes that fine-tuned generative AI can outperform the prior benchmark for auto-scoring, but in this dataset GPT-4 produced the strongest human-rated feedback, and the authors note that feedback quality is constrained by noisy teacher training data and subjective evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: The fine-tuned LLM (GOAT) outperformed the prior SBERT-Canberra method and GPT-4 on automated scoring of middle-school open-ended math responses. On the held-out test set (n=1,000 responses), GOAT achieved AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, and Cohen’s kappa=0.422, compared with SBERT’s AUC=0.662, RMSE=1.364, kappa=0.362 and GPT-4’s AUC=0.639, RMSE=1.16, kappa=0.266.
finding.measure: Automated prediction of teacher scores for open-ended mathematics responses; evaluated with AUC, RMSE, and Cohen’s kappa against teacher-assigned scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies automated scoring and feedback generation as a way to reduce teacher grading and feedback burden. The authors argue that GOAT and SBERT-style systems can support teachers by automating parts of scoring, while GPT-4 and GOAT can generate feedback that teachers may use as a starting point; no direct workload effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Human evaluation of generated feedback and comparison of automated scoring/feedback systems intended for teacher support
finding.study_size: n=100 sampled responses for feedback evaluation; n=1,000 test responses for scoring

paper_profiles.title: PARAMANU-GANITA: Can Small Math Language Models Rival with Large Language Models on Mathematical Reasoning?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a small, domain-specific generative language model trained from scratch on mathematical text can rival much larger language models on mathematical reasoning, and whether such an approach is more cost-efficient and environmentally sustainable. The authors build PARAMANU-GANITA, a 208M-parameter decoder-only model pretrained on a curated math/code corpus and then further fine-tuned with Chain-of-Thought instruction tuning on MetaMathQA.

The model is evaluated on a suite of benchmark math and reasoning tasks, including GSM8K, MATH, MMLU math subtests, AGIEVAL math items, and LogiQA. The paper reports that PARAMANU-GANITA achieves competitive or better accuracy than several general-purpose and math-specialized LLMs of much larger size on some benchmarks (for example, 36.77% on GSM8K and 10.34% on MATH, versus 36.40% and 18.00% for LLEMMA-7B on those same benchmarks), while using far fewer training hours.

However, the evidence is comparative benchmark evaluation only: there is no K-12 classroom intervention, no student assignment to conditions, and no direct measure of instructional impact on students. The paper’s main conclusion is that focused pretraining on mathematical corpora plus CoT fine-tuning can yield strong benchmark performance in a small model, but it does not establish that true generative AI improves K-12 mathematics achievement relative to standard instruction or non-AI digital tools.

finding.finding_summary: PARAMANU-GANITA, a 208M-parameter math language model pretrained from scratch and CoT fine-tuned, performs competitively on mathematical reasoning benchmarks. The paper reports 36.77% accuracy on GSM8K and 10.34% on MATH, with especially strong comparisons against several generalist and math-specialized LLMs; however, these are benchmark accuracies rather than K-12 learning gains.
finding.measure: Benchmark accuracy on GSM8K and MATH; also MMLU math subtests, AGIEVAL AQuA-RAT and SAT-Math

paper_profiles.title: MathOdyssey: Benchmarking Mathematical Problem-Solving Skills in Large Language Models Using Odyssey Math Data
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces MathOdyssey, a new benchmark dataset for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on mathematical problem solving. The authors argue that existing math benchmarks are either too familiar to models from training data or do not adequately cover the range of difficulty needed to test advanced reasoning, so they curate 387 original problems spanning Olympiad-level, high school, and university-level mathematics.

The paper evaluates several open-source and closed-source LLMs, including GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-3.5 Turbo, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Claude 3 Opus, Llama-3-70B, and DBRX-Instruct, using chain-of-thought prompting. Performance is highest on high-school items and much weaker on Olympiad-level problems, with GPT-4 Turbo scoring 47.03% overall, Gemini Math-Specialized 1.5 Pro at 55.8%, and Olympiad-level accuracy around 10% or lower for the strongest models. The work is a benchmark study of model capability, not a study of student learning, instruction, or classroom outcomes, so it does not provide evidence that generative AI improves K-12 mathematics achievement relative to standard instruction or non-AI digital tools.

finding.finding_summary: The paper benchmarks LLM performance on mathematics problems across high school, university, and Olympiad levels, but it does not test instructional effects on students. On the MathOdyssey benchmark, the strongest reported model results were 55.8% overall for Gemini Math-Specialized 1.5 Pro and 47.03% overall for GPT-4 Turbo; however, Olympiad-level accuracy remained very low (e.g. GPT-4 Turbo 10.14%, Llama-3-70B 9.46%).
finding.measure: Accuracy on MathOdyssey mathematics benchmark problems (high school, university-level, Olympiad-level)

paper_profiles.title: The Invalsi Benchmarks: measuring the Linguistic and Mathematical understanding of Large Language Models in Italian
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces three Italian-language benchmarks for evaluating large language models (LLMs): Invalsi MATE for mathematical understanding, Invalsi ITA for Italian language understanding, and Olimpiadi MATE for more difficult mathematical reasoning. The authors use publicly available school assessment items from Italy’s INVALSI tests and the national math Olympics, manually verify the question-answer sets, and evaluate 10 LLMs in a zero-shot setting using likelihood-based scoring, with additional human inspection and pattern-matching analyses for some tasks.

The central question is whether general-purpose and Italian-adapted LLMs can solve Italian math and language benchmark items, and how they compare with each other and with Italian students. The models include English-first Llama variants, multilingual Mistral/Mixtral models, and Italian fine-tunes such as Camoscio, Llamantino, and Anita. On Invalsi MATE, the strongest model is Llama 3.1 405B instruct (0.71 accuracy), with multilingual models generally outperforming English-first models and Italian fine-tuning providing only marginal gains. On Invalsi ITA, Llama 3.1 405B instruct reaches 0.88 accuracy and most models outperform student averages on language items, while on the harder Olimpiadi MATE benchmark even the best model reaches only 0.45 accuracy.

The paper does not test an educational intervention with students; instead, it provides comparative benchmark evidence about model capability across grades and question types. The authors conclude that multilingual pretraining helps more than Italian fine-tuning for Italian tasks, that mathematical reasoning transfers across languages better than language understanding, and that current LLMs remain far from reliably solving complex Italian math problems. The comparison to student results is descriptive and not statistically rigorous because the student aggregates include additional items and visual questions not present in the benchmark.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates LLM performance on Italian mathematics benchmarks (Invalsi MATE and Olimpiadi MATE). On Invalsi MATE, the best model, Llama 3.1 70B instruct, reaches 0.71 accuracy (Table 1), while multilingual models like Mixtral instruct outperform similarly sized English-first and Italian fine-tuned models; however, on the harder Olimpiadi MATE benchmark, even the best model reaches only 0.45 accuracy (Table 3).
finding.measure: Accuracy on Invalsi MATE and Olimpiadi MATE mathematics benchmark questions
finding.study_size: n=1039 total math questions across benchmarks; Invalsi MATE n=420; Olimpiadi MATE n=619

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates LLMs on Italian language-understanding items from Invalsi ITA. Llama 3.1 70B instruct achieves 0.88 accuracy overall on the benchmark, and most models outperform the aggregated student averages on multiple-choice/binary language questions, though performance drops relative to math on harder later-grade items.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Invalsi ITA language-understanding benchmark questions
finding.study_size: n=1264 total language questions in the benchmark; table of student comparators aggregates n=1615 across grades/question types

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation Report on Large Language Models Solving High School Mathematics Questions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report evaluates how several large language models perform on high school mathematics exam questions drawn from Chinese college entrance examinations (2019-2023). The paper asks whether different LLMs can answer math questions accurately, quickly, and with logical coherence, and whether prompting strategies can improve their performance.

The study compares eight LLM APIs, including GLM-4-Flash, ERNIE-Speed-128K, Spark-lite, Hunyuan-lite, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, gemma-2-9b-it, Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Yi-34B, across single-solution and multi-solution settings. It analyzes multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, and comprehensive mathematics questions, and reports metrics for accuracy, response time, logical reasoning, guidance sensitivity, and creativity/richness of solutions. The context is high school mathematics, but the paper is a model benchmarking report rather than a student learning intervention study.

Main findings are comparative rather than instructional: different models excel on different metrics. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and ERNIE-Speed-128K were strongest on answer accuracy for comprehensive and multi-solution tasks, while gemma-2-9b-it and Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct were often fastest on some item types; GLM-4-Flash produced the most solutions and highest complexity in multi-solution settings but was slowest overall. The authors conclude that LLMs show promise for educational use, but their reasoning, creativity, and efficiency vary substantially, and the evidence here does not test effects on student mathematics achievement versus standard instruction or non-AI tools.

finding.finding_summary: This paper benchmarks eight LLMs on high school mathematics exam questions rather than measuring student learning. Performance varied by metric: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct achieved the highest multi-solution correctness (0.64) and tied/led on several accuracy measures, while ERNIE-Speed-128K was also strong on comprehensive questions (0.95) and multi-solution accuracy (0.63). However, absolute single-solution accuracies were modest overall (e.g., multiple-choice accuracy ranged from 0.10 to 0.20; comprehensive accuracy from 0.70 to 0.95), and the study does not evaluate achievement gains for students.
finding.measure: Accuracy on high school mathematics exam questions; single-solution and multi-solution correctness across multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, and comprehensive items

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly compares model response times on mathematics questions. Some models were much faster than others: Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and gemma-2-9b-it were among the quickest on several single-solution item types (e.g., 0.32-0.57 s on some categories), while GLM-4-Flash was much slower on comprehensive items (16.01 s) and multi-solution tasks (7,400 s total reported). In the authors' weighted summary, gemma-2-9b-it ranked first on efficiency, whereas GLM-4-Flash ranked poorly on speed despite strong accuracy/complexity.
finding.measure: Response time in seconds for single-solution and multi-solution math problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The report includes a logic/reasoning evaluation based on chain-of-thought prompting and guidance attempts, which is an indirect proxy for reasoning quality rather than student durable skills. Hunyuan-lite performed best on the authors' guidance/logic criterion, requiring about 3 attempts to guide incorrect questions to correct answers, while other models ranged roughly from 4 to 6 attempts; the authors also note varying logic scores across models (e.g., 0.42 for Hunyuan-lite, 0.406 for Spark-lite, 0.362 for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct). This is a model benchmark, not a measure of learner critical thinking.
finding.measure: Logic/guidance score derived from chain-of-thought prompting success and number of guidance attempts

finding.finding_summary: Beyond accuracy, the study assesses creativity/richness of multi-solution mathematical responses. GLM-4-Flash generated the most solutions overall (472 total; average 4.5 solutions per question) and had the highest complexity score (68), while Yi-34B showed the lowest complexity (33). These findings indicate substantial variation in generative breadth and diversity across models, but again they do not measure student outcomes or compare against classroom instruction.
finding.measure: Number of solutions, solution richness, and solution complexity in multi-solution math prompts

paper_profiles.title: EZYer: A simulacrum of high school with generative agent
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents EZYer, a generative-agent system designed to support high school mathematics teaching and learning. The system has three modules: a Teacher Module that generates structured teaching materials and LaTeX Beamer slides from user input and a text corpus or LLM generation; a Student Module that simulates classroom interaction through five roles (Teacher, Assistant, Top Student, Struggling Student, and Note Taker); and a Controller that filters, scores, and corrects content to improve academic appropriateness and technical correctness.

The paper’s main goal is engineering and concept demonstration rather than testing learning outcomes. To evaluate the system, the authors generated 100 Beamer decks and 100 Notes documents and had five large language models score them on content accuracy, knowledge coverage, usability, formatting correctness, and visual design/appeal. Reported scores were generally high (e.g., average Beamer content accuracy 4.74 and Notes content accuracy 4.70 on a 0–5 scale), suggesting the generated outputs are of good quality and potentially useful for high school mathematics classrooms.

However, the evidence is limited to automated LLM-based evaluation of generated instructional artifacts; there is no student learning experiment, comparison against standard instruction, or comparison with non-AI digital tools. The paper also explicitly notes the lack of manual evaluation and calls for future testing with actual teachers and students. As a result, it provides weak comparative evidence for whether true generative AI improves K-12 mathematics achievement.

finding.finding_summary: EZYer-generated high school mathematics materials and notes were rated highly by five large language models, suggesting strong content quality for math instruction. Across 100 generated Beamer files and 100 Notes documents, average content accuracy scores were 4.74 and 4.70 respectively on a 0–5 scale, with knowledge coverage also high (Beamer 4.70+; Notes 4.53-4.81 across models).
finding.measure: LLM-rated quality of generated high school mathematics Beamer slides and Notes on content accuracy, knowledge coverage, usability, formatting correctness, and visual design/appeal

finding.finding_summary: The system is designed to reduce teacher workload by automatically generating structured teaching materials, exercises, Beamer slides, and notes from user input. The paper argues that this could improve lesson-preparation efficiency, but it does not report a direct time-saving experiment or teacher workload effect size.
finding.measure: System functionality and intended workflow for automated courseware/notes generation

finding.finding_summary: The Student Module is intended to increase learning interaction, interest, and engagement through simulated classroom roles and conversational notes. This claim is supported only by design rationale and LLM-based quality ratings of the generated notes, not by direct learner-reported motivation or engagement measures.
finding.measure: Designed interactive learning experience and LLM-rated usability of generated notes/materials

paper_profiles.title: Combining Large Language Models with Tutoring System Intelligence: A Case Study in Caregiver Homework Support
paper_profiles.venue: LAK 2025 (The 15th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how large language models (LLMs) can be integrated with an intelligent tutoring system to support caregivers who help children with math homework. The authors focus on a hybrid tutoring setting in which caregivers join students working in an equation-solving tutor and receive live, AI-generated message recommendations through a new tool called the Caregiver Conversational Support Tool (CCST).

The system combines contextual data from the tutoring system (e.g., current equation, correctness, hint use, and possible next steps) with prompt-engineering techniques and examples of effective tutoring practices.
