The study combines an anonymous survey of 32 teachers in the Department of Information Technology at Uppsala University with institutional statistics on cheating investigations from 2004 to 2023. Teachers rated cheating prevalence, cheating trends over time, whether using generative AI for writing is cheating, and how common student AI use is. The paper also compares responses by teaching experience (<5 years vs. >5 years) and relates perceived cheating trends to the university’s reported cheating-investigation counts.

The main finding is that teachers generally do not see cheating as highly prevalent, but most believe it has increased over time. Many do not classify generative AI use as outright cheating, yet they believe students use it widely. Reported perceptions broadly align with institutional cheating statistics, including a notable rise during the COVID-19 period, suggesting that instructors are aware of changing academic dishonesty patterns even if they do not treat AI use itself as always cheating.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers’ perceptions of cheating trend closely aligned with institutional cheating-investigation statistics from 2004 to 2023. The paper reports a noticeable rise in cheating investigations, including a peak in 2020-2021, and states that teacher perception scores tracked these objective trends.
finding.measure: Teacher survey perceptions of cheating prevalence trends; annual cheating investigations at Uppsala University
finding.study_size: n=32 survey respondents; institutional statistics from 2004-2023

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on student cheating and the academic integrity implications of generative AI in higher education. Teachers generally rated current cheating as not very prevalent, but most believed it is increasing and that generative AI is widely used by students; many did not equate AI use with cheating.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey items on cheating prevalence, cheating trends, whether generative AI use is cheating, and perceived student AI use

paper_profiles.title: Mathify: Evaluating Large Language Models on Mathematical Problem Solving Tasks
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS’23 Workshop on Generative AI for Education (GAIED)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of evaluating and improving large language models (LLMs) for high school mathematics problem solving, particularly on NCERT 11th- and 12th-grade content. The authors argue that existing open datasets are too simple and therefore curate a new dataset, MathQuest, from Indian NCERT textbooks to better reflect the complexity of school mathematics.

The study also constructs an augmented arithmetic training set (Math-401*) and fine-tunes three LLM families: LLaMA-2, WizardMath, and MAmmoTH. The models are then evaluated with exact-match accuracy on MathQuest and several public math reasoning benchmarks. The experiments are not classroom-based and do not involve student participants; instead, they benchmark model performance before and after fine-tuning.

Across the reported results, fine-tuning improves exact-match accuracy on the evaluated datasets, with larger models generally outperforming smaller ones. On MathQuest specifically, MAmmoTH-13B performs best after fine-tuning, reaching 24.0% exact-match accuracy, but the authors also note that MathQuest remains challenging and overall accuracy is still low. The paper concludes that MathQuest is a useful benchmark for complex school mathematics and that instruction-tuned LLMs can improve their math problem-solving performance, though important limitations remain for harder expressions and multi-step reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improved exact-match accuracy in mathematical problem solving after fine-tuning on the augmented Math-401 dataset. On MathQuest, the best-performing model after fine-tuning was MAmmoTH-13B with 24.0% exact-match accuracy; the authors describe this as the strongest baseline among the tested models, though performance remains low overall on the harder dataset.
finding.measure: Exact-match accuracy on MathQuest and related math reasoning benchmarks
finding.study_size: n=100 test samples per benchmark (reported tables); MathQuest dataset n=223; fine-tuning set n=302,000 augmented Math-401 samples

paper_profiles.title: E-EVAL: A Comprehensive Chinese K-12 Education Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces E-EVAL, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on Chinese K-12 educational content. The authors identify a gap in existing evaluation suites: prior benchmarks focus heavily on general language understanding, professional exams, or higher-level knowledge, while missing the full breadth of primary, middle, and high school subjects in the Chinese context.

E-EVAL contains 4,351 multiple-choice questions drawn primarily from homework, practice questions, and mock exams across 23 subjects. The benchmark is split into arts and science subsets and evaluated with zero-shot, five-shot answer-only, and five-shot chain-of-thought prompting. The study tests 15 advanced open-source and proprietary models and reports accuracy across subjects, school levels, and prompt settings.

The main findings are that Chinese-dominant LLMs generally outperform English-dominant models on Chinese K-12 material, but all models struggle especially on mathematics and other science subjects. Performance is consistently stronger in arts than science, and several models perform unexpectedly worse on primary-school questions than on middle-school questions, suggesting that mastery of higher-level knowledge does not guarantee mastery of simpler content. Few-shot prompting helps most models slightly, especially in arts, while chain-of-thought often hurts overall performance but can help on complex science tasks.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark results show that nearly all evaluated models performed poorly on mathematics relative to arts subjects, and the paper repeatedly notes that logical and quantitative reasoning remain a weakness. At the same time, chain-of-thought prompting improved performance on complex science subjects such as mathematics in some cases, indicating that prompting can help on harder math reasoning tasks even though overall math accuracy remains subpar.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on primary, middle, and high school mathematics questions
finding.study_size: n=4,351 total questions; math subset included primary, middle, and high school mathematics items (exact math-only n not reported in the excerpt)

finding.finding_summary: Across science subjects, model performance was lower than in arts subjects, showing that science reasoning remains difficult for LLMs in this benchmark. However, the paper reports that chain-of-thought prompting improved performance on complex science questions, especially middle- and high-school mathematics and other structured science items, suggesting some benefit for reasoning-heavy science tasks.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on science subjects including physics, chemistry, biology, science, and mathematics
finding.study_size: n=4,351 total questions; science subset included 10 subjects (exact science-only n not reported in the excerpt)

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s core contribution is a K-12 educational benchmark spanning Chinese, English, politics, history, geography, ethics, and other non-STEM school subjects. Models performed substantially better on arts/language-heavy subjects than on science subjects, and few-shot prompting especially improved performance on liberal arts items. This outcome is central because a major result is that LLMs are comparatively stronger on arts-oriented academic content than on science content.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on arts and humanities subjects across Chinese K-12 levels
finding.study_size: n=4,351 total questions; arts subset included 13 subjects (exact arts-only n not reported in the excerpt)

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly analyzes reasoning-related prompting behavior, finding that chain-of-thought prompting generally reduced average accuracy, but helped on structured science reasoning tasks. It also observes an unexpected failure on very simple elementary math problems, which the authors interpret as evidence that models may not generalize from higher-order knowledge to lower-order knowledge, a finding relevant to metacognitive and reasoning robustness.
finding.measure: Accuracy under zero-shot, few-shot-answer-only, and few-shot-chain-of-thought prompting; performance by school level

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark is designed as a standardized evaluation tool to help developers and educators rapidly assess and improve LLM capability in Chinese K-12 education. The paper claims E-EVAL can support faster diagnosis of model strengths and weaknesses, especially across subjects and school levels, but it does not measure time savings or workflow effects directly.
finding.measure: Benchmark utility for evaluating model performance across K-12 subjects and prompt settings

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames E-EVAL as a public benchmark intended to improve governance of LLM use in Chinese K-12 education by reducing contamination risk and providing a more complete assessment standard. It argues that the benchmark can inform development, comparison, and deployment of educational LLMs, though it does not directly evaluate policy or institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Creation and public release of a Chinese K-12 evaluation benchmark; leaderboard-based model assessment

paper_profiles.title: Environmental large language model Evaluation (ELLE) dataset: A Benchmark for Evaluating Generative AI applications in Eco-environment Domain
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces ELLE-QA, a benchmark dataset for evaluating large language models and related generative AI systems in the ecological and environmental sciences. The authors argue that existing LLM evaluations are too general and do not adequately test domain-specific professionalism, clarity, and feasibility for eco-environment applications. To address this, they create 1,130 expert- and source-derived question-answer pairs spanning 16 environmental subjects, with metadata for subject area, difficulty, and question type.

The benchmark was built using a mix of questionnaire-based expert contributions, manual extraction from textbooks, exams, and professional consultations, followed by multi-round expert screening and validation. The paper describes the dataset composition and the proposed evaluation protocol, in which models are scored on professionalism, clarity, and feasibility, while answers are withheld until after evaluation to reduce bias. The main contribution is methodological: a standardized evaluation resource for ecological and environmental GenAI, not an intervention study or a learner-outcome study.

Because the paper is focused on benchmark construction rather than an educational treatment, it does not study K-12 learners, schools, or mathematics instruction directly. It reports dataset characteristics and an evaluation framework for domain-specific AI assessment, with only preliminary mention that initial assessments using ELLE-QA yielded insights about current model strengths and weaknesses. No learner outcomes, subgroup effects, cheating behavior, retention, or productive-struggle measures are reported.

paper_profiles.title: A Systematic Review of Computational Thinking in Early Ages
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews research on computational thinking (CT) in early childhood, focusing specifically on kindergarten and children ages 2-5. The authors ask which tools and strategies have been used to encourage CT development at these ages, and they survey work from 2010-2020 across Scopus, ACM, IEEE, and Web of Science using PRISMA-style procedures.

The review synthesizes 34 included papers and organizes them into three broad categories: curriculum, review, and tools. It highlights block-based, robot-based, and block-plus-robot solutions such as Bee-Bot, KIBO, ScratchJr, Happy Maps, Blue-Bot, and related prototypes, as well as curriculum approaches like TangibleK and Coding as Another Language (CAL). The paper describes these initiatives as generally supporting early CT, programming vocabulary, collaboration, and engagement, while also emphasizing that the evidence base is still limited and that more rigorous validation is needed.

Across the reviewed literature, the authors note a growing research trend and substantial use of case studies and pretest-posttest designs, but they also stress that many studies are small and mainly evaluate short-term outcomes. The review concludes that early CT initiatives show promise for kindergarten and preschool settings, yet long-term impact on children’s later life outcomes remains largely unexamined. The paper also argues for more conferences, more validation studies, and continued curriculum development to support early introduction of CT.

finding.finding_summary: The review includes curriculum studies suggesting that programming activities can support early mathematics learning, especially spatial thinking. For example, Palmer (2017) reports a four-month intervention in two Swedish preschools with 8 children (5 girls, 3 boys) aged 3-4.5 years, using programming to facilitate preschoolers’ learning of mathematics and spatial thinking; the paper reports favorable pre/post change but does not provide effect sizes.
finding.measure: Math learning and spatial thinking assessed through pretest/posttest classroom intervention tasks and child responses

finding.finding_summary: Multiple included studies reported gains in motivation, engagement, collaboration, and confidence when young children used programming or robotics tools. For example, Bers et al. (2019) studied 172 preschool children (ages 3-5) in three Spanish centers and found that a 'coding as a playground' experience promoted communication, collaboration, creativity, and teacher motivation/confidence; Papadakis et al. (2016) similarly reported that ScratchJr made learning fun and increased engagement among 43 preschoolers.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, collaboration, creativity, and classroom participation observations/surveys
finding.study_size: n=172 (Bers et al. 2019); n=43 (Papadakis et al. 2016)

finding.finding_summary: The review centrally emphasizes that early CT activities develop problem-solving, sequencing, collaboration, and deep reflection. Reported studies include a quasi-experimental robotics intervention with 131 kindergarten students in Spain showing improved CT and programming skills, and a mixed-methods ScratchJr study with 222 students and 6 teachers indicating that children engaged in deep reflection as they solved problems and collaborated with peers.
finding.measure: Computational thinking, sequencing, problem-solving, collaboration, and reflection measures in classroom interventions

finding.finding_summary: The paper also reviews evidence that early coding and robotics can support broader academic learning beyond mathematics, particularly foundational programming concepts and literacy-related storytelling. For instance, studies on ScratchJr and related tools report that children learned new programming vocabulary, assimilated concepts, and could retell stories through animated sequences, indicating gains in early coding knowledge and related academic skills.
finding.measure: Programming concepts, coding vocabulary, storytelling/animation tasks
finding.study_size: n=43; not_reported for other cited studies

paper_profiles.title: Guardrails for avoiding harmful medical product recommendations and off-label promotion in generative AI models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates a safety and governance problem in generative AI: whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) produce off-label medical product recommendations that could be harmful or unlawful. The author argues that general-purpose GenAI systems trained on broad internet data can learn unvetted product–indication associations and then surface them in user-facing responses, creating public health and regulatory risks.

To study this, the paper proposes a post hoc detection pipeline for off-label promotion. The pipeline standardizes the input, applies biomedical named entity recognition, matches detected products and indications to FDA label data, and flags non-approved product–indication recommendations using a zero-shot classifier. The method is demonstrated on Anthropic Claude 3 Sonnet in a shopping-style product question-answering setting, where the user provides a product-label image and asks about it.

The evaluation uses synthetic red-teaming prompts generated from 35 pharmaceuticals with 143 known off-label uses, producing 14,300 queries. The model produced responses flagged as off-label in 15.4% of cases, and the detector achieved 85.75% precision, 80.47% recall, and 83.02% F1 on a 2,000-response annotated sample. The paper concludes that off-label promotion is a real failure mode for generalist GenAI and that post-hoc guardrails may help filter harmful recommendations before they reach users.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that a general-purpose MLLM can generate off-label medical product promotions, which the author frames as a regulatory and public-health risk. In a synthetic evaluation with 14,300 queries over 35 pharmaceuticals, 15.4% of responses were flagged as containing off-label indications, suggesting a nontrivial institutional governance problem rather than an isolated error.
finding.measure: Rate of model responses containing off-label indications; detector precision/recall/F1 on annotated sample
finding.study_size: n=14300 synthetic queries; n=2000 annotated sample; 35 pharmaceuticals

paper_profiles.title: Foundations of GenIR
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter provides a conceptual overview of modern generative AI for information access (IA) systems. It contrasts generative AI with traditional AI and IR approaches, emphasizing two central paradigms: information generation, where models directly produce tailored content, and information synthesis, where models combine external sources with generation to produce grounded responses.

The paper surveys foundational components of generative models, including Transformer architectures, scaling laws, training stages (pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF), prompting, and multimodal extensions. It then focuses on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), generative retrieval, and domain-specific modeling as ways to improve reliability, reduce hallucination, and incorporate external knowledge. The chapter is written for researchers and practitioners in information retrieval and related AI fields rather than a specific learner population.

The main conclusion is that generative AI substantially expands the design space for information access systems, but also introduces important limitations and open questions. These include hallucination, retrieval planning, model controllability, updateability, and the high computational costs of large models. Rather than reporting an intervention study or empirical evaluation, the chapter synthesizes prior work and identifies promising future directions for combining retrieval and generation in more reliable, explainable systems.

paper_profiles.title: Tinkering in Primary School: From Episode to Science Practice
paper_profiles.venue: The Primary School as a Playful Space
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how tinkering—an open-ended, constructionist learning practice—can be integrated into primary school classrooms as a bridge between exploratory activity and formal disciplinary learning. The authors propose a model called TIDE (Tinkering, Ideas generation, Disciplinary connection, Exploration) to connect tinkering workshops with curricular work, especially in physics and light-related phenomena, while preserving tinkering’s openness and student agency.

The paper reports on a multi-school project in Bologna, Italy, involving 13 primary classrooms, 24 teachers, and approximately 300 students over the 2021–2022 school year. Data came from teacher questionnaires completed by 20 teachers, classroom documentation, and fishbowl reflection protocols. The findings suggest that tinkering can increase engagement, participation, collaboration, and access to knowledge, especially for students who struggle in traditional schooling, but it can also surface vulnerabilities among some high-performing students. The study also finds that teachers often felt unprepared to pursue the scientific questions generated by students, especially in physics, and tended to shift integration toward language, storytelling, or expressive activities rather than disciplinary science. The authors conclude that tinkering has promise for inclusive science learning, but that teachers need stronger disciplinary support and more robust documentation practices for the model to be fully realized.

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that tinkering can surface authentic scientific questions and support inquiry, but teachers often did not feel prepared to sustain or extend those questions into disciplinary science learning. In the light workshop, students generated a substantive question about how to produce white light with filters, but the teacher left it unresolved because of inadequate disciplinary confidence; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections, fishbowl documentation, questionnaire responses about science integration and student inquiry

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that tinkering increased student engagement, participation, motivation, and persistence, especially after pandemic-related disruption. In the questionnaire, 70% of teachers reported unexpected or partially expected behavior, noting that many students became enthusiastic, sustained attention over time, and managed frustration more effectively during tinkering activities.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire, classroom observations/documentation, fishbowl reflections

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that tinkering fostered collaboration, mutual assistance, self-reflection, hypothesis testing, and willingness to revise ideas, with some students becoming group leaders and showing improved ability to work through failure. Teachers specifically noted gains in collaboration and process-focused reasoning, while some high-achieving students were challenged by the need to tolerate mistakes and could become frustrated.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire responses and qualitative analysis of classroom documentation

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that tinkering prompted teachers to rethink classroom routines, documentation practices, and the relationship between open exploration and curricular objectives. At the institutional level, the authors argue that integrating tinkering into formal schooling is feasible but requires teacher preparation, disciplinary support, and co-design structures to avoid reducing tinkering to isolated or recreational activity.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire, implementation analysis, and reflection on school integration of the TIDE model

paper_profiles.title: AI Safety in Generative AI Large Language Models: A Survey
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a technical survey of AI safety issues in generative AI large language models (LLMs), written from a computer science perspective. Its main purpose is to organize the literature on risks and safety challenges associated with LLMs, including toxicity, bias, privacy leakage, copyright infringement, misinformation, evaluation problems, prompt attacks, alignment, and safety at scale.

The survey does not evaluate a specific educational intervention or classroom deployment. Instead, it synthesizes prior research across NLP and machine learning venues and categorizes safety concerns by component of the LLM pipeline: training data, model behavior, prompting, alignment, and scaling. It also discusses how these issues arise technically, such as through pretraining data contamination, hallucination, prompt injection, and limitations in current evaluation protocols.

The paper’s conclusions emphasize that LLM safety requires more precise taxonomies, better evaluation methods, and stronger alignment and oversight mechanisms. It argues that many current safety problems are rooted in model design and training choices, and that future work should focus on identifying the technical origins of harms and developing more robust safeguards. The paper is broad and conceptual rather than empirical, and it is not specific to K-12 education.

finding.finding_summary: This survey identifies a broad set of systemic risks and governance challenges for generative AI/LLMs, including bias, privacy leakage, copyright infringement, misinformation, prompt attacks, alignment failures, and weak evaluation protocols. It does not report new empirical results; instead, it synthesizes prior literature and argues that safety failures can propagate across deployment contexts and require stronger governance and evaluation.
finding.measure: Literature synthesis of AI safety risks, taxonomies, and evaluation frameworks

finding.finding_summary: The survey notes that in-context learning and prompting allow LLMs to handle new tasks without explicit fine-tuning, which reduces computational overhead and can make deployment more efficient. This is a conceptual claim drawn from prior literature rather than a measured effect in this paper.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of in-context learning and reduced need for fine-tuning

paper_profiles.title: Mathematical Capabilities of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates the mathematical capabilities of two ChatGPT versions (9-January-2023 and 30-January-2023) and GPT-4 on a new benchmark suite, GHOSTS, plus a smaller subset called miniGHOSTS. The authors designed 709 prompts spanning graduate-level textbook exercises, proof completion, olympiad-style problems, symbolic integration, MATH benchmark items, and search-engine-like retrieval of mathematical facts and definitions.

The study is not an educational intervention but a benchmark analysis of model performance across increasingly difficult mathematics tasks. It compares model outputs using human ratings from 1 to 5 and fine-grained error/warning codes, with 1,636 manual ratings in total. The paper reports that ChatGPT performs inconsistently and falls well below graduate-student level overall, while GPT-4 improves substantially but still struggles with graduate-level reasoning and proof tasks.

The context is advanced mathematics rather than K-12 instruction, but the authors explicitly discuss how ChatGPT could be used as an assistant or search engine for mathematically proficient users who can verify its output. Their main conclusion is that these models are useful for fact lookup and some undergraduate-level work, but they are unreliable for high-level proof, computation, and robust mathematical reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: Across 709 prompts and 1,636 human ratings, the 9-January-2023 ChatGPT version averaged 3.20/5 (SD=1.23) on the GHOSTS benchmark, while the 30-January-2023 version averaged 3.29/5 (SD=1.28). GPT-4 performed better on the miniGHOSTS subset with an average of 4.15/5 (SD=1.12), but still failed on graduate-level difficulty and was vulnerable to simple calculation mistakes. The paper concludes that ChatGPT is strongest as a factual/math lookup tool, but overall mathematical performance is below graduate-student level.
finding.measure: Human-rated mathematical task performance on GHOSTS/miniGHOSTS (ratings 1-5), covering proofs, computation, symbolic integration, olympiad problems, and fact retrieval

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the models, especially ChatGPT, often produced confident but wrong answers and rarely expressed uncertainty, even when the output was completely incorrect. This suggests weak metacognitive calibration and unreliable reasoning support rather than sustained productive struggle or self-monitoring. No direct intervention or delayed retention measure was studied, but the evaluation highlights limitations in deeper reasoning and proof completion.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of answer style, uncertainty expression, and reasoning failure modes during mathematical problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The authors conclude that ChatGPT can be useful as a mathematical assistant for querying facts and acting as a search engine or knowledge base interface, which could speed up lookup tasks in a mathematician’s workflow. However, this benefit is limited to users who can already judge correctness, and the paper does not report a formal productivity experiment or effect size.
finding.measure: Observed usefulness for fact querying, definition retrieval, theorem naming, and proof-outline search tasks

paper_profiles.title: EXPTRIALMNG: A Universal Experiment Trial Manager for AR/VR/MR Experiments Based on Unity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents ExpTrialMng, a Unity-based library intended to make it easier for researchers to build and run AR/VR/MR experiments. The authors identify two practical barriers in immersive research: the programming burden of creating experiment logic in Unity and the risk of data loss or experiment failure when head-mounted displays or tracking systems malfunction.

To address these problems, the library separates trial randomization from experiment execution by using a pre-generated CSV file, automatically records trial results to CSV, and can resume an interrupted experiment from a specified trial index. The paper describes the library’s design and workflow rather than evaluating it through a user study or experiment. The intended users are researchers conducting HCI, psychology, or design experiments in VR/AR contexts, not K-12 students.

The main conclusion is that a lightweight, general-purpose trial manager can reduce implementation effort and help preserve data when unexpected errors occur during immersive experiments. The paper argues that this could broaden access to VR/AR experimentation for researchers unfamiliar with Unity and improve experiment robustness, but it does not report empirical effectiveness data for educational or learner outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Beyond the “Wow” Factor: Using Generative AI for Increasing Generative Sense-Making
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how generative AI can be designed to support, rather than replace, generative learning in education. The authors argue that much GenAI research is technocentric and insufficiently grounded in learning theory, so they develop ChatTutor, a theory-informed chatbot that prompts students to teach, self-explain, and receive scaffolded feedback aligned with generative learning theory.

The study reports two between-subjects experiments. Study 1 involved 175 university students in an authentic cognitive psychology course and compared ChatTutor with ChatGPT-4 and a teaching-as-usual condition. Study 2 replicated the design with 234 high school students, comparing ChatTutor with ChatGPT-4 and a re-study control. In both studies, students used the system during a short follow-up activity on the Sternberg memory scanning experiment, and outcomes included conceptual knowledge immediately after the lesson and at delayed follow-up, plus self-efficacy, trust, enjoyment, and behavioral intentions.

Main findings were mixed but encouraging for the theory-informed system. ChatTutor significantly improved trust and enjoyment relative to ChatGPT in both studies, and behavioral intentions in Study 1, but did not significantly improve self-efficacy. For learning, ChatTutor did not significantly outperform the comparison conditions on immediate post-test knowledge, but it did outperform teaching-as-usual on delayed conceptual knowledge in Study 1 and on delayed follow-up/new items in Study 2, suggesting some benefit for retention when GenAI is designed to elicit generative sense-making.

finding.finding_summary: Across two experiments, the theory-informed ChatTutor improved conceptual knowledge relative to comparison conditions in delayed or follow-up testing, but not consistently on immediate post-tests. In Study 1 (n=175), immediate conceptual knowledge did not differ significantly across groups (F(2,172)=1.886, p=0.155), but ChatTutor outperformed teaching-as-usual at 4-week follow-up (M=7.26, SD=1.50 vs M=5.93, SD=2.15; p=0.001). In Study 2 (n=234), ChatTutor also outperformed the re-study control on follow-up conceptual knowledge and new conceptual questions.
finding.measure: Conceptual knowledge test (post-test and delayed follow-up); new conceptual knowledge items at follow-up
finding.std_deviation: Study 1 follow-up: ChatTutor SD=1.50, teaching-as-usual SD=2.15; Study 2 SDs not fully reported in excerpt

finding.finding_summary: ChatTutor produced higher trust, enjoyment, and behavioral intentions than ChatGPT, indicating stronger motivational and affective responses to the theory-informed system. In Study 1, ChatTutor scored higher than ChatGPT on trust (M=3.64 vs 3.29, d=0.60, p=0.002), enjoyment (M=3.65 vs 2.99, d=0.86, p<0.001), and behavioral intentions (M=3.28 vs 2.73, d=0.57, p=0.016), all measured after or at delayed follow-up. Self-efficacy did not differ significantly (p=0.100).
finding.measure: Trust, enjoyment, behavioral intentions, self-efficacy surveys
finding.study_size: Study 1 n=175; follow-up subsamples smaller for some measures
finding.std_deviation: Trust SDs: 0.58 and 0.59; Enjoyment SDs: 0.91 and 0.52; Intentions SDs: 0.96 and 0.98

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines generative sense-making, self-explanation/teaching, and retention of conceptual understanding, which are durable learning processes. The strongest durable-skill-related evidence is that ChatTutor improved delayed conceptual knowledge relative to controls, suggesting better longer-term retention and sense-making rather than only immediate performance. The authors frame this as evidence that theory-informed GenAI can support generative processing and reduce the risk of GenAI acting as a mere crutch.
finding.measure: Delayed conceptual knowledge retention; generative sense-making/teaching activity quality as part of the intervention

paper_profiles.title: Cognitive Pathways: From Language Processing to Pedagogical Practice
paper_profiles.venue: University of Northern British Columbia dissertation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This dissertation examines cognitive mechanisms underlying learning across three related investigations: single-word processing, flashcard-based learning strategies, and the use of generative AI (GenAI) tools in postsecondary education. The GenAI component is the most relevant to the paper’s educational-technology focus, asking how AI-assisted learning affects cognitive load, learning efficacy, metacognitive engagement, test anxiety, and the quality of student processing when interacting with AI-generated explanations and writing samples.

Across the GenAI studies, students completed structured activities in which they critically evaluated AI-generated explanations and essays, cross-referenced outputs with reliable sources, and reflected on their own understanding. The dissertation argues that structured AI use can improve learning outcomes and academic confidence, but only when students are guided to engage critically rather than rely passively on AI outputs. It emphasizes AI literacy as a safeguard against shallow processing, cognitive offloading, and misinformation.

Although the dissertation also includes non-AI chapters on word recognition and flashcard learning, the GenAI chapter situates AI as a study aid in postsecondary coursework rather than as an autonomous tutor. The overall conclusion is that GenAI can support learning when used in an intentional, metacognitive way, but it also introduces risks related to overreliance, superficial engagement, and inaccurate outputs, so pedagogical framing and AI literacy are essential.

finding.finding_summary: Structured AI use was reported to improve learning outcomes and academic confidence while encouraging students to critically assess AI-generated explanations and writing samples. The dissertation emphasizes that these benefits depend on metacognitive engagement and AI literacy, suggesting GenAI can support critical thinking and self-monitoring when used intentionally, but can also promote shallow processing if used passively. Reported quantitative analyses are described as demonstrating improved learning outcomes, but no effect size, confidence interval, or sample size are provided in the available text.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes, academic confidence, metacognitive engagement, and critical evaluation of AI-generated content

finding.finding_summary: The GenAI chapter reports that AI-assisted learning improved students’ academic confidence and was studied in relation to test anxiety. The dissertation frames GenAI as potentially reducing anxiety by providing low-stakes, personalized learning support, though it also notes that anxiety may not be fully resolved by AI alone and depends on broader psychological factors.
finding.measure: Academic confidence and test anxiety

finding.finding_summary: The dissertation includes an intervention-like exploration of GenAI-supported study activities in postsecondary education, focusing on conceptual understanding and writing-sample evaluation rather than a specific school subject. It reports that structured AI use improved learning outcomes, but the available text does not provide numeric estimates, sample size, or inferential statistics for the GenAI studies.
finding.measure: Conceptual understanding and evaluation of AI-generated essays/explanations

paper_profiles.title: Global Trends and Priorities in STEM Teaching and Learning: A literature review
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and broader STEM education populations (mixed; review of international literature, including K-12 focus in parts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a scoping literature review of global trends and priorities in STEM teaching and learning. It asks how STEM education has evolved, what pedagogical and policy trends are shaping it, and what barriers remain to effective, inclusive STEM integration across countries. The review synthesizes recent research from Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, plus foundational sources, to identify themes such as interdisciplinary integration, technology use, equity, leadership, and workforce preparation.

The paper does not test a new intervention in a single setting; instead, it surveys the literature on STEM education across national contexts including the U.S., UK, Europe, Asia, and emerging economies. It highlights the promise of AI, VR, project-based learning, and dialogic/inquiry-based pedagogy for improving engagement and problem-solving, while also emphasizing persistent constraints such as curriculum fragmentation, teacher preparation gaps, resource shortages, and inequitable access for under-represented groups. The author concludes that sustained progress in STEM education requires balancing innovation with equity, supported by leadership, teacher development, infrastructure investment, and inclusive policy.

Because the paper is a narrative/scoping review rather than an empirical study, its conclusions are synthesized from prior studies rather than original data. It is especially concerned with how STEM systems can better support interdisciplinary learning, future workforce readiness, and access for marginalized learners.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that STEM-integrated and inquiry-based approaches are associated with stronger problem-solving, critical thinking, and scientific reasoning than fragmented, memorization-heavy instruction. It cites literature suggesting AI, VR, project-based learning, and dialogic teaching can improve student engagement and reasoning, but it also notes that these benefits depend on teacher preparation, resources, and equitable access.
finding.measure: Literature synthesis of STEM pedagogy, problem-solving, critical thinking, and inquiry-based learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses mathematics as a core STEM domain and notes that many national systems prioritize math literacy and numeracy within STEM policy. However, it does not report original quantitative effects of any intervention on math achievement; instead, it synthesizes evidence that integrated STEM and problem-based approaches are intended to strengthen mathematics learning and real-world application.
finding.measure: Literature synthesis of mathematics literacy, STEM integration, and PISA-related performance discussions

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly states that innovative STEM approaches can improve student engagement, motivation, and participation, and that inclusive STEM programs can reduce barriers for under-represented groups. These claims are drawn from prior studies and examples, rather than a single original dataset, so the finding is best treated as synthesized evidence of positive engagement-related associations.
finding.measure: Literature synthesis of student engagement, motivation, participation, and inclusion in STEM contexts

finding.finding_summary: A central conclusion of the review is that STEM education supports durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, creativity, and adaptability. The paper argues that interdisciplinary, inquiry-based, and project-based STEM models are designed to build these competencies, and that countries with stronger integrated-STEM systems emphasize them as future workforce skills.
finding.measure: Literature synthesis of critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, creativity, and adaptability in STEM education

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s strongest emphasis is on systemic and institutional issues: policy priorities, curriculum integration, teacher training, infrastructure, leadership, and equity initiatives. It concludes that STEM improvement depends on national and institutional action, including standardization efforts, professional development, and targeted inclusion programs, but it does not quantify a single institutional effect size.
finding.measure: Literature synthesis of STEM policy, curriculum, leadership, infrastructure, and equity initiatives

paper_profiles.title: Global Trends and Priorities in STEM Teaching and Learning: A literature review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a scoping literature review of global trends, priorities, and challenges in STEM teaching and learning, with a particular emphasis on innovation, equity, and the role of leadership in implementing STEM reforms. It asks how the literature has evolved over time, what approaches are currently shaping STEM education, and what barriers still limit effective integration across science, technology, engineering, and mathematics.

The review synthesizes peer-reviewed articles, books, and conference papers identified through searches of Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, drawing on works from roughly the last 15 years alongside foundational theory. It highlights recurring themes such as interdisciplinary integration, inquiry-based and project-based learning, digital technologies including AI/VR/AR, inclusive access, teacher professional development, and leadership models that support implementation. Across the literature reviewed, the author concludes that STEM education is moving toward more integrated, student-centered, and technologically supported instruction, but that progress remains constrained by definitional ambiguity, limited teacher preparation, resource gaps, rigid curricula, and persistent inequities affecting under-represented learners.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that integrated STEM education is associated with stronger mathematics-related learning when curricula emphasize problem-solving, quantitative benchmarks, and real-world applications. It cites PISA 2022 mathematics performance patterns and literature suggesting that interdisciplinary, inquiry-based approaches can support mathematical reasoning, but no new effect estimate is reported in this paper.
finding.measure: mathematics literacy performance, STEM achievement trends, problem-solving skills

finding.finding_summary: The paper concludes that STEM approaches that are interdisciplinary, inquiry-based, and project-based are intended to improve scientific literacy, critical thinking, and problem-solving. It discusses international PISA science results and reviews literature indicating that STEM integration is linked to better scientific understanding, but it does not report original statistical findings.
finding.measure: science literacy performance, scientific literacy, problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: A central theme of the review is that STEM education develops durable skills such as critical thinking, collaboration, creativity, adaptability, and problem-solving. The paper repeatedly links project-based learning, dialogic teaching, and interdisciplinary work to these skills, but provides no original quantitative estimate.
finding.measure: critical thinking, collaboration, creativity, adaptability, problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests that student-centered, inclusive STEM approaches can improve engagement and participation, while rigid curricula, high-stakes testing, and inequitable access can suppress motivation and involvement. It references engagement and participation disparities for under-represented groups, but does not report a study-level effect size.
finding.measure: student engagement, participation, equity in access and involvement

finding.finding_summary: This is one of the paper's main focus areas: the review argues that leadership, curriculum policy, teacher development, infrastructure investment, and equity-oriented programs are essential for successful STEM integration. It synthesizes literature on national strategies, policy reforms, and institutional supports, but does not present original outcome data.
finding.measure: policy implementation, curriculum integration, leadership, infrastructure, institutional support

paper_profiles.title: Global Trends and Priorities in STEM Teaching and Learning: A literature review
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and broader STEM education populations discussed in the literature review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative literature review of global trends, priorities, and challenges in STEM teaching and learning. It asks how STEM education has evolved historically, what pedagogical and policy trends are shaping its present form, and what future directions may improve innovation, equity, and workforce readiness.

The paper synthesizes published research, policy documents, and examples from multiple countries rather than reporting a new empirical study. It discusses integrated STEM, leadership, teacher professional development, inclusion, and the use of AI, VR, and other digital tools as ways to strengthen STEM instruction. The review emphasizes that effective STEM implementation depends on interdisciplinary curricula, strong leadership, adequate teacher preparation, and resources.

The context is global, with attention to English-speaking countries, Western Europe, Asia, and developing nations, and it highlights both high-performing systems and systems facing structural barriers. The main conclusion is that STEM education is moving toward more integrated, student-centered, and technology-rich models, but persistent inequities, fragmented implementation, and insufficient teacher capacity remain major obstacles. The paper argues that innovation and equity must advance together for STEM education to be effective and sustainable.

finding.finding_summary: The review discusses mathematics literacy as a core part of STEM education and cites international PISA results, but it does not report a new intervention effect. It notes that countries such as Singapore and Japan lead in mathematics performance and frames integrated STEM reforms as intended to improve mathematical problem-solving, but no study-specific estimate is provided.
finding.measure: PISA mathematics literacy performance; literature on STEM-integrated mathematics learning

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that STEM integration and inquiry-based approaches are associated with stronger scientific literacy, critical thinking, and problem-solving. It cites PISA science performance and claims that integrated, student-centered STEM curricula are intended to improve scientific reasoning, but it does not present a single primary empirical estimate.
finding.measure: PISA science literacy performance; literature on STEM integration and inquiry-based learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly links STEM innovations such as project-based learning, dialogic teaching, and AI-supported personalization with increased student engagement, resilience, and motivation. These claims are synthesized from prior studies rather than newly tested here, and no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, resilience, and participation in STEM learning

finding.finding_summary: A central theme of the review is that integrated STEM instruction strengthens durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, creativity, and inquiry. The paper supports this with literature across STEM pedagogy and leadership, but the evidence is synthesized narratively and no pooled effect is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, creativity, and inquiry-based learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that STEM outcomes depend heavily on policy, curriculum integration, teacher preparation, leadership, and resource allocation. It highlights systemic barriers such as ambiguous definitions, insufficient funding, weak professional development, and inequitable access, while describing policy initiatives intended to improve implementation and participation.
finding.measure: Curriculum policy, leadership, teacher training, resource availability, and participation/equity in STEM systems

paper_profiles.title: Global Trends and Priorities in STEM Teaching and Learning: A literature review
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and broader STEM education contexts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews global trends, priorities, and historical developments in STEM teaching and learning, with attention to how STEM education has evolved from isolated subject instruction to more integrated, interdisciplinary approaches. It asks how leadership, innovation, inclusion, and policy shape successful STEM implementation, and it synthesizes literature on frameworks such as sociocultural theory, Bernstein’s pedagogic discourse, mathematical modelling, and communities of practice.

The review is not an empirical study of a single intervention; instead, it draws on international literature, policy documents, and illustrative examples from multiple countries to describe common challenges and promising directions. Across the paper, the author emphasizes that effective STEM education depends on curriculum integration, teacher professional development, equitable access, and supportive leadership, while persistent barriers include rigid curricula, insufficient training, limited resources, and unequal access to technology.

The paper’s main conclusion is that future STEM progress requires balancing innovation with equity. It argues that technologies such as AI, VR, and digital learning platforms can enhance engagement and problem-solving, but only if schools also address structural inequities, invest in teacher capacity, and create inclusive policies and learning environments.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that integrated STEM education and mathematical modelling approaches support students’ mathematical literacy, problem-solving, and application of mathematics to real-world contexts. It cites international evidence such as PISA 2022 mathematics performance and literature on interdisciplinary STEM curricula, but it does not report a new effect size from a primary study.
finding.measure: Mathematics literacy / problem-solving outcomes discussed in reviewed literature

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes literature suggesting that STEM integration, inquiry-based learning, and AI/VR-supported instruction can strengthen scientific literacy, critical thinking, and problem-solving. The review discusses PISA science results and international examples, but no single empirical estimate is reported in the paper itself.
finding.measure: Science literacy / scientific problem-solving outcomes discussed in reviewed literature

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly frames STEM innovation as supporting student engagement, motivation, and resilience, especially through hands-on and inquiry-based learning. It also notes that inclusive and student-centered approaches may reduce disengagement, although the paper provides no direct study-level effect sizes.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, and participation described in reviewed literature

finding.finding_summary: A central theme of the paper is that STEM education builds durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, creativity, and adaptability. These benefits are supported through thematic synthesis of prior studies and policy examples, but the paper itself reports no original quantitative estimate.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, creativity, adaptability

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that STEM reform depends on leadership, curriculum policy, teacher professional development, infrastructure investment, and equity-oriented systems change. It identifies persistent institutional barriers—such as rigid curricula, low teacher preparedness, and unequal access to technology—and argues that coordinated policy and leadership can improve implementation and participation.
finding.measure: Policy, leadership, curriculum integration, teacher development, participation equity

paper_profiles.title: Global Trends and Priorities in STEM Teaching and Learning: A literature review
paper_profiles.population: Not reported; broad international STEM education literature with K-12 references
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews global trends, priorities, and historical developments in STEM teaching and learning, with a focus on how integrated STEM education has evolved and what continues to constrain its implementation. The review asks how leadership, innovation, equity, and interdisciplinary pedagogy interact in efforts to improve STEM outcomes, and it synthesizes literature from the past fifteen years alongside foundational theoretical works.

The approach is a scoping literature review drawing on articles, books, and conference papers identified through Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Although the paper is framed as a global review, it repeatedly discusses school-based STEM education and K-12-related initiatives, including examples from the U.S., Europe, Asia, Australia, and developing contexts. The review argues that STEM education has shifted from siloed subject instruction toward more integrated, inquiry-based, and collaborative models, but that implementation is still limited by definitional ambiguity, teacher preparedness, resource constraints, rigid curricula, and inequities in access.

A major conclusion is that innovation and equity must be advanced together: digital tools, AI, VR/AR, project-based learning, and interdisciplinary approaches may improve engagement and problem solving, but only if supported by teacher development, leadership, and inclusive policy. The paper is primarily descriptive and synthetic rather than empirical; it does not report original experimental data. Its main value is as a broad narrative and thematic review of STEM education trends and policy priorities rather than a test of a specific intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that integrated STEM, inquiry-based learning, and AI/VR-supported instruction can strengthen students' critical thinking, problem-solving, and scientific literacy, but it also notes that implementation is often undermined by rigid curricula, inadequate teacher preparation, and resource gaps. No original effect sizes are reported; the paper synthesizes prior literature and examples such as PISA comparisons and cited studies of technology-enhanced learning.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, scientific literacy, and STEM achievement as discussed in the literature

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly claims that innovative STEM approaches can increase student involvement, motivation, and engagement, especially when learning is hands-on, personalized, and connected to real-world problems. These claims are drawn from the reviewed literature rather than from a single empirical dataset, so no effect size is available.
finding.measure: Student engagement and involvement in STEM learning

finding.finding_summary: A central theme of the review is that STEM education builds durable skills such as critical thinking, problem solving, collaboration, creativity, and adaptability. The paper does not report original quantitative estimates; instead, it synthesizes literature arguing that interdisciplinary and project-based STEM instruction supports these competencies, while high-stakes testing and fragmented curricula can limit them.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, creativity, and adaptability

finding.finding_summary: The review strongly emphasizes system-level effects of STEM policy, leadership, curriculum integration, teacher professional development, and equity initiatives. It argues that successful STEM improvement depends on coordinated leadership, funding, infrastructure, and inclusive policies, but it does not provide original causal estimates or outcome data.
finding.measure: Policy implementation, curriculum integration, leadership, teacher training, and institutional capacity

paper_profiles.title: Complexity Growth Patterns in the Stelliferous Era of Big History. Preliminary Observations.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines long-run complexity growth in the universe during the Stelliferous Era as part of a Big History framework. The authors ask how cosmic complexity changes over time and whether the commonly used narrative of a simple transition from decelerating cosmic complexity to accelerating biosocial complexity is too simplified.

The approach is theoretical and quantitative, drawing on prior models of hyperbolic change and on astrophysical proxies such as star formation rate and metallicity. The paper argues that the growth of universal chemical-physical complexity can be approximated by the dynamics of stellar formation and supernova-driven enrichment, with a lag between star formation and complexity increase. It proposes that the universe’s complexity growth rate rose to a maximum around 11–10 billion years before present and then declined, and that metallicity, star formation rate, and mean stellar mass density are better proxies than free energy rate density for this phase.

The paper is not an empirical study of people or schools; it is a cosmological and conceptual analysis aimed at refining Big History periodization. Its conclusions are that complexity growth in the Stelliferous Era likely followed a non-uniform pattern with an early rise, a peak, and subsequent deceleration, and that existing complexity measures have important limitations when applied to universal-scale evolution.

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents a theoretical/quantitative argument about complexity growth in the universe, using astrophysical proxies such as star formation rate and metallicity rather than any educational intervention. It offers a model of universal complexity dynamics (including a proposed peak around 11–10 billion years before present), but it does not report student learning outcomes or any directly measurable educational effect sizes.
finding.measure: Theoretical modeling using star formation rate, metallicity, and mean stellar mass density as proxies for complexity growth

paper_profiles.title: Visual Analytics of Student Learning Behaviors on K-12 Mathematics E-learning Platforms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to interpret rich learning-log data from K-12 mathematics e-learning platforms. The authors argue that while these platforms record detailed traces such as grades, login time, and mouse trajectories, educators still lack tools for understanding how students solve problems and for identifying weaknesses in question design.

To address this, the paper proposes a visual analytics system that combines correlation analysis with visualizations of fine-grained mouse-movement logs. The system includes an overview of performance, a heat map of interaction density, a transition map of movement between regions of interest, and a data analytics view for exploring relationships among learning attributes and performance.

The paper evaluates the system using real log data from a K-12 math e-learning platform through three case studies. The findings suggest the system can help instructors spot potentially miscalibrated question difficulty, distinguish different problem-solving/thinking patterns, and infer detailed solution steps from student interactions. The contribution is primarily a visualization and exploratory analytics tool rather than an intervention intended to change student outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The system was used to analyze student performance on K-12 math questions and compare it with designer-labeled difficulty. In one case study, some questions labeled 'easy' had lower mean scores than expected, suggesting that the assigned difficulty levels were not always accurate and needed re-evaluation. The paper does not report inferential statistics or effect sizes, but it does provide descriptive evidence from real platform logs.
finding.measure: Mean scores on K-12 mathematics questions; comparison with labeled question difficulty

finding.finding_summary: The visualization system was used to infer students' thinking patterns and problem-solving steps from mouse trajectories, supporting interpretation of different approaches such as additive versus subtractive reasoning. The paper suggests the tool helps educators understand and reason about students' problem-solving styles, but it does not measure durable skills directly or test improvement over time.
finding.measure: Mouse-movement logs and problem-solving interaction patterns

paper_profiles.title: Human Agency and Creativity in AI-Assisted Learning Environments
paper_profiles.venue: Oxford Handbook of Human Creativity x Generative AI in Education (forthcoming chapter / preprint)
paper_profiles.population: Not directly studied; conceptual paper with K-12 references
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter is a conceptual/theoretical review of how generative AI (GenAI) reshapes student agency and creativity in AI-assisted learning environments. It examines four perspectives on agency—instrumental, effortful, dynamically emergent, and authorial—and argues that GenAI can both support and constrain creative learning depending on how students use it, how learning tasks are designed, and how classroom and sociocultural contexts shape interactions.

The paper proposes a person-centered framework of agentic engagement for AI-assisted learning, extending Reeve’s notion of agentic engagement to include how students initiate, direct, selectively adopt, seek outside help for, and reflect on their interactions with GenAI. It links this framework to mini-c creativity, emphasizing personally meaningful, process-oriented creativity rather than only final products. The chapter’s main conclusion is that meaningful AI-assisted creativity depends on students remaining active, reflective, and ethically responsible participants rather than passive consumers of AI outputs.

Although the chapter is not an empirical study, it highlights several concerns relevant to K-12 education, including overreliance on AI, reduced critical thinking, weakened authorship, and the need for transparent, ethically grounded classroom practices. It also notes that cultural context matters: agency and creativity may be interpreted differently across educational settings, especially in collectivist or hierarchical contexts. The paper’s focus is theoretical and forward-looking, calling for future empirical work on how students use GenAI to support creative process and performance.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that GenAI can support durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, and reflective engagement when students use it to initiate, revise, evaluate, and reflect on outputs. At the same time, it warns that overreliance may produce metacognitive laziness and reduce critical scrutiny, with the paper citing prior studies rather than reporting original data.
finding.measure: critical thinking, metacognitive reflection, self-scrutiny, reflective learning

finding.finding_summary: The chapter emphasizes effortful agency, motivation, persistence, autonomy, and competence as central to creative engagement with GenAI. It suggests GenAI may reduce frustration and help students stay in a productive zone of challenge, but also warns that passive use can erode autonomy and intrinsic motivation.
finding.measure: motivation, persistence, autonomy, competence, engagement

finding.finding_summary: The chapter discusses creative expression and writing-related authorship in AI-assisted learning, including multimodal production, authorial voice, and student ownership of outputs. It argues GenAI can scaffold expressive work, but overreliance and undisclosed use raise integrity concerns and may weaken students’ authorial voice.
finding.measure: authorship, authorial voice, creative expression, multimodal output

finding.finding_summary: The chapter raises institutional concerns about authorship integrity, disclosure norms, assessment design, and how AI reshapes teacher and student authority in classrooms. It argues that ethical integration of GenAI requires revised assessment practices, transparency, and attention to cultural and institutional context, but does not provide empirical estimates.
finding.measure: authorship integrity, disclosure, assessment design, classroom authority

paper_profiles.title: What Should Developers Be Aware Of? An Empirical Study on the Directives of API Documentation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates what kinds of directives appear in API documentation and how they can be systematically classified. The authors ask which kinds of natural-language constraints and guidelines are embedded in documentation for object-oriented libraries, and they develop a taxonomy of directive kinds from a large manual analysis of Java API docs.

The study is based on more than 6,000 pieces of Java API documentation from the JDK, Eclipse JFace, and Apache Commons Collections. Using a combination of syntactic pattern searches (e.g., must, should, override, thread, null) and collaborative manual coding, the authors identify and organize 23 directive kinds, including not-null constraints, return-value requirements, exception-raising rules, method-call sequences, and subclassing-related contracts.

The paper’s main conclusion is that API documentation contains a rich and recurring set of directive forms that can be systematically categorized and potentially used for tool support, documentation analysis, and contract recovery. It is an observational empirical study of software documentation rather than an intervention study, and it does not evaluate educational or learner outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The study is centered on documentation structures that help developers use APIs more efficiently, and it argues that identifying directive kinds could support future tools for documentation analysis, contract checking, and highlighting important phrases. However, it does not test a tool intervention or report productivity effect sizes; its contribution is a taxonomy built from more than 6,000 API documentation items.
finding.measure: Manual coding of API documentation directives; taxonomy construction; abundance of directive kinds
finding.study_size: n=20574 API documentation elements in corpus; >6000 pieces manually read

paper_profiles.title: Juxtaposing Controlled Empirical Studies in Visualization with Topic Developments in Psychology
paper_profiles.venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper surveys and compares controlled empirical studies in visualization with topic developments in psychology. Its central question is how empirical visualization research relates to the broader landscape of psychology, and what this comparison can reveal about common phenomena, missing questions, and opportunities for cross-disciplinary collaboration.

Methodologically, the authors combine close reading of 129 controlled visualization studies with distant reading of psychology journals and textbooks. They build taxonomies for psychology and for visualization studies, then use those taxonomies to classify prior work by study objectives, knowledge scope, tasks, behaviors, and study platform. They also perform a text-based topic analysis of papers from Behavioural and Brain Sciences and Psychological Review from 1978–2017 using Voyant Tools and ThemeRiver visualizations.

The paper’s main conclusion is that many visualization studies align with established psychological topics, especially around perception, attention, memory, and cognition, but the visualization literature also poses distinct task-related questions that psychology has not fully addressed. The authors argue for a shared taxonomy and tighter collaboration between visualization and psychology researchers to support new hypotheses and better empirical study designs. This paper is primarily a conceptual and survey contribution rather than a study of learner outcomes or educational interventions.

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Effect of Pretesting with Conversational AI on Retention of Needed Information
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether pretesting improves learning and retention when students use conversational AI, specifically ChatGPT, to obtain information needed for solving a problem. The authors build on prior “thinking before googling” research and ask whether asking learners to attempt a problem before accessing AI assistance leads to better subsequent recall and transfer than giving immediate access to ChatGPT.

The study was conducted in an intermediate-level statistics course with 61 undergraduate information sciences students at a large public university. Students first learned basic one-way chi-square analysis, then worked on a more complex two-way chi-square cybersecurity problem that required information not yet covered in class; one group attempted the task before using ChatGPT (pretest group) and the other used ChatGPT immediately (no-pretest group). A delayed multiple-choice transfer test showed that the pretest group outperformed the no-pretest group, suggesting that pretesting can strengthen retention and application of statistical concepts even in AI-supported learning environments. The paper also frames the effect as potentially related to productive failure and better metacognitive calibration before seeking external help.

finding.finding_summary: Students who attempted the problem before using ChatGPT scored significantly higher on the delayed final transfer test than students who accessed ChatGPT immediately. The final test covered concepts from chi-square analysis and concept transfer to a related scenario; the pretest group (n=29) outperformed the no-pretest group (n=31) with M=91.85 vs. M=78.59, SD=9.52 vs. SD=7.62, t(58)=-5.974, p<.001, Cohen’s d=8.59.
finding.measure: Delayed multiple-choice transfer test on chi-square analysis concepts

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that pretesting before using ChatGPT improves retention and supports deeper engagement with the task, indicating benefits for metacognition and productive problem-solving. Recall test performance did not differ between groups (t(58)=0.584, p=.562), but the later transfer test favored the pretest group substantially, suggesting better memory preparation and self-regulated engagement before seeking AI help.
finding.measure: Recall test and delayed transfer test performance
finding.effect_size: Final test d=8.59; recall test not_reported
finding.std_deviation: Recall test: Pretest SD=13.72, No-pretest SD=11.01

finding.finding_summary: Although the content area was statistics rather than a science subject, the task required applying chi-square reasoning to a cybersecurity scenario and interpreting statistical information. The pretest group showed significantly better understanding on the delayed test of the two-way chi-square task than the no-pretest group, indicating improved reasoning with statistical concepts after pretesting before ChatGPT use.
finding.measure: Transfer questions on two-way chi-square analysis in a cybersecurity scenario

paper_profiles.title: Prompt Complexity Dilutes Structured Reasoning: A Follow-Up Study on the Car Wash Problem
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether the STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) reasoning framework retains its effectiveness when moved from a short, isolated prompt into a much longer, production-style system prompt. The motivating question is whether structured reasoning methods that perform well in clean experimental settings still work when embedded among many competing instructions, formatting rules, and persona constraints.

Using the car wash problem (“Should I walk or drive?”), the author compares three conditions on Claude Sonnet 4.6: STAR embedded in InterviewMate’s full 60+ line production prompt with two different profiles, and STAR-only in the original 10-line prompt. The STAR-only condition achieved 100% accuracy (verified at n=100), while the production-prompt conditions fell to 0% and 30%, respectively, with accompanying drops in constraint detection. The paper concludes that prompt complexity can dilute structured reasoning by forcing conclusion-first output before reasoning unfolds, and that model upgrades improved STAR-only performance from 85% on Sonnet 4.5 to 100% on Sonnet 4.6.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly tests structured reasoning performance under prompt competition and shows that reasoning quality degrades when STAR is embedded in a complex production prompt. In the full InterviewMate prompt, STAR accuracy fell to 0% (0/20) for the Anthropic-oriented profile and 30% (6/20) for the default profile, compared with 100% (20/20; verified at n=100) in the STAR-only prompt. This indicates that added prompt complexity can undermine reasoning execution and increase post-hoc rationalization rather than genuine deliberation.
finding.measure: Car wash problem accuracy / correct answer selection and constraint detection under STAR prompting
finding.study_size: n=20 per production-prompt condition; n=100 verification for STAR-only

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that production prompt complexity can reduce the operational reliability of an AI system. STAR worked at 100% in isolation but degraded to 0–30% inside the deployed InterviewMate prompt, implying that adding formatting, style, and profile rules can make the system less dependable in practice.
finding.measure: Prompt-conditioned response accuracy in a production interview-coaching system
finding.study_size: n=20 per condition; n=100 verification for one condition

finding.finding_summary: The study focuses on the gap between experimental validation and real production deployment, showing that a reasoning method validated in a clean prompt may fail in the actual system prompt used in practice. The author emphasizes that prompt evolution can invalidate earlier findings and that production AI systems require environment-specific evaluation.
finding.measure: Difference in STAR performance between experimental and production prompt environments
finding.study_size: n=20 per condition; n=100 verification for STAR-only

paper_profiles.title: On Learning Sets of Symmetric Elements
paper_profiles.population: Not a human population; machine learning models and synthetic/benchmark image, point-cloud, graph, and video datasets
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of learning over unordered sets whose elements themselves have internal symmetries, such as images with translation symmetries, point clouds, or graphs. The authors argue that prior set-learning methods either process each element independently or only aggregate set information late in the network, which can miss useful low-level interactions between elements.

They propose Deep Sets for Symmetric elements (DSS), a family of linear equivariant layers for sets with element-level symmetry group H and set-level permutation symmetry Sn. The paper characterizes all such linear equivariant layers for the product group Sn × H, then proves universal approximation results for invariant and equivariant DSS networks under mild conditions. The work is theoretical, with supplementary experiments on synthetic signal classification, frame selection, image quality selection, color-channel matching, and burst deblurring.

Across these machine-learning benchmarks, early aggregation via DSS layers generally improves performance over DeepSets and Siamese baselines, especially on tasks where joint processing of set elements matters. The strongest gains are reported on classification, selection, and image reconstruction-style tasks, while some variants (notably mean-removal aggregation) perform inconsistently depending on the task. The paper is about neural network architecture design for set-structured data, not educational intervention or generative AI use in K-12 classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main empirical contribution is that DSS layers improve performance on several non-educational machine-learning benchmarks involving set-structured inputs. Across tasks such as signal classification, frame selection, color-channel matching, and burst deblurring, DSS(sum) or related DSS variants generally outperform Siamese+DeepSets and other baselines; for example, on signal classification DSS(sum) achieves the best accuracy across training sizes, and on frame selection it reaches 76.39% accuracy on UCF101 versus 36.41% for Siamese+DS.
finding.measure: Classification accuracy; selection accuracy; mean absolute error per pixel
finding.std_deviation: Reported as mean ± std over 5 random initializations in tables, but no single aggregated std value is given across all tasks
