finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that early aggregation can improve learning efficiency and model effectiveness compared with late-aggregation architectures, but this is demonstrated in the context of model performance rather than human workflow efficiency. The authors report that DSS(sum) often achieves better accuracy or lower error than Siamese+DS with roughly matched parameter counts, suggesting more effective use of representational capacity and better task efficiency for the network design.
finding.measure: Task performance at matched parameter counts; accuracy and error metrics
finding.std_deviation: Reported as mean ± std over 5 random initializations in tables, but no single aggregated std value is given across all tasks

paper_profiles.title: The Modern Mathematics of Deep Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a mathematical review of deep learning, not an empirical study in education. It surveys classical and modern theory for understanding why deep neural networks work, focusing on generalization, approximation, optimization, the role of depth, and how architecture affects learned representations and performance.

The article is organized as a broad tutorial-style synthesis of results from statistical learning theory, approximation theory, VC theory, Rademacher complexity, and stochastic gradient descent analysis. It argues that classical theory alone does not fully explain observed deep learning phenomena such as interpolation with good test performance, robustness of optimization in non-convex settings, and the advantages of depth. The paper does not study K-12 learners, teachers, classrooms, or generative AI use in mathematics instruction; instead it provides foundational mathematical background for deep learning research.

Because the paper is theoretical and survey-oriented, it contains no original intervention, no sampled population, and no direct empirical outcomes relevant to student achievement or classroom behavior. Its relevance to education research is only indirect, via conceptual background on deep learning models rather than evidence about educational uses or harms.

paper_profiles.title: Is the study of Indigenous mathematics ill-directed or beneficial?
paper_profiles.venue: Gazette of the Australian Mathematical Society
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a review/article arguing against claims that Indigenous Australian mathematics is not “real mathematics” and defending the inclusion of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander mathematical knowledge in the F-10 Australian curriculum. The authors respond to five published critiques that deny or diminish Indigenous mathematics, focusing on issues such as the absence of writing, numeral systems, measurement, kinship rules, and weather/season prediction.

The paper does not report an intervention or empirical study with participants; instead, it synthesizes historical, ethnographic, and ethnomathematical literature to rebut the “gatekeeper” view that mathematics is exclusively Anglo-European. The authors present examples from Australia and other Indigenous traditions—such as counting systems, calendrical knowledge, astronomy, kinship structures, and weather prediction—to argue that mathematical reasoning is culturally diverse and deeply embedded in Indigenous practice.

Its main conclusion is that Indigenous mathematical knowledge is legitimate, pedagogically valuable, and potentially enriching for mainstream mathematics education, including the Australian curriculum. The article frames exclusionary views as a form of gatekeeping with colonial roots and advocates two-way learning between Indigenous and non-Indigenous mathematics. It is primarily a conceptual/review piece, not an outcomes study.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that Indigenous Australian and other Indigenous groups have well-developed numeral systems and arithmetic practices, including base-5, base-20, and other counting systems, as evidence that these traditions do constitute mathematics. It cites examples such as Yolŋu turtle-egg counting, Anindilyakwa numerals up to 20, and Papua New Guinea counting systems, but does not report original participant data or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Descriptive accounts of numeral systems, counting, arithmetic, and quantification practices

finding.finding_summary: The article presents Indigenous astronomy and meteorology as mathematically grounded systems of observation, prediction, and explanation. It describes examples such as tide prediction from lunar phases, eclipse prediction, stellar scintillation used to forecast weather, and seasonal knowledge based on plant and animal indicators, but provides no quantitative evaluation.
finding.measure: Descriptive evidence on astronomy, tides, seasonal calendars, and weather prediction knowledge

finding.finding_summary: A central aim of the paper is to influence curriculum and institutional attitudes toward Indigenous mathematics by countering gatekeeping critiques and supporting inclusion in the F-10 Australian curriculum. The authors argue that recognition of Indigenous mathematical knowledge can reshape school and university mathematics norms, policy, and professional practice, but they do not measure institutional outcomes empirically.
finding.measure: Curriculum inclusion, disciplinary legitimacy, and educational policy argumentation

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Code Quality of AI-Assisted Code Generation Tools: An Empirical Study on GitHub Copilot, Amazon CodeWhisperer, and ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This paper evaluates the quality of code generated by three AI-assisted code generation tools: GitHub Copilot, Amazon CodeWhisperer, and ChatGPT. The authors ask how well these systems generate valid, correct, secure, reliable, and maintainable code, and whether code quality changes when docstrings are removed, function names are replaced with dummy names, and newer tool versions are used.

finding.finding_summary: Using the HumanEval benchmark (n=164 problems), the tools showed mixed performance on code generation quality. ChatGPT had the best code correctness (65.2% correct, average code correctness 78.1%), followed by GitHub Copilot (46.3%, 59.85%) and Amazon CodeWhisperer (31.1%, 51.95%); all tools produced valid code around 9 out of 10 times (93.3%, 91.5%, and 90.2%, respectively).
finding.measure: Code validity, code correctness on HumanEval unit tests, and code quality metrics (security, reliability, maintainability)

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests these tools can improve developer efficiency by generating mostly valid code quickly, but the benefits depend heavily on prompt quality and may require iterative human correction. The authors report that removing docstrings substantially reduced correctness (e.g., ChatGPT from 65.2% to 22.0%), implying that practitioner input is important for efficient use.
finding.measure: Code validity/correctness under different prompting conditions; average technical debt for smells

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides evidence that the tools only partially capture user intent and often need iterative refinement, which has implications for problem solving and debugging rather than direct instruction of durable skills. Partially correct generations were common (Copilot 23.2%, CodeWhisperer 40.2%, ChatGPT 22.6%), indicating that users must exercise judgment and debugging skill to convert outputs into correct solutions.
finding.measure: Proportion of partially correct code generations; correctness changes when prompts were simplified or function names were dummy variables

finding.finding_summary: The study has implications for tool adoption and institutional guidance, emphasizing that practitioners should not rely on these tools without testing because they can produce invalid code, bugs, and code smells. The authors conclude that secure code was not a differentiator on this benchmark, but maintainability issues and occasional bugs were common enough to warrant governance around use.
finding.measure: Security rating, bug counts, code smell counts, and technical debt from SonarQube

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (position paper; no empirical study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper asks how large language models such as GPT-3 and ChatGPT may be used in education, and what opportunities and risks they create for learners and teachers. Rather than presenting a new intervention study, the authors synthesize early applications and recent research to outline potential uses in content generation, feedback, tutoring, assessment, and educational dialogue across grade levels and higher education.

The paper discusses student-facing applications such as generating quizzes, practice problems, explanations, and pedagogical agents, as well as teacher-facing uses such as lesson planning, personalized feedback, automated scoring, and exercise generation. It also highlights important limitations and risks, including bias, overreliance, privacy, plagiarism, sustainability, and difficulty distinguishing model-generated from human-generated work.

For K-12 contexts, the paper is primarily forward-looking: it suggests that middle and high school students could use language models for subjects including mathematics, but it does not report a direct generative-AI mathematics intervention, comparator group, grade-specific treatment effects, or persistence of gains after tool removal. Its main contribution is a conceptual and ethical framework, with mitigation strategies emphasizing teacher oversight, critical thinking, fact checking, and responsible integration of LLMs into curricula.

paper_profiles.title: The cognitive paradox of AI in education: between enhancement and erosion
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (opinion paper; synthesizes evidence across student populations, including undergraduate and high school examples)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This opinion paper examines the promise and risks of artificial intelligence in education through the lenses of Cognitive Load Theory, Bloom’s Taxonomy, and Self-Determination Theory. The central question is whether AI in learning environments functions as a cognitive enhancer that supports personalization, efficiency, and engagement, or whether it leads to cognitive offloading, reduced retention, weaker critical thinking, and lower intrinsic motivation.

Rather than reporting a single intervention study, the article synthesizes prior empirical and conceptual work on AI-based learning tools such as adaptive systems, conversational AI, and ChatGPT. It highlights examples from higher education and secondary education, including studies on retention, critical thinking, creativity, and STEM learning, and argues that AI can improve performance on lower-order tasks while risking deeper learning if students over-rely on tool-generated answers.

The paper concludes that AI should complement, not replace, human instruction. It recommends teacher mediation, reflection prompts, AI-free practice, and balanced integration so that students remain actively engaged in problem-solving and metacognition. The paper also calls for future research on long-term cognitive effects, including whether gains persist when AI access is removed.

finding.finding_summary: The paper cites a secondary report that Stanford research found a 15% increase in standardized test scores for students using AI platforms compared with traditional instruction, but it also notes evidence that ChatGPT-assisted high school students performed worse on a concept-understanding test even while solving more problems correctly. Because these are cited, secondary summaries rather than a directly reported intervention in this paper, the math-specific evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive.
finding.measure: Standardized test scores; concept understanding test; problem-solving accuracy
finding.effect_size: 15% score increase; 17% lower concept-understanding score; 48% more problems answered correctly

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that excessive reliance on AI can reduce engagement, autonomy, and intrinsic motivation, and it cites prior work suggesting that students may become less motivated when AI does the thinking for them. These claims are presented as synthesis rather than as original measured outcomes in this article.
finding.measure: Engagement, autonomy, intrinsic motivation (reported from prior studies/theoretical synthesis)

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s core claim is that AI can support lower-order performance but may erode durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, and creative confidence when learners over-rely on tool-generated answers. It cites prior studies on retention, critical thinking, and divergent thinking, but does not present new original effect estimates in this opinion article.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, retention, divergent thinking, metacognitive engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that AI-based technologies can reduce redundant work and personalize instruction, thereby improving efficiency and allowing students to focus on more important cognitive operations. This is a conceptual conclusion supported by cited prior work rather than a new efficiency study in the paper itself.
finding.measure: Instructional efficiency / reduction of redundant work

paper_profiles.title: Sparks of Artiﬁcial General Intelligence: Early experiments with GPT-4
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an early, largely qualitative exploration of GPT-4’s capabilities across a wide range of domains, including mathematics, coding, vision, language, and human interaction. The authors argue that GPT-4 shows broad, general-purpose intelligence-like behavior and use hand-crafted prompts, comparisons with ChatGPT, and illustrative examples to probe strengths and limitations. Because the model version tested was text-only and still under development, the paper emphasizes that the results are exploratory demonstrations rather than formal benchmark evaluations.

The mathematics portion is not an intervention study and does not involve K-12 learners or educational treatment conditions. Instead, it shows examples of GPT-4 solving mathematical prompts, including a high-school-level proof about infinitely many primes and other reasoning tasks. The paper’s main conclusion is that GPT-4 can perform impressively on many problems, but the evidence is informal and not tied to learning outcomes, classroom implementation, or persistence effects after access is removed.

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 successfully solved an example described as a high-school-level mathematical problem and produced a correct proof-style response for the infinitude of primes. The paper does not report an educational intervention, student learning gains, or a controlled comparison; the evidence is limited to qualitative prompt-response examples.
finding.measure: Correctness of mathematical problem solving / proof generation from prompts

paper_profiles.title: Testing for Reviewer Anchoring in Peer Review: A Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether reviewers in conference peer review anchor to their initial scores when they later receive new information. The authors frame the problem around the rebuttal stage of peer review, where authors respond to reviewers and reviewers may revise their scores, and they investigate whether any apparent lack of score change is due to anchoring rather than genuine judgment.

To test this, the authors ran a randomized controlled trial with 108 adult participants who were PhD students or PhDs in computer science-related fields. Participants acted as reviewers for a mock conference paper; the experimental group initially saw a flawed version of the paper (a frozen GIF showing weaker results) and then, after debriefing/deception, saw the corrected animated version and could revise their ratings. The control group saw the correct version from the start. The review form included overall score and five subcategory scores, especially an Evaluation category tied to the paper’s evidence and results.

The main finding is that the manipulation successfully changed initial perceptions of paper quality, but the study found no significant evidence of anchoring when experimental participants revised their scores. Revised scores were statistically indistinguishable from control scores for both Overall and Evaluation ratings, suggesting that in this experimental peer-review setting, reviewers did not systematically cling to their original scores after seeing better evidence. The paper therefore concludes that muted score changes in rebuttal settings may arise from factors other than anchoring.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized controlled trial with 108 participants, the study found no significant evidence that reviewers anchored to their initial scores after seeing corrected information. Revised scores were statistically indistinguishable from control scores for both Overall ratings (Vargha-Delaney A=0.5048, adjusted p=0.6064) and Evaluation ratings (A=0.4863, adjusted p=0.6064).
finding.measure: Peer-review scoring of a mock conference paper (Overall score and Evaluation category score)
finding.effect_size: A=0.5048 (Overall revised vs control); A=0.4863 (Evaluation revised vs control)

paper_profiles.title: AI for Proactive Mental Health: A Multi-Institutional, Longitudinal, Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a generative AI-powered mobile app, Flourish, can proactively improve student mental health and well-being through strengths-based support. The study is motivated by concerns that most digital mental health tools are deficit-focused and reactive, and asks whether an AI system can instead deliver personalized, science-based, just-in-time well-being interventions at scale.

The intervention was a six-week randomized controlled trial conducted across three U.S. higher-education institutions (two four-year universities and one two-year community college) in Fall 2024. A total of 486 undergraduate students were randomized to either receive access to the Flourish app with instructions to use it at least twice per week, or to a waitlist control condition with existing school supports but no app access. The app included an AI chatbot (Sunnie), personalized recommendations, interactive activities, weekly insight summaries, and safety guardrails for high-risk language.

The primary outcomes were emotional, social, and overall well-being measures, including positive and negative affect, loneliness, belonging, closeness to school, resilience, mindfulness, and flourishing. The treatment group showed significant improvements in positive affect, loneliness, belonging, resilience, mindfulness, and flourishing, while negative affect did not change significantly. Effects were generally modest but consistent with both boosting and buffering patterns; the authors conclude that generative AI can support proactive, scalable well-being interventions, though the study does not test educational learning outcomes or post-removal persistence of performance gains.

finding.finding_summary: Compared with waitlist control, students assigned to the Flourish app reported significantly higher positive affect over time (Condition × Time b = 0.22, SE = 0.10, p = .020). Week 4 and Week 6 treatment-control differences were d = 0.23 and d = 0.33, respectively, and the intervention also boosted calm and buffered declines in mid-arousal well-being.
finding.measure: Subcomponents of Affect Scale (positive affect; calm, well-being, vigour)
finding.effect_size: d = 0.23 to 0.33 for Week 4 and Week 6 positive affect contrasts; b = 0.22 for Condition × Time

finding.finding_summary: The intervention reduced loneliness relative to control and improved belonging and perceived closeness to the university. The condition-by-time interaction was significant for loneliness (b = -0.05, SE = 0.02, p = .038) and belonging (b = 0.06, SE = 0.03, p = .030), with a marginal effect for closeness to school (b = 0.04, SE = 0.02, p = .070).
finding.measure: UCLA 3-item Loneliness Scale; campus belonging item; Inclusion of Other in the Self scale for closeness to school
finding.effect_size: b = -0.05 for loneliness; b = 0.06 for belonging; b = 0.04 for closeness

finding.finding_summary: The app improved broader well-being-related skills/resources, including resilience, mindfulness, and flourishing. Condition × Time interactions were significant for resilience (b = 0.11, SE = 0.06, p = .047), mindfulness (b = 0.19, SE = 0.09, p = .045), and flourishing (b = 0.19, SE = 0.09, p = .032), indicating small but reliable benefits relative to control.
finding.measure: Brief Resilience Scale; state Mindful Attention Awareness Scale; Flourishing Scale
finding.effect_size: b = 0.11 for resilience; b = 0.19 for mindfulness; b = 0.19 for flourishing

paper_profiles.title: SECRETS: Subject-Efficient Clinical Randomized Controlled Trials using Synthetic Intervention
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of making clinical randomized controlled trials (RCTs) more subject-efficient. The authors argue that standard two-arm parallel RCTs often require large samples because of between-subject variability, and they propose a framework called SECRETS to improve power without using external data.

SECRETS simulates the variance-reduction benefits of a crossover design by estimating individual treatment effects for both control and treatment arms using synthetic intervention (SI), a counterfactual estimation method. It then applies a custom data-driven hypothesis test designed to handle the dependencies induced by shared donor pools in SI. The method is evaluated on three real-world Phase-3 clinical RCT datasets (CHAMP, ICARE, and MGTX), where it increases power and reduces required sample sizes relative to a standard two-sample t-test baseline.

The paper is purely about clinical trial methodology and does not study educational interventions, students, or schools. Its empirical findings show that SECRETS improves statistical power by 6-54% over the baseline and can reduce required sample sizes by 25-76% while maintaining roughly comparable significance levels. The work also reports that the proposed hypothesis test better controls the false positive rate than standard one-sample or bootstrap alternatives when the estimated individual treatment effects are dependent.

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI Toolkit - A Framework for Increasing the Quality of LLM-Based Applications Over Their Whole Life Cycle
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes the Generative AI Toolkit, an open-source framework for automating development and operations workflows for LLM-based applications across their lifecycle. The toolkit is positioned as an LLMOps/DevOps solution that supports agent creation, custom evaluation metrics, repeatable test cases, model/prompt comparison, CI/CD integration, GUI-based debugging, and monitoring via logs and traces.

The paper’s main aim is to improve the quality, test coverage, and operational efficiency of generative-AI applications rather than to evaluate an educational intervention or learner outcome. The authors illustrate the framework with representative software-engineering use cases: a text-to-SQL agent, a restaurant RAG agent, an in-car voice assistant, and a model-comparison setup. These examples are used to show how the toolkit can shorten development cycles, automate testing, and surface optimization opportunities.

The paper does not study K-12 learners, math instruction, or educational attainment. It reports illustrative use cases for software developers and emphasizes lifecycle automation and monitoring for production LLM systems. No direct student learning outcomes, teacher mediation effects, or persistence-after-tool-removal effects are reported.

finding.finding_summary: The toolkit is presented as improving developer productivity and shortening release cycles by automating agent creation, testing, deployment, and monitoring. The paper states that the framework can significantly reduce cycle time and manual work, but it does not report controlled effect sizes or quantitative estimates for these gains.
finding.measure: Developer workflow efficiency, cycle time, manual work reduction, test automation coverage

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the toolkit supports CI/CD, audit-proof logging, scalable monitoring, and standardized evaluation for LLM applications, which could improve organizational quality assurance and deployment practices. However, these claims are based on framework demonstration and example use cases rather than institutional outcome measurement.
finding.measure: CI/CD integration, logging/monitoring infrastructure, deployment workflow standardization

paper_profiles.title: One Small Step for Generative AI, One Giant Leap for AGI: A Complete Survey on ChatGPT in AIGC Era
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (no primary study participants; survey paper)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of ChatGPT in the AIGC era, aiming to synthesize the model’s underlying technology, capabilities, applications, limitations, and potential future trajectory toward AGI. Rather than testing a new intervention, it reviews early post-release literature and examples across scientific writing, education, medicine, software development, management, and other domains.

Within education, the paper discusses how ChatGPT has been used for teaching/learning tasks and for subject-specific applications such as physics, mathematics, economics, law, psychology, and engineering. The treatment of mathematics is limited to a brief descriptive mention that ChatGPT can search for mathematical objects and related information and may outperform other mathematical models on a reverse-definition retrieval task; the paper does not report a K-12 mathematics intervention, comparator, teacher mediation/guardrails, or any learning-outcome persistence after tool removal.

Overall, the paper’s main conclusion is that ChatGPT is a powerful general-purpose language model with promising educational applications, but it also has important limitations, including factual errors, logical inconsistency, and susceptibility to misuse such as plagiarism and overreliance. The authors emphasize that ChatGPT should be used cautiously, especially in educational settings, and that further research is needed before it can be relied upon as a robust instructional tool.

finding.finding_summary: This is not an intervention study and does not report K-12 mathematics learning gains. The paper only briefly notes that ChatGPT can search for mathematical objects and related information and that, in one cited work, it outperformed other mathematical models on Reverse Definition Retrieval; no educational outcome data, comparator, or effect size are provided.
finding.measure: Reverse Definition Retrieval / mathematical object search (descriptive citation within survey)

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Effect of Activity-Based Method of Teaching Mathematics on Nigerian Secondary School Students’ Achievement in Mathematics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether an activity-based method of teaching mathematics improves achievement more than the conventional lecture method for Nigerian secondary school students. The motivation is the persistent low performance in mathematics in Nigerian secondary schools, particularly in topics that students find difficult, such as circle geometry and construction.

The intervention compared an activity-based teaching approach against a lecture-based approach in intact Senior Secondary II classes in two government schools in Calabar Metropolis, Cross River State, Nigeria. The sample included 96 students (48 experimental, 48 control). Students completed a 20-item researcher-developed Mathematics Test as both pretest and posttest, and ANCOVA was used to control for pretest differences.

Results showed a statistically significant advantage for the activity-based group on posttest mathematics performance after controlling for pretest scores. The paper reports a large group effect on posttest variance (partial eta squared = 0.261), indicating that the activity-based method outperformed lecture instruction for the targeted math topics. The authors conclude that activity-based instruction can improve secondary students’ mathematics achievement and recommend teacher training and provision of activity materials to support implementation.

finding.finding_summary: Students taught with the activity-based method scored substantially higher on the posttest mathematics achievement measure than students taught with the lecture method, after controlling for pretest scores. The study reports a significant group effect (F=114.461, p=0.000) and partial eta squared of 0.261 for the teaching method, indicating a large positive effect on mathematics performance.
finding.measure: 20-item Essay Mathematics Test (MT) on circle geometry and construction; pretest and posttest achievement scores
finding.std_deviation: Experimental posttest SD=8.84; Control posttest SD=6.22

paper_profiles.title: Demystifying Instruction Mixing for Fine-tuning Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how mixing different instruction-tuning datasets affects the performance of large language models (LLMs). The authors ask whether combining general chat instructions, coding instructions, and NLP task instructions helps or hurts downstream capabilities when fine-tuning LLaMA-2 models.

The study fine-tunes LLaMA-2 7B and 13B on combinations of three datasets: Alpaca for general instructions, CodeAlpaca for code generation, and P3 for reformulated NLP tasks. They evaluate the resulting models on zero-shot NLP benchmarks, HumanEval code generation, and FLASK-based alignment skill assessments. The setup is a controlled benchmarking study over multiple data mixtures rather than a human-subject or classroom intervention.

The main findings are that specialized instruction data improve performance in their own domain, but mixtures do not uniformly help all tasks. Alpaca generally improves alignment and NLP benchmark performance, CodeAlpaca improves coding and can also support alignment when combined with general instructions, and P3 improves NLP benchmark performance but tends to reduce alignment/chat abilities. Larger models benefit more from diverse instruction mixtures, and performance tends to plateau once fine-tuning data exceed about 10K instances per type. This paper does not study K-12 learners, mathematics instruction, or educational outcomes in schools.

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teachers should remain “in the loop” when using generative AI to personalize middle school mathematics tasks. The central question is not whether ChatGPT can generate math content, but how teachers interact with ChatGPT when modifying existing Illustrative Mathematics problems to better reflect students’ popular culture interests, and what trade-offs emerge in terms of personalization quality, student reactions, and teacher time.

Seven 7th-grade math teachers from six U.S. schools were trained to use ChatGPT/GPT-4o to personalize 143 problems from two IM units: Unit 4 (Proportional Relationships and Percentages) and Unit 6 (Expressions, Equations, and Inequalities). Teachers used the AI in live Zoom sessions, with their prompts, audio, and logs analyzed. Students then completed the resulting assignments in ASSISTments and provided interest/closeness ratings and open-ended feedback. The study found that teachers used generative AI in complex ways to manage grain size, depth, and ownership of personalization, but making a single problem took about 4 minutes on average and did not clearly become faster over time. Students tended to prefer finer-grained, specific popular-culture references, while teachers often had to correct realism and quantity issues in AI outputs. The paper concludes that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can support professional learning and quality control, but it remains time-consuming and tends to produce broad-grain personalization that may not fully match student preferences.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies personalized middle school mathematics problem creation and reports student ratings of the resulting math tasks, but it does not measure mathematics achievement or learning gains. Teachers generated 143 personalized problems for 521 7th-grade students, and students rated tasks as more interesting/closeness-matched in Unit 6 than Unit 4 (interestingness B=0.33, p=0.0012; closeness also improved significantly), yet these are preference measures rather than performance outcomes.
finding.measure: Student ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to students’ interests for personalized math problems; teacher prompting/time while creating math tasks
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.24 (interestingness rating), SD=1.28 (closeness rating); SD=2.6 prompts/problem; SD=165.7 seconds/problem

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that personalization affected students’ interest and perceived relevance, with most of the student-level evidence coming from 1–5 survey ratings and open-ended feedback rather than achievement measures. Across 52 rated problems, average interestingness was 2.46/5 and closeness was 2.53/5, and students gave more favorable ratings when teachers used 3–5 prompts to craft a problem; that prompt range was associated with about a 0.24-point increase on the 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, p=0.0073).
finding.measure: Student interest/interestingness ratings; perceived closeness to interests; open-ended student feedback
finding.study_size: n=521 students overall; ratings collected for 52-53 problems; open-ended responses from 446-454 responses per item

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally evaluates whether teacher-in-the-loop GenAI is time-efficient for creating personalized math problems. Teachers used 558 prompts to create 143 problems (3.2 prompts/problem) and spent an average of 246 seconds per problem; efficiency did not clearly improve over time, and in fact Unit 6 took longer than Unit 4 (286 vs. 204 seconds/problem; B=70.4, p=0.0189) while requiring more prompts (4.6 vs. 3.2 prompts/problem; B=1.26, p=0.0025).
finding.measure: Time to create each personalized math problem; number of prompts per problem
finding.effect_size: B=1.26 prompts/problem (Unit 6 vs Unit 4); B=70.4 seconds/problem (Unit 6 vs Unit 4)
finding.std_deviation: SD=2.6 prompts/problem; SD=165.7 seconds/problem; Unit 4 SD=153 seconds, Unit 6 SD=169 seconds

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper is not a direct assessment of durable skills, it substantively examines teacher prompting, revision, and problem-posing practices that involve monitoring realism, clarity, and appropriateness. Teachers iterated prompts to improve contextual realism and mathematical clarity, and the authors interpret this as evidence of developing prompting skill, but they do not measure transfer, metacognition, or collaboration outcomes independently.
finding.measure: Teacher prompting patterns and iteration strategies while using ChatGPT for problem-posing

paper_profiles.title: Qwen Technical Report
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (general language model technical report; no K-12 sample studied)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This technical report introduces QWEN, a family of large language models developed by Alibaba Group, including base pretrained models, chat-aligned models, code-specialized models, and math-specialized models. The paper focuses on model design, pretraining data and architecture, supervised finetuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, tool use, code interpreter use, and agent capabilities.

The mathematics-related component is MATH-QWEN-CHAT, which is trained via supervised finetuning on augmented math instructional data and evaluated on benchmark datasets such as GSM8K, MATH, Math401, and Math23K. The report does not study a K-12 instructional intervention, does not compare classroom conditions, and does not examine teacher mediation, guardrails, or removal of tool access in an educational setting.

Overall, the paper reports benchmark performance improvements for the math-specialized models relative to the base and chat models and to several open-source baselines. However, these are offline benchmark evaluations of general LLM capability, not direct evidence of learning gains for K-12 students. As such, the paper is not a direct generative-AI mathematics intervention study for schooling, and it provides no evidence on persistence of gains after tool access is removed.

finding.finding_summary: MATH-QWEN-CHAT improves benchmark math performance relative to the base chat model and several open-source baselines. On GSM8K, MATH-QWEN-7B-CHAT reached 62.5 and MATH-QWEN-14B-CHAT reached 69.8, compared with QWEN-CHAT at 50.3 and 60.1; on MATH, scores were 17.2 and 24.2 versus 6.8 and 18.4. These results come from benchmark tests, not K-12 learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Benchmark mathematics reasoning accuracy on GSM8K, MATH, Math401, and Math23K

paper_profiles.title: Distributed agency in second language learning and teaching through generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a conceptual/emerging-technologies column about how generative AI is changing second language learning and teaching. Rather than reporting a single intervention study, it synthesizes early examples of ChatGPT and related tools in language learning, with emphasis on agency, ecological/sociomaterial perspectives, AI literacy, ethics, and the changing role of teachers and learners.

The piece argues that generative AI creates new forms of distributed or shared agency between humans and AI systems. It discusses how learners may use AI for brainstorming, drafting, revising, feedback, and practice, and how teachers can use it to create materials and assessments, while also warning that AI has limitations in pragmatics, cultural context, and reliability.

The paper is aimed broadly at language-learning stakeholders rather than a specific experimental sample, and it does not present original quantitative data. Its main conclusion is that effective use of generative AI in education will depend on critical AI literacy, careful prompt use, reflective pedagogy, and awareness of ethical and equity issues, especially as AI becomes more embedded in educational and everyday tools.

paper_profiles.title: The RefinedWeb Dataset for Falcon LLM: Outperforming Curated Corpora with Web Data, and Web Data Only
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents REFINEDWEB, a large-scale English pretraining dataset built exclusively from CommonCrawl web data using a new filtering and deduplication pipeline called MacroData Refinement (MDR). The authors argue that web data alone, if carefully processed, can match or exceed the quality of curated corpora traditionally used for large language model pretraining.

The study evaluates 1B, 3B, and 7B parameter decoder-only language models trained on variants of the dataset (raw, filtered, and fully refined) and compares them with models trained on other web corpora and curated corpora such as The Pile. Results are reported on zero-shot language-model benchmarks, showing that filtering and especially deduplication improve performance, and that models trained on RefinedWeb can match or outperform models trained on curated data in the authors' evaluation setup.

This is a dataset and language-model pretraining study, not an education intervention study. It does not involve K-12 learners, teachers, mathematics instruction, or any classroom implementation. There is no comparator related to educational treatment, no grade band, no math topic, no teacher mediation/guardrails, and no evidence about whether learning gains persist after tool removal.

paper_profiles.title: Democratizing Signal Processing and Machine Learning: Math Learning Equity for Elementary and Middle School Students
paper_profiles.venue: Submitted to IEEE Signal Processing Magazine
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a practitioner-oriented perspective piece arguing that early mathematics support is essential for later success in signal processing, machine learning, and STEM more broadly. The authors frame arithmetic fluency and early algebra readiness as equity issues, emphasizing systemic barriers that prevent many elementary and middle school students from building a strong foundation in math.

Rather than testing a formal intervention, the paper describes and reflects on three out-of-school math support programs associated with the authors: CyMath (Iowa State), Algebra by 7th Grade (Purdue), and Math Motivators (Actuarial Foundation). These programs combine tutoring/mentoring, adaptive practice with ALEKS, homework or at-home resources, family outreach, and occasional STEM enrichment. The article reports program observations and a few descriptive student outcome examples, such as percentile gains on MAP and iReady for CyMath students and a reported association between completing a grade level in ALEKS and higher ILEARN proficiency for Ab7G participants, but it does not present a controlled causal evaluation.

The main conclusion is that sustained early math practice, parent awareness, supportive mentoring, and school-university partnerships may help close foundational gaps before they become difficult to remediate later. The paper also offers practical recommendations for schools, such as emphasizing regular math practice, providing parent information, and using summer and extracurricular support to address learning loss. Because it is primarily an opinion/perspective article with descriptive program information, the evidence is limited and should be interpreted cautiously.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports descriptive gains for students in the authors' tutoring programs, but without a comparison group or causal design. For CyMath, one student moved from the 40th percentile to the 85th percentile on MAP and then the 92nd percentile on iReady; another moved from the 20th to 38th to 60th percentile. For Ab7G, the paper cites Womack et al. reporting significant growth among n=20 students who completed a full grade level in ALEKS each year and a relationship with proficiency or higher on Indiana's ILEARN math test.
finding.measure: MAP, iReady, ALEKS progress, ILEARN math proficiency
finding.study_size: CyMath descriptive cohort: not_reported; Ab7G cited study n=20

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that mentoring, parent engagement, and reward structures such as game time after math work can support motivation and persistence, but it does not provide a controlled estimate of social-emotional change. Evidence is mostly programmatic/observational, including descriptions of student recognition for meeting ALEKS goals and the role of mentor-student connection in sustaining participation.
finding.measure: Program participation, engagement, persistence, mentor-student connection

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes institutional and community-level effects of university-led math support programs, including partnerships with school districts, parent outreach, and access to technology and transportation. It argues that these structures help recruit and retain students and expand support for under-represented learners, but it does not evaluate policy change with a formal design.
finding.measure: Program reach, school partnership functioning, recruitment/retention, parent outreach

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how elementary students and teachers perceived a generative-AI-supported creative mathematical writing activity. The authors were interested in the educational benefits and challenges of using GenAI to help children generate and revise math stories, particularly in relation to creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and classroom experience.

The study implemented a GenAI-powered platform in six elementary classrooms with 79 fifth-grade students and six teachers in two U.S. schools. The instructional sequence had three phases: Ask (analyze the math story), Represent (visually model ideas), and Transform (use GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 to co-create or revise culturally relevant math stories). Students and teachers then participated in interviews, and researchers triangulated those data with open-ended surveys and classroom observations.

Because the study is qualitative and focused on perceptions rather than achievement testing, it does not report direct learning gains, comparator conditions, or persistence of effects after access to the tool was removed. The main conclusions are that GenAI-supported math story writing was perceived to support creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, interest, curiosity, and ownership of learning, but it also raised challenges such as overreliance on AI, lack of feedback, limited autonomy, weak social interaction, and accessibility concerns.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived the GenAI-supported creative math writing activity as helping students understand math ideas, represent mathematical knowledge, and uncover misconceptions. However, this paper reports qualitative perceptions only; it does not provide achievement scores, effect sizes, or a comparison against an alternative condition.
finding.measure: Interview themes about mathematical understanding, knowledge representation, and misconception detection during creative math story writing

finding.finding_summary: Participants perceived the activity as increasing interest, curiosity, and ownership of learning. Students reported that working with AI made math more fun and motivating, while teachers noted greater engagement with personally meaningful story topics.
finding.measure: Interview themes on interest, curiosity, and ownership of learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students used prompt engineering strategies, revised requests, and evaluated AI strengths and weaknesses, suggesting gains in critical thinking and metacognitive monitoring. These were qualitative perceptions from students and teachers rather than measured performance outcomes.
finding.measure: Interview themes on prompt engineering, critical evaluation of AI output, and story revision

finding.finding_summary: The study centers on creative mathematical writing and story generation, with students and teachers describing improved ability to draft, modify, and elaborate written stories. The paper does not report standardized writing scores or any pre/post writing assessment, so the evidence is limited to perceived writing support.
finding.measure: Qualitative perceptions of story writing, drafting, and revision with GenAI

paper_profiles.title: An Experience of Introducing Primary School Children to Programming using Ozobots (Practical Report)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This practical report describes an outreach project that introduced primary school children to programming using Ozobot Evo robots. The authors focused on a step-by-step workshop design intended to bridge unplugged activities, pen-and-paper line-following tasks, and eventually block-based programming in OzoBlockly. The paper is motivated by practical challenges in early programming education, including limited teacher preparation, hardware access, and the transition from concrete, tactile activities to screen-based coding.

The intervention consisted of two-hour workshops delivered at eight primary schools in Germany and Austria between October 2018 and October 2019, targeting grades 3–5. Children first explored the robots’ features, then completed worksheets that introduced line following, color-code commands, randomness, control tasks, and finally a debugging/programming challenge on tablets. The workshop format was informed by cognitive load theory and the use-modify-create framework, and was designed to actively involve children while keeping tasks simple and achievable.

The paper is not an experimental learning-outcomes study; instead, it reports implementation experiences, practical lessons learned, and qualitative observations about children’s engagement and difficulties. The authors conclude that Ozobots were generally well suited to primary-school programming outreach, especially for introducing basic sequence concepts, but note constraints such as battery life, occasional confusion with remote-control features, language limitations, and the need for teacher/instructor support. They also state that while the pen-and-paper activities seemed effective as an introduction, it remains unclear whether these activities support later learning of more advanced programming concepts.

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that most children were enthusiastic, enjoyed programming with the Ozobots, and responded positively to the hands-on workshop format. They note that all children stated they enjoyed programming with the robot, and that the activities seemed to build confidence and positive attitudes toward programming, though no standardized affect measure was used.
finding.measure: Observed enthusiasm, enjoyment, and reported attitudes toward programming

finding.finding_summary: The workshop was explicitly designed to develop introductory computational thinking and programming skills such as sequences, testing, and debugging. The authors report that children were able to program functioning dances and that the concept of sequences could be transferred in some cases to BeeBots, but these are qualitative observations rather than measured learning gains.
finding.measure: Observed ability to execute sequences, debug a preloaded program, and transfer sequence concept

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports several implementation advantages and challenges related to workshop delivery. Ozobots were portable and useful for bridging unplugged and programming modes, but battery drain, pairing issues, and the need to manually preload incorrect programs increased instructor workload and complicated delivery.
finding.measure: Instructor observations of workshop logistics, battery life, pairing, and preparation burden

paper_profiles.title: Celestial mechanics, from high-school to Newton’s Principia
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a classical mechanics problem originally posed as a high-school physics contest exercise and uses it to develop multiple proofs of the relationship between orbital geometry and kinetic energy loss. The motivating question concerns a spacecraft that changes from a circular orbit to an elliptical orbit that touches a planet’s surface, and asks what proportion of kinetic energy is lost. The author treats this as a pedagogical example in mathematical physics, emphasizing that the problem can be solved with elementary methods suitable for high-school students as well as more advanced university-level methods.

The paper does not study an AI intervention or any instructional technology. Instead, it offers a series of mathematical-physical derivations using Kepler’s laws, conservation laws, the radial equation, Frenet formulas, the Runge-Lenz vector, hodographs, and classical results from Maxwell and Newton. The context is the Hungarian Eötvös high-school contest tradition, where students may use all documents and tools, and the paper argues that such problems can foster creative reasoning and even lead to research-level insights.

The main conclusion is that the relative kinetic-energy loss in the described orbital transition equals the numerical eccentricity of the ellipse, specifically \(\epsilon = (r-R)/(r+R)\), which is 1/19 for the numerical values given. Overall, the paper is a mathematical exposition and historical discussion about problem solving in physics education, not an empirical study of learning outcomes, classroom implementation, or AI-mediated tutoring.

paper_profiles.title: Deep Inelastic Scattering with Application to Nuclear Targets
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a reconstructed set of lectures on deep inelastic electron scattering from nuclear targets, originally delivered in 1985 and reposted to arXiv in 2022. Its central question is how to use inclusive lepton scattering to probe quark and antiquark distributions in nuclei, with special attention to the EMC effect and what it implies about nuclear structure at the quark level.

The approach is theoretical and pedagogical rather than experimental: it develops the kinematics of inclusive scattering, dispersion relations, the Bjorken limit, the parton model, and then applies these tools to nuclear data on iron, deuterium, and other targets. The paper discusses the EMC collaboration and follow-up SLAC, BCDMS, and neutrino data, emphasizing how ratios like F2^A/F2^D deviate from naive nucleon-sum expectations. It argues that the data indicate valence-quark degradation, possible sea-quark enhancement, and longer quark correlation lengths in nuclei, especially at higher nuclear density.

The paper does not study AI, generative AI, or any educational intervention, and it does not contain K-12 learning outcomes. It is a physics lecture note rather than an empirical education study. Accordingly, there are no outcome assignments relevant to the requested educational categories.

paper_profiles.title: Can AI Understand Cultures? Evaluating Cross-Cultural Miscommunication through Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: Digital Maadili 14 - 18 July 2025 — DIGHUM (First African Digital Humanism Summer School 2025 Proceedings)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether leading multimodal generative AI systems can understand and reproduce culturally grounded greeting practices across five societies: Baganda (Uganda), Luo (Kenya), Hausa (Nigeria), Chinese, and Brazilian. The authors focus on a culturally sensitive prompt-evaluation task rather than an educational intervention, using norm-compliant and norm-violating scenarios to test whether models can recognize social protocols such as deference, eye contact, gendered behavior, and body proximity.

The approach compares GPT-4o, Gemini, and Grok on both text and image outputs. Outputs were reviewed by native cultural experts in a human-in-the-loop process, and the study reports recurring Western-centric defaults, mistranslations, stereotype-laden visuals, and weak handling of culturally specific norms. GPT-4o performed best overall, especially on visual fidelity, but all models still failed to achieve deep cultural fluency.

The paper’s context is not K-12 education; it is a cross-cultural AI evaluation framed within digital humanism. Its main conclusion is that current generative AI can mimic surface features of culture but does not reliably understand culturally embedded meaning, implying a need for community-anchored, pluriversal evaluation and dataset design.

paper_profiles.title: Solutions to Problems at Les Houches Summer School on EFT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a set of worked solutions to problem sets from the 2017 Les Houches Summer School on Effective Field Theory (EFT) in particle physics and cosmology. It is not an education intervention study; rather, it is a technical physics document that walks through derivations and calculations in renormalization, EFT power counting, discrete symmetries, operator identities, decay rates, matching, and anomalous dimensions.

The document compiles solutions corresponding to lecture series by several physicists, covering introductory EFT, renormalization group methods, SMEFT, and applications to QCD, QED, and scalar field theory. The intended audience is graduate-level or advanced physics students attending the summer school, but the paper contains no educational experiment, no K-12 context, and no learning-outcome evaluation. Its main contribution is pedagogical exposition of physics problem solutions, not empirical evidence about teaching or learning.

paper_profiles.title: Cosmic rays studied with a hybrid high school detector array
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings / conference paper (venue not explicitly stated in text)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the LORUN/NAHSA hybrid detector array, a pathfinder project combining cosmic-ray particle detectors and radio antennae for both research and education/outreach in astro-particle physics. The system was installed largely by students on public/high-school buildings, and it uses coincidences between scintillator detectors and radio antennae to identify candidate air-shower events.

The main goal is technical and scientific: to demonstrate that a hybrid radio-plus-particle setup can work in a school-linked environment and can be extended to larger high-school arrays. The paper reports the detector setup, data acquisition, offline matching, and three candidate cosmic-ray events observed between January and August 2005, with estimated primary energies above 0.2–0.3 EeV. It emphasizes student hands-on involvement and the outreach potential of high-school cosmic-ray arrays, but it does not evaluate a generative-AI mathematics intervention or any learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports successful detection of candidate cosmic-ray air showers using a hybrid high-school-linked detector array. Three candidate events were identified between 2005-01-01 and 2005-08-01, with HiSPARC and LORUN measurements consistent with working coincidence detection and estimated primary energies above 0.2–0.3 EeV.
finding.measure: Detection of coincident cosmic-ray air-shower events in hybrid particle/radio instrumentation

paper_profiles.title: CMATH: Can Your Language Model Pass Chinese Elementary School Math Test?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks a benchmarking question rather than testing a learning intervention: to what grade level of Chinese elementary-school mathematics do popular large language models (LLMs) correspond? The authors introduce CMATH, a dataset of 1.7k math word problems drawn from Chinese elementary workbooks and exams, annotated by grade along with counts of reasoning steps and digits. They use the dataset to evaluate several commercial and open-source LLMs in zero-shot settings.

The main approach is comparative model evaluation, not classroom implementation. Models tested include GPT-4, ChatGPT, and multiple open-source Chinese LLMs. The paper also creates a small distractor set to test robustness to irrelevant information. GPT-4 is the only model that achieves at least 60% accuracy across all six grades and remains robust under distractors; ChatGPT performs well on lower grades but degrades on higher grades and with distractors, while most other models fail broadly.

The study population is elementary-school math content, not students or teachers, and there is no instructional treatment, comparator curriculum, or evidence about persistence after access is removed in a learning sense. The results are useful for understanding model capability on K-12 math word problems, but they do not provide direct evidence of student learning gains from a generative-AI intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates LLM accuracy on 1.7k Chinese elementary-school math word problems (CMATH) across grades 1-6. GPT-4 is the only model to reach success defined as accuracy ≥60% across all six grades, while ChatGPT succeeds through grades 1-4 and other models generally fail at higher grades or across all grades.
finding.measure: Accuracy on elementary school math word problems

paper_profiles.title: School Management Information Systems: Challenges to Educational Decision-Making in the Big Data Era
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal on Integrating Technology in Education (IJITE)
paper_profiles.population: School administrators and educators in K-12 schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how school management information systems (SMIS) are used to support educational decision-making in the era of big data. Rather than testing an intervention, it reviews the literature on SMIS features, benefits, and barriers, emphasizing that schools often have abundant data but lack the infrastructure, training, timeliness, and usability needed to turn it into actionable decisions.

The paper proposes a five-phase conceptual model for improving SMIS use: identification, design, application, decision, and result. Across these phases, the author argues that schools should identify inhibiting factors such as poor data quality, inadequate training, limited technical support, and user resistance, then address them through stakeholder buy-in, usability-centered design, and ongoing professional development.

The context is U.S. K-12 schooling, especially administrative and instructional decision-making. The main conclusion is that SMIS can improve efficiency and decision quality only if schools intentionally address implementation barriers and align system design with user needs; however, the paper is conceptual and does not report empirical learning outcomes or student achievement effects.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that SMIS can reduce workload, improve access to timely student data, and support faster administrative decision-making, but these claims are based on cited literature rather than original empirical testing. No effect size, sample size, or statistical outcome is reported in the paper itself.
finding.measure: Administrative decision-making efficiency, data access, workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on how SMIS can shape schoolwide data-driven culture, governance, and institutional decision-making in K-12 schools. It proposes a five-phase conceptual model intended to improve educational management, but provides no direct empirical evaluation of institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Schoolwide data use, decision-making processes, institutional governance

High school studies are mentioned only in summarized media reports; the sweep lacks primary comparative studies with clear mathematics outcomes from secondary sources.

The thread asks for stratified evidence by grade band and mathematics outcome type, but the current sweep does not systematically capture outcome categories such as achievement, problem-solving, reasoning, attitudes, engagement, self-efficacy, or transfer across studies.
The search appears to miss broader K-12 generative AI interventions beyond word problem solving, including tutoring, feedback, exam preparation, and classroom use.
The current Scopus hits are promising but too narrow and too few to support a confident synthesis of grade-band stratification.

The sweep is still dominated by general AI/LLM discussion and secondary/indirect evidence; it has not yet surfaced a robust set of K-12 mathematics studies that clearly meet the criterion of being generative-AI-specific empirical evidence.
The found items appear mostly to involve pre-service teachers or upper-secondary contexts, not clearly K-12 student studies, so the target population coverage is incomplete.
There is no clear separation yet between generative-AI-specific studies and broader AI/intelligent tutoring/blended-learning/design/perception studies, which is the core audit requirement.

Missing are likely key K-12 math studies on ChatGPT/LLM use by in-service teachers, students, problem posing/solving, feedback, and classroom implementation, as well as explicit exclusion of non-generative AI studies.
The sweep has not yet clearly separated true generative-AI-specific K-12 mathematics studies from adjacent broader AI/ITS/blended-learning/perception literature.
It appears to miss direct evidence involving K-12 students or in-class implementation; the surfaced item is pre-service teachers preparing to teach secondary math, not K-12 learners.
No clear coverage yet of elementary, middle, or secondary student studies that actually use ChatGPT/LLMs in mathematics instruction, tutoring, problem solving, or assessment.
The results shown are too sparse and partially off-target, with irrelevant papers and only a small number of generative-AI math items; this is insufficient to confidently answer the thread.
No clear evidence yet of true K-12 math outcome studies; the result shown is a conceptual/qualitative ChatGPT-in-calculus paper, not a comparative achievement study.
Missing direct comparisons against standard instruction and non-AI digital tools (e.g., textbook/software/control conditions).
No randomized trials, quasi-experiments, or classroom intervention studies identified that measure K-12 mathematics achievement gains.
Search coverage appears overly dependent on Semantic Scholar, which returned 403 errors and likely missed key education databases and conference proceedings.
The current sweep does not yet establish the strength of comparative evidence, especially whether effects are causal, replicated, or limited to higher education/non-math contexts.

The sweep has mostly captured broad reviews/meta-analyses and a couple of upper-secondary/high-school studies, but it does not yet establish evidence specifically for K-12 mathematics achievement versus standard instruction and non-AI digital tools.

There is an important evidence-type gap: the thread asks about comparative strength of evidence, but the sweep lacks clearly identified K-12 math RCTs or quasi-experimental classroom studies with achievement outcomes and appropriate control groups (teacher-led instruction, textbook/workbook, or non-AI digital tools).
The current findings skew toward perceptions/acceptance and one physics study, which is adjacent but not directly responsive to K-12 math achievement.
It is unclear whether any elementary or middle-school GenAI math interventions were found; these populations are underrepresented relative to the research question.

The sweep does not yet separate true generative AI tools (LLM/chatbot/tutor feedback) from broader AI, adaptive learning, or non-generative digital tools, which is necessary to answer the comparative effectiveness question.
The sweep currently surfaces a living meta-analysis and only partial/failed search results, but not the underlying empirical K-12 studies needed to answer implementation questions.
Grade-band coverage is unclear: no distinct evidence for elementary, middle, and high school mathematics implementations.
Math-topic coverage is unclear: no specific studies on algebra, geometry, arithmetic/number sense, problem solving, or proof are identified.
Teacher mediation and guardrails are not yet evidenced in concrete classroom implementations (e.g., teacher prompts, supervision, verification routines, safety constraints).
Dosage/exposure is not captured: no information on intervention length, frequency, session structure, or classroom integration model.
Curriculum/prompt alignment is not demonstrated: no studies on lesson-plan alignment, curriculum mapping, standards-based prompt design, or task sequencing.
The current evidence base appears biased toward broad synthesis; the sweep still needs primary studies, case studies, design-based research, and pilot interventions in K-12 math.
The sweep has not yet surfaced concrete K-12 implementation studies of generative AI in mathematics; the visible result is a meta-analysis rather than primary studies.
Grade-band coverage is unclear or missing: no evidence yet for elementary, middle, and high school implementations separately.
Topic coverage is incomplete: there is no clear mapping to specific math domains such as arithmetic, fractions, algebra, geometry, word problems, or proof/problem solving.

The core implementation dimensions in the research thread are still undercovered: teacher mediation, guardrails/safety controls, dosage/frequency of use, and prompt or curriculum alignment are not yet evidenced in the findings.
It is unclear whether the sweep captured classroom-based trials, design-based interventions, or teacher-led deployments, which are central to answering how the tools are implemented in practice.
The sweep is dominated by general commentary and detection-oriented papers, not direct empirical studies of K-12 mathematics outcomes or behaviors.
No clear evidence yet on delayed retention, follow-up performance, or durability of learning after generative-AI-assisted math tutoring.

Equity/subgroup effects are not yet well covered; there is no focused evidence on impacts for learners by prior achievement, SES, language background, disability status, or other subgroups in K-12 math.
Academic integrity is only indirectly addressed; the sweep has not surfaced K-12 math-specific studies on homework cheating, answer copying, or assessment misuse.
Overreliance and reduced productive struggle in math problem solving are not yet substantively covered by classroom or experiment-based studies.
The sweep appears to miss randomized trials, classroom interventions, or observational studies in elementary/middle/high-school mathematics that evaluate post-test retention and transfer.
The sweep currently appears mostly conceptual and does not yet surface empirical K-12 mathematics studies with measured outcomes on delayed retention/post-test follow-up.
Subgroup/equity effects are not actually evidenced yet; there is no clear coverage of differential impacts by prior achievement, SES, language status, disability, or access conditions.
Cheating/answer-copying concerns are described in general terms, but there is no dedicated coverage of K-12 math homework or assessment studies examining AI-assisted dishonesty or detectability.
Overreliance and reduced productive struggle are mentioned conceptually, but there is no evidence from classroom or experimental studies showing these effects in K-12 mathematics.
The one surfaced paper appears to be a calculus case study rather than K-12, so the thread’s age-band focus remains under-covered.

The sweep has not surfaced any direct intervention studies in K-12 mathematics using generative AI/LLMs that report actual learning outcomes; current results are mostly broad reviews, benchmark papers, or non-intervention system descriptions.
Comparator type is unresolved because no eligible experimental/quasi-experimental math intervention papers have been identified.
Grade-band coverage remains incomplete, especially for lower elementary, middle school, and high school math settings.
Teacher mediation/guardrails and post-removal persistence of gains cannot be assessed from the current findings because no qualifying study with a before/after or retention design has been found.

The current search appears constrained by Semantic Scholar API failures; alternative sources (ERIC, Google Scholar-style web results, Crossref/OpenAlex, publisher sites, arXiv) were not yet exploited for direct study retrieval.
No clearly verified direct K-12 mathematics intervention study with actual learning outcomes and a bona fide generative-AI comparator has been fully established from primary sources.

The sweep is still missing rigorous identification of comparator type, grade band, math topic, teacher mediation/guardrails, and especially whether gains persist after tool removal for each candidate study.

Current findings include at least one likely non-intervention or non-K-12 item (AI literacy/over-reliance) and one secondary/summary-style result, but not enough primary evidence to answer the thread with confidence.

Middle-school and elementary interventions need deeper coverage; the sweep has not yet surfaced likely candidate classroom trials/RCTs/quasi-experiments from education journals, ERIC, or publisher sites.

The persistence-after-removal question remains essentially unanswered; follow-up should target post-test/delayed-transfer/novel-item retention measures and studies that explicitly disable the AI tool after training.
